H. EDWARDS.

The Committee on Credentials reported the presence of
more than a Constitutional number of Representatives present
from chartered Lodges, and requested further time in which
to make final report, which was granted; and the Grand
Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with music by the choir
and prayer by the Grand Chaplain.
Past Grand l'Iaster E. I1. Fitzgerald of the jurisdiction of
Nevada was introduced and received with due honors.
The Grand l\faster ·then delivered his annual address as
follows:
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:

. This occasion must necessarily give rise to varied and peculiar re·
flections and impressions. The renewal of friendship that we experience
and .the social intercourse that distinguishes this week probably above
all the other weeks of the year will fill our minds with intense gratification, and, in contemplation of this feature of our convocation, we
may well rejoice that we are permitted to be here. The communion and
interchange of views of congenial spirits engaged in a high task of com·
manding duty, devoted to a common purpose of transcendent worth and
moving together and in co-operative effort toward the achievement of
definite and imperishable ideals, must be the source also of infinite
pleasure and delight. We are gratified also at the reflection that this
and other similar institutions having in view the happiness and welfare
of mankind have made substantial and enduring growth and develop·
ment within the past year, that an immense amount of practical benevo-

7

This feeling of joy and elation however, is somewhat tempered and
restrained as we recall how far short of the needs of humanity our ef·
forts have fallen, how little we have done in comparison with the stupendous work that has challenged our attention, and how grossly inadequate have been our personal sacrifices and puny endeavors in the holy
eause of humanity.
It is indeed a time for serious and searching introspection, for a
new and resolute dedication and consecration of ourselves to this high
purpose and for a reaffirmance of our faith in the gospel that our
Institution proclaims and of the reasons why we invite and claim the
approval of rational and righteous men.
It might cause many of us a large measure of chagrin and discom·
fiture if we seriously and solemnly considered the following questions
and reflections: How much time have I personally and individually
devoted to the practical, vital work of the Orderf Have I been really
interested in the welfare of my neighbor or have I been principally or
exclusively concerned in the gratifications of my own selfish desires and
purposes f Have I been satisfied to enjoy the good things of the world
while around the corner or perhaps in the same block children have been
crying for breadf ~ave I practiced any considerable self-denial that
the necessity of others might be supplied! Have I been satisfied with
a profession of faith in the beauty and efficacy of Masonic principles
while neglecting and refusing to demonstrate by the practical and enduring expression of benevolence and love the deep sincerity of my
avowal of these principles! Have I thanked God for the favor of
Heaven in the blessing of advantages superior to those of my neighbor
without using to the utmost, or at all, my superior gifts to lessen the
chasm that separates me from other and less-favored sons of the
Almightyf

What I wish to emphasize is that this is a personal consideration,
and that not only is the Institution collectively but each individual
member is solemnly pledged to the advocacy and support of the moral
sentiments taught in our ritual and to their persistent application to
the daily and ordinary affairs growing out of our relations to our fellow
men; and my earnest desire and prayer is that we may go away from
this convocation better equipped and more thoroughly inspired for the
great tasks that confront us.
· As to the principles themselves constituting the foundation stones
of this great Institution there can be no doubt that they are consistent

9

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

with enlightened morality, that they constitute a sound and safe creed
of personal conduct, that individuals as well as nations can adopt no
better guide in their dealings with one another, and that their universal
application would largely destroy discontent, inefficiency and unhappiness, and contribute immeasurably to the highest development of human
character and the largest degree of national greatness.
·we content ourselves with the mere statement of these propositions,
as no argument is necessary to convince a body of Masons of their
verity.
There is some reason, however, to fortify ourselves against discouragement over the apparent disinclination of mankind generally to
accept these sentiments as the rule and guide of their conduct and to
place themselves under the beneficent dominion of these lofty ideals.
'fhe world is distracted by strife, contention, selfishness and brutality, a large part of the human race is waging a ruthless war of
death and destruction, and some of us may be ready to conclude that
fraternity has become a mere empty phrase and that love as a principle
of conduct has lost its charm and power.
Not so, my brethren. The principles we teach are the only influence
that can save and redeem the world1 and their beauty and potency will
yet be aeknowledged by all mankind. Out of this bitterness, hatred,
devastation and death will come a realization of the futility of violence and war, and the glory of love and peace and fraternity will be
revealed to mankind as never before in the history of the world.
This madness will pass away, and yet, as E.dwin Markham says,
there will be still unrest and contention, but it will have in view, not
the destruction of men, but the achievement of real freedom and the
highest development of character.

born in the morning of antiquity, whose genealogy in every page drips
with the red blood of innocence; it respects neither the feebleness of
infancy nor the sacredness of virtue, and walks iron-shod ruthlessly and
impartially over the form of the weakling or the form of the giant; it
makes puppets of kings, princes of paupers, courtiers of courtesans and
thieves of respected subjects; empires melt before its breath as does
the mist before the morning sunlight; famine, want and misery follow
in its path; it lays waste grainfields and stills the land of industry; it
pillages the land of its resources and contributes nothing of benefit to
mankind, leaving pestilence to stalk ghostlike in its wake and eomplete
the work of destruction. It lays heavy tribute upon its most loyal subjects for the maintenance of its establishment; it squanders the vitality
and lives of those who serve it faithfully, yet it returns to the world
nothing but ruin and ashes. The baubles of fame it confers on some
are but empty shells of false standards wherein the license to commit
murder and rapine is held to be the insignia of glory by a mistaken
civilization. It can offer no excuse for having come into existence, nor
ean it give one plausible reason why it should not cease to be otlrnr
than that so long as men who wield influence are permitted to gratify
their selfish desires and ambitions at the expense of many wlio must
carry the burdens and endure the suffering, so long will it continue to
exact its toll of sorrow, devastation and death. For it is pitiless, devoid
of all feeling. It fears neither man nor God. It is amenable to no
law, and is itself the law and the last resort.''

8

"Yet the black smoke of battle it will passSome time, some time,-like vapor from a glass;
There will be rest for all the weary flags,
And rest for bugles on the battle crags;
Still there will be no rest for man's strong soul;
Before him shines an ever-flying goal;
Still must he seek for freedom ever-more;
No halt for any soul on any shore;
Man is the conscript of an endless quest,
A long divine adventure without rest;
Each hard-earned freedom withers to a bond;
Freedom forever is beyond,-beyond.''
We must do our part as a Fraternity .and as members thereof to
hasten the time when the world shall realize that war is unnatural, inhuman and brutal; that it was properly characterized by an anonymous
writer who declared: ''It was conceived in passion, envy and greed,

If our .principles were atlopted by men generally1 instead of war
there would be friendly emulation among the nations of tlie earth as to
which could contribute most to the development of civilization and the
l1appiness of mankind. The world woul<l realize, as Mr. Root said, ''that
no nation can live unto itself and continue to Jive, tliat each nation's
growth is a part of the development of the race; that there may be
laggards, and there may be leaders, but no nation can long continue
very far in advance of the general progress of mankind, and no nation
that is not <loome<l to extinction can remain very far behind. A people
whose minds are not open to the lessons of the world's progress, whose
spirits are not stirred by the aspiration and achievements of humanity
struggling the world over for liberty and justice, must be left behind
by civilization in its steady and beneficent advance.''
And so, my brethren, with the individual: He cannot live unto himself alone and continue to live a wholesome, helpful and successful life.
He must recognize the fact that he is but one unit of this great aggregation constituting the race; that his own progress and happiness are
inseparably linked with the history and destiny of his fellow men; that
there is a law of unity and common interest binding us together and
emphasizing the importance of all we do in relation to other human
beings. We must realize that there will be for us no real life, no per-

10

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

manent progress, no substantial growth and development, and no abi<ling
sueeess or supreme happiness, if we attempt to live ourselves apart from
others or to exclude from consideration the happiness and success of
the rest of mankind. We can only booome greater1 stronger, better and
happier in an honest, earnest and persistent endeavor to be of vital
and helpful service to others.

November 24th, I visited Union Lodge, Sacramento, and witnessed
the third degree conferred by the Past Masters of that Lodge, Brother
Ben Wilson presiding decorously and efficiently in the East.

The great mission of Masonry is indeed to make us servants of
others, for their welfare as well as our own.
I regret exceedingly that I have not had the opportunity during the
year of urging these matters upon the attention of more of the membership.
I was, however, as you probably know, stricken with a severe illness
which seriously interfered with my plans and prevented me from making
many of the visits that I contemplated. I had the pleasure, though, of
meeting with the brethren as follows:
VISITATIONS,

October 16th, assisted by other Grand Officers, I instituted Bethlehem Lodge No. 455 at the Masonic Temple and installed their officers.
Monday evening, October 18th, I performed a like service for
Crocker Lodge No. 454 at San Mateo.
October 21st I visited Oak Grove Lodge No. 215 of Alameda, The
occasion was graeed by the presence of Brother Scott, Past Grand
Master of the jurisdietion of Illinois, who, by his inspiring words
increased our admiration for this great Institution. Brother Scott has
since joined the invisible host of the Grand Lodge above, ''where the
Supreme Grand Master of the Universe forever presides."
November 10th, I visited Orland Lodge No. 265 at Orland.
November 11th, Redding Lodge.

installed their officers.
·
November 13th, visited McCloud Lodge, Siskiyou County.
November 15th, was given a joint reception at Yreka by St. John's
and Howard Lodges of that place. I must say a word as to the zeal and
interest of these mountain lodges in the progress of the Fraternity. In
my judgment, no more earnest and intelligent Masons can be found
anywhere. They show by their conduct that they regard Masonry as
one of the greatest instrumentalities in the world for the progress and
happiness of mankind. At Yreka I had the great pleasure of meeting
Dr. Nutting, Past Grand Master of this jurisdiction. He is a power
for good in that community, and the brethren who were present will not
soon forget his impressive and eloquent speech in behalf of the Fraternity.

OTHER SPECIAL COMMUNICATIONS.

. December 23rd I received from a Brother who asked me not to reveal
h_is name the sum of $21,000 in giltedge bonds to be used in the construction of a dormitory at Covina, Los Angeles County, in connection with

February 16th, in company with William P. Filmer, Past Grand
Master and Sovereign Grand Inspector General; Rev. John A. B. Fry,
Grand Chaplain; William H. Waste, former Grand Orator; John Whicher,
the Grand Secretary; and other brethren, I exchanged greetings through
the long distance telephone from the company's office in San Francisco
with the Most Worshipful Grand Master Seering of New ,Jersey, who
was in attendance at a banquet in Ridgway of said State celebrating. the
installation of Herbert R. Talbot as Master of Fidelity Lodge No. 113.
of said city. It was a novel and wonderful experience. We were over
3000 miles apart, yet the conversation was carried on as expeditiously
and understandingly as though we were in the same room. It was,
indeed, as the Grana Secretary wrote, difficult to get away from the conviction that the brethren gathered there at the festal board were very
near in body as well as in spirit.
Brother Talbot first spoke to me as follows: "Brother Albert G..
Burnett, Most Worshipful Grand Master of the Most Ancient and Honorable Society of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California,
I greet you in the name of the members of Fidelity Lodge No. 113 of
Ridgway, New Jersey, who are assembled before me with their ladies,.
450 in number. I am informed by a representative of the telephone
company here present that we now have the distinction of being the first
representatives of Masonic bodies, assembled as such, to converse across
the continent .. I am quite sure that in years to come, when transcontinental telephoning has become one of the commonly-accepted public
utilities of our great country, you and I will look back to this occasion.
with more pleasure. Surely, this demonstration is a marvelous triumph

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

14

15

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

for science. We hear much of traveling from east to west and from
west to east in our Masonic experience, but surely nothing :Masonic has
ever before traveled as speedily as the sound of our voices tonight, for
I am told that the distance is 3400 miles and the time required for transmission is one-fifteenth of a second. The Most Worshipful Grand Master
for the State of New Jersey is seated at my right, and will in a few
minutes greet you on behalf of the Grand Lodge and the brethren of
New Jersey. In conclusion, I wish to assure you that the opportunity
to' address you in the language of fraternal greeting is much appreciated
by me. The company now assembled will listen with pleasure to your
reply."
I then replied: "Through me as Grand Master of this jurisdiction,
the Masons of California, sixty thousand strong, send most cordial and
fraternal greetings to the Most Worshipful Grand Master and brethren
of the jurisdiction of the splendid state of New Jersey. Though separated by more than 3000 miles of territory, we are bound together by
the indissoluble bonds of brotherly love, relief and truth. May we rejaiee in the consciousness of our membership in an Order that is inspired
by the highest considerations for the welfare and happiness of mankind,
and has for its ideals the purest and noblest conceptions of human
greatness. The principles we teach are as everlasting as the throne of
God; they are as sound and efficacious as any doctrine ever promulgated
for the development of individual character and the perpetuity of
society; and though madness and barbarism seem now to dominate a
large part of the so-called civilized world, yet the madness will pass,
the barbarism will give way to a better civilization than has ever been
known, and the doctrine of peace and love will yet bind together the
children of men in a holy and imperishable eompact. God grant that we
may be true and faithful and do our part in the mighty work of civilization and humanity that belongs to the craft."
The address of the Most Worshipful Brother Edward M. Searing
was as follows: "The kind message so distinctly heard, although your
voice has traveled 3500 miles, is greatly appreciated, and as Grand
Master of New Jersey, I shall take great delight in conveying it to the
42,000 Masons of this grand jurisdiction, and in return allow me to
extend to you, Most 'Vorshipful Sir, also to the brethren of the grand
and beautiful State of California, the same cordial and fraternal greet·
ings from the craft of New Jersey. It is said that distance lends enchantment, but the distance between us this evening seems but a few
yards and yet the delight in speaking with you is beyond description.
Were we not affiliated with this world-wide fraternity and linked together

On August 10th, I sent the following communication to the constituted Lodges:
''Dear Brethren: When I was elected Grand Master of this jurisdiction I fully expected to visit every Masonic District in the State and
meet personally as many of the brethren as possible. I was actively at
work in pursuance of that purpose when, on the seventeenth of March last
I was stricken with a serious illness which confined me to my bed for
twelve weeks and left me weak and incapable of performing the task
that I contemplated. I am now feeling quite well, but my normal strength
has not been fully restored. I have resumed my official duties on the
bench, but I cannot with safety to myself undertake much additional
labor. Indeed, my physicians advised me to abstain from all unneees·
sary effort for two or three months longer. This advice I have not
strictly followed, but I am sure that for some little time I shall not be
as active as formerly. I need not assure you that the enforced change
in my plans has been a great disappointment to me. I cannot tell you
how strongly I desired to visit the Lodges and meet the brethren in
the various parts of the State face to face. I thought I might, in the
providence of God, be of some service to the Fraternity that fills such
a large space in our thoughts and affections. During my long illness
this consideration was almost constantly in my mind, and I was unccas·
ingly and deeply concerned as to the welfare of the Order and the
progress and happiness of the membership. Thus, through circumstances
over which I had no control, I have been deprived of the unspeakable

The Pascoe case is one also of long standing. The ledger of Rising
Star Lodge shows that he was first suspended for non-payment of dues
in February, 1895, and reinstated April 6th of the same year. He was
again suspended March 30th, 1901. He then owed for dues for more
than four years.
Brother Pascoe 's application for reinstatement was made upon the
ground, a~ he states himself, "at the time of my suspension and f?r
some years previous thereto I was totally blind,'' and it may be said
that there were affidavits presented to the Lodge in support of the
statement. In his written communication he said he sought reinstatement "not for the purpose of securing aid from your Lodge" but "to
place myself in a position to meet my fellow brothers on a~ equal un.derstanding." He seemed to think that where "a member is placed rn a
position where he can no longer earn a livelihoo.d and .having no means
of obtaining funds to pay his assessments he is considered a member
in good standing and is exempt from dues".
The Lodge, however, declined to reinstate him unless he paid the
full amount due. The Lodge may have been influenced in its attitude
by the belief that Brother Pascoe had not always treated the Lodge as
a Mason should. In a letter among the papers in the case a former
Master of that Lodge says that he had heard it stated in the Lodge
that ''Brother Pascoe has neglected to pay his dues when he was well
able to do so" and that he was present when Brother Pascoe was suspended and that he had an opinion at the time that Brother Pas~oe
had not acted fairly in obtaining a certain letter of recommenclation
"under false pretenses and used it for a different purpose from that
for which he induced me to write it".
The evidence shows that the Lodge acted legally in suspending the
brother. They had no knowledge or notice of his disability as far as
the record shows. He should have notified the Lodge of his aftliction,
but, here, of course, there was excuse for his failure ~n consequence of
the nature of his trouble. While the brother has no right to demand a
restoration, I think out of consideration for his great misfortune and
moved by that brotherly love which is the cardinal tenet of the Order

we might well advise his restoration that he may go down to his grave
with all the privileges and honors of a Master Mason.
DECISIONS,

My first impression was to spare you a recital of the decisions rendered, but upon reflection I concluded that such an innovation would be
unfair to you and also hardly be in consonance with the requirement of
the law that the Grand Master shall "present at each annual Communication, a written message therein setting forth all his official acts during
the year,'' etc. It may be, though, that some of the minor decisions will
be omitted:
1. An application was made for the degrees in a Lodge and the
fee was deposited, an investigating committee was appointed, but before a report could be made the applicant moved to China.
He sought to have the fee returned, and I decided that there was
no authority for the Lodge to refund the fee as the application was
still pending according to section 101 of the Const.itution1 and that as
long as the application was pending and the Lodge was willing and
ready to confer the degrees the applicant was not entitled to have the
fee returned. It seemed to constitute a hardship in that particular case
and the law might well be amended to meet such a contingency.
2. A controversy between Temple Lodge No. 6 of Albuquerque,
New Mexico, and Coronado Lodge No. 441, of this jurisdiction, in
reference to the conduct of a petitioner in applying for the degrees. in
the latter Lodge while apparently a resident within the jurisdiction of
the former, was brought to my attention. I suggested that charges
should be preferred against him in order that his apparent fraud upon
the Lodge at Coronado might be investigated and justice meted out,
that it might be determined, in other words, whether there was an honest
mistake or a willful misrepresentation of a material fact on his part.
3. A circular was sent out by certain members of a Lodge asking
for a contribution for the purchase of a ''suitable remembrance'' for
the retiring Master, and I was asked if such conduct was in violation of
section 127 of the Constitution, and I replied that: ''As I understand
the facts, the said circular was not ordered to be sent by the Lodge,
and therefore the first. clause of said section does not apply. Without
doing violence to the spirit or letter of the law, I think it may be said
that the presentation of a suitable testimonial to a retiring Master who
has done many years of faithful work for the Lodge is a 'matter or
thing' Masonic in its nature, and I am of the opinion that the members
of the Lodge may properly, if they deem it advisable, make a contribution or solicit one among themselves for such purpose. Of course, it
is a matter of some delicacy, but it can be safely left to the good
judgment and sense of propriety of the members of the particular
Lodge.

4. I was asked whether the tenn ''total revenue' ' as used in section 89 of the Constitution means the ''gross'' or ''net'' income of
the Lodge for the year. I held that the word ''total'' is one of the
definitions of the word ''gross'' and that the Grand Lodge used the term
with that sig)llification. Of course, as it was suggested, under this inter·
pretation the brethren may sometimes indulge in extravagant expenditure for social purposes, but we must repose confidence in the judgment
and conscience of the members of the constituent Lodges, and if the
law is deemed to work a hardship the subject should be brought to the
attention of the Grand Lodge that the needed change may be effected.

10. In balloting for a candidate a mistake was probably made in
placing a black ball in the box. There were, however, two unfavorable
ballots in the box, and the Worshipful Master declared the candidate

and inquiry was made as to how it could be remedied, and I replied

eourse to pursue.
11. I decided that a member of a lodge that had surrendered its
charter could become a member in good standing of another Lodge ''by
affiliation and election in the ordinary way", he furnishing a satisfac·
tory explanation in writing of inability to furnish a demit.
12. On a motion to amend the by-laws of a LO(lge, there being
ten members present, :five voted for it, three against it, and two did not
vote. The Master, acting on the presumption that ' 1 all present not
voting are presumed to dissent to the action taken," (Section 77h of the
Constitution), counted the two members not voting as though voting in
the affirmative, and therefore declared the amendment adopted, it requiring a two-third vote to carry it. The brother who seconded the motion
did not vote, but afterward movetl for a re-consideration and the \Vorshipful Master being in doubt as to the propriety of the procee<1ing did
not entertain the motion. I held that the amendment was not .carried as
the law requires the vote of two-thirds of those present. 'fhis necessarily exacts actual participation in the ballot and does not contemplate
"constructive voting"· The presumption as to those not voting is that
they ''assent to whatever disposition may be made of a proposition by
those who do vote". (Proceedings of Grand Lodge for 1884, Page
738.) Furthermore, the brother who did not vote was not entitled to
move' for reconsideration. (Mackey 's Masonic Parliamentary Law, page
143.) I also held that the Worshipful Master is not required to announce that a two-thirds vote is necessary to amend the by-laws, as the
brethren are presumed to know the law, but it is advisable for him to
do so to put the brethren upon their guard.

5. These two questions were submitted to me: 1. Can a Lodge of
either Entered Apprentices or Fellow Crafts be opened more than once
in twen.ty-four hours for the conferring of degrees in the maximum of
five different candidates at each meeting~ and 2. Can a Lodge of
Entered Apprentices be opened and :five degrees conferred and later a
Lodge of Fellow Crafts opened and :five degrees conferred on other
candidates, all within twenty-four hours? I answered that in my
opinion the questions must be answered in the negative, that the natural
and reasonable interpretation of the law is that no more than :five
degrees should be conferred by the same Lodge in any period of twentyfour hours.
6. I held that where the installation of Officers was to take place
in a building other than where the Lodge regularly met the Lodge
should open in the Lodgeroom and then repair to the place of installa·
tion.
7. It was held that a Mason who has demitted from his Lodge may
petition for affiliation with a Lodge in another jurisdiction while he
still holds residence in the jurisdiction from which he has demitted.
(See Proceedings of Grand Lodge of 1915, page 295.)
8. A candidate for the degrees was balloted for, and a black cube
appearing, another ballot was taken. This ballot was also unfavorable
and the Worshipful Master declared the candidate !ejeeted. Some discussion then ensued, it being suggested that possibly a mistake had
been made; and a brother admitted that he had made a mistake in
easting the black ball. Another ballot was thereupon had which resulted
in the election of the candidate. I held that the third ballot was a
nullity under section 104 of the Constitution. I am pleased to say,
however, that I granted a dispensation for another ballot under section
106 of the Constitution and the candidate was regularly elected and
afterward initiated.

boundaries beyond those of the city of San Fernando and so as to
completely surround the latter. He therefore inquired: ''Has not the
Masonic jurisdiction of the city of Los Angeles by virtue of the above
named facts enveloped and absorbed the Masonic jurisdiction of San
Fernando Lodge No. 343 f and consequently does not San Fernando
Lodge now hold concurrent ,iurisdiction with the rest of the Lodges
located within the jurisdiction of the City of Los Angeles T"
I replied: ''I can find no ground for holding that San Fernando
Lodge has concurrent jurisdiction with the Lodges of Los Angeles City.
s.ection 82 of the Constitution, relating to concurrent jurisdiction, provides that 'If two or more Lodges are located within the corporate
limits of any city, town or place, they shall have concurrent jurisdiction
therein,' but in the sense of said expression, your lodge is not within
the corporate limits of Los Angeles but it is within the corporate limits
of San Fernando. I do not think a Lodge can be within the corporate
limits of two cities at the same time. You are a part of the municipality of San }'ernando but not of Los Angeles, 1tlthough surrounded
by the latter. This view necessarily operates to reduce the territorial
extent of your jurisdiction, and I regret the result, but under the laws,
as I understand it, I can see no other alternative. At the time said
provision was adopted no one probably anticipated such a complication
as has arisen in your city and the law should probably be amended to
meet the situation."
15. Wilshire Lodge No. 445 adopted resolutions changing the by·
laws relating to fees for degrees and dues, with. a proviso that the
change should not go into effect until the membership of the Lodge
should have reached three hundred. The Deputy Grand Master decided
(and I concur) that no amendment could be properly made to take
effect at an indefinite date; that "the time for such amendments will
be opportune when the membership shall have reached the specified
number and all members will have had an opportunity of expressing
an opinion thereon.''

27

In reply to an inquiry whether examination of visiting brethren
I.Jo held at any place other than a room or place adjacent to the
hotly of said Lodge", I answered that the Constitution contemplates that
~11 1 ·.h examination shall be made within the jurisdiction at least of the
I ,odgo which the visitors desire to attend.
17. I held that a man who ''has lost his right leg seven inches
lu•low the knee'' is not qualified to receive the degrees .
18. I held that it was proper for the Secretary at the stated meetiui.: in June to read the names of all who owed for dues, but that needi«•HH humiliation of any member should of course be avoided.
19. I decided that it was not proper to hold Masonic services over
the ashes of a brother whose body had been cremated.
20. In reply to a question whether a brother's dying request that
his funeral services be conducted by the Masons and Odd Fellows, I
held that the language of Section 164 of the Constitution should be
construed as liberally as possible, but that it certainly means nothing
less than tnat the whole service should be under the direction of the
Masonic Lodge· but that out of respect to the wishes of the deceased,
and as a matt:r of courtesy to the other great fraternal organization,
the Worshipful Master ~f the Lo.dge might properly request the Odd
Pellows to render their service or a part of it at the Chapel, it being
understood that the Masonic Lodge shall have charge of and conclude
the service". (Proceedings of Grand Lodge of 1891-1892, Page 215.)

MASONIC TEMPLE.

One subject of tremendous importanoo to which I must not fail to
call your earnest attention, involves our interest in the Masonic Temple.
As has been said by my immediate predecessors, our faith has been
pledged to this enterprise, and we cannot afford, as I am sure we have
no disposition to shrink from, our responsibility in the premises. We
must go forward until the debt is entirely obliterated and this splendid
building is placed upon a sure foundation of safety and profit. Let there
be no laggards in this matter. We will bear the burden cheerfully,
knowing that the reward will be commensurate with the sacrifice we
are called upon to make. I recommend that we follow the example set
by the last Grand Lodge, and that we purchase $25,000 worth of the stock.
MASONIC HOMES AND OTHER AGENCIES,

I am pleased to say that the members generally are proud of the
practical agencies adopted and conducted by the Fraternity for the amelioration of distress and for the aid of those who need assistance. I
have not been able to devote much personal attenti~n to these instrumentalities, but I am satisfied that those having them in charge are fully
alive to the importance of their work and are striving earnestly and
efficiently to discharge their sacred trust. I believe they are imbued

28

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

with the true spirit of Masonry and are glad of the opportunity to be
of some service to the Order and to mankind. Of course, no one who
does not love the Order and his fellow man should undertake to admin·
ister these practical functions of benevolence and helpfulness nor should
he spare himself in his efforts to secure economy and effieie~cy if he is
called upon to represent the Order in these important executive duties.
There shonld be, of course, no favoritism nor partiality. Strict attention to duty should be required of all subordinates, and full value should
be obtained if possible for every dollar of the Fraternity's money that
is expended.
'
My visit to the Homes certainly made a deep impression upon my
mind. As far as one can judge from appearances, you would say that
conditions are almost ideal. It is unneoossary to go into detail, but
they certainly appear to be Homes indeed wherein reside contentment
love and happiness. May they ever be the object of our most earnest and
prayerful consideration to the end that we may discharge our full duty
to those entrusted to our guardianship.
The Boards of Relief and employment agencies are also of tremendous importance and they demand our most careful attention. Full information will be given you no doubt as to the work by those who know
whereof they speak, and I trust that it may receive the attention that
it deserves. I will state here that of the $1200 allowed for my expenses
I have turned back the sum of $580.65.
PROGRESS OF THE ORDER.

Speaking generally, I may say that the Order has made substantial
progress during the year. We have grown in numbers our enrollment
now being nearly 58,000. That constitutes, my bre~hren, a mighty
army of soldiers of peace and fraternity. We will soon be one hundred
thousand strong in this state. I believe also that our membership is
growing in appreciation of the significance of Masonry and in ihe practical exemplification of the tenets of our Order. The reports of the
Inspectors show that great care is being exercised as to the character of
those elected to receive the degrees and that in the various communities
the people regard Masons as standing for the highest and best in our
civilization, and they look upon it as one of the most potent agencies
for the promotion of human welfare and happiness.
SUGGESTIONS,

Various suggestions have been made to me whereby it is thought
?ur work may be im.proved. Probably none of these is of commanding
importance, yet I thmk I may trespass upon your time to call your at·
tention specifically, to a few of them. Of course we are all vitally interested in the subject of endowment for our Homes, and in this connection
one brother suggested that the Lodge be permitted•to spend a portion
of the social fund for the insurance of some of the members in favor

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

29

of such a fund. Another suggestion was that a specific day should be
designated by proclamation of the Grand Master to be known throughout
the jurisdiction as "Endo'll<ment Day," and that on that day it would
be expected ''that every Master Mason should contribute toward the
fund whatever he could, that the Inspectors should be instructed to
actively stimulate interest and through the Inspectors the Masters of
subordlnate Lodges could be induced to send letters explanatory of the
economic and sentimental desirability of the fund"·
Another suggestion was that the procedure should be simplified so
that ''for the purpose of examination only a lodge of the third degree
may be called from labor in that degree to work i~ the second degree
without closing and reopening in the respeetiv!l degrees'' and when the
cxamina tion has been concluded "the Lodge shall be purged and work
forthwith resumed in the third degree".
Another brother thought that the '' degree teams'' of which we hear
so much should be subjected to examination by a committee consisting
of the Grand Master, Grand Lecturer and Grand Secretary, who should
be authorized to pass upon their efficiency in the work.
These suggestions, together with a letter of advice to Masters of
Lodges by Brother Leo Bruck, are worthy of attention and I commend
them to you.
NECROLOGY.

The Grim Reaper has been busy in our midst during the year.
Many of our brethren have fallen, but in consequence of a life well
spent they could exclaim with the great Apostle: ''Oh death, where is
fhy sting¥ Oh grave, where is thy victory~" Many of the members of
the constituent Loc1ges who have passed away have not sought honor
or worldly distinction. They have been content to pursue· the even tenor
of their way, performing their daily tasks in a quiet, unostentatious
manner, satisfied with the approval of their conscience and leaving be·
hind them an enduring monument of self-sacrifice and devotion to the
welfare of others. We pay them the tribute of our admiration and com·
mend their example to those who are remaining here for a little while.
Of the members of this Grand Lodge we have to regret the loss of
William Abraham Davies and John Morton Eshleman.

How forcibly this record of the dead reminds us that we too are
passing away. The places that know us now will soon know us no more
forever. Whatever may be the distinction we now enjoy, we will soon
meet upon the common level of the tomb. How true is the language
of Senator Ingalls: ''In the democracy of the dead all men at last are
equal. There is neither rank nor station nor prerogative in the republic
of the grave. At this fatal threshold the philosopher ceases to be wise
and the song of the poet is silent. Dives relinquished his millions and
Lazarus his rags. The poor man is as rich as the richest, and the rich
man is as poor as the pauper. The creditor loses his usury and the
debtor is acquitted of his obligation, There the proud man surrenders
his dignities, the politician his honors, the worldJ.ing his pleasures, the
invalid needs no physieian and the laborer rests from unrequited toil.
Here at last is nature's final decree in equity. The wrongs of time are
redressed. Injustice is expiated, the irony of fate is refuted, the unequal
distribution of wealth, honor, capacity, pleasure and opportunity, which
makes life sueh a cruel and inexplieable tragedy ceases in the realm of
death. The strongest there has no supremacy, and the weakest needs
no defense. The mightiest captain succumbs to that invincible adversary,
who disarms alike the vietor and the vanquished.''

32

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Let us, my brethren, h!!ed the lesson of the grave; but may we also
never close our eyes to the light that streams through its gloomy portals,
revealing the glory ineffable that lies beyond.
God grant that we may make the most of the present life, that we
may work while it is called to-day, knowing that "the night cometh
when no man can work'', that we may endure unto the end in the
earnest, unremitting and faithful discharge of our duties and at the last
great day receive the final judgment of the Supreme Grand Master of
the Universe: "Well done, good and faithful servant".
ALBERT G. BURNETT,
Grand Master.

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY.

report of the transactions of the office of Grand Secretary for the
year, and such other matters as may be of interest:

The membership for the year ending July 31, 1915, was 55,341,
and the membership as reported to the end of this fl.seal year, July 31,
1916, is 57,856, a net gain of 2,515 for the year. The gross gain was
4,702, and by suspensions, deaths and withdrawals, the gross loss was
2,228. The suspensions alone were 638, and the restorations only 126,
and I repeat my remarks of a year ago, that ''suspensions are not•
always the result of depressed business conditions, but that in many
instances the members in arrears might be kept in good standing and
Masonic usefulness by studied effort on the part of Masters and See·
retaries. The largest Lodge in this jurisdiction, with a membership of
more than nine hundred, lost no member last year by reason of suspension or non-payment of dues.· . • • . One. of the principal committee.a is a ''Committee on Delinquent Members,'' and it is the duty
of this committee to ascertain the cause of delinquency-with the
happy result that if a member be in destress, his dues are promptly
remitted, and if he be negligent, he ls shown the error of his ways and
his duty to his fellows.'' This particular Lodge, pursuing its usual
splendid committee work on delinquents, reports the loss of four
members only this year by suspension.

UNFINISHED BUSINESS.

At the Annual Communication in 1915 the following resolution
was presented by the Los Angeles Board of Relief, referred to the
Committee on .Jurisprudence, which Committee reported baek reeom·
mending that it be referred to the incoming Committee on Jurisprudence, to be reported at the Annual Communication in 1916:
"Whereas, the Boards of Relief are frequently called upon to
give aid to the daughter of a Master Mason, living or deceased; and
'"Whereas, many of such el'l!lls are from and in behalf of such
daughters who have passed the age of majority, and from and in
behalf of daughters who have been or are married; therefore be it
"Resolved, that the term 'orphan' is construed to include both
male and female under the age of twenty-one years, and that the
claim to Masonic aid at the age of twenty·one years shall cease as a
matter of right, and that aid vouchsafed to such orphans after they
shall have attained the age of twenty.one years shall be in the dis·
cretion of the Masonic bodies dispensing charity.
"Resolved, that section 163i, now reading 'That the daughter of
a Master Mason in good standing, whether of tender or mature years,
is entitled to relief,' be amended to read:

40

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

'' 'That the daughter of a Master Mason in good standing, under
the age of twenty-one years, is entitled to relief as a matter of right,
but the daughter of a Master Mason who has attained the age of
twenty-one years shaill not as a matter of right be enHtled to aid, but
may receive aid at the discretion of the dispensing body.' "

The Trustees of the Masonic Homes presented their Annual Report, and inasmuch as printed copies were in the hands·
of Representatives present, the reading thereof was omitted
and consideration of the Report was made special order for
11 o'clock Wednesday morning. The Report is as follows:
REPORT OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE
MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California herewith
submits for your consideration and approval its annual report for the
year ending September 30, 1916.
The Most Worshipful Grand Master reappointed William S. Wells,
vice self, term expired, and the Board held its annual meeting at the
office of the Grand Secretary on October 16, 1915, electing William 8.
Wells President, Motley H. Flint Vice President, and Elmer E. Stone
Secretary. During the year the Board has held its regular and special
meetings at both Decoto and Covina.
Th~ report of the Secretary is submitted herewith, made a part of
this report, and referred to for more particular information regarding
the condition of both Homes.
DECOTO HOME.

The new dormitory, of fireproof concrete construction, which was inspected by the members of the Grand Lodge at its last session, was regularly opened immediately after the adjournment of that Body. All applications for admission have received prompt attention, and at present all
rooms are occupied, with the exception of five rooms in Simino:H' Temple,
four rooms in the cottages for men, and seven rooms for women on
the third floor of the main building. All rooms in the new dormitory
are filled.
The general affairs of the Decoto Home have moved along with
gratifying smoothness during the year past. Among the important repairs and improvements which have been made are the following:
A brick blacksmith shop building has been added to the power
house and equipped with furnace, drill and emory wheels operated by

An irrigating system has been installed to water the trees and
flower plants on the road leading to the main entrance of the Home
grounds, the lily pond being used as a reservoir.

Five cottages for reside~ts, three cottages for employes, the dairy
barn, and stable have been pamted to harmonize with the brick buildings.
A row of walnut rees has been planted along the entire front of
~he county road, inside the boundary fence of the Home property 1 adjoinmg land owners entering into a similar agreement.
_The deep well pump has been overhauled and put in order, and all
repairs to the hot and cold waterpipes and heating system have been
made.
The following improvements are recommended:
The hospital building is inadequate to the needs of the Home. There
are. fifteen beds, and during the past year at times more than twenty
patients w~re careu for, the extra room being secured by placing beds in
the op~ratrng room and crowding the space in the wards. The building
of a wrng to the present structure is recommended.
A large warehouse is needed to house farming implements, wagons
and to store feed corn and grain. This would enable the Home to pur'.
chase a year's supply when the market is low.
The porch floors of the main building and cottages should be
painted.
.
The frame work of the hospital building on the outside needs paintmg and .the woodwork an~ walls of the halls and rooms need a general
overhaulmg to put them rn good condition.
.
All roads on the Home grounds need grading, crowning and gravelrng.
. The activity .at the Home is shown by the enlargement of the
chicken ranch, which now contains two thousand chickens, the improvement of the dairy herd of :fifteen cows, and the enlargement of the vegetable garden, which furnishes all vegetables for table use and greens and
stock f~ed for farm department. This year two tons of sugar prunes
were dne~ at Deco~o, and a large quantity of stock corn raised and stored
f~r use m the chicken and hog ranches, the latter of which contains
sixty-five hogs. A combination auto truck and bus is needed to reduce
the number of horses now used.
COVINA HOME,

The pa.st year has been a most active one at Covina. Few persons
can appreciate the amount of detail necessary in moving so large a

54

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

family with .attending conditions of leaving a large roomy building
with very old but generous equipment, and placing them in a comparatively small building with limited appurtenances. The children, however,
ent~red into the spirit of the affair and assisted in many helpful ways.

The Temporary Buildings, Covina.

The New Buildings, Covina, Sept. 20, 1916.

Your Trustees had agreed to deliver possession of the old San Gabriel
property 'on January 1, 1916. Immediately after the close of Grand
Lodge, construction . was begun on a temporary building to house the
children during the construction of the new buildings. It was constructed economically, but was very convenient, though somewhat crowded.
Materials of such dimensions and quality as to make the greatest sal-

55

vage when the present purpose was accomplished, were selected, and the
construction was adjusted to minimize the waste when the material
•hould be used in other buildings. At a cost of approximately $7,000 the
work was completed, and the children moved to the new building on
Saturday, December 18, 1915. They enjoyed their holidays in the new
home, and started their school work the first of the year without any
interruption of their studies.
The Masons and citizens of Covina are deeply interested in our
Home, and assisted in every way to secure all necessary conveniences. We
met with no disappointments, and few inconveniences with the public
utility companies. Although two miles from Covina, we had water, electric lights, gas, power and telephone all in service before occupying the
building. We were obliged to provide a pressure tank and motor for
waier, but the supply is ample, and we now have arranged for pressure
~ater from the street mains for the new buildings. For heating, an
odorless gas fµrnace was provided in each of the rooms. This was not
ideal, but met the need.
In the construction of our new buildings we desired the greatest
possible efficiency in arrangement and construction, with the view of
economical maintenance when completed. The Trustees therefore personally visited many similar institut ions, corresponded with every Masonic Home in the United States for suggestions and recommendations,
and consulted the best authorites on eleemosynary institutions to secure
for our dependent children all possible advantages consistent with judicious expenditure.
Architects of Los Angeles, members of the Fraternity, were invited
to submit completed drawings and brief notations for specitlcations.
Three of our most prominent firms responded with carefully drawn plans
and complete perspectives. Needam & Cline, John F. Blee and Train &
Williams submitted their odrawings without identifying marks to indicate
to whom they belonged. All of the plans possessed much merit,' so the
Board called in another architect to assist in the selection, and had a
responsible contractor estimate the cost of each set of plans. The selec·
tion finally fell upon John F. Blee, whose plans most nearly met the
need of the institution. All of these architects deserve t he thanks of
the Fraternity, for .they manifested much sincere interest in the Home
and gave generously of their time to render us a good service. All are
experienced in t his character of work and have designed creditable school
buildings for the Los Angeles B oard of Education.
The Board ordered Mr. Blee 's plans moditled to meet many needs
not known at the time to the architect. Floor plans and elevations were
approved February 26, 19161 and the contract let for the foundation
and first floor on April 5, for $21,445. The foundation and a portion of
the first floor were completed by May 20, at which time the cornerstone
of the building was laid.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
LAYING OF CORNERSTONE.

The ceremony of laying the cornerstone was one of the most inter·
esting events in the history of Masonry in California, and the interest
of Southern California Masons was evidenced by their great attendance
on this occasion. Credit for success of details is due largely to a com·
mittee on arrangements, consisting of representatives of Masonic, Municipal officers and business men's organizations of Covina. The following
account of this splendid occasion, written by our Very Worshipful Grand
Secretary John Whicher, best reports the event:
The most important public event of the year was the laying of the
cornerstone of the new Home for Children. The buildings, as described
above, will be located on our recently-acquired holdings two miles east of
the beautiful city of Covina, in Los Angeles county. The foundation
stone was laid in the northeast corner of the main structure on the
20th of May, 1916, by Right Worshipful Francis V. Keesling, Deputy
Grand Master. It was an ideal day, and the little city of Covina was
decked out in flags, bunting and flowers, while thousands of people
lined the avenues along the line of march to the Rome. Of automobiles
alone there were six hundred parked near the place of the cermonies.
Grand Lodge was convened in the hall of Covina Lodge No. 334, and
under the able direction of Frank Clarke Prescott, Past Master of
Vallee de France Lodge No. 329 of Los Angeles, the eseort was formed
as follows:
Seventh Regiment Band, N. G. C., of Pomona.
The Grand Commandery Knights Templar of California, Right
Eminent Sir Elmer E. Stone, Grand Commander, escorted by two battalions commanded by Eminent Sir Benjamin F. Bledsoe, Grand Captain
General.

Los Angeles Commandery No. 9, K. T.
Southern California Commandery, No. 37, K. T.
Pasadena Commandery No. 31, K. T.
Long Beach Commandery No. 40, K. T.

Commander, commanding:

Arriving at the site of the Home, the officers of Grand Lodge and
of the other participating bodies, with the Trustees of the Home and
all the children of the Home and their attendants, were assigned to seats
on a platform. Golden West band rendered a piece of music, and
prayer was offered by Very Reverend William MacCormack of Corona
Lodge No. 324, as follows:
"0 God, our Heavenly Father! We come into Thy presence to-day
supplicating Thy bfossing and seeking Thy guidance in what we are
about to do. Forasmuch as without Thee we are not able to please
Thee, mercifully grant that Thy holy spirit may in this gracious work
of mercy lead us in the way in which we ought to go. Direct us in
this and in all things with Thy most loving favor, and further us with
Thy continual help that in all our works, begun, continued, and ended
in Thee, we may glorify Thy holy name. We praise Thee most of all
that Thou didst put it into the hearts of Thy servants to erect this
building for the care and protection of Thy homeless and needy children.
May Thy presence brood over it. Be with the offi.iers and teaehers in
their blessed work. Bring to all a realizing sense of the responsibility
of the task committed to them, and of the privilege of serving Thee and
their fellows in the edueation and training of the young. Keep the
workmen employed from every harm and danger. May they labor not
as eye-servants or men-pleasers, but with this thought that they are
building this house in the blessed service of human redemption. Grant
that this consciousness may inspire them while they labor, and may it
perfect and beautify the efforts of their hands.
"We would ask as well Thy blessing on the Grand Lodge, and on
all the Lodges of our ancient eraft. May the ideals that are lifted up
for our contemplation be actualized in the lives of our members. We
pray Thee that each Mason, wherever he may be found throughout the
world, may be a living monument of the truth which his lips profess.
All this we ask in His name who has taught us to pray, saying: Our
Father which are in heaven, hallowed be Thy name. Thy kingdom come.
Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our
daily bread. And forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who
trespass again!!t us. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us

from evil: For Thine is the kingdom, and the power, a.nd the glory, for

When the boy had finished, there were tears in the eyes of every

reply, which he did in part as follows
"No one within the hearing of little Herbert's voice but who has
been profoundly affected. WoukJ that the entire membership of the
Fraterntiy were here for. the beneficent effect this incident would have
bad.
''This is a great work which the Fraternity is doing, but it is not
the greatest work done by the Institution. The greatest work is that
which promotes good citizenship, thereby insuring life, liberty and the
pursuit of happiness, under which circumstances such great work as this
may be done. The environment of the Home is entirely befitting. Here
God's sunshine is less interrupted. Here the mountains are majestic
and the plants and trees bloom anil fructify in bountiful beauty. May
the happiness resultant from it all, assisted by the efforts of the Fraternity in its ministrations, be transfused into the hearts and souls of
the little ones who will be our wards in this institution.''

Brother Samuel E. Burke, Grand Orator, then delivered the following address: ·
''Suffer little children come unto Me and forbid them not; for of
such is the Kingdom of Heaven.''
Surely these, my friends, are the most beautiful words of all time.
Of all the utterances of our Lord none has been more quoted-songs have
been written around its theme, sermons have been preached, and whole
volumes have been written, and still the words strike as sweetly the ear
of the hearer today, as they did those many, many centuries ago when
they were :first uttered to the people of Judea.
And while we are laying this eornerstone today, let us remember
that we lay not only the comerstone of the building whieh shall give
to these children temporary shelter, but rather that we lay the cornerstone of character, the building·stone of souls. It is not enough that
we gather here today to see that stone placed which shall mean to these
little ones a home,-a place where thir physical bodies shall be fed, and
clothed and kept warm; it is more that the building which shall here be
erected shall be the fostering place ·of noble manhood and true womanhood; that here the little feet may be started in that narrow path that
leads to a lofty goal; the little hands taught to fashion, not mischief
and wrongdoing, but deeds of love and honor; that here into the little
hearts shall be instilled a love of truth, a love of country, and a love
of God.
We who have made possible this ceremony today are not dispensers
of sweet charity. Instead1 we are the recipients of a wonderful privilege. To be permitted to have in our keeping these youthful minds
and souls at the very time their characters are being moulded for all

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

61

the years to come; to be able to give to the world in after years men
and women of integrity, with sane minds in sound bodies, is an honor
far greater than ever conferred by medal or silken ribbon. It is at once
not only the greatest honor that could be bestowed on us today, but t?e
greatest responsibility. We are thankful to God for the honor; we will
not shirk the responsibility.
Do you not sometimes travel back, back into the day of yeste!J'.ea~,
back to that fairyland of your childhood, and do you not :fincl there mc1dents that stand out in your memory as landmarks, sometimes even
turning·points in your life' Perhaps to you then they were only an ~­
usual occurrence in the daily routine of your little life, but now, holding
aloft the lamp of experience, you view them differently. You view them
in their real importance and estimate them at their true worth. Perhaps
it was only an earnest talk with your father, but does not his. kindly
word of advice or warning sound in your ear today, though the hp that
uttered it may now be with yesterday's seven thousand years' Or perhaps it was the death of your mother, for how ofttimes has it happen~d
that the last loving look of a mother, the last tender clasp of her dear
hand, her last gently whispered word1 has had more influence for good
in the life of her boy than all the sermons and arguments that were
ever conceived in the brain of man.
Thus it is with us now: We sow, and we reckon not the harvest.
There may perhaps come a time in the more mature years of these chil·
dren when some lesson here learned, some precept impressed, shall stand
as a guide·post at the parting of the ways, helping them to know the
right path from the wrong, the wheat from the tares.
Then let us as Masons never think of this sheltering spot of our
'
'
.
Masonic children with a glow of righteous pride for our splendid munificence and generosity, but rather with hearts humble with thanksgi:'ing
for the gracious kindliness of Almighty God, that He has permitted
us to be the tool of His hand, that into our keeping He has seen :fit to
place this sacred trust, this priceless casket of His jewels, the lives of
His little children .
.Then let us make it our constant aim to make always the needs and
wants of other men our very own, to give the affection of our hearts
to those to whom we minister the gifts of this world's goods; to enter,
insofar as we ma.y, into the feelings of another, to make his sorrows our
own· to enter the shadow of his life and realize its pall. In this way
only: my Brethren, may we be of real service one to another. It is
tho hand of fellowship that strengthens, it is the word of cheer that
brightens the dull life, it is the assurance of brotherly. love that lightens
the burder for the weary heart.
To lift another's burder too hard for him alone to bear, to whisper
the word of warning to the erring one, to soothe the Grphan 's woe, and

.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

wipe away the widow's tear; to dedicate our lives to service and to
sacrifice, to labor and not sigh for rest, to give and never oount the
cost, to fight and never heed the wound: these, indeed, are the :fruits
and :flowers of true Masonic brotherhood, and the primal reason for the
existence of our Fraternity.

Every one is familiar with the stupendous increase in prices of all
materials since the beginning of the European war1 and we have suffered much from this fact. · However, taking into counsel many of the
best men of the Fraternity, and judging from market conditions that
further delay would only be more expensive, your Board saw nothing
to do but accept the situation and let the contract. Therefore, after
four weeks' deliberation, we awarded the general contract to Brother
G. H. Whyte, for $91,000, feeling that the Fraternity is being well
served, and that the success of· the children who have gone from the
Home to take their places in the world's work merits all we can do for
those who are and will be under our care.
The contract for heating, plumbing, refrigeration, laundry, vacuum
cleaning, etc., was delayed for a time because of contention among the
bidders. This matter was adjusted to the satisfaction of both the Board
and the bidders finally by the contestants themselves determining the low
bidder, and a committee from their own number was selected to supervise the work. The contract was accordingly awarded to Brother
William McArthur, for $26,431.40.

Masonry, too, imposes upon as as bounden duty the leading of
pure and upright lives1 being charitable men and useful citizens. It
bids us in every condition and circumstance of life to remember our
high calling; to know and do Charity, not only in the relief 'of financial
distress, but in every ministration that love dictates to the just and
generous heart; to never forget our duty as citizens of the State, and
in all the responsibilities of citizenship be true; that in the home rela·
tions, our lives shall be such that content and happiness shall reign;
that in this journey of life we shall ever hold aloft the unfailing and
unquenchable light of Truth, that we may make light the paths of those
who follow.
And, in. this way, as time goes on, this noble Institution of Morality, Friendship and Brotherly Love shall radiate its perpetual influence
of charity among men, till cruel superstitions shall only be a humiliating
memory and a record of forgetfulness; because
The poor, oppressed, honest man
Had never sure been born,
Had there not been some ~eeompense,
To comfort those that mourn.
Golden West Commandery band then played Old Hundred, which
was joined in by the entire audience, after which Brother MacCormack
closed the ceremonies with the following benediction:
"The Lord bless thee, and keep thee; the Lord make His face shine
upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; the Lord lift up His countenance
upon thee, and give thee peace. Alnen. ''
The Board approved detail plans of the buildings on May 18 and
bids were received and opened July 22. Upon openings the bid:, the
Board was much disappointed to find that the amounts were in excess
of estimates. The bids for the foundation were slightly under estimate,
and we were encouraged to feel that the superstructure might also be
more rea!!onable. Many demands, however, were made upon the Board
by those sincerely interested in having the Masons of California make
suitable provision for the dependent children of the craft, and some additions were jleemed advisable to make a complete institution, particularly
in thoroughly equipped hospital rooms, operating rooms, sterilization,
surgical, dental and preparation room oti the second :floor of the main
building, and a substantial class of machinery for all needs in the basement.

Good bonds have been furnished with both contracts, and the work
is progressing very satisfactorily.
While this preliminary work bas been going on with the buildings,
we have not been idle with the farm end of the new location. About
four acres has been graded for alfalfa, and garden work has done well
since the water reached it. We have laid a system of pipes to reach all
of the lower grounds and constructed a septic tank for the new buildings, which we are using temporarily as a reservoir. The trees on the
plaee, while few in number, are doing nieely, and a small vineyard on the
terrace yielded a fairly good crop this year. The general farm improvements have not been made because they are a part of a general scheme
and contingent upon some work that cannot be done yet.
Altogether it has been a year of wonderful activity and splendid
progress, The buildings will stand as a monument to the noblest in
Masonry, and what is even better, our children are having a happy,
healthy and useful childhood.
Fraternally submitted,
WM. S. WELLS,
MOTLEY H. FLINT,
THOMAS FLINT,
E. B. SPENCER,
EI,MER E. STONE,
Trustees.

During the year there have been admitted to the Home, 37 men and
l:! women. There are now at the Home, 100 men and 52 women.
'l'lwrc are 14 members being eared for at the Coleman Hospital. In
vinw of the increased membership of the Home, additional room at
J.ho lmspital is urgently needed.
The water supply has been pl!lntiful for household, garden and
Irrigating purposes. The reservoirs have at all times 700,000 gallons of
w11tcr in storage.
The greater part of the hill ranch has as heretofore been leased
11it.hcr on shares or for cash rental.
The farm has supplied plenty of fruit for table use, the surplus
hoing sold in the San Francisco market. A large quantiy of corn and
11toek feed and hay has been raised for the dairy, hog and chicken
mnehes. Two tons of dried prunes are on hand. The vegetable and
lmrry gardens gave good returns. Enough of the vineyard has been

70

retained for Home use and the balance of the acreage has been cultivated for e<>rn and hay. The hay crop was fair. The new orchard is
doing well. A row of walnut trees has been planted along the entire
front of the Home property inside of the boundary fence.
The operation of the heating, laundry, pumping and cold storage
plants and the blacksmith shop have been satisfactory.
The chicken ranch has supplied all the eggs for kitchen and table
use and a large number of eggs have been put up for winter use. The
dairy has furnished plenty of milk and the hog ranch has given good
returns.
All the mending and household linen has been made by the women
of the Home. A number of the brethren have contributed to the welfare
of the Home by their labor in the carpenter, shoe, tailor and barber
shops, also the woodyard and in the care of flower gardens, lawns, library
and reading rooms, and light work in a general way.
There are 2600 volumes on the library shelves. Many magazines,
periodicals and daily papers are received, which are placed on the tables
of the library, men's club rooms and the ladies' reading room.
Moving picture, stereopticon and musical entertainments are given
from time to time in the Siminoff Temple and the Assembly Hall. An
orchestra consisting of a violin and piano has been organized and takes
part in all our entertainments. The Thursday evening social, games and
dances, the Friday evening song practice have been regularly held in
the Assembly Hall. The usual services are held on Sunday afternoon,
followed by a musical concert.
The men's club room in the new building has been furnished with
a billiard table, a pool table, two eard tables (drop lights being over
each table), two counting racks, twelve arm chairs and twelve Vienna
chairs. The brethren enjoy their new quarters, and greatly appreciate
the comforts affordecl them there, which was made possible by the
generosity of the Lodges of San Francisco. The opening of the club
room was a formal affair, the ladies of the Home acting as hosts, and
the brethren the guests.
The Regina music box and twenty Regina records, presented to the
Home by Mrs. M. E. Waldren, has been placed in the men's new club
room.
A beautiful Westminister chime clock, six feet high, was presented
and installed in this room by Mrs. Leo Bruck.
A large and beautiful silk American flag, with gold cord and tassel
and standard and pedestal was presented to th13 Home by officers of the
Grand Lodge, Inspectors of the Bay counties and Brother B. Pasquale.
It has been placed in the Assembly hall.
Arrangements have been made whereby each month the members
of our family-a few at a time-may visit Alameda Lodge No. 167,

a~~ Orient Chapter No. 177, 0. E. S., at Centerville. Oeeasionally
v1s1ts are made to Lodges and Chapters at Oakland1 San Francisco and
other cities near the Home.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
THE COVINA HOME.

We ean most effectively introduce the new Home at Covina to the
Grand Lodge1 by quoting a portion of a letter written by one o~ o~r
older girls to a girl who left the home two years ago. The quotation llJ
modified only to avoid personalities mentioned in the letter:
"The dry stubble of a recent grain field in the midst of the orange
groves of Covina was disturbed one October morning by a string of
teams hauling in lumber, and the stillness of the spot was soon broken
by the noise of hammers and the hum of saws. In a few .we.eks the
scene was transformed as dozens of eqildren raced on the h1lls1de and
shouted in childish joy of the outdoor life.
''A new building, crowded, odd, no ceilings, no plaster, but convenient, novel and jolly, and the children were happy. A little cold in
the winter a little hot in the summer, but oh, so homelike and pleasant,
The schoo{ was new but so much better. Better playmates, better build·
ing and an auto tru~k to call for the children and bring them home again.
No church was near and no Sunday school room was provided in the
building, but it was' just so nice to bunch up all together in the living
rooms and have a Sunday school all their own. One of the Trustees
acted as Superintendent, one of the girls as pianist, and each Sunday
new quartettes and solos were arranged. Then one Sunday the Trustee
couldn't come out and he asked one of the older girls to lead the school.
It was :fine. Then one of the boys wanted to try it, and now the different children eagerly wait their turn to conduct the Sunday school. No
Sunday school in all California is more interesting.
''Soon flowers were planted, geraniums in green banks, the tall
cosmos and dahlias did so well and the violets, pansies, daisies, and
asters all rewarded us for the care we gave them. And the wild :flowers
were so plentiful and several million poppies right in front of the house.
It may. take a long time to grow big trees, but the sweet :flowers come to
us quickly and plentifully.
·
''And now the big buildings are going up. How wonderful they
are. How instruetive as it is all explained, and how generous Masons
are to do all this for children''.
The above quotation presents ii: true expression of the splendid
manner the children displayed in adjusting themselves to the new conditions, and their evident appreciation of the necessary steps contingent
to such a move.
The Home life was only intensified by the move. Inspired to greater
effort by new surroundings, the same spirit prevailed in their lessons,
training and discipline.
Their music has continued the same. Their dancing, ,art work,
sewing, etc., occupy the girls, and the boys have built pens for rabbits,
houses for pigeons, and laid out small tracts of grounds for vegetables.

83

Under the skilled direction of Eddie Maier and Doc White of the
"Tigers", the boys have advanced in base ball and have taken many
honors. Never in the past has Charter Oak school, where the boys
attend, ever had representatives to qualify for the track meet. This
year, with our boys alone, they won the greater number of points in the
valley schools, competing against well trained teams.
The indoor diversions of the children are many, and while our
Matron is most resourceful in providing something new from time to
time, the children display much originality in occupying their play hours
with healthful and suitable amusement. A social evening is given once
a week for dancing, card games, etc., for the older ones, and lighter
games for the little ones. A reading or ''story hour'' occurs practically
every day and their music, both instrumental and chorus work, is conducted in such a manner as to inspire interest and cause them to anticipate the new features with the greatest pleasure. Each child 'e birthday
is celebrated with a large cake and candles, and suitable floral decorations are placed on the table at which the child is seated. The child
cuts the cake and personally passes it to the children. A ringing
''call'' is always given and the event is thus pleasantly recognized.
All holidays, patriotic events, and anniversaries are celebrated in
suitable ways. St. Valentine's Day v.ith appropriate cards, Easter with
lilies and "rabbit eggs"· May .Day with baskets, Memorial Day with
flags, Fourth of July with pyrotechnics, Halloween with pumpkin faces
and masked party, and even St. Patrick's Day and All Fools' Day are
becomingly recognized. The birthdays of Lincoln, and Washington,
and Admission Day are remembered, and Thanksgiving Day is always a
treat.
'The children are given impromptu holidays by the Lodges, Shrine
an.d Eastern Star Chapters, and many visits of Grand Officers, Lodges,
or other Masonic Bodies, are turned into active occasions by something
novel, arranged either by the visitors or by the children. It is not practical to mention all visitations, but those particularly pleasant and en·
joyable since our last report were as follows:
October 3d. Grand Master and Mrs. Bledsoe visited the children
and so.t at the table with them at supper. The children gave an impromptu program and Brother Bledsoe gave them one of the most
pleasant and beneficial talks they ever heard. Our good Brother seemed
inspired for the occasion.
October 6th. Harbor Chapter No. l'i4, 0. E. S., o~ San Pedro,
visited the Home and left a dozen very attractive single comforts. for
the little girls' beds. The children responded with a program.
October 30th. Judge and Mrs. Wells took part in the Halloween
party of ghosts, fairies, imps, gargoyles, gnomes, pumpkin faces,
witches, etc.

84

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

November 1st. No one is ever more welcomed among the children
than Brother John Whicher. Every child feels intimately acquainted'
with him. They made this occasion pleasant for him, too.
November 14th. Golden West Commandery Band made their annual
visit to the Home and played a number of selections. Thia Band of
good hearted Masons has a strong claim on the children, who have not
the opportunity of seeing even the street parade of a circus or political
meeting, where bands are playing. This is a valued treat for the
youngsters.
November 14th. Brother William Henry Gaynor, Grand High Priest
of California, with his wife and daughter, and Brother Harry Ascroft,
Grand Lecturer of the Grand Chapter, visited the Home and had dinner
with the childrel'. Brother Gaynor is no stranger to the Home, and is
much interested, while Brother Ascroft has been adopted by the childl'.en
as their own. He is always prepared with new jokes and stories and
they would not trade him for the whole Orpheum circuit.
December 12th. Long Beach Chapter No. 173, 0. E. S., visited
the Home. This most generous Chapter and its strong ally, the Shrine
Club of Long Beach, are strong in heart and pocket for our children.
These good ladies and brethren are thoughtful the year around, and
are always providing for both the pleasure and comfort of the children.
They not only give the sunshine of their presence and spirit to the
children, but also fruits, melons, etc., and the big thirty pound bucket
of candy from the Shrine Club always comes along with ''Pop'' Bennett,
Brother Cleveland or some other good brother. Each year this Chapter
has presented one dollar to the personal account of every child, which
starts a saving fund as an inspiration for the child to add to it. The
Board of Trustees are much indebted to these representatives of Long
Beach.
December 19th. Jasmine Chapter No.145 of Azusa always visits us
the Sunday before Christmas. This is positively "Jasmine Day". This
year caught us just the day after we moved and in much disorder, and
our "Sunday clothes" not yet unpacked. We believe our visitors en·
joyed the situation all the more, and especially the fact that we had
moved so close to them, being now but half a dozen miles from their hall.
They left the usual big box of home made candy for each child and gav:e
us liberal Christmas greetings. The children responded with a program ..
December 23rd. The Masons of Covina and their families gave the
children a good House warming in their new temporary buildings. It
was an overflow of heart and soul. Nothing could convince the BoarcJ.
of Trustees more than this meeting that they had selected a truly Masonic
neighborhood where the children were among friends. The welcome
was most gratifying. We believe all reading this report would be
interested in their program.
