April 24th. East Gate Lodge No. 290 gave a "Home Evening" at
their hall which was largely attended by ladies. Four of our girls were
on this program and an address was given by a member of the Board.
May 13th. Al Malaikah Shrine, under the direction of ''Daddy
Silverwood", Potentate, secured special c11-rs and took the children to
the Shrine picnic at Eagle Rock Park. Every concession, games, merrygo-round, pictures, etc., was given them. The only thing short was time
to take them all in. They were generous in their prizes for races, etc.,
and our children received special prizes of unusual merit.
May 14th. Visit of Brother Leo Bruck, wife and friends. Brother
Bruck has won the children not only by his deep interest which he manifests so generously at times, but his music stands to them as a milestone
for them to reach, which he modestly tells them is easy to do. The ?hildren swarm around him at the Home and keep him playing at the piano
for hours. Brother Bruck is only a little older child himself, and puts a
spirit in the game when he is with them.
May 20th. Corner-stone laying. (See Brother Whicher 's account

with some of the leading performers of the country, and over three
hundred others participating. The expense of the camp, exclusive of
maintenance and supplies, is provided from the Christmas fund which is
sent in by many lodges every Christmas. If these thoughtful and generous lodges could visit this camp in a body and witness the round of real,
healthy childish joy, they would feel many times compensated for their
Christmas remembrance aside from the delight of Christmas time. The
camp is operated under self government. The children nominate and elect
their officers at a primary and general election, and the work is all done
by committees. Advancement on committees is made on a thorough merit
system, and the entertainment and disciplinary features excel many
organizations composed of older people.
Many favors from active and interested Masons have been received
and en,ioyed the past year. Some have inconvenienced themselves much
to be of service.
Brother Percy L. Nash, who first called our attention to our new
site, bas been of much assistance in arranging with all the utility companies, and gave us valuable counsel in our farm work. His pleasing
personality bas won the children and we count him one of our fast friends.
Our exceptional health record is largely due to the always timely and
willing attention of Dr. J. M. Dunsmoor, assisted by his wife, Dr. Nannie
Dunsmoor, and son, Dr. Robert Dunsmoor. Our reports have been strong
in commendation of Dr. Dunsmoor's work, which grows with our big
family each year.
A new and valuable friend of the children is Dr. C. Deichmiller of
Oriental Lodge, who has given much special attention to the children's
teeth. He bas examined every child's teeth and done much work for
them. The Doctor's only compensation is the gratitude of the children,
and appreciation of the Fraternity.
Miss Dorothy Lyndall continues faithfully to give our girls their
classic dancing, although our present quarters makes her work a little
difficult. Miss Lyndall 's work with the girls is much appreciated by all
friends of the Home, and particularly the girls benefited by her instruction.
Miss Theresa Costa with the string instruments, and Mrs. Lela
Buckham with the piano, have brought out splendid results, particularly
with the beginners.
Miss Leta Nash, a popular and gifted son~stress of Covina, daughter
of Brother P. L. Nash, has given the children training in chorus work
and bas added much to musical instructions of the Home.
Brother William Schneider, of Silver Trowel Lodge, extends favors
every month in the year with generous treats and gifts of clothing, etc.
At camp this year he brought out thirty-five sides of lambs and barbecued them for the children. He also brought his own dressings and a
big sack of rolls. The children photographed him for their records, but

The Report of the Committee on Endowment was presented, and consideration thereof was fixed for 11 o'clock
Thursday morning. Following is the Report:

Because of these needed improvements, and others which will arise,
it is absolutely essential that a large endowment fund be raised as early
as possible, in order that the tax upon the individual Mason and upon
our subordinate lodges be reduced at the earliest possible time. From
the figures following, you will note that progess has been made.

REPORT OF ENDOWMENT COMMITTEE, MASONIC
HOMES OF CALIFORNIA

Endowment Fund-July 31 1 1914:

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
We, members of your Endowment Committee, Masonic Homes of
California, appointed by the Grand Master at the close of the last Grand
Lodge, beg to report that this very important matter has received our
most thoughtful and careful consideration.
The results secured during the year, while eminently satisfactory,
have not been as great as we had hoped, having in view the splendid
object for which we are striving.

In a speech delivered by the Hon. Henry D. Estabrook, a short time
ago, on "Truth-Business and Political," he said among other things:

''Our Vice-President, Mr. Marshall, occasioned much ribald laughter
in some quarters because he said in one of his speeches that the right
to inherit was not an inherent or natural right, but was founded altogether on custom or statute, and therefore subject at all times to legislative regulations. There is nothing in this statement to laugh at. Mr.
Marshall uttered a truism, and I predict that as this truth becomes more
'generally recognized, we will witness a development of the principle of
the inheritance tax that will cause laughter out of the other corner of
the mouth. For the state has the power to say, and I am not sure that it
is not its duty to say to· every man: Have your fling-get all the fun you
can out of life-work. not only for your necessities, but for the joy of
working-gain what knowledge you can-gain what wealth you canspend your wealth as you please, or not at all-give it aw~~ to those ~ou
love or to those you hate-but know this: that your domm10n ends with
your life! All you can hold in your dead, cold hand is what you have
given away! In other words, by givin 'in presenti,' you may evade the
law without cheating it, for the law leaves you the alternative, Give or
surrender! I am not sure, I say, but what this would be best for the
state, for the man himself while living, and for all parties concerned
after he has ceased to live.''

94

PROCEEDINGS OF 'rHE

No greater truth ever was spoken than is contained in the excerpt
above, and the quotation is sent to our brethren with the hope that when
they are preparing their wills, such amounts as they feel they can give
will be bequeathed to the :\Iasonic Homes of California. Ask your
lawyer in preparing your will to provide for this bequest.
Some of our brethren, among them two residing at San Fernando,
Los Angeles County, have taken out life insurance policies in favor of
the Masonic Homes of California, and have forwarded these policies to
the Secretary of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes, with instructions
that they be notified when premiums are due.
Many of our members could take out such policies for reasonable
amounts, making the Masonic Homes of California the beneficiary, and
this without any very serious burden, financially. Such a plan would
ultimately result in materially increasing our Endowment Fund.
One of our very distinguished Masons, an Inspector of a Masonic
district, is arranging for what is to be known as "Endowment Day,"
one day specifically designated as that upon which every Mason shall
contribute what he feels able toward the Endowment Fund. Such gen·
eral publicity not only acquaints the individual Mason with what we
are trying to do, but gives enthusiastic interest in this splendid work.
Another excellent suggestion, made by one of the Masonic brothers
in Los Angeles, is that each Mason in our jurisdiction set aside ten
cents each week for one year, to be ~dded to the Endowment Fund. Such
a plan would involve no real sacrifice on the part of any one, and would
amount, in round figures, to a very greatly increased Fund, for we have
over 50,000 Masons in our jurisdiction, and the $260,000 which the
working out of such a plan would add would be of material assistance.
Some of our brethren also are sending us small cash donations, all
of which are very thankfully received.
While the work of the Endowment Committee has progressed very
satisfactorily, if all of our brethren could appreciate the great good
that would be accomplished by bringing this Fund to such a figure that
the income therefrom would pay for the maintenance of these splendid
Masonic charities, our Fraternity would be a much greater factor in
the world's welfare than is possible now.
·
Reflect upon the suggestions that have been offered, write us what
you think of them, and give us any other icleas which you believe would
help in the creation of an adequate Endowment Fund.
Fraternally yours
(Signed by the Committee)
At the suggestion of Brother George F. Rodden, Inspector of the
35th Masonic district, who had given the matter very careful thought,
it was decided to hold an annual endowment Day, until our Fund shall

reach an amount of sufficient size, the income from which will support
our Home.
Thanksgiving Day, November 30, 1916, was decided upon as En·
dowment Day for this year, and through the office of the Grand Secre·
tary form letters are being supplied to the master of each lodge, to be
mailed by him to every one of his members, advising them fully of
our purpose and urging their support. The letter is as follows:
ENDOWMENT DAY

For the
MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
THANKSGIVING DAY, NOVEMBER 30, 1916

Dear Sir and Brother:
Disregarding all other considerations, the Masonic jurisdiction of
California fulfills the purpose of its being, by the tender care and protection extended to its needy old at the Masonic Home at Decoto and
the dependent young at Covina.
But, glorious as the work is, and approved by the Most High as it
must be, it is accomplished only after the imposition of a per capita
tax upon the subordinate lodges which many of them find difficulty in
meeting, and which must result, in many cases, in financial compli·
cations.
Our own lodge, for instance, at the tax rate of $1.50 per member,
is called upon to remit annually for the maintenance of these Homes
approximately $ - - - - , which amount, added to the 90 cents per capita
for Grand Lodge dues, makes no inconsiderable sum.
Recognizing these facts, the Grand Lodge some years ago appointed
an Endowment Committee, with the purpose of raising an Endowment
Fund of $1,000,000, fr-0m the earnings of which the Homes could be
maintained, and as a result of which the subordinate lodges would be
relieved from all further taxation.
With the idea of aj!sisting the Endowment Committee so far as
possible, a plan was evolved by Brother George F. Rodden, Inspector of
the 35th Masonic district, which, submitted to the Grand Master, Chairman of the Endowment Committee, and many other wise and experienced
leaders, has met with hearty approval and support.
The plan simply contemplates the cooperative assistance of our
sixty thousand brethren. It provides that once each year the Grand
Master shall specify a day, to be known throughout the jurisdiction
as "Endowment Day", when it is expected that each Mason will con·
tribute toward the Fund whatsoever his means will permit.
It must be obvious that even so small a sum as one dollar from
each one of us added to the many contributions from other sources
will soon bring about the happy result.

Every lodge must do its part, and every Mason his share. Thanks·
giving Day, November 30, has been designated "Endowment Day'',
and I am convinced that your apprecin.tion of the tremendous i:m·
portance of this movement, together with your love ol' and pride in
the craft, will prompt a ready and generous response at that time.

The enthusiastic support of every member of this Grand Lodge is
needed for the success of Endowment Day, so that on next Thanksgiving
Day the Fund will be very materially increased. The plan is one which
should have the hearty approval and earnest cooperation of every brother
of our Grand Jurisdiction, for it is only in this way that Endowment
Day can be made a complete success.

'rhe Grand Lecturer then read his Annual Report, as

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER.
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Once more have we assembled in Annual Communication to give
an account of our duties performed during the year. We thank the
Great Giver of all good for the bountiful prosperity our beloved Fraternity bas enjoyed, as the increase of membership and the number of
new Lodges indicate.
I have visited all the Districts throughout the length and breadth
of the State, and have held schools of instruction, both day and night
sessions, which were well attended by the officers and members, all

99

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

anxious to perfect themselves in the ritual. I have also given much in·
struction in my office to Inspectors, officers and members, and I am at
all times ready and willing to instruct the brethren when requested. I
did not however, visit the two Lodges compos~ng the 11th Masonic Dis1
trict, located in Mono county, the officers of these Lodges being so scattered, except during the winter months, that it is impossible to get
them together for instruction.
The Lodges generally have had a marked increase in the number of
petitions, which would indieate the general prosperity existing throughout the jurisdiction from a financial standpoint. Many Lodges are building new Temples, which add in a great measure to the interest of the
officers and members.
I have received reports from an the Inspectors, and they report
the Lodges under their supervision to be generally prosperous, and conforming to the ritual and floor work as taught by the Grand Lodge;
many of these reports showing in detail the average attendance at stated
and special meetings as well as giving a complete financial statement of
the Lodges in their Districts. It is a pleasure to note in these reports
the great increase of candidates who are learning and in open Lodge
are passing examinations in the Candidate's lecture of the Third degree,
and receiving therefor a Grand Lodge diploma certifying to their proficiency. Several of the Inspectors suggest that this lecture by made
compulsory, many jurisdictions making this obligatory. Personally, I
do not think it necessary in this State, as the Lodges are so generally
taking this up now by merely suggesting to the candidates that they
learn the lecture, that the purpose thereof is accomplished without the
necess.ity of a Constitutional requirement.
It has been my pleasure to accompany the Most Worshipful Grand
Master on many of his visits. These visits are greatly appreciated by
the J,odges, and do much good, by stimulating new interest in the Lodges
and among the brethren, making us all better and better Masons for
having heard the beautiful sentiments expressed, and by coming in contact with such an exemplary character. The fraternity regrets as well
as he that his health would not permit of the visits to the Lodges which
he had anticipated.
I desire to express my thanks and appreciation to the Inspectors
and brethren for their courtesies and assistance, which has not only
made my duties pleasant, but the performance much more satisfactory
and beneficial. The ·efficient work of the Inspectors cannot be too highly
commended, for their untiring efforts in maintaining and effectually
raising the standard of the work throughout the jurisdiction, whicll cannot be gainsaid, has greatly improved.
I am greatly indebted to the Very Worshipful Grand Secretary
for his ever ready and willing counsel at all times, and also for many

~ourtesies extended to me in his office, whieh has been of material help
rn my work.
The Sehools of Instruction for the benefit of the Inspectors and
Brethren in attendance at the Grand Lodge were held October 8th and
9th. These schools were well attended by the Inspectors and brethren
all manifesting a keen desire to perfeet themselves in the ritual am~
fioorwork.
0~ Wednesday evening, October 11th, the thircl degree will be
exemplified by brethren of Redwood City Lodge No. 168, for Starr King
L~dge No: 344, on a candidate to be furnished by Presidio Lodge No.
3a4, of this City.
On Thursday e\'ening, October 12th, the officers of Occidental Lodge
No. 22 will exemplify the first degree. These Lodges will endeavor to
exemplify the work as near letter perfect as it is possible and I am
s1'.re the brethren will not only be pleased, but materially benefited by
witnessing the eonferring of these degrees.

BOARDS OF RELIEF.
The Grand Secretary presented the reports of the several
Boards of Relief, all which were referred to the Committee
on Finance.
To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:
We, hereby present the following report for the year beginning
August 24, 1915, and ending August 28, 1916, both dates inclusive:
The work during the past year has been nothing unusual, and the
amount expended for relief about the same as the average year, and
there is very little upon which we can comment. We have been given
assistance at all times by a great many Brethren of the Fraternity on
whom we called upon various matters, and have always found a ready
response and willingness to co-operate on all occasions.
We find the Fraternity at large very willing and anxious to do
something for the great Brotherhood, and believe that it is only from
lack of opportunity that a more active part is not taken by the membership of the Lodges.
We particularly desire to thank the following Brethren who havei
assisted us at all times with their professional skill and ability, and
their only compensation has been the thanks of those benefitted thereby.
It must be a source of great satisfaction to them to know the immense
amount of good that they have done during the year, from which came
no glory and no publicity. It is such work as these men are doing that
we may call true Masonic Charity. We refer to:
Doctors Winslow Anderson, H. I. Bloch, J. C. Egeberg, D. E. F.
Easton, George C. H. Franklin, Otto Freyermuth, A. S. Green, William
P. Read, Jacob Schwartz, George A. Wood, Wilhelm Waldeyer, and
A. W. L. Zillmer.
We want to call the attention of the Masters of the various
Lodges to the fact that the membership should be instructed in matters
pertaining to the actual management and work of the Lodge. The
amount of ignorance on this subject leads to a great many misunderstandings by the public in general, and by families of deceased Brethren. A little instruction will make better Masons and better men.

REPORT OF THE MASONIC EMPLOYMENT BUREAU
OF SAN FRANCISCO.
The Officers of the Masonic Employment Bureau hereby present the
annual report of their labors for the year ending August 31, 1916, for
your kind consideration and perusal.
We desire to express a deep sense of gratitude to the Members of
the Fraternity who have so ably assisted us during the year to obtain
employment for a great many worthy Masons and their families, thereby
relieving Lodges of the expenditure of unnecessary relief, and allowing
them to retain their self respect rather than become objects of Charity.
Although the Bureau has been hampered somewhat in its work by
the lamentable illness of our Secretary, Wm. H. Mitchell, who has so
ably fulfilled the duties of Secretary until this summer when he was
stricken with paralysis, and it became necessary to fill the office temporarily until such a time that he has recovered, and we are pleased to
be able to report that according to all indications this desirable end
will not be far distant.
Under these conditions, we thing the work accomplished is phenomenal, and we again wish to commend the good Brethren who keep us in
mind, ,and who make this success possible, and say to the ''KEEP UP
THE GOOD WORK".
Fraternally yours,
ARTHUR JOEL,

President.

J. W. FELT,

Secretary pro tern.

MASONIC BOARD OF RELIEF OF LOS ANGELES.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The Masonic Board of Relief of the City of Los Angeles, herewith
presents the following report of its labors from September 1, 1915, to
August 31, 1916.
The Masonic Board of Relief is composed of the Masters (ex-officio)
of the 26 Blue Lodges of this city and two members appointed by him,
together with the Past Grand Masters residing within the City of Los
Angeles, the Inspectors of the several Masonic Districts of Los Angeles
City, one repressntative from each of the several Royal Arch Chapters,
the Council, the Commanderies, the Scottish Rite bodies and the Shrine,
the manager of the Masonic Employment Bureau, and one Past Worthy
Matron of the Order of the Eastern Star.
The conditions for the year 1915-16 are very much as they have
been during the last two years, only more intensified by the prevailing
conditions existing throughout the civilized world.
The cost of living has increased in proportion to the depreciation
of business. The number of unemployed Masons bas also increased, and
in desperation these Brothers have really become ''rovers' '-going from
place to place seeking employment. These men ask for only $2.50 to
$5.00, which seems too small an amount to ask a sister jurisdiction for
reimbursement, and also it is too small an amount to refuse to contribute
when the appeal seems meritorious.
We are sorry to note an increased number of wife-deserters and
abandonment of children. These wives and children must be aided,-at
least temporarily. This may not be in conformity with the Strict Letter
of the Masonic Law, but we believe it is carrying out the broad principle
of Masonic Charity.
INVALIDS.

Brethren:
Please observe the following paragraph:
This is no place for a really sick man unless he has plenty of means
and is willing to part with his money. He can't live on climate alone,

APPLICATIONS CANCELLED.

Nineteen applications cancelled during the year for good and sufficient reasons.
Six applications cancelled for placing their various labor unions before Masonry and refusing good paying positions.
Six applications cancelled for refusing good paying positions because they were out of the city.
Three applications cancelled for drunkenness.
Four applications cancelled for failing to report for duty after positions were secured.

goes without saying, but the policy of the Board is that it is far more
charitable to assist the guilty than to permit any worthy brother to
suffer. The Board, in its communications with Lodges in some jurisdictions, finds that they have eliminated the words "to aid and assist"
from their rituals, and reply that ''our dues are only one or two dollars
a year and we have no funds.''
We have established an Employment Bureau, to which the Board
contributes $25 a month, and many positions have been secured through
the agency of the Bureau for members of the fraternity, their widows,
daughters and sons. Others eontributing to the Bureau are the Chapter
of Royal Arch Masons, the Commandery1 Consistory, and Chapters of
the Eastern Star. Brother Charles H. Wixson is in charge, and he may
be found at Masonic club rooms every day from 9 to 12.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS.
Brother Hugh J. Owen, Chairman of the Committee on
Accounts, reported as follows:
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Accounts beg to report that since the last Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge it has regularly met on the
last Saturday in each and every month in the Grand Secretary's office,
examined and audited all bills presented throughout the year, none
having been paid without the approval of .the committee; your committee being at all times most agreeably assisted by our genial, most efficient
and worthy Grand Secretary and his aole Assistant.

AMENDMENTS TO CONSTITUTION.
A proposed amendment to Section 210 of the Constitution
was presented by Brother Leo Bruck, as follows:
Resolved, That Section 210 of the Constitution be amended by adding
after the words "a stated meeting next preceding," the following:''and provided further, that whenever a trial has been transferred to a
Lodge other than the one of which the brother is a member, and he is
found guilty and sentenced, he must apply for restoration to the Lodge
of which he was a member at the time of his suspension''; thus making
the whole section and amendment to read as follows:
Sec. 210. All sentences of suspension shall be for an indefinite
period; and a Lodge may, at any stated meeting, by the votes of twothirds of the members present, annul any sentence of suspension pronounced by itself, and restor~ the Mason thus suspended to all his
Masonic rights and privileges; provided, that notice of a resolution for
such restoration shall have been given at the stated meeting next preceding; and provided further, that whenever a trial has been transferred
to a Lodge other than the one of which the brother is a member, and
he is found guilty and sentenced, he must apply for restoration to the
Lodge of which he was a member at the time of his suspension. And,
in case of such restomtion, the Secretary shall at once notify the restored
party and the Grand Secretary thereof.

REPORT OF TE.J!IPLE ASSOCIATION.

DISBURSEMENTS.

Brother William P. Filmer presented the ·report of the
Directors of the Masonic Temple Association, as follows:
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
In accordance with its usual custom, the Board of Directors of the
Masonic Temple Association of California presents herewith its annual
financial statement for the fiscal year ending August 31st, 1916. In
doing so we are pleased to report an encouraging eondition, inasmuch
as our income has been increased some $2000.00 over that of last year,
by additional rentals of halls to Masonic bodies, and from the tenancy
of one of the stores on the ground floor.
The statement also shows a marked decrease in the interest charge,
due to the payment of nearly $39,000.00 on the indebtedness.
A further encouraging feature is that while the annual loss for
the fiscal year of 1915 was $7 ,256.69 that of 1916 was $5,344.04, a difference of $1,912.65.
Considering the location of the Temple, which now, and perhaps
for eeveral years to come, is distant from the business center of San
Francisco, the Board of Directors regard the financial showing as very
ss.tisfactory; in fact, were it not for the large annual interest charge,
it would be possible for the Association to pay a small dividend.
This interest charge, which causes our annual deficit, is the chief
reason why there is still need of further assistance from the Grand
Lodge.
Our reports for the years 1914 and 1915 set forth clearly our dependence upon the Grand Lodge to further assist in financing the
Temple, and both reports refer at length to the several resolutions
adopted by the Grand Lodge from time to time, pledging its assistance
to the extent of its financial ability.
We are therefore again obliged to repeat our request for action by
the Grand Lodge tending to permanently finance the Temple, to the
end that the Grand Lodge subscribe and pay for stoek to the amount
of $25,000.00 at this communication, and $25,000.00 at each annual
communication thereafter until the Temple shall be self-sustaining.

WHEN IS A PE'rITION RECEIVED 1
Brother H. E. Verble, Master of Traver Lodge No. 294,
presented the following:
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
I would like to call attention to the following occurrence which is
not covered in our Constitution or By·Laws:
A petition for degrees was filed with the Secretary, and read at a
stated meeting. As soon as the Secretary had finished reading said petition, a brother arose and objected to the petition being received.
What decision should the Master have madei Does this applicant
stanQ the same as one objected by a committee or rejected at the ballot
box~ How long a time should elapse before his filing another petition,
and should said objections have been reported to the Grand Lodge'
There is some question as to whether or not the brother had· a
right to file objections at this time. On this occasion the Master merely
stated that the petition would not be received, and instructed the Secreary to return the fee to the applicant. I have also been informed that
there is a parallel case to this, only it being an application for membership.
Further: When is the petition received1 When placed in the hands
of the Secretary, or after being read in Lodge~
I think some decision should be made covering these various questions, so that in future like occurrences may be taken care of.

Referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.

'l'he Grand Secretary presented, the report of the Committee on Masonic Education, as follows:
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic Education, continued from last year
to formulate plans for reSBarch aml study, beg to report as follows:
We feel it to be not only a duty but a pleasure to <lo our full part
in furthering the cause whieh should and will he of more and more im·
portance as the years roll by, notwithstanding the action of Grand Lodge
last year in refusing to adopt our then proposed plan of lectures.
We are especially anxious that the Grand Lodge should give its
active and unqualified support to the cause of Masonic Education. Last
year, as indicated above, the essential portions of our report and recom·
mendations were referred to the Finance Committee and not reportetl
back, thus leaving the balance of little effect.
If ever there was a time in the history of our fraternity when men
need enlightenment and understanding that time is now. They neell
the understanding which sball help them to umlerstanll themselves. They
need the understanding which shall deepen their sympathies for their
fellows. They need the understanding which shall broaden their outlook
in life. They need the understanding which shall make them more kind
and tolerant of all men, particularly of those they call their brethren.
The trend of events the past year or so will verify all this.
In our Masonic Lodge rooms the great principles of human brotlier·
hood should be so sanely voiced that our members will see in them real
beauty and understand that they can endure only when harmony prevails.

The basic principles for which we stand should be so earnestly aml
eloquently impressed both on our candidates and our members that all
will be aroused by a mighty inspiration.
In our work, we should depend less oh formalism and more on
enlightenment. We owe more to the camliclates who knock at our doors
than we sometimes give them after they have crossed the portals. Mere
ritualism alone will not suffice--it is appealing so far as it goes-bnt
it does not go far enough; not every man is prepared to grasp its
hidden meaning.
At the very outset of his ).fasonic career, the candidate sbouhl be
thrilled with the 'Vital principles and purposes or the l''raternity-a11ll
tbese should be made known to him as clearly as pure English can define
them. Nor should that interest be allowed to wane and become inactive
through any fault of ours.
We have among our members many men of ability who can ahl
materially in accomplishing this work. How shall we go about iU J,et

us only reiterate what we asked for last year, and hope this time we will
receive the hearty co-operation of the Grand Lodge.
We, therefore, sum up this report by submitting the following points
for eonsi<leration, being the same four paragraphs that appeared in our
report last year, and as found on page 508 of the printed proceedings
of 1915, as follows:

First, that a committee on Masonic Education consisting of three
members be appointed by the M.". W.". Grand Master to serve for the
ensuing year. That it shall be the duty of this committee to exercise
a helpful influenee toward all Lodges who desire their counsel and advice.
That this committee shall foster and encourage throughout this jurisdiction the study and research of Masonic tradition, history, literature, law,
philosophy and dominant purposes of this institution.
Second, that a series of lectures to he read in our Lodges at stated
intervals, shall be prepared under the direction of such Committee. Such
lectures to be submitted to the M. ·. W. ·. Grand Master for his approval,
and afterward printed. One lecture to be mailed each month to e\•ery
Lodge in this jurisdiction, but only on request.
Third, that a series of three lectures be prepared under the direction
of the Committee on Masonic Education, along exoteric lines, appropriate
respectively to the E. A., F. C. and M. M. degrees. Sueh lectures to be
first approved by the M.". W:. Grand Master and afterward printed.
These lectures to be placed in the candidate's hands after he has received
each degree. The lectures to be sold to the Lodges desiring them at cost.

The number of members from outside jurisdictions who have affil·
iated with us considerably exceeds the number who have withdrawn. It
would seem, however, that with proper attention given to the nonaffiliated members in our midst, this proportion should be considerably
increased.
The suspension for non-payment of dues should receive attentiQn.
It is to be noted, as a general rule, that the Lodges which are remiss in
making reports have the largest proportionate number of suspensions.
. This leads to the conclusion that if proper attention were paid to the
delinquents the number could be materially reduced. We believe if the
Masters and Secretaries of the various Lodges will give this matter
proper attention this can be accomplished. We think continual effort
should be made by all Lodges toward this end. It would seem that as
much time and effort should be given to maintaining a member on the
rolls in good standing after he is once there as is given to putting him
there in the first place.
Respectfully submitted,
J. D. ABRAMS,
C. D. BARNETT,
GEO. W. LEMOIN,
ARTHUR S. CRITES,

Your Committee notes with great satisfaction that generally speaking
there has been a material improvement in the manner in which trials
have been conducted, and in the form in which the transcripts have been
prepared.
In this connection special mention should be made of the record
of the trial commission in Record No. 198, from Silver Gate Lodge No.
296. The transcript is not only a model for a record of proceedings be·
cause of the care and exactness with whieh it has been prepared in strict
compliance with the requirements of the constitution (with one exception
to be hereafter noted), but it is in itself, of its kind, a work of art.
The typing is extraordinarily clear and distinct, with no erasures or inter·
lineations, and it appears as a bound book in a handsome leather cover,
lettered in gold. The testimony was reported and the transcript prepared
by Brother Norton Langford; and it is to be especially noted that
Brother Langford made no charge whatever for his services.
The one departure from a strict compliance with the requirements
of the Constitution, to which we have referred (and to which no refer·
ence would ·be made except for the fact that we have declared the record
to be a model), consists in having the transcript of testimony constituting
the reeord signed by the witnesses. The transcript transmitted to the
Grand Secretary is presumed to be merely a copy of the original which
is filed in the archives of the Lodge. It is the original which should be
signed by the witnesses, and not the copy transmitted to the Grand
Lodge. The only originals in that transcript should be the certificates
required by the Constitution. The other practice, however, has become
so common that in recent years it has not been questioned.
We offer the following resolution:

REPORTS OF COMl\IIITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE.
Past Grand Master Angellotti, Chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports:
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration that
portion of the Address of the Most Worshipful Grand Master which
states the decisions on questions of Masoanic law rendered by him
during the year.
Decisions numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16, 18 and
20 are so clearlv in accord both with the letter and the spirit of our
written law and the decisions made by this Grand Lodge thereunder,
that no comment on our part is necessary. We recommend that all of
the decisions specified be affirmed by this Grand Lodge.
As to decision No. 5, we are of the opinion that there is nothing in
our law that prohibits the conferring by the same Lodge of more than
five degrees in any period of twenty-four hours. There is nothing in
the law as written to prohibit the holding of more than one called
meeting within the period of twenty·four hours, that matter bein~ left
to the discretion of the Master, and the only limitation being as to
the character of the business that may be transacted at such a meeting.
Section 115 simply prohibits the conferring of degrees on more than
five candidates at any one meeting, the conferring of more than one
degree on any one candidate at any one meeting, and the conferring of
degrees on more than one candidate at a time. We are not at liberty
to add by decision to the prohibition thus clearly expressed, and if any
change in this respect is desired it must be accomplished by legislation.
We recommend that the decision be not approved.

Adopted.
Decision No. 12 is in accord with the ruling Grand Master Murphey
in 1914, which ruling was approved by the Grand Lodge. (Sec. 135p.)
We recommend that the decision be approved.

Adopted.

153

Decision No. 14 is in strict accord with our law. The Grand Master
suggests that perhaps the law should be amended to meet such a situ·
ation as was presented in the case brought before him and discussed
in his decision. Vv e are noting this decision simply to suggest that in
the year 1912 our Constitution was amended so as to provide for a
modification in special cases of the general rule as to territorial juris·
diction of Lodges, such modification to be made by the Grand Lodge.
The amendment is section 92A of the Constitution.
We recommend that the decision of the Grand Master be approved.

Adopted.
As to Decision No. 17, we must assume in favor of the ruling of the
Grand Master that the p~oposed candidate, by reason of his physical
defect 1 was not able to conform substantially to the requirements of
the various degrees, and, so assuming, the decision must be held to have
been correct. The test in all cases is whether the candidate is thus
able to substantially conform. It would seem that Lodges should be
able to apply this simple test without the necessity of advice or ruling
on the part of the Grand Master.
We recommend that the decision of the Grand Master be approved.

Adopted.
At the last communication of the Grand Lodge it was proposed to
amend our Constitution by making it provide "that the daughter of a
Master Mason, in good standing, under the age of twenty-one years, is
entitled to relief as a matter of right; that the daughter of a Master
Mason who has attained the age of twenty-one years, shall not as a
matter of right be entitled to aid, but may receive aid at the discretion
of the dispensing body.''
If any such amendment is desired it should be added to section
163 of the Constitution, which now provides ''every Master Mason in
good standing, his widow and orphans, when in distress, has and have
the right to ask for and receive relief,'' etc.
The word ''orphan'' as used in this section has always been construed to include a daughter, whatever her age, and regardless of
whether she has been married. If in distress, such a person has always
been considered as entitled to Masonic aid.
We are of the opinion that our law in this regard shonld not be
changed, and especially should not be changed so as to exclude the
daughter of a Master Mason simply and solely by reason of the fact that
she has attained the age of twenty-one years.
We recommend that the proposed amendment be not adopted.

Report concurred in.

Your Committee on Jurisprudence make the following report as to
certain matters submitted to them for consideration:

3. It is proposed to amend the Constitution by authorizing subordinate Lodges to adopt by-laws providing that members who have belonged to the Lodge for a period of not less than twenty-five years and
have arrived at the age of sixty-five years or more, shall thereafter be
exempt from the payment of any Lodge dues.

1. A proposed resolution has been introduced, the object of which
is to exempt Lassen Lodge No. 149, at Susanville, from the general rules
as to territory over which it shall have jurisdiction, by giving it jurisdiction over certain specified territory not within its jurisdiction under
such general rules. The change proposed would affect the jurisdiction
of Janesville Lodge No. 232,
No recommendation of the Grand Master has been made in such
matter. No notice of this application or resolution has been given to
Janesville Lodge. Our law on this matter (section 92A, Constitution),
expressly provides that no such resolution shall be adopted except upon
the recommendation of the Grand Master, and further, that notice of
application for any such resolution with a precise statement of the
boundaries of the proposed territory shall be given by the applicant
Lodge at least thirty days prior to the commencement of the Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge at which the same is to be made,
to each Lodge whose jurisdiction will be affected by the proposed resolution.
We recommend that the proposed resolution be not adopted.

Recommendation adopted.
2. It is proposed to amend section 95 of the Constitution which,
among other things, provides that no lodge shall receive an application
for the degrees from a person unless he shall have been a resident
"within the jurisdiction of the lodge ( i. e., nearer thereto than to any
other lodge existing under this Grand Lodge) during six months next
preceding the date of his application'', by adding thereto a proviso
as follows: ''Provided, that the petition of an applicant for degrees
may be presented to the nearest Lodge, or, :vhen the nearest Lodge is
not in the county in which the applicant resides, then to the nearest
Lodge in that county.''
We can see no good object in thus changing the general rule in
regard to jurisdiction of Lodges. One of the effects of this particular
change would be to make the question of jurisdiction dependent to some
extent on the option of the applicant for the degrees. We believe that
if in any particular case the circumstances are so exceptional as to make
it desirable that special rules of jurisdiction should be made for a
particular Lodge, resort should be had to the provisions of section 92A
of the Constitution under which this Grand Lodge, with the approval of
the Grand Master, may prescribe such rules.
We recommend that the proposed amendment be not adopted.

Recommendation adopted.

Similar propositions have been made before, and it has uniformly
been thought that any such change in our law was undesirable. The
well-settled policy of this Grand Lodge is that all members of the fraternity who are able to discharge the obligation resting upon them as
Masons of contributing their share in the great work of the fraternity
should continue to do so, regardless of any question of age. It is
doubtless true that there are few, if any, who are thus able to contribute
who desire to shirk such an obligation. We see no good reason for any
change in our policy in this regard and recommend that the proposed
amendment be not adopted.

Recommendation adopted.
4. Certain questions have been submitted to the Grand Lodge and
referred to this Committee as to the effect of an objection made by a
member to a petition for degrees when such petition was read at a stated
meeting, the objection to the petition being received. It appears from
the statement made in connection with these questions, that the Master
ruled that in view of such ob;jection the petition would not be received,
and instructed the Secretary to return the fee to the applicant.
The various questions asked in connection with this matter may be
sufficiently answered by stating that the objection to the petition being
received thus made by a member was under our law ineffectual for any
purpose. This matter is practically covered by a decision made in 1915,
which is reported as foilows: "When objection is made before a ballot,
if the report of the investigating committee is favorable, a ballot must
be had. If the candidate is elected, ob;jection may then be made. An
objection before ballot is not provided for in our Constitution: the
remec1y by a black ball being considered ample to prevent the election
of unworthy petitioners." (lllc)
In the case at bar the Master should have disregarded the objection,
and, at least unless by a majority vote the lodge declined to receive
the application, should have appointed the usual committee on investigation.
The question is further asked ''when is such a petition received f ''

We are satisfied that it cannot be helc1 to have been received by a
Lodge until it is read to the Lodge at a stated meeting. In this connection, however, it is proper to note that the prohibition as to subse-

156

157

GRAND LODGE OF CALJFOR::\'IA

quent withdrawal of such an application is applicable only after the
same has been referred to a committee.
We recommend that these answers be approved by the Grand Lodge.

Th'e Grand Master in his Acldress has submitted certain correspondence between the Grand Lecturer and the Inspector of the 64th Maf!onic
District at Honolulu relative to a portion of the third degree work as
given by Oceanic Lodge No. 371, at Honolulu. It appears that a certain
portion of that work, namely, the so-called ''French'' work in the
second section, differs in certain respects from our regular ritual. This
particular work, as we understand it, has been followed in that Lodge
ever since its institution, its original charter having been granted over
sixty-five years ago. The departures from our prescribed ritualistic
work, as we understand the matter, in no wise affect the substantial
principles and teachings sought to be inculcated by our ritual. They are
of the same character as the departures that have at all times been tacitly
allowed to our French-speaking lodges in· San Francisco and Los Angeles.
At the same time we cannot question the views of the Grand Master
that these departures are violations .of section 121 of our Constitution.
However, we cannot feel that it is the dfaposition of the Grand Lodge
to actually prohibit the uniform practice in these Lodges, a practice
which has been acquiesced in and practically approved during the whole
history of this Grand Lodge. We do think, however, that if the practice
is to continue it should not be in violation of our written law. This
fraternity cannot witl1 decency or dignity occupy such a position.
We would therefore recommend that section 121 of the Constitution
be amended by adding thereto a proviso reading as follows.
"Provided, however, anything in tl1is section to the contrary notwithstanding, that the Lodges in this jurisdiction whose long established
ritualistic work is in part a departure from the uniform ritual of this
jurisdiction, may continue to perform such work as the same is now being
performed in so far as the same may not be disapproved by the Grand
Master and the Grand Lecturer.''

Section 121 of the Constitution was thereupon amended
as above by unanimous vote.

Your Committee to whom was referred. the amendment to section
192 of the Constitution, proposed by Brother Ben Levi, have had the
same under consideration and respectfully report as follows:
Brother Levi proposed to amend section 192 by inserting in said
section after the word "duty" in line 6, page 152, the following:
"The Master of the Lodge of which such Mason may be a member,
to forthwith obtain a certified copy of such final judgment of conviction,
and said judgment shall be presented to said Lodge and read into the
record thereof at its next stated meeting, and it shall thereupon be
the duty of the Master of said Lodge to declare such Mason forthwith
expelled.''
We deem this proposed legislation entirely too radical. It would
be inequitable and in a great many cases absolutely unjust to assess the
penalty of expulsion in every case of conviction involving moral turpi·
tude. The fact of conviction in a State or Federal Court should not be
sufficiently conclusive evidence of guilt as to absolutely preclude the
possibility of the facts and circumstances in connection with the offenses
being presented to a Masonic tribunal in order that a just punishment
may be inflicted.
The Grand Lodge placed itself on record last year (proceedings of
1915, page 482) as to its conception of the proper procedure in cases of
this character, and we do not feel disposed to recommend any deviation
therefrom.
It said, "Upon the trial of that charge the record of the conviction
in the State Court, if duly authenticated, may be properly introduced
as prima facie evidence of the proof of the charge. Then if the accused
desires to introduce evidence in his own behalf he may do so, notwithstanding the fact that he has been convicted in the State Gourt. The
Commission is then called upon to decide whether or not, in the judgment
of the Commissioners, the accused is guilty of the offense charged. If
no testimonv at all is introduced on behalf of the accused the Commis·
sion of cou;se has no discretion in the matter and must find a verdict of
'guilty. ' "

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

158

159

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

This we think is a rational, logical and satisfactory manner of
procedure in this character of cases. We therefore recommend that the
amendment be not adopted.

The report was adopted and the proposed amendment
was lost.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration Decision No. 19 contained in the Grand ::\faster 's Address, and beg to report
thereon as follows:
The Grand Master decided that it was not proper to hold Masonic
services over the ashes of a brother whose body had been cremated. We
cannot agree with the broad general statement contained in the decision;
but on the contrary, we are of the opinion that when a Masonic funeral
is requested, it is eminently fit and proper to pay respect to the memory
of a departed brother, in whatever form his mortal remains may be
presented for the performance of the ceremony.
We therefore recommend that this decision be not approved.

The report was adopted and Decision No. 19 was disapproved.

Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom was referred a resolution presented by Brother Bruck of the San Prancisco Board of Relief,
providing for the amendment of Section 210 of the Constitution, would
fraternally report that the purpose of the proposed amendment is to
provide that a suspended Mason tried by a Lodge other than his own,
might be restored to membership through the vote of his own Lodge.
Section 210 now provides that a suspended Mason may be restored
only by the Lodge pronouncing sentence of suspension. If that Lo(lge
refuses, application may then be' made to the Grand Lodge.
It is to be observed, however, that the latter body restores to membership at large, but that restoration by the trial Lodge, restores to the

Lodge of former membership. It can easily be seen :hat serious objection to such restoration might exist in the last ment10ned Lodge; and
that, under our law as at present, the peace and harmony of t?e f~­
ternity might easily be strained if a Lodge were thus forced agarnst its
will perhaps, by the action of another Lodge, to receive an unwelcome
member into its own ranks.
On the other hand, we think that ordinarily the trial Lodge, presumably impartial and ,possessed of all the facts, i~ best fit:ed to p~ss
upon the question of restoration. An error upon its part rn refusmg
restoration can be corrected by an application to the Grand Lodge. An
error in restoring a suspended Mason, due to partiality or ignora~ce of
the facts, could not be corrected, and might subject the fratermty to
conshlerable criticism.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That Section 210 of the Constitution be and the same
is hereby amended by adding thereto, at the end of the first sentence the
following: And provided, further, that if the Mason suspended was not
a member of the Lodge adjudging suspension, the application for restora·
tion shall be refused unless the consent of the Lodge in which member. ship was held, if it be in this jurisdiction, is given. The request for
such consent shall lie over at least one stated meeting."

Report adopted, and Section 210 was amended by unanimous vote.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom was referrerl the three
proposed amendments to the Constitution presented by Brothers Dunsmoor, Test and Burke in behalf of the Southern California Past Masters
Association, would fraternally report that the first deals with section
165 of the Constitution and aims to relieve the fraternity in California
of the burden of taking care of Masons demitted from other jurisdictions who, out of standing in their own ;jurisdietions, place and keep
themselves in standing here by the simple device of applying for mem·
bership every six months.
Under our decisions, promulgated many years ago, a non-affiliate
living in this ,iurisdiction, though unable to join any Lodge herein, can
keep himself in standing by making application for membership at least
every six months and accompanying such application with six months
dues.
Your Committee is fairly of the opinion that good standing in this
State should not be based upon such an unsubstantial foundation. They
are equally of the opinion, however, that any legislation of this Grand
Lodge aimed to curtail or abrogate the privilege herein above referred

160

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

to should be limited to those not in good standing upon their entry into,
or' assumption of residence in, California. True Masonic courtesy to
brethren from foreign jurisdictions compels us, in our judgment, to give
full Masonic recognition to those in good standing in such foreign
jurisdictions if they conform to our laws while residing here. We believe
the law should be amended, therefore, so that those coming to California
in good standing in their own jurisdictions, or regaining such good
standing after their arrival here, should be entitled to full Masonic
consideration.
We, therefore, recommend. the adoption of the following resolution:
Resolved, that section 165 of the· Co~stitution be and the same is
hereby amended by adding at the end thereof the following:
''Provided. further, that a Mason demitted from another jurisdiction who is not ,in good standing therein at the time he enters, or becomes
a resident of this jurisdiction, shall in no case be entitled to any Masonic
rights or privileges unless and until he shall be elected a member of some
Lodge in this jurisdiction, or shall be restored to membership by the
jurisdiction from which he holds his demit.''

The recommendation was adopted, and Section 165 of the
Constitution was amended by unanimous vote.
The second proposal coming from the Southern California Past
Masters Association is intended to relieve subordinate Lodges from the
payment of any per capita tax to the Grand Lodge upon members
whose dues may have been remitted.
With the principle of this purpose we are in full sympathy. Lodges
ought always to remit the dues of their members who are unable to pay
them, and no restraint upon this commendable act of Masonic charity
should be imposed by the Grand Lodge by requiring per capita contributions as for the member whose dues have been thus remitted. Our chief
difficulty, however, has been to devise a plan of procedure calculated to
effect the purpose in mind and yet affording sufficient protection to the
financial affairs of the Grand Lodge.
In this spirit we submit the following resolution and recommend. its
adoption:
Resolved, That section 41 of the Constitution be and the same hereby
is amended by adding at the end thereof the following:
''Provided, nevertheless, that no contribution of any sort, in the
nature of a per capita tax, shall be payable by a Lodge upon any
Mason whose dues at the stated meeting in ,July of the calendar
year in which such tax would otherwise be payable, shall have been
remitted for the next preceding twelve months period, because of the
inability of such Mason to pay such dues. Each subordinate Lodge's
annual report, in addition to any other matters required, shall contain a

161

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

list of the names of Masons whose dues have been remitted, together
with the cause of such remission, as to whom non-payment of per capita
tax contribution is to be had.''

The recommendation was adopted, and section 41 of the
Constitution was amended by unanimous vote.
The third deals with a proposal to amend the Constitution by adding
a new section thereto, to the effect that any Entered Apprentice or
Fellow Craft who fails, without good cause, for one year, to present
himself for the remaining degrees shall, after notice, be stricken from
the roll of members and a waiver of jurisdiction be given to him. Under
the law an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft who fails to present
himself for the remaining degrees possesses but one right, and that of
a very unsubstantial nature: He may visit his own Lodge when it is
open in the degree in which he may have been advanced.
The only purpose of the proposed amendment is to relieve the Secretaries of Lodges from carrying these Entered Apprentices or Fellow
Crafts upon their rolls and, since the discontinuance of the publication
of the Roster in Grand Lodge Proeeedings, we are constrained to believe
that this purpose is of but negligible import. Some record, obviously,
should be kept of the fact of the qualified membership attaching to
Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts, and we believe that no permanent
and substantial good can be accomplished by the adoption of the amendment proposed.
We, therefore, recommend that this proposal be not adopted.

Your Committee on Appeals and Grievances, to whom was referred
trial record No. 189, Delano Lodge No. 309, reports as follows:
In this case the accused was charged with unmasonic conduct in
that on a certain day he entered into an agreement to steal and <leliver
to a party named, a certain number of cattle, and that said accused did
steal and deliver a certain number of cattle in accordance with said agreement.

•

This is an appeal by the accuser from a verdict of acquittal. The
accused was brought to trial on a charge of unmasonic conduct preferred,
if not at the direction, at least upon the suggestion, of the Grand
Master. The conduct complained of consisted in the accused having
prepared and caused to be sent by mail to every member of his Lodge
a circular letter seriously reflecting upon the Master of the Lodge and
imputing to him and to the Secretary conduct for which, if guilty, they
should be brought to trial before a Masonic tribunal. In that letter the
writer gave the details of a Masonic trial in which he had been the
accuser and with the result of which he was not satisfied, arnl clearly
intimated, if he did not indeed directly charge, that a notice of appeal
which had been filed by him in the case referred to bad been suppressed
by the Master; and that a review by the Committee on Appeals and
Grievances of the proceedings of that trial had thereby been prevented.
The fact that such a letter had been written was called to the
attention of the Grand Master, who caused an investigation to be made;
and who thereafter rendered his opinion to the effect that even though

166

167

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRA.ND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the ,writer believed that he had cause for eomplaint, the method adopted
by him was illegal and unmasonie, and eould result only in evil.
The aeeused having elaimed that he eould not obtain a fair trial in
his own Lodge, and the Master of that Lodge (the sueeessor of the
Master referred to in the circular), while disputing that claim, having
requesteu that the case should be transferred to some other Lodge, the
aceused was brought to trial in a Louge designated by the Grand
Master.
The case was apparently trieu by the Commissioners upon the theory,
advanceu by the accused and disputed by the accuser, that if the Com·
missioners should find that the accused had given a notice of appeal
whieh had been suppressed by the Master (and which the Master denied),
that then they could not find him guilty of unmasonie conduct, because
he would then have been justified in sending out the letter eomplained of.
That theory, of course, as was indicated by the Grand Master, is
absolutely untenable and would be subversive of the basic principles upon
which is established the government of a Masonic Lodge.
If it were within the province of the members of a Lodge to review
the acts of their Master, the accused might perhaps be heard to say that
his sole purpose was to seek from the members a remedy for a wrong
suffered at the hands of the Master; but the accused, a lawyer and a
Mason of more than ordinary intelligence, as is apparent from the manner
in which he conducted the case, must certainly have known that no action
the members might take as a result of that letter could result in the
reversal by the Lodge of the action of the Master; and that the only
possible effect would be to disturb the peace and harmony of the
Lodge.
As stated by Mackey (Mackey 's jurisprudence, page 240), "there
is no principle of Masonic jurisprudence more familiar to the craft than
that which prohibits an appeal from the decision of a ]\faster to the
Lodge. It is of course true that the power of the Master is thereby to
a great extent rendered despotic in his Lodge; but on the other hand,
by the wise provisions of the same law, this despotism is restrained by
the most salutary checks.. The Master himself is bound by the most
solemn obligations to the faithful discharge of his duties, and the impar·
tial administration of justice and equity; and as a still further safeguard
the Grand Lodge as the Appellate Court of the jurisdiction is ever ready
to' listen to appeals, to redress grievances1 to correct the errors of an
ignorant Master, and to punish the unjust decisions of iniquitous ones."
There would therefore appear to be absolutely no justification for
the writing of such a letter; and the question of the truth or falsity of
the statements therein contained, and the motive which prompted the
action of the accused, ·were material only insofar as they might perhaps

have properly influenced the judgment of the Commissioners in fixing the
punishment.
While we have no doubt that the accused in this case was guilty
of unmasonic conduct in adopting the course he pursued, and should be
by this Grand Lodge held amenable therefor, we c'an not escape the con·
viction that we will not have fully performed our duty with merely thus
disposing of this particular proceeding without a further consideration
of the facts disclosed by the record.
From the fact that a verdict of acquittal was rendered, ..we must
assume that the Commissioners must hia.ve been of the opinion that a
notice of appeal had been filed in the case referred to; and in view of
the fact that this Grand Lodge may, in its discretion, without remanding
the case for retrial, adjudge the accused guilty of unmasonic conduct
and fix the punishment, it is only fair to him to say that there was
testimony introduced upon which might have been predicated a finding
that a notice of appeal had been given. Not only, however, was that
not an issue, but there was no such finding made. It would therefore
not be proper for this Grand Lodge to determine that question upon
this proceeding. If, however, there was in faet an appeal filed in the
case referred to. justice will not have been clone until the proceedings
in that trial shall have been reviewed by the Committee on Appeals and
Grievances and its report thereon rendered to the Grand Lodge.
Indeed, the principle by which we are guided in our decision in this
proceeding is depen<lent upon the doctrine that where there is a wrong
there must be a remedy; and that it is only because there is a proper
and orderly method provided whereby a brother believing himself injured
may seek redress, that he is precluded from adopting other methods which
couhl lead only to discord and confusion.
The humblest member of the fraternity, when he supposes himself
to be injured on unjustly treated by his superiors, is entitled to his redress in an appeal to the Grand Lodge; and no matter what may be his
relation with the other members of the Lodge, or the opinion whieh
they may entertain of him, or the motive by which tlwy believe him
to be actuated, his right to be heard must not be denied. Through mis·
take or otherwise he may have been guilty of the commission of a Masonic
offense for which he should be punished; but he must not on that account
be denied a remedy to which he is entitled.
The accused in this proceeding was the accuser in the case referred
to. Concerning that case it is not necessary, and in the jrnlgment of
your Committee, it is not proper at this time to say anything more than
this: That the offense charged was one of the most serious of which a
Mason could be accused; that there was a verdict of guilty; and that
the sentence was, it was contended by the accuser, grossly incommen·
surate with the nature of the offense.

168

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In fairness to all concerned (and particularly to the Commissioners),
until the contrary is shown upon a review of the proceedings in that case,
we may assume that there were extenuating circumstances which war·
ranted the infliction of a lighter punishment than otherwise would have
been decreed; but likewise, in fairness to all concerned, this Grand
Lodge should determine for itself whether the sentence in the case re·
ferred to is to be regarded as a commendable exemplification of that
brotherly love and affection which should induce us, when dealing with
an erring brother, to temper justice with mercy, or on the other hand,
as a reprehensible dereliction of ·duty resulting in a gross miscarriage· of
justice.
Whatever may have been the motive by which the Commissioners
were actuated, if the accuser, dissatisfied with the verdict, filed a notice
of appeal, in due time, and in accordance with the provisions of the
Constitution, the proceedings should be reviewed even though, whether
through accident or design, the record itself discloses no notice of
appeal; and it ought to be unnecessary to say that if an appeal having
be.en filed it was intentionally suppressed, the person or persons liable
therefor should be dealt with as the occasion demands.

the receipt thereof, no person except the members thereof being present
in either Lodge.

ORATION.
Brother Samuel E. Burke, Grand Orator, then delighted
the Grand Lodge with a most scholarly and entertaining oration, at the close of which and after prolonged applause,
Brother Filmer moved that the thanks of Grand Lodge be and
are tended to Brother Burke, that he be requested to furnish
a copy of the oration to be printed in the proceedings and that
it be printed, together with the Address of the Grand Master
in sufficient number to supply all Lodges with copies thereof'.
which motion prevailed. The full text of the oration is as
follows:
Most Worshipful Grand Master, and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
I am honored beyond my deserts by being accorded this opportunity
to address you, and, as I look into your faces, I can say with the ancient
Greek orator, "I have with me the best of Athens."
. Centuries ago our Lodges were composed of operative masons.
W1th trowel and square and plumbline they constructed the temples and
palaces of mediaeval Europe. They were the friends of order and the
allies of religion, and actually labored with the tool as well as the pre·
cept. Ever before the eyes of the humblest Mason who wielded the
trowel was the vision of Grand Master Solomon directing the construction
of that great temple in whose building the founders of our Institution
worked for more than seven years under cloudless skies.
The temple of Solomon 11as crumbled in the grasp of four thousand
ye~rs; the frat~rnity which he aided to organize has ceased to be oper-

ative, and the implements of the craft have become Byplbols instead of
tools. Today we construct temples of character instead of temples of
stone'. and those edific~s which we build will be unaffected by the ravages
of Time, for they will accompany us and shelter us into the Great
Beyond toward which we are fast journeying.
It was well said by a great Mason who long since climbed the path
to immortality, "The Masonic Institution itself is more wonderful than

170

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

any edifice which it ever eonstrneted from the perishable materials of
earth. It has an unspoken language older than any living language of
Christendom. It has survived wars and revolutions, and is ever ascending
to loftier planes of usefulness. It looks to the heavens for its model,
and in its work imitates the Divine plan of nature.''

the attainment of knowledge. Good is the vital principle of ::\fasonry,
and it is universal good, for the Mason who is good to his brother Mason
is incapable of being bad to the rest of the world.
Time destroys material monuments erected by man. Beneath the
waves of the mid-Atlantic are buried the relics of the cities of the lost
Atlantus. The cities of Palestine are ruins; the pyramids and the sphinx
are slowly decaying; in our own domain the ruins of Casas Grandes and
of prehistoric acqueducts may be seen. But the principles of Truth, of
Justice, of Equity, of Fraternal Love, of Charity, of Faith, of Hope,
are indestructible, and because they are attributes of God, they cannot die.

The sun draws in vapory tributes the moisture from the ocean; the
invisible >Vinds carry it in clouds. over the globe and distribute in refreshing showers the liquid treasures of the skies. In like manner, Masonry
draws its strength and resources from the deep sea of human sympathies,
and employs them to redress the wrongs and relieve the sorrows of
humanity.
The dominating spirit of Masonry is Charity. Down the aisles of
nineteen centulies comes the voice of Paul, saying, ''Though I speak mth
the tongues of men and of angels, and have not Charity, I am become as
sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal. And though I have the gift of
prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I
have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not Charity,
I am nothing. Charity suffereth long, and is kind; Charity envie th not;
Charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up. Charity never faileth.''
Said Brother Starr King fifty years ago, in an address: ''Do we
ever get tired of the tolls and tax of charityt Suppose the sun did t
What does he receive in homage or obedience from the orbs that swing
round him in comparison with what he gives-all his light, all his heat,
all his vitality, for the blessing of four-score worldst Shall we complain
of the demand upon our treasulies, or our private purses, for the sacred
funds of the Masonic Board of RelieH What if the sea grumbled at the
assessment which the mighty sun, the Most Worshipful Grand Master of
the solar system, levies upon its substance. Every day the sun touches its
stores with its wand of light, and says, GIVE, GIVE, and the sea obeys.
Evaporation is its tax, constantly demanded, constantly given. Every
eloud we see, whether stretched in a beautiful bar across the east at
sunrise, or hanging in pomp over the gorgeous pavilion of the retiring
day, is part of the contribution for the general relief of Nature, assessed
by the lordly sun. The water which the ocean keeps is salt. Pour a
bucket of it on a hill of eorn or a garden bed, and it kills it. The water
which the ocean gives is fresh, and descends in blessing after it rides in
beauty or majesty on the viewless couriers of the air. Nature tells us
that to give is t<: live.''
Truth is the dominant virtue of Masonry, and Truth is immutable,
immaculate, and immortal. Experience dissolves in its clear light the
eloud-capped fancies of youth, and the passions and plans of manhood
vanish amid the infirmities of age; but neither time nor decay can impair
Truth. In Masonry, allied to this noblest of virtues, are the discipline of
the mind, the subjection of the emotions to the dominion of reason, and

lil

Masonry, in the vast number of its members and in the extent of its
sway in all countries, is the most powerful, the most wonderful and the
most beneficient social organization in all the world. Operative masonry
is the oldest mechanical trade. Deep excavations made in modern
Jerusalem have uncovered massive masonry of the time of King Solomon,
which underlies work done in the age of Zerubbabel. Above these are
specimens of mason work laid in the age of Herod the Great; and finally
there appears, but still below the level of the present city, stones laid
in the reign of Justinian.
The past of speculative Masonry, like that of operative masonry,
is beneath us, but not like the grandeur of a ruin. It is beneath us like
the roots beneath one of the giant sequoias of the Sierras-they still
give life and strength to the great tree which has for four thousand years
given shelter to all who gathered beneath its far-spreading arms.
Solomon's temple, which our ancient brethern constructed, was not
comparable with the living temple of our Institution. Under the direction
of Hiram of old, the stones of the first temple were prepared at the
quarries. They were brought to the temple-site and laid in massive walls
and arches in reverent silence, without sound of hammer or chisel or any
metal tool. Thus have our living temples been constructed in every land
and every age, without boasting and without noise. The best of the
manhood of the land are the stones of this living temple. The strife
and the selfishness of the world may roar outside the Lodge room but
they do not penetrate within its walls, and the sound timber and approved
stones are somewhere fitted to their places daily, without noise or confusion, in tens of thousands of Lodges in our land.
The walls of our Lodges never echo a sentiment that is not kindly
and their doors never open for an evil deed. When those of us who are
here today have been gathered to our fathers, our Masonic Lodges mll
look upon a field of labor and supply larger than we can dream of.
Twenty millions of people will dwell in our California. Temples of art,
and .industry, and science, and religion, and benevolence, will send ten
thousand spires to the skies. The outreaching arms of our iron Briareus
will bring to our doors the trophies of a conquest which commerce shall

172

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

achieve from Alaska to Patagonia, and which will extend over the western
sea to where sinks the sun.
And stiU as Yosemite in the presence of awe-struck tourists, tosses .
her soft white laee of falling waters into the air, as simply and as purely
as in the days when she was alone with the forests, and the meadows,
and the mountains, so will the maxims and the deeds and lifo of our
Institution bear themselves serene and unchanged amid the din of human
industry and the selfishness of human struggle.
Solomon's temple, where operative and speculative Masonry conjoined
in organization and operations, stood as it was .built, until its pillars and
domes were levelled by the weight of centuries. It could not enlarge
itself or recuperate itself. But our temple of speculative Masonry can
know no decay, for it is a house not built with hands. It is .an edifice of
immortal and ever-rejuvenating vitality. It is like the cedars of Lebanon,
which repair their waste and renew their leaves. Masonry fLlls in its
losses, enlarges its sweep and sway, and stands in its old proportions,
though in greater amplitude, symmetrical, mysterious, sublime.·
Masonry inculcates patriotism-love of country, love of the flag,
and love of freedom. It especially thrives on American soil. Not American in that narrow sense which questions a man's birthplace, or inquires into his theological or anti-theological opinions, but American
in a broader and more comprehensive definition; American as Niagara
is an American cataract; and the Columbia an American river.
There are Masonic Lodges near the icy glint of lakes which lie
far beyond the northern confines of our Republic; there are Lodges
shadowed by the forests where Orizaba's purple summit shines. The
Order invites to its membership all worthy men, whether aliens or citizens, wherever born and of whatever creed. It is American in the sense
that its spirit is the spirit of the mountains, the forests, the prairies,
the cataracts, the white-tipped lightning, and the thunder's voice. It
gathers its tradition from ages and ages gone. Traces even of its pre·
historic existence may be found in this western hemisphere. There are
Masonic symbols in the Casas Grandes of New Mexico, in the ancient
fortifications in the Mississippi valley, in the sculptured monoliths of
Copan, and the ancient· aqueducts of Arizona. Masonry evidently ex·
isted among races whose carvings in stone and whose ornaments in pot·
tery, and metal, in shell, obsidian and porphyry, are often unearthed all
the way from Lake Superi~r to the Belize; races whose temples are
crumbled, whose gods are vanished, and whose records exist only in the
undecipherable hieroglyphics of a language lost and gone.
Our Lodges are dedicated to the use of an order whose chief object
is brotherhood and charity; an order which accomplishes its benign
purposes through the love that comes from knowledge of each other,
and the .strength that is born of association and cohesion.
