Perhaps there are not in the whole vast vocabulary of human speech,
syllables more articulate with honorable emotion than the one word
''dedicate.'' In the beginning, when the morning stars sang together,
the first grand dedication w.as made, and I wonder that painters of the
pre-Raphaelite S<lhool did not choose this subject above all others for
their master effort. A new and swinging world, plucked out of the
stilly and starless unknown; her brooks filtrated from the mists of
' chaotic wastes, her fields unblown, her :first-born forests yet succulent
with Nature's milk, her airs .warm with wooing motion, and her freshlytinted skies painting the crest of creation upon new-made lake and
river. Suns unshorn of a virgin beam and moons unpropelled along
unplowed paths, and stars yet untaught in sentinel duty over all the
songless world. What though put a dewdrop hanging from the finger
of the Great Author 'I It was a world set apart for the uses of mortal man,
and dedicated in the presence of the angels to universal brotherhood.
There is no taint of evil in MaB1Jnry. Its temples are dedicated to
Love and Charity, and still retain the master idea of ages old; still
rear their proportions a perpetual rebuke to tyranny, and always a
stronghold of rectitude and justice, catching glints even through the
quagmires of the superstition of heathen nations, or the jungles of
obscure faiths, of that celestial light that shall endure forever.
Wherever there is Masonry, there is progress, and charity, and
good deeds, and kindly words. Where the eloquence of art speaks in
thrilling tones through lips of marble and bronze, or shines through
canvassed walls; where music breathes the symphonies of Heaven's own
tongue; where the dramatic art throbs in lifeful verity its lessons to
men-there the Lodges of Masonry are erected.
Where the doors of hospitals swing open at the sight of human
suffering; where libraries yield their treasures and professors their
erudition without cost to the seeker for learning; where the brandingiron and thong have been banished from penal institutions-there the
spirit of Masonry walks abroad. Where the pageant of power rushes
daily over millions of miles of iron rail, where the lightning sounds the
paean of progress upon Thought's million-chorded lyre, where the iron
barges of commerce smite the abject seas with their conquering foreethere the triumphs of Masonry are sung.
Where the sun draws pictures, and the microscope reveals the
secrets of life, and discovery and invention have made the existence' of
the day laborer more comfortable than that of a barbarian king-'there Masonry is a force for right doing and right thinking. Where
science has pursued unchecked and encouraged, her mighty march unti:l
the voices of the living may be heard through the air thousands of
miles, and the voices of the dead speak from the mouth of the phonograph, and men sail in great ships above the clouds and under the

174

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

seas-there sits Masonry, smiling, saying to her votaries "Do not believe that of this mighty panorama of human progress, you will eatch
but the fleeting glimpse afforded by the brief life of earth for the ages
live with you and with them you shall live."
Masonry in its march keeps step with civilization, and is the
apostle of liberty, and the conservator of order. Masons have been
inventors, artists, organizers and promoters of industries, authors,·
orators, statesmen,--ever foremost in every field of benifieent effort.
Masonry requires only that its members shall be ''free born and of
good repute. " It demands of an applicant for admission that he shall
be an honest man who believes in the existence of an Almighty God.
It does not ask upon what soil he was born, or to what religious creed
he professes allegiance. In Masonic Lodges kings have obeyed the or·
ders of subjects seated in the Worshipful Master's chair, and major
generals and corporals have clasped hands in fraternal grasp. Multimillionaires and mechanics, college professors and hand-laborers, mer·
chants and clerks, meet on terms of equality which elsewhere is theoretical, but in the Masonic Lodge is actual. By the couch of the sick
and the bier of the dead, Masonry alleviates human suffering and sympathizes with human sorrow, and its succoring ministrations are given
to the widow and the fatherless. :Neither the restlessness of change
nor the march of time have impaired its strength or altered its
principles.
Mutual assistance is a fundamental principle of Masonry. The
man of wealth does not become a member in order to increase his holdings, the politician does not expect to influence the vote of a brother
Mason, nor does the college professor enter our Lodge room in order to
add to his knowledge of Greek or Latin. The help that Masons give
to each other is not sordid and not the result of bargaining. The Mason
seeks and obtains counsel of his brother in health, care in sickness,
assistance in difficulty, and defence when needed. Masonry seeks to
improve the characters rather than the worldly condition of its membership. Unless calamities of Nature, such as :fire or disease overtake
our brothers, they do not apply to their fraternity for aid. Want is
not often a visitor in a Lodge room, for Masons are intelligent, indus·
trious and frugal. Artificial social distinctions which wealth and station
create, have no place in our fraternity. Masonry does not deny ministration to the physical wants of its members, but it seeks to promote an
expansion of their sympathies. It promotes the fellowship of manliness,
not that of political or ecclesiastical or social distinctions. Its basis is
the brotherhood of man and the fatherhood of God. In the Lodge
room, rich and poor, learned and unlearned, public official and private
citizen, meet upon a basis of absolute equality, and all contribute equally
ta a common treasury.

No man can be a Mason at heart, unless he worships God and loves
his· n~ighbor. No charlatan, no glutton, no adulterer, no hypocrite, no
miser, no man who does not aspire and labor to obey the moral law,
can ever become a true Mason through any process of admission. Perfection in this life we cannot attain, but we can reach toward it with
faithful hearts and steady eyes. It should be our task amidst the team·
ing vitality of California, under the institutions by which we are protected, in the spheres of labor to which we are respectively called, not
merely on holy days, but every day, by the cheerfulness and persistence of
our industry, by the promptness and punctuality with which we keep
our engagements, by the modesty of our pretensions, by the general
probity of our conduct, by our firmness and patience under affliction, by
our unaffected sympathy and charity, by our strong control over appe·
tite and passipn, and by our temperate enjoyment of pleasure, to spread
the light and Wal'mth of Masonry.
Whether a man is a Christian, a Jew, a Buddhist, a Parsee or a
Mahomedan, if he believes in a God, in an existence after death;
and in the supremacy of good, he may become a Mason. If he is an
Athf>ist, who denies the existence of an Almighty Power, lie cannot
become a Mason.
Masonry teaches that ''it is not all of life to live, nor all of death

to die.'' Masonry teaches its members to lead clean lives and to respect
the rights of others. Masonry is a bulwark of order and a dove of
peace. Masonry is the foe of ever materialistic philosophy.
We are steadily toiling up the mountain-heights seeking knowledge.
Below us are the tangled undergrowth out of which our fathers crawled.
Above us tower the star-lit peaks which our children may ascend. And
now there steps from out the wayside shadows the gloomy presence of a
cold, and pitiless philosophy. It says, "Fatigue not yourself with trying
to climb higher. There is no future. There is no Divine Law. Faith is
a folly. Hope is a delusion. Good and Evil are only words. The uni·
verse is only a charnel house of dead languages, dead faiths and dead
gods. Go back to the bliss of ignorance. Eat, drink, and be merry, for
tomorrow you die.''
A Mason will not accept this creed of these apostles of Annihilation.
He says, ''I decline to consider myself as an intelligence unfit to survive
the death of my body. I prefer to believe that there is ceaseless and
progressive life. I prefer to believe that the Almighty has placed by
every bed of death a waiting cradle for the soul, and that death itself is
but ''that first breath which our souls draw when we enter Life, that is
of all life, center." Masonry believes that materialistic philosophers
are mischief-makers. They are like the ruffian who kicks the crutches
from under the arms of a cripple and leaves him no other support by
which he can limp away from the storm. Their dogmas tend to paralyze

176

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the consciences and strangle the nobler impulses of men and banish tl:~em
from the white light of later centuries, to grovel among the cave dwellers
of a prehistoric age.
Masonry believes that faith in a future existence where a man shall
reap what he has sown in earthly life, is an armed guard, whose arresting hands are laid upon the selfish, the savage and the criminal impulses
of man, and that even from a more worldly and economic point of view,
society cannot afford to snatch .the star from the breast of the Invisible
Guardsman, and trust for protection to a creed of personal irresponsibility based upon the hypothesis of personal annihilation after the
death of the body.
Masonry says to the Materialist: "Have all the formative forces
of the universe been exhausted in producing Man' Is he the crowning
and ultimate feat of all creation f Of course, we of the human race are
very wise and very great, but after all, we are far from perfect, even
physically. Even with our aeroplanes any wild goose can outfly us, any
dog or rabbit outrun us, and relative weight considered, any grasshopper
can outhop us.
Masonry places God's message to man upon its altars and emblazons God's initials on its walls, because Masons believe that Man is
but one link in the endless chain of existence which stretches out over
the purple path of space from the depths of night to the home of the
singing stars. Masonry says that if evolution demonstrates that man
has been developed from a lower order of being, does it not follow that
in turn a higher order of being will be evolved from man f If we start
with the mollusc, must we stop with the human f Surely the difference
between a clam and a materialist is greater than. the difference between
a materialist and almost any kind of an angel. If an advocate of materialism can trace himself backward to the time when he was an. invertebrate, wriggling a slimy argument against a future life, or a saurian insisting that beyond crocodilism there could be no further development, or any icthyosaurus babbling to his fellow-fishes about the impossibility of there being any other world than the watery one in which
they were swimming, why cannot he project himself forward into another
existence where he will have an opportunity to explain to the other
devils how it was that he came to make such a mistake in this one'
I cannot better conclude this address than by a quotation from a
brother who long since journeyed on: ''There is,'' said Frank Tilford,
"no eternity to matter. No work of man can resist the ruthless hand
of violence or the unsparing scythe of time. Even the temple which
our ancient craftsmen erected on the sacred mountain. that marvellous
structure of consummate beauty, bas not escaped the universal doom.
Note the changes wrought on our planet since the era of authentic
history. Science reveals to us the unchangeable decree of the Infinite

tba t. the time must arrive in the grand procession of the ages, when
all hfe shall cease upon our globe. The atmosphere with its gorgeous hues
and banner of clouds will pass away; the rivers and oceans will disappear; the myriad voices of nature will no longe rise to the heavens
in songs of rejoicing, and the mighty monuments of the past will remain, tombs of generations that have died amid the awful solitudes of
a dead world; but the principles of Masonry cannot die. They must

IN MEMORIAM
JOHN MORTON ESHLEMAN
By Harvey D. Loveland, Past Master San Francisco Lodge No. 360.
''Friend after friend departs,
Who hath not lost a friend~''

Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of .the Grand Lodge.:
i\. we turn back 0 'er the pages of Memory's book, upon wh1eh the
assin~ years have stamped their indelible record, as we read t~ere the
~ames of those who no longer answer to our roll-call, as we realize that
in th'e language of the Persian astronomer and poet,
''The moving :finger writes, and having writ,
Moves on· nor all your piety nor wit
Can lure it back to cancel half a line,
Nor all your tears wash out a word of it,"
the truth comes home to us with startling distinctness that ''man was
made to mourn.' '

Gathered as this Grand body is at this time to direct the destinies
of this great Order within the jurisdiction of our beloved commonwealth,
it is peculiarly meet and fitting that these brothers for whom we mourn
today, who have left their ''footprints upon the sands of Time'' should
be remembered. I am asked to speak to the memory of one whom I
knew and loved. Of one whom to know was to love. Of one whose life
offered convincing evidence of the truth of the oft-repeated saying that
''war is not necessary to the development of heroes and heroism.' ' Aye,
and of one whose passing into the Great Beyond proves the truth of
that other adage that ''Death loves a shining mark.'' It seems but
yesterday, my brethren, that we felt the honest, sincere clasp of his hand
in friendship and in fe11owship, and listened to his kindly voice, which
ever uttered words of thoughtful and disinterested helpfulness. It seems
but yesterday that many of us gathered around his bier with a great
concourse of those who loved and respected him in life, to pay our last
sad tribute to his earthly remains and to listen to the beautiful eulogy
pronounced by his friend, the honored Chief Executive of our State, who,
next to our brother's immediate family, probably felt his loss most
keenly. It seems but yesterday that, with bared heads and heavy hearts,
we stood around his last resting place in the beautiful cemetery down
there in that fair city of sunshine and flowers where he had chosen to
make his future home, and listened to our beloved Grand Master im·
pressively repeat in a manner which stamped them as coming from his
heart, the last touching words of our burial service, ''Soft and sweet
to thee, our brother, be thy earthly bed'', and as we turned from that
lonely grave the thought must have come to others, as it came to me,
that the green graves of our own loved ones on different hillsides bore
mute but eloquent testimony to the depth and sincerity of the sympathy
which we felt and still feel for those nearest and dearest to our brother,
and there echoed in our hearts the beautiful plea that o'er that silent
tomb "may the sweetness of the summer's last rose linger longest."
Tenderly we laid him away under a wealth of beautiful flowers, last
silent offerings of love and friendship.
The gentle breeze wafted from o'er the bosom of the broad Pacific,
whose mighty, resistless energy his character seemed to typify, wedded
to the rustling leaves of the trees which spread their shadows o'er his
grave, seemed fitting requiem to a soul at rest and as, with a last lingering look, I turned from the grave of my friend, unbidden there came
to my mind the words of the old sweet hymn sung to you and to me
in years gone by, by voices now members of the celestial choir,
"Sleep sweetly,, brother; far from thee
Thy kindred and their graves may be;
And yet it is a blessed sleep
From which none !rl'er wake to weep."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Although all this seems but the events of yesterday, two-thirds of
that larger period by which we measure the seasons have passed since
we left him to his last long sleep. Yet such is the nature of genuine
grief, his memory lives in our hearts in unfading tenderness.
Thus, my brethren, I have spoken of his death. What shall I say of
his life and character and of the great work which he crowded into the
few short years allotted to him i Born in Illinois, of parents rich in
honesty and purity of life, but poor in material wealth, his life from
childhood to man's estate was ever and always a struggle to respond to
that honest and exalted ambition which spurred him on. With a mind
that knew no limits in its aspiration, with a soul attuned to the music
of the spheres but with a body weakened by tuberculosis and by his
prodigious mental effort in securing an education, in early manhood he
sought health and opportunity in California. While he did not find the
one permanently, he created the other. Improved in health by a season
of outdoor life in a railroad construction camp, he again answered Ambition's call to fit himself for the larger and richer life to which he
aspired, and entered the University of California.
That great institution, Alma Mater to many who are writing their
names high in the halls of Fame and Success, points with pride to his
scholastic record, and at a meeting of the faculty and the student body
shortly after his death, a beautiful eulogy of the life and work of
Brother Eshleman was pronounced by Senator Guy C. Earl, one of the
regents of the University.
Graduating with distinguished honors, he entered upon the practice
of law, but even that jealous mistress, devoted as he was to his profes·
sion, could not blind him to the fact that life has large responsibilities
incident to our complex civilization, which can only be accepted by sacrifice, and he became a member of the Legislature. There he at once took
bis place as a leader of men of moral aspiration, who were willing to
engage in the battle of life for high ideals and pure polities. Again his
health failed and, accompanied by she who had been his classmate in
college, with whom he had selected to go hand in hand alo_ng life's
pathway, he was taken from the halls of legislature to the Imperial
Valley, as his friends feared, to die.
Indomitable will power and life-giving, life-sustaining sunshine prevailed, and his health again improving, he entered upon the practice
of his profession and became District Attorney of Imperial county, a
county which he was largely instrumental in creating.
Later he was elected to the office of Railroad Commissioner. Of his
work in that :field, where for four years I was in daily association with •
him, I need not speak. You all know that he became a State and
National figure and authority in public utility regulation.

Answering again that which he regarded as duty's call, he accepted
the nomination for Lieutenant-Governor, and the majority by which he
was elected attested the esteem in which he was held. Here I may
properly refer to Brother Eshleman 's Masonic record. He was initiated
passed and raised in Durant Lodge No. 268, F. and A. M., of Berkeley;
California; reeeived the :Master's degree on May 26, 1905. The following
year he became a member of Berkeley Chapter No. 92, R. A. M.; received
the Royal Arch degree on December 12, 1906. In 1908 he became a
member of El Centro Lodge No. 384, and was Master of that Lodge in
1909. He withdrew from Berkeley Chapter in 1910 and became a
charter member of El Centro Chapter No. 109. Brother Eshleman,
shortly before his death, was elected to membership in Imperial Valley
Commandery, U. D., at El Centro, and was .on his way to receive the
Orders of Knighthood when he died.

185

Brethren, the tale is almost told. As was said in the beautiful
eulogy delivered at his funeral, "ever and always the grim spectre of
death stalked at his side.'' Bravely he fought, like a hero he died.
Alone in the early morning hours, just as the dawn of another day was
breaking, separated from those nearest and dearest, he made his last
fi~ht and lost.. Shall we say "lost," or rather shall we say, in keeping
with the sentiment of the beautiful poem recited by Brother Gunzen1
dorfer, ' He made his last fight and won, won the crown of immortality,'' for there was in him that nobility of character and faith in the
ultimate which robs the grave of its victory. and death of its sting.
That dawn was to him the morning of eternity.
. Our ea~thly associations with him have ended, but his memory rema1?s and is a monument in the hearts of his friends prouder than
stoned urn or chiseled marble pointing to the skies. I would, indeed,
my brethren, that in the brief moments remaining to me, I could impart
to you that knowledge of his character which fntimate association gave
me. I cannot, and hoping still to fail not in the performance of the sad
yet pleasureable duty assigned to me upon this occasion, I appeal to one
of the master minds of other times, and say in the language of Tennyson,
''He had in him that gentleness which, when
wed to manhood makes the man.'' .
I close my simple tribute to my friend and our brother with a little
story appropriate because of its allegorical application in keeping with
the manner in which the science of our Order is taught. It is called
the Story of the Immortal Bell:
Upon the side of one of the steepest and highest of the mountains
of Switzerland a monastery is located. So inaccessible is it that few
tourists ever visit it, but from the reports of the few who have braved
the dangers incidental to reaching it, it is famed for three things: First

186

187

·,,'?ROCEl<JDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and second, for a cordial and a liqueur made by the monks, dear to the
hearts of the epicures; and third, for the possession of a bell east three
hundred years ago. So fine was it C',ast and so perfect of tone, that
although rung for the first and only time three centuries ago on Christmas
morning, it is still giving out its sweet and perfect tones to the wonder
and awe of all who behold it.

Denson and Past Master Loveland, together with the entire
program, were ordered printed in the Proceedings.

Comparable to the perpetuity and sweetness of the notes of that
perfect bell, is the inftuenee ·which proceeds from the life and efforts
of our brother, whom we mourn today. Like the notes of the bell, that.
influence will go sounding down through the corridors of time with the
·influence of other men of pure anc1 high ideals, and our children's children
will reap what he and others like him have sown.

In life we honored :rnd respected Brother John M. Eshleman; in
death his memory is a heritage worthy of the respect we are today according it.
Just a word in closing of our brother in that sacred relation of
husband and father, whieh relation the teachings and tenets of Masonry
cherish and respect; and brethren, quoting from the immortal bard, I
would say, ''If you have tears, prepare to shed them now,'' nor think
it unmanly should Nature bid you weep through feelings of genuine
sorrow, for never yet was manhood shamed by permitting the eye to
pay tribute to grief that wrings the heart.
Down there in that once happy but now lonely and desolate home,
are those upon whom this dispensation of an all-wise Providence has
fallen most hi;avily. To that sorrowing girl-wife, for she is scarcely
more than a girl, and to the little ones who in childish innocence still
speak of daddy and wonder why he does not come, we extend our continued heartfelt sympathy, the depth and sincerity of which is measured
by sorrow second only w their own. May God in his infinite love and
mercy watch o'er and care for them even as he "tempers the wind to
the shorn lamb.''
Lost to sight, but to memory dear, there is left to us, his brothers
of the Mystic Tie, the fond hope, aye, the abiding faith, that up there
in that Lodge not made with hands, in the glorious presenee of our
Supreme Grand Master, our brother has found that light eternal which
was ever the objeet of his ~fasonic pilgrimage here on earth. Brethren
of the Grand Lodge, I respectfully ask that, with bowed heads and
reverent hearts, you join with me in the beautiful words with which
Masons ever conclude their supplications to the Throne of Grace, "So
mote it be. "

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PAY OF MEMBERS.
Brother Howard D. Kercheval, Chairman of the Committee on Pay of l\Iembers, presented the following report, whieh
was adopted :
'fo the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:

Your committee, charged with the duty of ascertaining the cost of

Past Grand Master Angellotti, for the Committee on
Jurisprudence, reported as follows:
To the Jf:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Brother William A. Sherman proposes to amend section 73 of the
Constitution by adding thereto the following:
''Resolved, that Section 73 be amended to read in the following
manner: '.l'o strike out the word 'and' in the last line but one, and add

* For items, see Report of Committee on Returns.

210

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

at the end of the section the following: 'and are thoroughly proficient
in those portions of the Constitution and General Regulations of the
Grand Lodge which relate to the government of a Lodge.' ''

The recommendation was adopted and section 115
amended by unanimous vote.

"As amended the section to read as follows:
Sec. 73. Upon the petition of twelve and not more than twenty-five
Master Masons in good standing, accompanied by the demits or certificates of the signers in the forms prescribed in Sections 159 aud 161,
being presented to the Grand ·Master, in the form prescribed in Section
235, he may in cases of manifest propriety and necessity grant them a
dispensation to open and hold a Lodge at the place therein to be named,
under such name as shall be approved by him, which shall not be the
name of any living person or chartered Lodge, with power to make
Masons and receive members by affiliation; and he shall therein appoint
the Master and Wardens of the new Lodge. But in no case shall such
dispensation be issued unless the petition be accompanied by a recommendation from the nearest or most convenient chartered Lodge (if from
a city or town where more than one Lodge exists, then from a majority
of such Lodges), setting forth, in the form prescribed in Section 237,
that the petitioners are all Master Masons in good standing, that the
establishment of the new Lodge is of manifest propriety and will conduce
to the good of the order, and that a safe and suitable Lodge-room has
been provided therefor; nor unless the petition shall also be accompanied
by a certificate from an Inspector whom the Grand Master shall select,
declaring that the Master and Wardens, proposed in such petition are
fully competent properly to confer the three degrees of Masonry, to
deliver entire the lectures thereunto appertaining, and are thoroughly
proficient in those portions of the Constitution and General Regulations
of the Grand Lodge which relate to the government of a Lodge.''

Brother Elmer E. Stone proposes an amendment to section 30 of
our Constitution by adding thereto the following:

The effect of the proposed amendment would be to make the
requisite qualifications of the Master and Warden of proposed Lodges
U. D. the same as those of the Master and Warden of chartered Lodges.
We, therefore, recommend its adoption.

The report was adopted and section 73 amended by unanimous vote.
Brother Lemuel L. Test proposes to amend our Constitution so as
to prohibit the conferring of more than five degrees by any Lodge in any
one day. It has been decided that the law as now written contains no
such prohibition. Believing that no Lodge can confer more than five
degrees in one day in an effective and creditable manner, we are in
entire sympathy with the proposed amendment. We therefore recommend that section 115 of the Constitution be amended by adding thereto
the following:
"Nor shall it confer more than five degrees in any one day."

211

"The Committee on Jurisprudence, on Grievances and on Finance
shall convene at the place of holding the annual communication of G;and
~o.dge, at l:ast twenty-four hours previous to its opening. All propositions subJect to reference to the above said Committees· must be
presented in writing and delivered to the Grand Secretary prior to the
time of convening of said Committees.''
As will be seen, this proposes quite a radical change one of the

effe~ts ~hereof being to prevent the consideration at any Annual Com·
mumcat10n of any resolution or proposition subject to reference to the
Committee on Jurisprudence or Finance or Grievance unless presented
to the Gran~ Se~retary at least ~~enty-four hours before the opening of
the Commumcat10n. The propos1hon was not introduced until the third
day of this Communication and, as is apparent, consideration thereof at
this· Communication may well be held to be inconsistent with its terms.
In any event, we believe that we should not act hastily in the matter
and recommend that consideration be deferred until our next Annual
Communication.

The recommendation was adopted.
A proposition is made to amend section 17 of the Constitution so
as to fix the time of t.he ~lection of Grand officers for the second day of
each Annual Commumcation. The proposition was not introduced until
the third· day of this Communication. As at present advised we can
see no good reason for making the change in our existing law's in this
~atter; but we feel that the proposition is entitled to more consideration than can properly be given to it at this Communiootion and recomme~d that its consideration be postponed to our next Annu~l Communication.

The recommendation was adopted.

Adopted.
Brother Bernhard from the same Committee reported as
to Trial Record No. 191 as follows:
The case was tried by Bakersfield Lodge No. 224. At the trial
there were six Commissioners, and the accused was found guilty as
charged and the penalty fixed as suspension. T?e vote ~n the penalty
of expulsion was 3 to 3 and the vote on suspension was D to 1.
Your Committee feels that the evidence in this case juatifies the
severest penalty in our power, that the punishment of suspension was
inadequate to meet an offense of this kind and that the accused should
be expelled. We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved, That the verdict be sustained and the sentenee of suspe~­
sion be and the same is hereby reversed and the accused be and he is
hereby expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.

The resolution was adopted, and Hiram C. Hamilton of
Tehachapi Lodge No. 113 was thereupon expelled from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Your Committee also reports on Trial Record No. 190, from Fairmount Lodge No. 435, that the record is so incomplete and defective
and in such a condition that the Committee has never acquired jurisdiction of said matter and reports it back without action.

to have them reproduced in oil at the rate of not more than four each

Your Committee on Finanee bas devoted considerable time to the
study of the conditions surrounding the claim of Lassen Lodge No. 149,
of Susanville, California.
They are in brief as follows: Bro. L. S. York, a member of
Cement Lodge No. 431, of· th.e Grand Jurisdiction of Missouri, came
to Susamille in the fall· of 1914, and in a very short time became so
ill that he was unable to work for a period of seven or eight months.
His family consisted of a wife and six small children. They were entirely destitute. Lassen Lodge immediately took charge of the brother
and tenderly eared for him during his long illness. They expended on
behalf of his family $385.64, and have been reimbursed by Cement
Lodge to the extent of $50.00. Cement Lodge eonfesses inability to
pay more, and the Grand Lodge of Missouri will not assist. We therefore offer for adoption the following resolution:
Resolved, That the sum of $335.64 be and the same is hereby
ordered paid to Lassen Lodge No. 149 as reimbursement for moneys
expended on behalf of Bro. L. S. York.
The Masonic Board of Relief of Portland, Oregon, in its fraternal
ministrations, has extended aid to Agnes Brown, daughter of Wm. A.
Brown of Pescadero Lodge No. 239 (charter surrendered). The amount
advanced was $125.00 as evidenced by vouchers at hand.
We therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution:
Resolved, That payment be made to the Masonic Board of Relief
of Portland, Oregon, in the sum of $125.00 for moneys advanced on
behalf of Miss Agnes Brown.
There has been presented for the consideration of your Committee,
the claim of Humboldt Lodge No. 79, for $143.00 expenses incurred by
the burial of Mrs. Celia Benton, who died within the jurisdiction of
that Lodge on January 81 1916. Mrs. Benton was the widow of a nonaffiliated Mason in good standing at the time of his death, August 16,
1871 . .
While admitting that the claim, as such, is a proper. one against
this Grand Lodge, we are impressed with the belief that Humboldt Lodge
incurred a greater expense than conditions demanded, and the items of
the bill accompanying would seem to confirm that belief.
We feel that our subordinate Lodges should be admonished that in
similar cases no greater expense should be incurred than is eonsistent
with decency and respect.

Your Committee has examined a most voluminous correspondence
between the Grand officers of Nevada; Douglas Ledge No. 12, of Genoa,
Nevada; Carson Valley Lodge, and Palmyra Lodge No. 26 of Placerville, California, referring to a claim by Palmyra Lodge for moneys
expended on behalf of the widow of Bro. James W. Small, who was, at
the time of his death, a member in good standing of Douglas Lodge.
The amount involved was $415.00 of which $166.00 was returned, leaving
a balance due of $249.00.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The evidence gives conclusive proof of diligent effort on the part
of Palmyra Lodge to recover and of the fairness and fraternal spirit of
both the Grand and subordinate Lodges of Nevada, in their efforts
to reimburse. Financial inability on the part of Douglas Lodge prevented the complete liquidation.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, That Palmyra Lodge No. 26 be reimbursed in the amount
of $249.00 for moneys expended on behalf of Mrs. Susan Jane Small.
There has been referred for out consideration a letter signed by
Mrs. Frederick H. Colburn, Regent San Francisco Chapter, Woman's
Section of the Navy League, asking that the sum of $500.00 be set aside
for the purpose of erecting and protecting a monument, to replace one
which now marks the grave of Peter Lassen, a distinguished man and
Mason, near Susanville, Lassen County.
Your Committee is of the opinion that this matter, being one
wherein sentiment alone is involved, becomes largely a matter of policy
which should be determined by this Grand Lodge without regard to its
Committee, but owing to the many practieal and necessary demands upon
our resources, we cannot approve it.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved, That the request of Mrs. Frederick H. Colburn that the
sum of $500.00 be appropriated for the erection and protection of a
monument to Peter Lassen be regretfully denied.
GEO. F. RODDEN,

APPROVED DECISIONS AND AMENDMENTS TO
CONSTITUTION.
See. 41. (Add) Provided, nevertheless, that no contribution of any
sort, in the nature of a per capita tax, shall be payable by a Lodge
upon any Mason whose dues at the stated meeting in July of the calendar
year in which such tax would otherwise be payable, shall have been remitted for the next preceding twelve months period, because of the
inability of such Mason to pay such dues. Each subordinate Lodge's
annual report, in addition to any others matters required, shall contain
a list of the names of Masons whose dues have been remitted, together
with the cause of such remission, as to whom non-payment of per capita
tax contribution is to be had.
Sec. 73. (Add at bottom) And are thoroughly proficient in those
portions of the Constitution and General Regulations of the Grand
Lodge which relate to the government of a Lodge.
81d. The two-thirds required to amend is a two-thirds vote of all
the members present. It is not a two-thirds of the votes cast.
81e. An amendment to the by-laws to .become effective at an indefi·
nate elate will not be approved.
82c. A Lodge in an incorporated city which is entirely surrounded
by another city, has no jurisdiction outside its own municipal limits. A
Lodge cannot be within the corporate limits of two cities at the same
time.
88a. (Add) The matter of a suitable testimonial to a retiring
Master is a "matter or thing" Masonic in its nature, and members of
a Lodge may properly make a contribution or solicit one among themselves for such purpose.
89f. The term ''total revenue'' means gross revenue.
lOla. A petition is received when it is read by the Secretary at a
stated meeting, unless by majority vote of the members present the
Lodge declines to receive it. (The decision of 1900 is now void.)
104c. In balloting for a candidate, two cubes were in the box. A
mistake had probably been made in placing therein one of the eubes.
The Master properly declared the candidate rejected. The mistake
can only be remerlied by application for a dispensation to reballot.
115. (Add) Nor shall it confer more than five degreE's in any one
day.
118k. It is proper for the Secretary to read the names of all who
owe for dues, but needless humiliation should be ;,tvoi<led.
121. (Add) Provided, however, anything in this section to the
contrary notwithstanding, that the Lodges in this jurisdiction whose longestablished ritualistic work is in part a departure from the uniform

222

ritual of this jurisdiction, may continue to perform such work as the
same is now being performed, in so far as the same may not be disapproved by the Grand Master and the Grand Lecturer. (This affects La
Parfaite Union Lodge No. 17, Vallee de }'ranee No. 329, and Lodge le
Progres de l 'Oeeanie No. 371.)
125h. Examinations of visiting brethren shall be had ~thin the
jurisdiction of the Lodge which the visitors desire to attend.
135q. Where installation -is to take place in a building other than
where the Lodge regularly meets, the Lodge should open in the Lodgeroom and then repair to the place of installation.
1640. Out of respect to the wishes of the deceased, and as a courtesy to another fraternal organization, the Master might properly request
the other organization to render its service or a part of it, it being
understood that the Masonic Lodge shall have charge of and conclude
the service.
164p. It is proper to hold Masonic services over the ashes of a
brother whose body has been cremated.
165. (Add) Provided, further, that a Mason demitted from another
jurisdiction who is not in got>d standing therein at the time he enters,
or becomes a resident of this jurisdiction, shall in no ease be entitled
to any Masonic rights or privileges unless and until he shall be elected
a member of some Lodge in this purisdiction, or shall be restored to
membership by the jurisdiction from which he holds his demit.
210. (Add) And provided, further, that if the Mason suspended
was not a member of the Lodge adjudging suspension, the application
for restoration shall be refused unless the consent of the Lodge in which
membership was held, if it be in this jurisdiction, is given. The request
for such consent shall lie over at least one stated meeting.

ALABAMA.
1915.

95th Annual, Montgomery, Dec. 1 and 2.
Lodges, 554; Membership, 27,916; gain, 368.
ful

The Annual Communication was presided over by the Most Worshfp·
C. :!'.filler, Grand Master.

After the opening of the Grand Lodge, the Grand Master delivered
his annual address, replete with information touching masonic activities
during the preceding year. He mentions the formation of nine new
lodges under dispensation, as one of the evidences of pronounced masonic
activity and growth.
The Grand Lodg<i suffered within the year a severe loss in the death
of the distinguished and beloved Brother Angus M. Seott, for fifteen
years the Grand Lecturer of the Grand Lodge, probably the most generally known and best beloved mason in the jurisdiction.
Reference is made, with especial pride to the :Masonic Home, a
creation of comparatively recent years in this jurisdiction, and the
Grand Master assures the brethren that they are absolutely unable to
form any idea of the good accomplished by this institution except
through a personal visit to the Home. This institution is accomplishing
magnificent masonic woi;.k, and has in store for it a career of vast benefi·
cence and good.
The Grand Master falls in line with the tendency of very recent
years to get away from the idea of physical perfection, and disregard,
to a large extent, this tradition, which we have inherited from operative
masons, to the end that emphasis be placed upon our teaching that it is
the 'internal and not the external qualifications which recommend a man
to be made a mason. Grand Master Miller fails to see why a stiff knee,
or the loss of a first joint of a thumb, or some equally unimportant circumstance, should prevent a good man from becoming a mason.
The Grand Master is unquestionably correct, and, as stated, his
thought is simply in line with the drift of masonic opinion almost everywhere.
In connection with the visitation to subordinates, Grand Master
Miller appreciates, as possibly some Grand Masters do not appreciate,
the very great benefit which a subordinate lodge receives from official
contact ·with the ruling Grand Master, and he states that it is his firm
conviction that the Grand Mast<ir can accomplish great good, and render
a most genuine service by coming in contact with the members of the
several lodges, greeting them personally, and allowing them to feel the

4

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

warmth of his presence, and the genial friendship conveyed in the cordial
hand-grasp.
He voices his conception of the high ideal of masonry in the following paragraph from the conclusion of his splendid address:
''Today, as never before, has Masonry had the respect and admiratiQJl of all thinking people. Its stand for morality and right-living;
its stand for education and enlightenment; its stand for independence
in free thought and free speech and the right to worship our God according to the dictates of our own conscience, without infringing upon the
rights of any man, has endeared it to the hearts of all good and true
men, who honor their home, their God and their country.''
This jurisdiction has, in our opinion, an excellent method of passing
upon constitutional amendments, in that hasty action is prevented by
the method adopted in changing the fundamental law of the jurisdiction.
For instance, before an amendment can be considered, it must have a
vote of one third of the members present in the Grand Lodge when the
amendment is offered, and then the amendment is submitted to all of
the lodges of the jurisdiction, who are required to vote thereon within
the year following the submission of the amendment and make returns
of their vote upon the amendment to the Grand Secretary, and the
returns are then announced at the next Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge, and amendments can only be adopted by an affirmative
vote of two thirds of all of the lodges in the jurisdiction. This method
forces every lodge to consider carefully in its own meeting the proposed
amendment, and this affords an opportunity for all master masons to
express their opinions as to the wisdom of the proposed change. This
method of constitutiunal amendment prevents, as stated, hasty action,
and compels a knowledge upon the part of all of the lodges as to changes
that are made in the organic law.
In accordance with recommendations of the Committee on Foreign
Correspondence, fraternal recognitio"n was extended to the Grand Lodge
of Queensland, and fraternal recognition was also extended to the Grand
Lodge of the Philippine Islands, and in this connection it is worthy of
comment that the pretensions of the so-called Regional District Lodge
of the Philippine Islands, presided over by one Mendoza, were decided
as being without foundation or merit, and the protest against the recognition of the regular Grand Lodge of the Philippines was disregarded.

We have in some of our comments in former years, referred to what
has seemed to us the incongruity of the reception in the Grand Lodge
of masons, even when at ease, of delegates from the Order of the Eastern
Star.
We would not presume to criticise any jurisdiction for anything it
might, in its judgment, approve, yet, as stated, the reception of a dele-

Large appropriations were voted for the relief of distressed brother
masons in foreign lands, battling' hi Engiand 's cau,5e. The matter that
was naturally uppermost in all of .the· discussions throughout the various
Quarterly Communications was the life and death struggle in which
England is now engaged, and in which every British subject takes a
vital interest, and this paramount subject of vital interest was reflected
in the proceedings of the Grand Lodge. In one of the co.mmunications,
it was moved:
. .
.
''That each Private Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of England be required to examine the cases of all members who '
are of GBrman birth, to eall upon all such members whose retention of
membership is not approved by the unanimous vote of all the other
members of the Lodge to resign, and failing resignation, to forthwith
exclude such members from membership; or, in the alternative:
''That on the termination of the war each Private Lodge under
the jurisdiction of the. Grand .Lodge of England be required to ex:amine
the cases of all members who are of German .birth,· to refuse permission
to such members to resume attendance at Lodge, unless the resumption
of such attendance is approved by the unanimous· vote of all the otlier
members of the Lodge, to call upon all members of German birth the
resumption of whose attendance is not so approved, to resign, and failing i·esignation, to forthwith exclude su(lh members .from membership.
''The immediate withdrawal of this Grand Lodge's recognition of
the German Grand Lodges.
''The prohibition of the reception iri English ·Lodges of alleged
Masons belonging· to a Lodge under any German Jurisdiction, and the
prohibition of the entry of English Masons irito any Lodge existing
unde.r any German Jurisdiction."
Prolonged debate, in which the entire subject was comprehensively
discussed, took place, and this was adopted:
·
''Grave concern has been occasioned to the Board since the outbreak of the war by differences which have arisen in certain Lodges
owing to the presence therein of Brethren born in alien enemy countries.
These have given occasion not only for internaL diesention, but .in rare
instances for proceedings 1mauthorized by the Book of Constitut.ions.
Tlie Board considers that the time has .arrived when, in order to prevent the peace and harmony of the Craft being d'isturbe<l, it is necessary
that all Brethren of German, Austrian, Hungarian or Turkish birth
should be required by Grand Lodge to abstain from attendance, at any
Masonic meeting under the English Jurisdiction during the continuance
of the war, and a resolution will be submitted to that effect.''.
England is battling for her vetj' existence, and 'no outside jurisdiction has any right to criticise, as some Correspondents have done,
whatever action the Grand Lodge of England may see fit. to adopt in
support of the general obJigation. of common defense.

FLORIDA.·
1916.

87th Annual, Jacksonville, Jan. 18-19-20.
Lodges, 233; membership, 12, 724; gain, 663.
The 87th Annual Commul).ication of the Grand Lodge of this
jurisdiction was opened in Ample Form by Most Worshipful Cephas L •
• Wilson, Grand Master.
The Grand Master opens his Annual Address with attractive metaphor and simile, comparing masonry with the various beautiful phases
of nature, etc., all intended to exalt our institution as one of the most
beni:ficent powers and influences established among humankind.
The Grand Master then sets forth in a practical way the usual
Grand Lodge activities, referring with a glow of pride to the continued
prosperity of the jurisdiction, mentioning, among other things, the issuance of dispensations to form eight new lodges, and numerous dispensations to plaee corner stones, and referring particularly to a Special Communication of the Grand Lodge1 held for the purpose of placing the
corner stone of the new temple of St. Petersburg Lodge No. 139.
Apparently a large number of dispensations were granted to ballot
for and confer degrees short of time, a form of dispensation usually,
we believe, discouraged, and as a rule infrequently granted in most
jurisdictions.
Of the so-called rulings or decisions, none, we believe, were of more
than local interest, and are not, therefore quoted.
The Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence, Past Grand
Master Wright, reported a request of one Ramon Mendoza, alleged
Secretary of a so-called Regional Grand Lodge of the Philippines, protesting against the recognition of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine
Islands, recently established, and requesting recog:Dition for the body
which he represented. The report of Brother Wright was adverse to the
pretensions of this alleged masonic body and recognition was refused.
Brother Past Grand Master Wright presents again the report on
Foreign Correspondence and, as is usual with his reports, it possesses
great excellence.
He again discusses, as he did a year ·ago, the true province of a
Correspondence Committee, and, in his judgment, the correct position
is to steer a middle course between too much criticism upon the one
hand, which may create ill feeling, and too little comment on the other

A touch of eloquence is disclosed in Grand Master Ballard's conclusion, which we quote:
"We are the descendants of those ancient builders whose cunning
hand and fertile brain have filled the earth with most wo~derful works
of art. Marble blocks touched by their chi,sel speak of faith and hope,

''The hands which wrought, and. the fertile brains that planned these
wondrous works of art have long since perished from earth. A new form
of expression has supplanted the costly type used by our ancient brethren.
Ours is a nobler art, for we build in the hearts of men a living temple,
a temple of truth and honor, a temple as enduring as Eternity and as
everlasting as is truth itself. Beautiful Milan shall perish; magnificent
Cologne shall crumble and not one stone be left upon another; the
wintry blast shall sing a sad requiem over the spot where now. stands
glorious York, yet, the living temple which Masonry is erec,ting in the
hearts of men shall outlast all of these. For an angel's wing shall not
reach its journey's end, nor an angel's eye penetrate its extended destiny.
My brethren, we, as Masons, have a glorious past, a past filled with
wonderful achievements. Let this be to us an ever-abiding inspiration
to achieve nobler things in the future. Let us build as does the
Nautilus:

Leave thy low-vaulted past!

Leaving thine outgrown shell by life's unresting sea!"
Owing to the present crowded condition of the Masonic H,orne,
there is under consideration the proposition of securing another location
with the idea of transferring the Horne thereto, and a committee to
make investigations along these lines and report at the next Annual
Communication, was appointed.
The Most Worshipful Charles L. Bass, presents his fourth report as
Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, in which he
reviews the proceedings of the usual Masonic Jurisdictions, in which
California, 1914, has an hoI)ored place. He refers in complimentary
fashion to Grand Master Murphy's address, and makes liberal quotations therefrom.
He remarks, in his conclusion, that the year, so far as he has been
able to observe, was one marked by tranquility and prosperity with but
little to record out of the ordinary. The growth of masonry, he states,
has not only been gratifying but surprising as the year preceding had
been, in some respects, one of uncertainty and unrest, and contemplation of the awful war across the seas, has made more manifest to our
country the blessings of peace, and has raised in the hearts of the
brethren everywhere a profound. sense of gratitude to the Supreme
Architect of the Universe for the blessings we enjoy.

IDAHO.
1915.

48th Annual, Boise, Sept. 14-15-16.
Lodges, 64; membership, 4,640; gain, 227.
The Grand Lodge was opeiied in Ample Form by Andrew Christenson, Grand Master. Eleven Grand Officers were present, eight Past
Grand Masters; and representatives from 49 of the 64 lodges in the
Jurisdiction.
The Grand Master's Address is a straight-forward statement of his
official acts during the year. Three new lodges were constituted that
had received charters at the previous annual communication.
Various interpretations of the Masonic law of the Jurisdiction were
rendered by him, and he otherwise discharged in a capable manner the
functions of his high office.
He refers in his report to the somewhat prevalent practice in certain Grand Jurisdictions of electioneering and "log-rolling" for office
in tl:ie Masonic Grand Lodge. He regards this practice as degrading to
the institution of masonry and robbing the fraternity of one of its
greatest glories in that the spirit of the Institution is above the sordidness of selfish aims.
This jurisdiction having a membership of less than 5000, has
accumulated an Orphans Fund, amounting to $76,323.45, from the income
of which disbursements are made to orphans, indigent masons, and
widows of deceased masons, amounting last year to $2581.50, certainly
a magnificent work for a jurisdiction numerically no larger than that
of Idaho.
By amendment to the Constitution, additional safeguards were
thrown about the care and investment of this Fund whereby it is fully
protected from loss through improper investments.
The Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, Most
Worshipful George E. Knepper, who is now the Grand Secretary of
the Grand Lodge of Idaho, presents his fourteenth annual report, which
is filled with discriminating and interesting comment. California fails
to find a place in his report, our 1914 Proceedings apparently having
failed to reach him.
M.'. W.'. FRANCIS JENKINS, Grand Master, Moscow.
R. ·. W. ·. GEO. E. KNEPPER, Grand Secretary, Boise.

ILLINOIS.
1915.

76th Annual, Chicago, Oct. 12-13-14.
Lodges, 837; membership, 139,271; gain, 7,366.
Preceding the formal opening of the Grand Lodge there was a
musical program delightfully rendered by certain members of the Craft.
The Annual Communication was presided over by the Most W orshipful Henry T. Burnap, who at the opening of his address announces
glad tidings to the fraternity in that at the close of the second year of
his administration as Grand Master "increasing prosperity and continued harmony" obtain in the jurisdiction.
The Masonic year preceding was a busy one for the Grand Master,
the increasing number of lodges and the phenomenal addition to membership, resulting in a vast increase in the labors of the head of the
fraternity.
Feeling reference is made by him to the death within the year of
Past Grand Master Brother Edward Cook, who was a prominent figure
for a great many years in the Grand Lodge and whose influence was
pronounced in all of the important proceedings of the Grand Body in
the generation to which he belonged.
The Grand Master refers also to the death of Brother John Chas.
Black, Grand Orator. He served the Grand Lodge in this capacity at
the Annual Communication of 1894-5.
Dispensations to form twelve new lodges were granted within the
year. Grand Lodge ceremonies for the dedication of six masonic halls
took place and six corner stones of public buildings were laid by the
Grand Lodge with masonic honors.
Apparently the only decision rendered by the Grand Master, aside
from a few unquestioned interpretations of masonic law, was concerning whether a lodge might lawfully provide and maintain in apartments
adjoining its place of meeting, so-called Club Rooms, where n';embers
might spend leisure hours in reading, or the enjoyment of games or
other amusements in themselves unobjectionable. His decision was to
the effect that such places, if conducted, within reasonable limitations,
being closed during all sessions of the lodge, and such rooms as were
used as reading rooms only to be opened on Sunday, that a lodge might
lawfully maintain such apartments. Unquestionably a very sensible
decision which was endorsed by the Jurisprudence Committee and approved by the Grand Lodge.

REPORT ON .CORRESPONDENCE

The most important and interesting event of the year, and in some
respects, it is stated, the greatest in the history of the Grand Lodge of
Illinois, took place on the grounds of the Masonic Home at Sullivan on
Monday, July 5th1 the occasion being the dedication of the new Royal
Arch Memorial Hospital. In other words, ·the dedication of a magnificently equipped and thoroughly modern hospital in every respect, donated
by the Grand Chapter of Royal Arch masons of Illinois, a building and
equipment representing an investment of more than $50,000, a gift of
the Royal Arch Chapter Of Illinois, and certainly a magnificent offering
by this fine body of masons to this high form of charity.

Dispensations were granted for twelve new lodges, and to illustrate
the strength .of these new lodges, let it be noted that the charter roll of
Sincerity lodge, one of the new. lodges started in the City of Chicago,
contained three hundred names; another lodge .had one hundred and nine
members to begin with; another, one hundred thirty-seven, and still
another-Brotherhood Lodge- 'three hundred and nine names, as charter
members.

The Masonic Homes of Illinois continue to be administered with
unusual ability. There are now housed at the Orphans' Home at La
Grange, with its sheltering care, 94 children who are being carefully
reared to become useful members of society, and· at the Home for the
Aged and Infirm at Sullivan 150, or thereabouts, are kindly cared for.
The Grand Master refers approvingly to the George Washington
Masonic Memorial Association and bespeaks for it the support and
endorsement of his Grand Lodge.
Acknowledgment is referred to by the Grand ::\faster of the tender
of assistance by Grand Master Bledsoe of California in connection with
the river disaster in Chicago when the steamer Eastland overturned in
Chicago River, causing the loss of hundreds of 1.ives. Grand Master
Burnap gratefully acknowledged the generous tender of assistance by
Grand Master Bledsoe but stated that the Grand Lodge of Illinois coulc1
no doubt give such assistance as might be called for. The tender of aid
was none the less appreciated, and the generosity of California masons,
which is proverbial, was gratefully recognized.
A distinguished visitor in the person of the Grand Secretary
Brother William M. Anderson of Oklahoma was received with the usual
honors. In acknowledgement the courtesy of his reception, he announced
his pride in the state of Illinois, where, it appears, he was born, and
great praise was accorded by him to the wonderful jurisdiction of
Illinois.
Th!) Proceedings recorded the fact that the Grand Orator Brother
Delmar D. Darrah, delivered the annual oration, which met the enthusiastic approval of the Grand Lodge that extended by rising vote its
thanks and appreciation for the scholarly and eloquent effort. An order
was made to print the oration in the Proceedings, but through ·some
misunderstanding between the Grand Orator and the stenograhpic reporter, the oration was not taken down, and the Grand Orator was
unable to furnish a copy, hence we are deprived of the privilege and
pleasure of reading the production.

We have thought in California, if. a lodge started with a hundred
charter members, such as. the Charter Rock Lodge in Berkeley, it was
having a magnificent start, but lodges with an initial membership of
more than three hundred are certainly ''some infants''·
At this Annual Communication 806 lodges were represented, and
only 31 out of the entire jurisdiction that did not have representatives
to the Grand Lodge. This is an evidence of masonic zeal and enthusiasm that in a measure accounts for the wonderful progress of this
great masonic jurisdiction..
The report on Masonic Correspondence is from the gifted pen of
Most Worshipful Owen Scott, "Reviewer" as it is termed. In his
introduction, he estimates the total masonic membership in the world
as 2,221,999, a net increase for the year of 54,910. He states that
these figures are based upon ~fficial sources, except in a few rare
instances. ·we presume, for instance, that the membership of the
Grand Lodge of England is no more than an estimate, because so far
as we have been able to learn, this Grand Lodge does not give figures
as to lodges and membership. We observe that Brother Scott credits
England with 3160 lodges, with a total estimated membership of
210,000.
Concerning the conditions brought about by the war whereby
members of .masonic lodges in England of German birth or parentage
and vice versa members of masonic lodges in Germany of English
birth or parentage are denied the right to visit .their own lodges in
these times of war, Brother Scott has this to say:
''That the terrible, inhuman conflict in Europe would bring dis·
order and chaos was inevitable. Forms, rules and customs have been
wrecked. In this tumult masonry could not escape. In England, men
of foreign birth, though British citizens, have, by action of the grand
lodges been deprived of the privilege of attending meetings .of their
own lodges. Those born in Germany, Austria, Hungary or Turkey,
nations at war against the Allies, are debarred from attending English
masonic bodies during the war. In some cases they have been members
of local lodges for half a life time, but the fact of alien birth casts
them out. Of course there is no right, except that of might, for such
action. To avoid discord and strife this course was adopted. I<'or
further details, see under England.''

Self-preservation is not only the :first law of nature, but it is the
first law of national politics, and we presume is paramount to all
other laws, and it is, of course, the law of self-preservation in a nat1onal sense that has brought about this unmasonic condition where
the Brotherhood of masonry is at least temporarily sub-merged and
made to yield to the law of national expediency and preservation.

The Grand Master callS attention to the fact that in 1918, the
Grand Lodge of Indiana will pass the century mark of its existence,
and recommends that suitable arrangements be made to fittingly celebrate that great event.

32

Brother Scott reviews Califonia, 1914. He quotes from the
address and opinions of Past Grand Master 1\IIurphy. He praises the
oration of Worshipful Brother William H. Waste. He considers "a
doubtful precedent" the presentation of a "solid silver service" to
the retiring Grand Master, and looks upon this as in a sense commercial and mercenary. He approves the idea of a Gand Master's
jewel as a token to the retiring Grand Master, but, as stated, thinks
the presentation of a solid silver service to the retiring Grand Master
unmasonic or unwise, from which conclusion, we presume, it will be
conceded that we, and perhaps others, may dissent.
M.'. w:. RALPH H. WHEELER, Grand Master, Chicago.
R.'. W.'. ISAAC CUTTER, Grand Secretary, Camp Point.

INDIANA.
1916.

99th Year, Indianapolis, May. 23.
Lodges, 560; membership, 73,720; gain, 3,706.
Preliminary to the formal opening of the Grand Lodge an open
session was held consisting of a program of music and an address by
Past Master L. Ert Slack upon the spirit of masonry.
The formal opening of the Grand Lodge, in which a full corps of
Grand Officers was present, a large number of Past Grand Masters,
and Representatives of 554 of the 556 chartered lodges, then took place.
The Grand Master Charles P. Benedict presented his Annual
Address or "Allocution ", as it appears to be called in this jurisdiction, although it differs in no respect from the ordinary Grand
Master's address, wherein the Grand Master reports a most gratifycondition of the Craft throughout the State; he duly constituted
the lodges that received their charters at the preceding Annual
Communication; he lists the lodges to which he had granted dispensations within the year preceding; he gives a memorandum of Grand
Lodge ceremonies performed within the year; also masonic halls dedicated, and otherwise enumerates the usual official acts performed by
the Grand Master.

'

The Grand Master was active in visitations to subordinates within
the year, very much to be benefit and advantage of the various lodges.
He gives the Washington Memorial Association the stamp of his approval and expresses the hope that the Gaud Lodge will take some
favourable action looking to helpful cooperation in that worthy
enterprise.
Under the caption of "decisions", he states that numerous questions arose during the year, but in every case determination was made
by reference to the Rules and Regulations.
In concluding his excellent address, he states that he is in no
sense fearful of the future of masonry, that while certain characteristics may change to some extent, the fundamental truths will abide.
In his opinion, masonry is ''pure goM and needs no alloy'',. and therefore he is inclined to discourage the addition of the ''club feature''
used in some jurisdictions to emphasize social benefits and, in his
opinion such additions, thoug:i1 based upon a seeming demand, will
only, weaken our Ancient Institution.
There is in process of erection in this jurisdiction masonic home
buildings for the housing of the Home system, recently adopted.
Something in excess of $200,000, money actually in hand, was appropriated for the creation of the home plant, and of this $200,000, about
$125,000 has been expended in the buildings now approaching completion, and it is expected that within a year, the Home will be open
for the reception of guests.
A great deal of enthusiasm exists in this jurisdiction over .the
home project, and we doubt not that Indiana will take its place in
the front rank of the American jurisdictions that have adopted the
''Home System'' as a means of administering this form of masonic
benificence.
Decided interest has been aroused in the Grand Juriscliction of
Indiana in the last two or three years in the so-called ''study side''
of masonry. Special Grand Lodge committees have been appointed
to carry on this work among the subordinate lodges, and much zeal
and enthusiasm have been awakened.
This, ·we may say, is a subject that is not only arous~ng interest
in this jurisdiction but in many of our American jurisdictions as well,
and it is a subject that may very properly appeal to all American

''Certain qualifications of a candidate for initiation are derived

The Grand Secretary, in response to inquiries so often addressed
to him relative to what constitute the "land-marks" in masonry, prepared a statement of what in Indiana may be regarded as essential
land-marks,, and inasmuch as this is a subject in which we are all more
or less interested, it will not be amiss to enumerate what the Grand
Secretary considers as masonic land-marks:
''There has been a wide diversity of op1mon among Masonic
writers as to what and what are not absolutely landmarks. In some
jurisdictions they are restricted to. the o~li_g~ti?n, signs 1 tokens a~d
words. Others include the ceremonies of imtiat10n, passing and raising and the form, dimensions and support, orname~ts, furniture and
jewels or their symbols. In others they regard nothing as a landmark
beyond the peculiar secrets.
''The first requisite to a landmark is a custom or rule of action
that must have existed from time immemorial. Its integrity is its
essential element.''

*

*

*

''The mode of Masonic recognition is of all landmarks the most '
unquestioned.
''The division of symbolic Masonry into three degrees is a landmark and has been preserved without question.
''The legend of the third degree is an important landmark, the
integrity of which is one of the essential and important lessons in our
work.
''History tells us there is no rite of Masonry practiced in any
country or language in which the essential elements of the legend are
not taught.
The government of the fraternity by a presiding officer called a
Grand Master, who is elected from the body of the craft, is a landmark of the order, though under different titles in earlier years. The
prerogative of the Grand Master to preside over every assembly of the
craft wheresoever and whensoever held is also a landmark. It is not
from spcial enactment that the Grand Master assumes the chair, which
in England is called the ''Throne.''
"The necessity and privilege of Masons to congregate in Lodges
is a recognized landmark and the government of the brethren when
so congregated as a Lodge is also regarded as a landmark. The necessity that a Lodge when congregated should be tiled is a landmark of
the institution and is never neglected.
"It is a landmark of the order that no visitor unknown to the
brethren present or to some one of them as a Mason can enter a Lodge
without first passing an examination according to ancient usage.

"The belief in the exilltence of God as the Great Architect of the
Universe is one of the most important landmarks of the order.
"The book of the law constitutes an indispensable part of the
furniture of every Lodge and is unquestionably a landmark. It is not
necessarily the Old and New Testament but the book of the law is
meant that volume which by the religion of the country is believed
to contain the revealed will of the Great Architect of the Universe.
In all Christian countries the book of the law is the Old and New
Testament.''

In the opening portion of his address, he calls attention to the
foundation of our government by our masonic forefathers, who were,
in fact, the founders of the Republic, and they inaugurated a govern·
ment built upon the masonic precepts of >Equality, Liberty and Fra·
ternity, a country which they framed with the idea that it should
afford a welcome to all who believed in those great fundamental prin·
ciples, and to perpetuate these principles, the American people and the
institution of Freemasonry are at this date striving that this govern·
ment of the people and by the people may be preserved for remote
posterity.
The Grand Master recounts the very great pleasure which came
to him upon the occasion of the official visit which he paid to the
brethren of Burlington in commemoration of the 75th anniversary of
the first regular lodge in Iowa, and from that initial step, taken by
eleven dauntless and faithful brethren, the present Grand Lodge of
Iowa, with its 55,000 masons, has been evolved, and, in a sense,
masonry is still in its infancy in this wonderful jurisdiction.
The Grand Master mentions the constitution of the two lodges
that received charters at the preceding Annual Communication, and
refers to the Masonic enthusiasm with which these lodges have ent.ered
upon their careers of usefulness.
Especial pleasure is expressed by the Grand Master in mentioning
the large number of dispensations issued by him for new lodges, not
especially because the number was unusual but because they repre·
sented in each case a genuine demand for the light which masonry
brings in the several communities where the lodges were established,
and, beginning under such favorable auspices, he ventures the opinion
that they will each fulfil a splendid masonic destiny.
Numerous dedications of masonic halls were made by him; a large
number of corner stones were placed, and otherwise the year was one
of marked activity.
There is perhaps a minor note in his Address of unfulfilled hope,
in that the Grand Charity Fund, the noblest masonic activity of the
jurisdiction, is not receiving the full measure of support which shoul_d
be accorded to it by the Grand Lodge, and he voices the hope that this
magnificent charity may receive perhaps a more cordial, concerted
support by ap the lodges and brethren, than has been recently ac·
corded to it, to the end that the same may have sufficient annual ·reve·
nue to fully meet the requirements of all worthy applicants.
The Grand Charity Fund in this jurisdiction has always been a
source of especial pride, and with the Masonic Library, are the out·
standing features of Iowa masonry, and we doubt not that the breth·

The Deputy Grand Master delivered an address devoted largely
to a statement of the causes, as understood by him, leading up to the

No change was made in the list of Grand Officers, all of the
Grand Officers being reelected.
It is stated the Most Worshipful Grand Master had been unable
to attend the meetings of the Grand Lodge as frequently as in former
years, having been engaged for the greater part of the preceding

Expeditionary force in France.

Notwithstanding the strain and stress placed upon the country
because of the existing war, masonry, nevertheless, was prospering,
particular attention being drawn to the fact that six new lodges were
founded within the preceding year, two being attached to the military
corps.
A resolution was passed recommending to the subordinate loclges
that dues be remitted of all members on the active service.
The masonic charities of the jurisdiction a:Te well maintained, and
the great work of masonry goes uninterruptedly forward in Ireland,
notwithstanding the great E'uropean crisis.

The Committee on Foreign Correspondence makes a report concerning an elaborate request presented by one Ramon Mendoza of
Manila as ''Grand Secretary of the Grand Regional Lodge of the
Philippines, etc.'', the substance of the request being that Kansas
withdraw the reeognition which it had previously granted to the
Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands recently created. The learned
Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence of Kansas,
Most Worshipful Brother Matthew M. Miller, was unable to discove;
that Mr. Mendoza had made oµt a case to the effect that either the
Grand Lodge Regional of the Philippines, or the Grand Orient of
Spain had any particular ground for protest against the formation of
the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands, and as a logical consequence that any reason had been presented why fraternal recognition
to the. Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands should be withdrawn,
and his recommendations accordingly were unanimously adopted by
the Grand Lodge of Kansas.
The Committee which the Grand Lodge of California appointed
several years ago to investigate exhaustively the condition of masonry
in the Philippine Islands, arrived at the indisputable conclusion that
there was no regular masonry in· the Philippine Islands prior to the
establishment there of lodges chartered ·by the Grand Jurisdiction of
California.

The Grand Lodge was open<1d in Ample Form by the Most Worshipful George B. Winslow, Grand Master.
At the opening of his Annual Address, the Grand Master assures
the brethren of his appreciation of the honor conferred upon him in
electing him to the high office of Grand Master, and congratulates the
Craft that peace and harmony prevail throughout the jurisdiction,
notwithstanding the fact that slight differences are practically unavoidable.
He expresses appreciation of the excellent service given by the
Deputy Grand Master T. J. Adams, as Acting Grand Master, upon
several occasions of the unavoidable absence from the State of the
Grand Master himself.
He feelingly refers to not only the loss which the Grand Jurisdiction suffered, but his own personal loss that occurred within the
year, through the passing away of the beloved and brilliant Past
Grand Master Warren Larue Thomas.
Among the several events which called him from the State within
the year was the annual meeting of the George Washington Memorial
Association which he attended at Alexandria, Va., on Feb. 22nd.
He gives expression to the pleasure which he received upon this
occasion and bespeaks for the project the continued support and approval of the Grand Lodge.
Dispensations for the placing of corner stones to the number of
at least twelve were issued, as were three dispensations to form new
lodges.
He refers to the Masonic Homes, there being in this jurisdiction
an Orphans' Home, and also a Home for Aged Masons, with a feeling
of just pride and gratification, and it may be truthfully stated that
Kentucky occupies a foremost position in the jurisdictions of America in the matter of Masonic Homes, this State being one of the very
first, perhaps the first, to create this form of administering masonic
charity.

MARYLAND.

1915.
129th Annual, Baltimore, Nov. 16th.
Lodges, 116; membership, 17,135; gain, 648.
Within the year the Grand Lodge was assembled in Special
Communication on July 5th to celebrate the Centennial of the laying
of the corner stone of Washington Monument, which occurred on
July 4th, 1815. The occasion was in many respects a notable one,
and was honored by the presence of distinguished masons and officials
of the City of Baltimore.
On July 6, 1915, a Special Communication was held for the purpose of conducting the funeral ceremonies of the Most Worshipful
Brother .Tohn M. Carter, Past Grand Master. This Most Worshipful
Brother served the Grand Lodge as Grand Master 1878-79.
The regular Annual Communication was presided over by Most
Worshipful 'rhomas .T. Shryock, Grand Master, and, as usual, in this
Jurisdiction, he made no report, at least no written report, but at
the opening of the Grand Lodge paid a tribute to the memory and
character of Past Grand Master Carter.
Brother Shryock has served the Grand Lodge of Maryland as
Grand Master for thirty-one consecutive years, a world's record. During these thirty-one years, he has never, so far as we know, rendered
a single decision in interpretation of masonic law. At least no decisions by him of masonic law have ever been recorded, and he stated
several years since that it had never been necessary for him in the
course of a quarter of a century or more as Grand Master to render
a so-called decision, and, as stated, has never rendered a written
report, and the fact that the Grand Jurisdiction of Maryland is one
of the foremost masonic jurisdictions in the United States, and is
carrying forward the great work of masonry in a high and capable
manner within the jurisdiction, may be accepted as evidence that
Brother Shryock's methods are masonically very satisfactory, at least
to Maryland.
The one outstanding event within the year was the death of the
single surviving Past Grand Master, Most Worshipful Brother Carter,
and Maryland occupies the unique position among American juris·
dictions of being the only jurisdiction that does not possess a surviving Past Grand Master, and aside from the Grand Lodge of England, is probably the only jurisdiction in the world that does not
;have a number of surviving Past Grand Masters.
