The character of Correspondence Reports has, we believe, materially changed since the earlier days when it was quite the usual
thing for reporters to indulge in hostile and unseemly critieism in
their reviews of other jurisdictions, but this spirit has praetieally
passed away, and it is seldom, indeed, that anything but kindly referenees are made to other jurisdictions, although differences are
oftimes pointed out as to laws or practices of different jurisdictions,
or how the jurisdiction under review may differ from the one to
which the reporter belongs, and so long as this is done in a spirit of
courtesy and good will, no harm results, but rather as is often the
case, a great deal of good.
Another change has taken place in these reports, in that at the
present time, the reports are regarded as primarily for the purpose
of affording information to the reporter's own jurisdiction, whereby
the busy men of his jurisdiction, who do not have time to examine
the Proceedings of sixty-five or seventy Grand Lodges can gain a
knowledge in condensed form of what is taking plaee in the Masonic
world.
It may be quite true that i:f one is interested in going exhaust·
ively into one partieular subject, and knows exactly the subjeet he
wishes to investigate, he ean, as Brother Gallagher points out, go
into the office of the Grand Secretary of his own jurisdietion, and
obtain the report of the particular state, containing the information
he is after; but oecasions of this kind are extremely rare, and, on the
other hand, there are a great many wide-awake masons in every
jurisdiction that are glad to have in a condensed form a report of
what is going forward in the masonic world.

We have a great admiration for the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts; some of the ablest men the Republie has produeed have
• been active in the masonry of that Commonwealth. We partieularly
have a high regard for the personal qualities and great ability of
Brother Gallagher, as we have experieneed the toueh of his charm·
ing character and personality, yet we eannot quite agree with him in
his conclusions as to the value to a Grand Jurisdiction of a Committee on Foreign Correspondenee, and we ean scareely imagine

At the June Quarterly, a very learned address on the Causes of
Divergence in Ritual by R. vV. Roscoe Pound, Professor of La~ and
Juris1irudence in Harvard University, was delivered. He traces in an
inexhaustive manner the lineage of every American Grand Lodge
and shows how differences in ritual were inherited, and why, because
of this inheritance, differences in ritual still exist. The treatise, as
stated, disclose much painstaking and careful investigation of the
origin of the different American Grand Lodges.
Brother Gallagher at the June Quarterly makes a further report
upon the so-called ''.Regular and Independent Grand Lodge . of
Prance'' and his further investigation simply confirms the conclusion
he arriv~d at a year ago that this alleged Grand Lodge does not possess the essentials of independent sovereignty as a Grand Lodge, and
the recommendation of a year ago that recognition cannot be extended, is repeated and confirmed.

A very important question was presented by the Grand Master
in his Address at the September Quarterly Communication in the
request received from thirteen Master Masons, including .three Chinese brethren for the establishment of a lodge at Peking, China, to
?e known as the International Lodge, and one of the great questions
mvolved was whether a dispensation should be granted for a lodge
non-Christian in charaeter, in which the Holy Bible is not regarded
as one of the "Great Lights" but in which the Volume of the Sacred
Law is made up of the writings of Confucius and other philosophers.
The Grand Master discussed the unchangeable Ancient Landmark of belief in the Supreme Being, Omnipresent, Omniscient
Omnipotent, the Creating and Superintending Power in monotheism'
and believing in this unchangeable Ancient Land-mark, one ma;
properly be a mason whether he regards as his Sacred Book, the Holy
Bible of the Christian, the Old Testament of the Hebrew, the Koran
of the Mohammedan, or the Sacred Book, whatever it may be, of
other religions whose fundamental belief is in one eternal Supreme
Being.
It was therefore, properly decided that a dispensation for a
lodge under the Grand Jurisdiction of Massachusetts might issue to
these faraway masons in Peking, China, where the Volume of Sacred
Law'' would not be the Christian Bible.

At the Quarterly Communication Dec. 8th, which is also counted
as the Annual Communication, an exceedingly interesting event occurred at the opening of the Communication in the introduction to the
Grand Lodge of Brother Daniel Hollinger. He was introduced to the
Grand Lodge by the Most Worshipful Grand Master as one who is
probably the senior living Mason of America. Brother Hollinger
was, at the time of his introduction, more than one hundred years
of age, having been born in September, 1815, and was at the time of
his introduction 78 years a mason. It is a pretty close race between
Brother Hollinger and Past Grand Master Mitchell of Michigan. We
do not happen to have before us the exact date of birth of Brother
Mitchell, but we remember reading in the Proceedings of Michigan
several years ago of the introduction of Brother Mitchell to the Grand
Lodge at its Annual Communication, who at that time was certainly

not less than 96 years of age, and had been a Past Grand Master
much more than half a century. Brother Hollinger, it appears from
a subsequent note in the volume of Proceedings, died in December,
1915, which left Past. Grand Master Mitchell of Michigan, we believe,
the undisputed oldest mason not only of .Ameriea but probably of the
world. (Brother Mitchell died in February, 1916.)
The Grand ]\,faster in the opening portion of his address at this
Communication, refers at length to the controversy that had existed
between Massachusetts and California eoneerning the McGrew ease,
and to the happy solution, so far as the two jurisdictions are concerned, of this perplexing ease.
In our opinion, Massachusetts was extremely generous in her
attitude towards California, and California, we are sure, is very appreciative of the courtesy and consideration of Massachusetts and
of her action in finally restoring to full membership in Massachusetts
our unfortunate Brother McGrew.
The Past Grand officers of California, who visited the Grand
Master, and certain other of the prominent brethren of Massachusetts, will ever remember the kindly treatment extended to them
by these gentlemen in being afforded an opportunity of getting firsthand the Massachusetts side of the controversy, and they were able
to appreciate and understand the very great concessions made by our
Massachusetts brethren, as they understood the case, in order to restore the complete harmony and good will between the Grand Jurisdictions. The sad part of the transaction lies in the fact that while
Brother McGrew was restored to full standing in ]\,fassachusetts
before he passed away, which occurred on the very day following his
restoration, he himself was not acquainted with the fact that the
masonic cloud, which had rested upon him for so many years, had
finally been lifted. His death is recorded in the Proceedings of
Massachusetts in the State Communication of Dee. 28th, with his full
Masonic Title and Honors.

The constitutional number of lodges were represented and after
the opening of the Grand Lodge, the Grand Master delivered his
Annual Address.

masonry, and in this list are printed the names of twenty-nine American jurisdictions and fourteen foreign jurisdictions,

He spoke at the outset of the great difficulties which had beset
the various lodges in the jurisdiction because of the troubled conditions in Mexico, and because, also, many of the lodges belonging to
this jurisdietion are composed largely of Americans.
The Grand Master states that nearly all of his fellow-countrymen,
he himself being an American, were in the early part of the year
huddled together and escorted to the borders of the Republic, hun, dreds leaving all of their earthly interests behind, being compelled
from motives of personal safety to cross the border back into America.
The Grand Master gives a full description of this visit to the
. convention of Grand Masters held in the City of St. Louis, and refers
with a feeling of appreciation to the marked courtesies which he, as
representative of the Grand Lodge of Mexico, received upon that
occasion.
Two lodges in the jurisdiction were obliged, because of the conditions prevailing in the Republic, and the impossibility of keeping the
membership together, to surrender their charters, yet notwithstanding
the loss of these two lodges, the membership of the jurisdiction
showed but a very slight decrease, there being a net loss apparently
of thirty-eight members, and a total membership still remaining of
1156.
The Grand Master, in concluding his address, gave expression to
the pride whieh he feels in the jurisdiction, stating that he would
rather have the honor of being at the head of the little masonic army
in Mexico, than any other position that the world affords, stating
that the devotion and patriotism of the little group of York Rite
masons, who have stood so nobly by their colors, will never be forgotten, holding their organization, as they have, at the risk of their
lives, and he rests his belief in the perpetuity of masonic organization and principles in Mexico upon his knowledge of the high-class
material of which the membership is composed.
The usual reports of Grand Officers were rendered and in the
annual election the Grand Master was chosen to succeed himself in
that exalted station, the administration of his trust having met with
the universal approval of his brethren.
In the small Volume of Proceedings a list is given of the Grand
Lodges of the world that had extended fraternal recognition to the
York Grand Lodge of Mexico as a sovereign Grand Body of Craft

The last name on the list was that of Past Grand Master William
T. Mitchell, who was Grand Master of the Grand Lodge in 1865, and
who survived his Grand Mastership for more than fifty years, being
at the time of his death Feb. 6, 1916, undoubtedly the oldest Past
Grand Master of masons in the world.
The Grand Master upon this occasion made a feeling address in
memory of Past Grand Master Mitchell, concluding his remarks with
the following apt quotation from Goldsmith:
''Like some tall cliff that lifts its rugged form,
Swells from the vale and midway leaves the storm,
Though 'round its breast the rolling clouds are spread;
Eternal sunshine settles on its head.''
The year was evidently a busy one with the Grand Master; he

dispensations were issued to form three new lodges; Grand Lodge
ceremonies were held for the purpose of constituting four new lodges,
which received charters at the preceding Annual Communication; a
large number of corner stones of public buildings were placed, and
not less than eight masonic halls were dedicated within the year.

The Grand Master refers particularly to the subject of the contemplated Masonic Home. This is a project that the Grand Jurisdiction has been looking forward to for several years, having, however, previously agreed that the undertaking would not be entered
upon until at least $100,000 was accumulated for the purpose.
The accumulation of this fund is rapidly approaching the $100,000 mark and it is the expectation of the jurisdiction within the
next two or three years to actually enter upon the construction of
the Home.
On the first day of the Communication, the Grand Orator, Worshipful Brother Albert Lea, delivered an address, replete with tender
and sympathetic illustrations of some of masonic teachings applied to
every-day life. Our space only permits us to excerpt two or three
paragraphs from his· splendid address:
''The Masonic order is not a church, although the Holy Bible is
ever on our altar. It is not a system of religion, although it teaches
the reverential awe which is due from the creature to his creator; to
implore His aid in all laudable undertakings and to esteem Him as the
chief good. It is not a political organization, although it insists that
we be true to our government and just to our country. It is not an
insurance society, although it ever endeavors to afford timely relief to
misfortune and distress; nor is it a charitable organization, although
it enjoins charity, not alone the charity of alms, but the charity that
speaks no unkind word, harbors no evil thoughts, bears no malice or
revenge, which nurtures, loves and protects, which condones, forgives
and forgets.

''It is no one of these things, but rather a great fraternal organization, with the ideal of making its votaries wiser, better and consequently happier, with the ideal of dissolving the artificial cliques and
castes which keep men apart, and bringing them together upon a common platform. Masonic teachings should not only lead us in the great
things, but in every little act of life.''

''The life of service ever lives. Over in California, so many of
you have visited the mission of San Juan Capistrano. You have seen

61

the old church, racked by earthquake, the arches fallen, the padres gone.
They tell you how the old missions were founded, running from San
Diego, twenty-one of them, clear up to San Francisco, just about a day's
journey apart, and today most of them are in ruins. Here is the mission founded by Father Junipero. But it seems, for the moment, as if
the sacrifice of his life has come to naught. Then you go to the mission
play, over at San Gabriel and watch the expression of so many in that
great audience whose eyes are tear filled, touched by the self-sacrifice
of that eloquent old Francisco friar, of his love, for the Indians among
whom he lived. And though the walls of his mission have crumbled, and
though a great mass of the people are of another faith, his sacrifice and
his service will continue to inspire as long as California shall live.
''My Brothers, may the teachings of Freemasonry become really a
part of the warp and woof of our lives, evidenced by purity of life and
rectitude of conduct by nobler .deeds and greater aspirations. May
our eyes be more keen to observe the needs of our fellow-men, and our
hearts more sympathetic to the touch of misfortune so that when we
have reached the end of our toilsome ,journey, and from our hands have
dropped forever the tangled skein of this present life, it may be said,
of each of us: 'He loved his fellow men. He knew the words of
Masonic wisdom, and .he lived a Mason. ' ''

67

The Grand Master refers approvingly to the return of unused moneys·
contributed for the relief of the Ohio flood sufferers, which, however, has
become quite the proper thing in connection with relief work of masonry,
as this return of unused contributions to relief funds is now the common practice among masonic grand jurisdictions, and we may say that
perhaps this practice was established by the Grand Lodge of California
in 1907 in returning to donors over $60,000 of masonic relief funds contributed to sufferers in the earthquake of 1906. California, in that instance, returned more than 20% of the total of relief funds contributed
by outside jurisdictions.
Montana, notwithstanding the fact that it numerically is not a
strong jurisdiction, maintains a splendid Masonic Home. In this jurisdiction, this is rather an expensive form of masonic charity, there being
maintained at the Home at the present time not more than twelve or
fifteen guests at an average cost for the preceding year of about $350
per member. This average cost will, of course, gradually decrease as
the number of guests increases, and after the. unusual expenses incident
to early operation (the home being only a few years in existence) are
disposed of; but even when that shall have been done, it is, we believe,
a proposition of doubtful wisdom to endeavor to maintain a Homo in a
jurisdiction with a membership no larger than that of Montana.
Eloquent addresses were made in the evening of the first day of the
Annual Communication by the Grand Orator, Most ·worshipful Brother
E. C. Day, and by the Most Worshipful Past Grand Master Brother H.
S. Heppner. These addresses were greatly appreciated and by order of
the Grand Lodge were printed in full in the Journal of Proceedings.
The c:losing ceremony of the Annual Communication was the presentation of the Signet Ring. The retiring Grand Master Most Worshipful Brother Smith presented in a pleasing address the signet ring to
his successor, Most Worshipful Brother W. H. Allen. In the presentation he called attention to the many distinguished men of the jurisdiction that had worn the ring; he called attention to the symbolism of the
ring, and to the high ideals of service which it implied, and the sacredness of the trust which it imposed.
Grand Master Allen fittingly responded and assumed the responsibility which the signet ring impressed upon its bearer.

of masonic law.

The Grand Master presents a clean-cut, straight-forward statement
of his official acts within the year.
Under the heading of decisions, he states that many questions were.
propounded to him within the year, all of which were amply provided
for in the Digest, and none of them requiring anything in the nature of
an official decision.
He refers with pride to the Masonic Home, characterizing the institution as an_ expression of the ''noble work of the Fraternity.''
Reference is made in his report to an incident that occurred on
Feb. 16th, whereby through the courtesy of one of his subordinate
lodges, he was given the extreme and unique pleasure of a fraternal
visit with Most Worshipful Brother Albert G. Burnett, Grand Master
of California, by means of the great transcontinental "voice railway".
Our
orshipful Grand Master presented, through the telephone, the
comphments of the 60,000 masons of California to the Most Worshipful
Grand Master and brethren of the jurisdiction of the splendid State
of New Jersey, stating that though the two jurisdictions were separated
by more than three thousand miles of territory, they yet are bound
together by the indissoluble bonds of brotherhood, and that the principles which underlie the great Fraternity, whether it be in California
or New Jersey, are as ever-lasting as the Throne of God, and that
though madness and barbarism seem for the moment to dominate a
large part of the so-called civilized world, yet our Grand Master Burnett assured his Brother across the continent, that the madness would
pass and give way to a better civilization, founded upon the eternal
principles of the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man.

:1

The Most Worshipful Grand Master of New Jersey expressed to his
brother in California the reciprocal fraternal feelings entertained by the
Craft of New Jersey towards their brothers at the Golden Gate and
that while thousands of miles separated their persons, yet the 'voice
from. across the continent seemed but a few yards away, and that this
was m a sense typical of the close. bond of brotherhood that united
those in the Fraternity, though separated by the width of a continent.
The incident was certainly very delightful, and one that will no doubt
linger in the recollection of the distinguished brothers.

The first day of the Annual Communication was made.notable, in a
certain sense, by the reception of eminent brethren from other jurisdictions, reference being made to a fraternal visit from the Most Worshipful Grand Master of Pennsylvania, and the other Grand Officers
from this jurisdiction and from )Tew York and Delaware. They were
received with the usual Grand Honors and escorted to seats in the East.
The Grand Lodge accepted the custody at this Communication of
what is known as the "Old Masons' Hall" of :N"ew Jersey, the oldest
masonic building in America north of the Mason and Dixon Line.
This building was occupied as one of the :first school buildings in the
State of New Jersey, and was in the very center of the scene of stirring
revolutionary action at the time that Washington crossed the Delaware,
and fell upon his surprised and panic-stricken enemies, marking one of
the notable successes of Washington's military career.
This old masonic building had been acquired through the patriotic
activities of certain of the prominent masons of New Jersey, who at
this Communication handed over to the Grand Lodge the key of the
famous old structure ''almost as dear to the hearts of masons of New
Jersey", the Committee states, "as our :flag is dear to all of us who
love America".
Brother Wilbur F. Sadler, Jr., Chairman of the Committee, received
the grateful thanks of the Grand Lodge, with the assurance that the
old building would be for all times safe-guarded and protected.
Something of an innovation, so far as Grand Lodges are concerned,
obtains in this jurisdiction in that the Grand Master apparently appoints at each Annual Communication a committee of nine ladies who
have oversight of the domestic affairs of the Masonic Home. Very
proper and appropriate and extremely unselfiBh, so far as the ladies
are concerned, to assume this important and responsible task.
Worshipful Robert A. Shirrefs, Chairman, again presents the report
on Foreign Correspondence, and as usual, the report possesses a high
order of merit.

and the great Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons has become

"The very universality of our Order, so frequently our proud
boast, has, by reason of its all-embracing nature, produeed a cleavage
in the bonds that unite us.

Masonic body is beating in aetive and substantial sympathy with the

Grand Officers, to the Masonic Home at Utica, this being the one

The Grand Master refers with a certain measure of satisfaction
to the large amount raised by the various lodges for the so-called
"Redemption Fund", that is, for the redemption of a portion of the
debt standing against the New York City property, the amount now
accumulated towards this fund being $703,635.55, leaving about $40Q,.
000 still needed to complete the Fund.
We presume there is hardly another Grand Jurisdiction in the
world with the financial strength to lift such a tremendous financial
obligation.
A Balance Sheet is presented showing the total of the various
Funds and Properties belonging to the jurisdiction of $5,741,086.70,
against which there are liabilities consisting of outstanding bonds on
the New York City properties, and otherwise, of perhaps half this
amount. The obligations, however, are in a fair way of rapid liquidation, so that, within a reasonable time, this jurisdiction will have
property worth probably five and a half millions or six millions of
dollars, free of debt.
The Grand Lodge at this Communication was favored with distinguished visitors. The Most Worshipful I,ouis A. Watres, Grand
Master of Pennsylvania, accompanied by several of the Grand Officers

Grand Master ·watres referred to the Great Masonic charities of the

York. Speaking of these institutions, Grand Master Watres says:
"We have at Elizabethtown, midway between Lancaster and
Harrisburg, a Masonic Home that is perhaps one -0£ the largest in the
world. We have there 981 acres of land. We have there a Grand•
Lodge Hall that cost us over half a million dollars. We have invested
there a million and a quarter dollars. We have today 276 guests there,
the adults averaging 70 years old, and some as old as 94. We have
children there up to the age o.f 14 years. And in our State the heart
of every Mason is at Elizabethtown. That is the favorite of all of us
there. When a Mason wants to do something, he does it for the
Masonic Home at Elizabethtown. I believe that the work you have
done at Utica and the work we are trying to do at Elizabethtown, will
stand out as perhaps the noblest flower of all our efforts, and I believe
that, as time goes on, there shall be unveiled in the work at Utica
and Elizabethtown a spirit which is there manifest, which is being
developed there-I believe that perfection will finally be unveiled
there in the work we are doing and that the achievement will ~row

We would ilke to ask some of our masonic reviewers who oppose
the Masonic Home system, South Carolina for example, how they
would manage the widows and orphans and distressed aged masons
problems in such jurisdictions as New York and Pennsylvania, except
through the ''Home'' system~
The New York Masonic Home is a "family of five hundred", and
in the Pennsylvania Home 276 guests are now provided for, and the
Home establishment there is of comparatively recent creation.
Brother Leonard Wood, ranking Major General of the United
States Army, was also a distinguished guest of the Grand Lodge at
this time. He made some rather pertinent remarks upon the subject
of preparedness and the benevolent purposes of the United States in
bestowing the blessings of good government in certain instances
where it has intervened for this purpose, and we are glad to quote a
few of his remarks upon these subjects:
''This little Cuban flag, that you have up here this morning, is
really an American flag, in one sense. Its place there is due to the
philanthropic work of our own people.
"We intervened in Cuba to establish conditions of order and to do
away with certain conditions that we thought were undesirable. We
built up a little nation which is really living under our protection.
That is pretty good evidence to the world of America's spirit of fair
dealing and fair play. But the important thing to bring home to our
own people is, I believe, that fair dealing and fair play and national
morality will not protect us. We all know that the most blameless
nations have been ruthlessly overrun and deprived of their rights, and
we know that this has been done, not only in our own experience, but
it has been done in the experience of the past centuries. The story is
the same now as it has been for centuries. We also know that we
have something worth defending. I know we have, and so do you.
We have institutions that we believe are vital to humanity. We have
a government that we are going to defend to the last ditch. We have
homes that we are going to defend. Now, if we are going to do these
things, we as sensible men must recognize the fact that we cannot
"successfully defend them without some kind of reasonable preparation.''

There is also in this jurisdiction another officer peculiar to New
York, known as the Grand Historian, filled by the able and scholarly
Right Worshipful Ossian Lang, whose Dissertation at this time was
upon a subject assigned to him by the Grand Lodge, to-wit: "Was
Freemasonry derived from the Medieval Craft Gilds of Masons~"
The erudite treatise is, of course, too long to be quoted in this report,
but one or two if his ":findings" are given because they contravene
the ordinarily accepted theory that Speculative masonry was the outgrowth of original "Operative Masonry", whereby Operative Masonry gradually faded away and in its place was erected the Speculative Masonry of today.
His ''findings'' a Te as follows:
"If you accept my :findings, we shall agree:

(1) That Freemasonry, as we know it, is in nowise derived from
operative Masonry.
(2) 'fhat a 'symbolic' fraternity existed, whos~ members, under Anglo-Saxon conditions, frequently chose to obtam the freedom
of the Masonic craft gild by 'acceptance.'
(3) That the explanation foT the preference accorded t? ~he
Masonic gild may be inferred f;om the aspect. of cathedral build~~g
in the medieval age more especially the function of Masons, to gi: e
form to symbols of 'predetermined significance, the brotherhood striving to unite men of diverse interests and to preserve the 'geometry'
of sacred things.
(4) That on the Euro~ean ~ontinent t~e brotherhood h~d not
even an elbow-touch connect10n with craft gilds, the latter bemg exclusively trade organizations.
(5) That the history of the 'Laws, Porms and Usages' of the
Fraternity while of less significance than that of 'the Arts and
Sciences thereof,' nevertheless is of con~iderable interest, and serves
to interpret much that could not otherwise be accounted for.
(6) That 'Laws, Forms an? Usages' are largely derived from
association with Masonic craft gilds and form merely the outer shell
or mold into which the substance was poured which developed into
the kind of Freemasonry we know.''

1915.

26th Annual, Wellington, May 12th.
Lodges, 198; membership, 13,435; gain, 171.
The Grand Lodge was opened in the Annual Communication in

~U:ple

The matter probably of prime importance in this jurisdiction is
the presentation of the Balance Sheet, wherein the resources of the
Grand Lodge are set forth, a list of the various funds given and a
statement of income and expenditures, all set forth in an exc~edinglv
businesslike manner.
•
This Grand Lodge has now been in existence just twenty-five
years; it now has invested assets of about $175,000 and during its
existence has distributed in the way of charity an amount about
equal to its present total invested funds, that is to say $125,000,
representing in that manner amounts received of about $300 000 in
addition to expense of administration, surely an extremely gr;tifying
record.
One of the first orders of business in the Annual Communications
of this Grand Lodge is the election of Grand Master and under this
order of ?usiness, the Most Worshipful Brother John' Joseph Dougall
was unammously elected to succeed himself in that exalted station.
From the report of. the Board of General Purposes, which is the
business organization within the Grand Lodge, the general condition
of masonry is set forth, and, as one would naturally expect, the
principal topic discussed is the war in progress upon the continent of
Europe, and notwithstanding the :financial support which the Grand
Lodge is extending in the patriotic cause, the lodges, without ex·
ception, have not only carried on their charitable work as usual but
showed an improvement and advance over the preceding year. '
Partic~lar mention is made of the beneficial results accruing to
the subordmate lodges through the official visits made by the Grand
Master to many parts of the Dominion within the preceding year,

and the zeal and activity of the Grand Master is mentioned as greatly

NORTH CAROLINA.

appreciated by the Craft.
The Grand Master was in due course installed, following his reelection, and, after his installation, presented his annual address to
the Grand Lodge, which was made up principally of a resume of the
progress of the Grand Lodge from its formation to the present time,
this being the Twenty-fifth Anniversary of its foundation.

1916.

The Grand Lodge of New Zealand certainly overcame the great
difficulties and obstacles placed in the way of its formation by the
Mother Grand Lodges of England, Scotland, and Ireland, particularly of the persistent opposition of the Grand Lodge of Scotland.
The Grand Lodge of Ireland was the first of the three to accord
recognition, and this was followed a number of years afterwards by
the Grand Lodge of England, the favorable action of the Grand
Lodge of England having been brought about largely through the
kindly offices of the late King Edward, VII, before he ascended
the 'Throne, and while he was still the Grand Master of the
Grand Lodge of England, and recognition from the Grand Lodge of
Scotland was only grudgingly extended two years previously in 1913,
after New Zealand had achieved a membership of more than 13,000
with 190 or more subordinate lodges.
The Grand Master, in his address, contrasts the differences in the
policies of the Government of England towards her colonies, which
is marked with extreme liberality and the granting of well-nigh full
and unrestrained liberty of action, with the policy of the Grand
Masonic Lodges of England and Scotland, in accordance with which
freedom is denied to the very last possible moment, and ·only until
after the entire masonic world, outside of these grand lodges have
accorded independent recognition, has recognition been extended.
The experience of the Grand Lodge of New Zealand is acquiring
independence from the Grand Lodges of England and Scotland differs
in no material respects, so far as we have been able to discover,
from the experience of Australia and other Grand Lodges in achieving their independence of the so-called Mother Grand Lodges.
The report on Foreign Correspondence by the Right Worshipful
Brother Sydney Clifton Bingham is a comprehensive and intelligent
review of the various Grand Jurisdictions, in which California, 1914,
·has a prominent place, with quotations from the report of Grand
Master Murphy, the oration of Worshipful Brother Waste, reports
of committees, etc.

Walter L. Stockwell. He indicates what, in his .opinion, masonry consists of. He states what, in his judgment, is masonry's message, and
what, as he understands masonry, is its mission. Of what masonry
consists, ~e says in part:
·
''The Constitution of the United Grand Lodge of England
'Pure ancient Masonry consists of three degrees and no more;
tered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason, including the Supreme Order of the Holy Royal Arch'. This statement is made at
this time to emphasize the necessity of getting back to fundamentals,
at least occasionally. Anything else which is today grouped under
the head of Masonic degrees or orders, may be put down as the outgrowth of the zeal, the ambition, or the fertile brain, of some men or
group of men to achieve fame for themselves, and possibly render a
service to the seeker after higher light in Masonry. It is a well established fact that in the beginning the Royal Arch degree and that
of Knight Templar, were conferred in a Lodge of Master Masons.
Hence, we repeat that the Symbolic Lodge, the L-Odge of JI.faster
Masons, is fundamental; and anything which cheapens or commercializes the institution is, in our judgment, a serious reflection upon the
dignity and character of Masonry. How many men are t.here in your
acquaintance today who are seeking admission into our Lodges solely
because of the attraction that Ancient Craft Masonry has for them
with its wonderful lessons .and its opportunities for service. Too frequently we fear there is something else in our present scheme of socalled Masonic degrees which attract their attention. Do not get the
idea that we disapprove of the Royal Arch degrees or the Templar
Orders, or the Scottish Rite or the Shrine. We have them all, but it is
our desire tonight to impress upon yon the fact that when all is said
and done, Symbolic Masonry it was that has stood the test of opposition, of prejudice, of the anathemas of the church, and unless Masonry
in this form is kept strong and vigorous your whole scheme of higher
degrees falls. And we may add that we cannot disassociate our memberRhip in any of these other degrees or bodies with our capacity as
Master Masons. May we urge that nothing ever be done in a public
way which brings discredit upon Masonry in the eyes of the profane.
J,et us never forget that by our conduct as men is our institution
jm1ged. Our :Masonry is not a cloak that can be put on and off at will,
it must be a part of the life we live.''
Of Masonry's message, he says in part:
"Masonry teaches brotherhood and democracy; democracy and
brotherhood are the solutions of the world's problems today. Our
thoughts instinctively turn to the world conflict raging today, and the
extreme delicacy of our national position. May it not be our part to
lead the world out of the darkness which has fallen upon it. Let us
not lose our sanity. May not this nation, in which all the old world
elements and nationalities are being fused, show to the warring peoples of Europe that there is no reason why hatred should rule in their
lives; and in this time of our national crisis may we refrain from
saying the word or
the act which may imperil our safety and
our solidarity. Let us remember that there is but one name under

Concerning the subject of the war and the part that Nova Scotia
and the masons of Nova Scotia are taking, the Grand Master states:
"The British Empire is not engaged in this war for the purpose of
conquest, but in order to uphold the honour o.f our country, to protect
the weak and innocent from the ruthless hand of the strong wrongdoer, and to preserve to the whole world, freedom, honor and justice.
Many of the sons of Nova Scotia have voluntarily gone forth to assist
in the great struggle, which is now being carried on by the British
Empire and her allies against those nations which have disturbed the
peace of the world, destroyed the homes of the innocent, and who are
waging war against all that we hold most sacred.
''Among those who have gone to the Front, are many of our Masonic brethren and the sons of brethren of this Grand Masonic Juris·
diction. The end of that conflict does not appear to be near, and no
man can prophesy within measurable distance at what time the war
will end, nor what the outcome will be. It is our duty as Masons to
loyally support the Government in carrying on this war against those
who wonld trample under foot and destroy all the principles of our beloved Order. I believe that in the end, justice and right, although now
seriously threatened, will triumph, and that while we cling to the ancient landmarks, principles and charges of Freemasonry, and nobly do
our duty in whatever station it has pleased the Grand Architect of the
Universe to place us, we need have no fear of what the future has in
store for our Grand Lodge, nor for the brethren herein represented.
Let us pray for peace, but at the same time let us do our share of the
work necessary to be done in order to obtain and secure that peace we
hope and trust will come ont of this conflict, and will forever hereafter
prevail throughout the world.
"We cannot all enlist in the great army that is now fighting and
shedding its blood for King and country, but we can serve our King
and country as good and loyal citizens of this great and glorious Empire and fulfil the mission of Masonry by exerting ourselves to make
provisions for the care of the wounded soldiers, to help support the
families of those who fall, and to bring as much comfort as possible to
all those in distress and want. That I believe is the mission of the
Freemasons of this Grand Jurisdiction.''
Concerning the state of masonry, the Grand Master indicates that
the year ha,d been one of comparative quiet, the minds of the people
being fully absorbed with the war that very little time had been left
to consider the subject of masonry. The general condition, however,
of the Fraternity continues excellent; the finances of the Grand Lodge
are in flourishing condition, and the benificent funetions of the fraternity are discharged in a highly laudable manner.
The Grand Master rendered a few unimportant rulings concerning local law and made a number of official visits to subordinates

The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form by the Most W or·
shipful Grand Master Brother George L. Marshall.
As is usual in this Grand Jurisdiction, practically every subordi·
nate lodge was represented. In other words, out of the 541 chartered
lodges, only sixteen were without representation.
'rhe Grand Master reports a year of marked official activity. Dis-·
pensations were granted to form two new lodges; numerous emergent

communications were held for the purpose of constituting lodges, dedicating masonic halls, placing corner stones of public buildings, etc.
He manifested a degree of activity in visitations to subordinate
lodges, inspiring by his official presence, in the various portions of his
magnificent jurisdiction, interest and enthusiasm among the members.
Speaking of "Decisions", he states that numerous requests have
been made of him for opinions, etc., and that all have been answered
by reference to the Code or Proceedings, and he adds that in his
judgment, the jurisprudence of the jurisdiction should not be' encum·
bered with needless decisions which are nothing than constructions
of by-laws or code, stating, also, that through the work of the splendid
Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence, which, through the wisdom of a
long line of capable predecessors, has actually established the masonic
law of the jurisdiction, all attempts to confuse by the addition of new
decisions, are unwise and unnecessary.
In closing his address, Grand Master Marshall thus touches the
high points of masonry:

'' Poss.essed with a. la.nguage and history, Freemasonry has had
for centuries but one mrss1on, and that mission is to direct the minds
of me:r; t~ the one true living God, and to vitalize in the highest sense
the p~m.c1ples of human Brotherhood. Thus Masonry, the hand-maiden
of rehgrou, strengthens the Mason in his service to God, to his country, and to humanity, and is found a living force for .;ood in every
avenue of worthy effort. Our growth is therefore not ph~nomenal, b1{t
rather natural, and there can be no danger to the Institution in numbers. so long as the Ancient Principles govern and inspire the Craft.''

At the March Quarterly Communication, special refer~nc~ was
made b the Grand Master in his Address to the death w1th1~ the
ear ofyWorshipful James M. Lamberton, for sixteen years cha~rman
~f the Committee on Foreign Correspondence. Bro. Lamberton is de-

scribed as an eminent scholar, a zealous freemason who had enunciated
the precepts of masonry for many years and had exemplified these
precepts in his daily life, a man. whose work as Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence had helped to place Pennsylvania
in the front rank of Masonic jurisdiction of the world and Philadelphia, as it is claimed, the "premier Masonic city of America".
Brother Lamberton 's loss is a severe one not only to the jurisdiction of Pennsylvania but to American masonry as well, and the volume
of 1915 proceedings appears without the usual report of Committee on
Foreign Correspondence, no one having been selected to serve in that
capacity for the current masonic year.
At the December Quarterly Communication, which, as stated,
stands in a sense for the Annual Communication, 445 lodges out of a
total of about 490, were represented,-surely a fine representation of
the lodges of the jurisdiction.
At this Communication reports of the various Funds were presented, and an inspection of these reports reveals the wonderful financial strength of this jurisdiction, probably the richest jurisdiction in
the world, the total of its assets reaching the vast sum of $4,456,432.10.
This jurisdiction has invested in its vast Masonic Home properties
more than one million dollars, and the scope of the Masonic Home institutions being, in many respects, greater than any other jurisdiction in
the world.
From the report of the Committee on Masonic Homes, one learns
that there are now sheltered in this Institution, 245 guests, and at the
present rate of expansion, this total will unquestionably within a few
years reach five hundred.
In concluding its report on Masonic Homes, the Committee uses
the following eloquent language touching these beneficent institutions:
'"rhe Grand Lodge, we are sure, takes pleasure in contemplating
this cluster of Homes as the full flower of its noblest effort, plante<l
in love, nurtured in constancy, refreshed by the gentle <lews of
thoughtful an<l tender attention, and developed in the sunshine of
unselfishness.
''Here, apart from the shock and tumult of existence, the heart
may throb with no disquieting alarms to jar its perfect rhythm.
Within the shelter of this Masonic Garden of Content, the age([ may
rest in comfort at the close of the day and the young may take hope
and gather inspiration for the morning.
''Age and youth alike are beautiful. We cherish both here with
ties of tenderness, the one coming in from the the long road upon
which the other is preparing to enter. As our guests, they are entitled

other words these decisions are not passed upon by a Jurisprudence
Committee or by the Grand Lodge, the word of the Grand )faster
being final.
Among these decisions, we observe one to the effect that the Secretary of a certain lodge was not to furnish information requested by

the guests at the Masonic Homes were not to become members of the
Order of the East Star, and directing that certain activities in this
connection must immediately cease, from. all of which, it is fair to
conclude that the Order of the Eastern Star is not looked upon with
particular favor by this jurisdiction, if the rulings of the Grand Master
may be taken as reflecting the sentiment of the Grand Lodge.

'l'~e Fourth Annual Communication was presided over by the Most
Worshipful George R. Harvey, Grand Master.

He extends greetings, in his address, to the assembled masons
and congratulates the jurisdiction upon the prosperity which has at'.

. He calls attention to the substantial gain in membership of 119,

He refers feelingly to the death within the year of the Right
Worshipful Deputy Grand Master, Brother Burton Whitcomb, and
gives voice to the general feeling of loss which the jurisdiction sustained in the passing away of this distinguished and honored brother.
He refers with pride to the fact that fifty-three Grand Jurisdictions have already recognized his Grand Lodge as a sovereign Grand
Lodge of Ancient Craft masons,. and at the time of his report was rendered, there were not over six or seven American Grand Lodges that
had not already taken favorable action, and of the six or seven,
several, since the date of his report, have extended 'l'ecognition.
He refers at length to the protest entered by one Ramon Mendoza,
an alleged official of an alleged Regional Grand Lodge of the Philippines, against the action of the masonic world i~ recognizing the
Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands as the established masonic
power in the Archipelago, and in response to a request from Massachusetts, Grand Master Harvey goes extensively into this protest and
demonstrates absolutely and conclusively the utter absence of merit
in the pretense of this alleged masonic body, and that the protest is
entitled to no consideration whatever; and we may say that this has
been the attitude, so far as we have been able to discover of all the
Grand Lodges to whom the protest was addressed, and in not a single
instance has a doubt been expressed as to the propriety of the recognition already extended to the properly and legally formed Grand
Lodge presided over by Brother Harvey.
Perhaps the one outstanding event in the masonic activities of the
preceding year was the laying of the corner stone of the new Masonic
Temple at Manila on August 14, 1915, a building which when completed will be the most modern in design, construction, and general
equipment in the far East. It will be six stories high and will be far
the most conspicuous building in Manila, and in addition to its equipment as a business and office building, it will have not less than two
complete floors devoted exclusively to masonic purposes.
The Fraternity in the Philippines may well be proud of this visible evidence of power and influence, and the Fraternity is certainly
to be congratulated upon carrying forward to completion, in the face
of adverse conditions, this magnificent project.
A feeling of good will and amity prevails between the lodges belonging to the Grand Lodge and the one or two other outside lodges;
the Portuguese Lodge for example, which were in existence when the
Grand Lodge was formed, and which still retain their allegiance to the
Mother Grand Lodges, from which they received their charters. This
feeling of good will and friendship means much to the masonry of the

''And here, perhaps, it might not be amiss to note, that this is not
the first time the fate of civilization has been trembling in the balanc-e.

PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.

"Five hundred years before the Christian era Greece was the abode
of culture the home of art, the seat of philosophy, the centre of civilization and the cradle of democracy. Against the little state of Attica,
no larger than one-third of Prince Edward Island, came the Persian
hordes under Cyrus. On the field of Marathon the Greeks were victorious and Civilization was saved.
''A thousand years later Civilization was again threatened by the
invasion of the Huns, who swarmed from Asia over Central Europe.
''Again in the Eighth Century there was another turning l!oint in
the world's history, when at the great battle of Jours the. qi;iest10n was
decided whether Europe should be Mohammedan or Christian.
''The world reached another crisis one hundred years ago, when
the Corsican gunner stood upon the shores of France, gazing with
ambitious eye, across the English Channel to the land he!d by 'the
nation of shopkeepers.' He had trampled Europe under his feet; he
had waded through blood to gratify a boundless ambition; and he
wished to have England at his feet. The question then was, as it is
now, military despotism against democracy; but on the field of Waterloo the principles of liberty were vindicated and the arms of Napoleon were shattered.
"In the present supreme moment of .the world's exist~n~~ let. us
hope and trust that history may repea~ itself, ai;d that Civ:ihzat10n,
and Right and Truth may come off triumphant m the terrific clash
of arms that is deluging Europe with blood.''

In closing his brief and businesslike address, the Grand Master
craves the indulgence of the Grand Lodge in calling their attention to
the fact that he had served that Grand Body in different postions for·
ten years, and that he felt the time had arrived when he was justified
in laying aside the mantle of office, and transferring to other shoulders
some of the responsibilities that he had assumed, although very cheerfully assumed, in the preceding decade of time, assuring his brethren,
at the same time, that he would_ experience contentment and satisfaction in contemplating the carrying forward by other of the noble
work of the fraternity in the jurisdiction.

Notwithstanding the marked increase in numbers, the Grand
Master is certain this gain has not been made at the expense of quality,
and believes that the high standard of manhood demanded on admission in to the Craft has in no sense been relaxed.

After installation, the newly elected Grand Master, Most Worshipful Reuben Samuel Bemis, upon assuming his station, addressed the
Grand Lodge in an appreciative and feeling manner. He called particular attention to the line of grand and honorable men who had preceded him in the exalted station of grand Master, and expressed the
hope that he would receive the generous and kindly •consideration of
his brethren in endeavoring to not unworthily maintain the honor and
high standing of the Grand Body that had been won for it by his distinguished predecessors.
There is no report on correspondence.

He refers with feeling to the death within the year of Most Worshipful Brother John Leslie, Past Grand Master of the Grand Lodge. of
Manitoba, and Honorary Past Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
Saskatchewan.
On account of the serious illness of the former Grand Secretary,
he was forced to relinquish his office, with its duties and responsibilities, and his unexpired term was filled out by appointment of Right
Worshipful Brother Rev. W. B. Tate.
The Grand Master favored a number of the lodges of his jurisdiction with his official presence during the year and his visits were
so distributed as to reach nearly every part of the Province. Six
new lodges that received charters at the preceding annual Communication were duly constituted, and dispensations were granted by him
to form three new lodges.

9th Annual, Regina, June 16th.

The Annual Communication was presided over by Most Worshipful Lauchlin Taylor McDonald.
Welcome to the City of Regina was extended to the Most W orshipful Grand Lodge by the Mayor O'f the City, with suitable acknowlmerl't on behalf of the Grand Lodge by one of the officers designated
for that purpose.
The Grand Master, in his address, contrasts the present condition
of the fraternity in the jurisdiction with the condition that existed
only a few years before ill 1906 when the Grand Lodge was organized.
At that time there were within the Province, twenty-four lodges with
only 900 members, and within the brief span of ten years the lodges
increased to 116 with a membership of nearly 7,000.

Special reference is made by the Grand Master to certain catastrophes that had occurred within the preceding year, particular reference being made to the war precipitated in Europe, in which the Grand
Master naturally is a strong partisan of England, believing, as he does,
that the war was forced upon England through the machinations of
Germany.
In closing his address, he expresses the opinion that while the
preceding year had been a strenuous one, it nevertheless had been one
of masonic growth and prosperity, whereby masonry stands higher in
the Province than at any time since the formation of the Grand Lodge,
and he voices the opinion that the terrible war in which E'urope is involved has had the effect of causing the brethren more seriously to
consider what masonry stands for than it had ever done before.

SCOTLAND.
1915.

No change was made in the official roster of this Grand Lodge,
the Most Worshipful Col. Robert King Stuart, Grand Master.
From an inspection of the reports of the quarterly proceedings, we
observe that the business of the Grand Lodge went forward in much
the usual manner, during the preceding year.
Six new loilges were apparently created in the several provinces.
The reports of the Board of General Purposes, Board of Annuity,
Grand Stewards of Orphans' and Widows' were presented at the various communications, and adopted, and, inasmuch as practically the
entire business of the Grand Lodge of Scotland was transacted through
these boards, very little remains for the Grand Lodge to do at the
Quarterly Communications other than to ratify the actions of the
Boards, and to officially adopt their reports.
The charity scheme of this Grand Lodge seems to be in a sense
quite comprehensive, and under the annuity system in vogue here, a
vast amount of charity and good will is distributed to needy and deserving brothers, their widows .and orphans, not only in Scotland proper,
but throughout the entire jurisdiction, wherever Scottish lodges exist.
A letter is published from our own Brother W. B. Melish of Cincinnati, Chairman of the War Relief Committee of the United States,
and as expressive of the appreciation which the Scottish Grand Lodge
felt for the kindly action of our American brethren, the following was
adopted:

''Grand Commitee therefore resolved that if and when the claims
upon the funds of Grand Lodge grow to such an extent as to cause
anxiety, .the circumstances will be laid before the Executive Committee
of the Masonic War Relief Association of the Unitd States, and their
kind offer utilized for the purposes for which they design it.''
}~rom the above resolution, it will be observed that while the spirit of
benevolence manifested by our American brethren through this so-called
War Relief Association is appreciated, there is manifest a desire, which
has shown itself in other of the European jurisdiction, to permit their
own Grand Lodges to take care of the question of war relief themselves, and that if American masonic help is finally needed later, our
good American masons will be so advised.

13 9th Annual Charlestown, Dec. 13-14.
Lodges, 262; m~mbership, 16,712; gain, 438.

The Most Worshipful George T. Bryan, Grand Master, presided.
There were present at the Annual Communication . eight Past Grand
Masters, and 260 out of 262 lodges were represented.
The Grand Master reports issuing dispensations for three ~ew
lodges; constituting six lodges which received charters at the previous

The Grand Lodge received a deputation from the Grand Lodge of
Maryland in advocacy of the George Washington :N"ational Memorial
Association project, and voiced its approval of that project by voting
an appropriation of $3,000 to the enterprise.
1''rom the report of the trustees of the Masonic Home Fund, it
appears that thirty-one orphans and several widows received aid from
this Fund, a total expenditure of $3,510 being recorded.
Grand Lodge beneficenee in aid of widows and orphans is administered in this Jurisdiction through the Private Aid system, instead
of the Masonic Home system, the Masonic Home system having been
voted down a couple of years since, and the report of the Committee
on Foreign Correspondence is throughout sprinkled with illustrations
drawn from experiences of various Homes, showing the great expense
of this method of administration over the Private Aid system.
No one, so far as we are aware, has ever claimed that the Masonic
Home system was a money saver, and the expenditure of South Carolina last year of $3,500 to carry on its charity establishment is certainly very economical in comparison with the many thousands expended, for instance, by California in maintaining its two homes, the
one at San Gabriel for ehildren, and the one at Decoto for the aged
masons, with its modern hospital adjunct, etc.; yet masonry has never
been recommended, so far as we know, as either a money maker, or
money saver, and the question, we believe, that is ordinarily the one
considered in connection with caring for the orphans and widows and
infirm masonic brothers is not which is the cheapest but which is
the best method, and we believe that, without exception, every jurisdiction that has the Home system, while eoneeding that it is not the
cheapest system, believes that it is, by all odds, the best and most
comprehensive system; but, it is everything to be satisfied, and so long
as our good brethren of South Carolina are satisfied with their system,
and the good brethren of other jurisdictions are equally satisfied with
another system, no criticism or complaint should issue from either

114

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

side, but all should work along the lines best adapted to their own
ideas to advance the general good of masonry.
Some doubt seems to exist in the minds of at least some of the
brethren in South Carolina as to what particular Grand Lodge anniversary they were celebrating, some contending that the Grand Lodge
was holding its 179 Annual Communication instead of its 139th, a
trifle of forty years having, in some unaccountable way, slipped into
the discard, and in order to' settle the question authoritatively, a committee was appointed to make due investigation and report at the
next Annual Communication.
The best part of the Volume of Proceedings before us is the report
on Foreign Correspondence by Most Worshipful J. L. Michie, Past
Grand Master, and, whether one agree with him or not in the methods
followed in his review of Proceedings; his report is certainly exceedingly interesting and devoid of dullness. He does not hesitate to
criticise or express adverse opinions, yet we do not find his criticisms
contain a sting.
The distinguished committee in Massachusetts that recently made
a report adverse to the creation of a Correspondence Committee in that
State, advanced as one of the reasons why the policy of Massachusetts, in not having this committee, should not be departed from, that
Correspondence Committees frequently indulged in criticism of other
jurisdictions, that was unpleasant and ofttimes a cause of friction, and,
also, that these Committees were prone to usurp to themselves
an air of superior wisdom, etc.
In our judgment the distinguished Committee in Massachusetts is
hardly justified in assuming this position, and, aside from possibly one
other Chairman of our American Correspondence Committees, South
Carolina is as free to criticise as any, and yet, as stated, we fail to
discover anything in the comments of Brother Michie that even the
most sensitive could reasonably object to, and, as stated, we have
taken a great deal of pleasure in reading Brother Michie 's comments,
which are always interesting.
In his present report he reviews California, 1914, with kindly
reference to Grand Master Murphy's excellent address, and some of
the splendid qualities of California masonry.
He observes that the reports of the Committee on Grievances
disclose the fact that certain masonic trials do not take place in the
lodges where the charges are preferred but are frequently transferred
'for trial to some other lodge. Brother Michie asks for an explanation
of this procedure.
We may say that the rule in California is the same as in other
jurisdictions in reference to most masonic trials, and it is only the

TENNESSEE.
1916.
102nd Annual, Nashville, Jan. 26th.
Lodges, 461; membership, 28,300; gain, 219.
The Grand Communication was presided over by the Most Worshipful T. A. Hisey, Grand Master, assisted by a full corps of Grand
Of:ficers and Representatives of 437 of the 461 lodges of the jurisdiction, certainly a very :flattering representation of the subordinate
lodges.
The Grand Master refers, in the opening portion of his Annual
Address, to the severe affliction which visited the Grand Jurisdiction
within the year preceding in that no less than three Past Grand
Masters and the Grand Secretary, were summoned to the Supreme
Grand Lodge above. The beloved Grand Secretary, John B. Garrett,
who had served the jurisdiction in the capacity of Grand Secretary for
twenty years, was taken away in the early part of the year, and his
death was followed by that of Past Grand Master Henry H. lnger;wll,
Past Grand Master John T. Williamson, and Past Grand Master Kewton McConnell. Suitable memorials were prepared and presented on
all of these distinguished masons, wherein homage was paid to their
superior character and excellence.
The Grand Master indicated a year of unusual masonic activity;
not less than twelve corner stone ceremonies were held within the year,
various lodges were constituted, and a vast amount of correspondence
was carried on by the Grand Master in passing upon questions presented to him, and, in addition to a large amount of correspondence,
he paid fraternal and official visits to not less than forty-four of the
subordinate lodges, visiting praetically every nook and corner of the
Grand Jurisdiction, and, no doubt, bestowing vast benefit upon the
fraternity through his personal presence among so many lodges.
A large number of so-called rulings were made by him construing
the local law of the jurisdiction, but that a great many of these rulings were hasty and ill-advised may be judged from the fact that a
large number of them were disapproved by the Jurisprudence Committee, and the findings of the Jurisprudence Committee were in all
cases up-held by the Grand Lodge, which illustrates the wisdom of the
Grand Master first submitting to the Jurisprudence Committee his decisions and modifying them according to the superior judgment which
this Committee ought naturally to possess.
This excellent method was adopted by one of our recent Granil
JYfasters in California, and it would be, in our judgment, a 'l'.ery desirable custom to establish permanently.

The "Widows and Orphans' Home in this jurisdiction has always
been managed with a great deal of skill and economy, the per capita

There is a proposition to open in addition to the Widows and

The Grand Master voices his belief in the true and genuine worth
of the people of his Commonwealth, and how they are so often misunderstood, in the following sympathetic terms:
''How I wish, oh, how I wish that some hand, guided by love,
sympathy and understanding, would take up the task of preserving in
poem, story and history the simple, unaffected, honest, friendly life
of the people of Tennessee and the South. New England, the North,
and the West each have had this labor of love done in their behalf,
but the true stories of the home life of the South are yet to be written.
Too many tales of the passions and the free use of the pistol in the
hands of angry and thoughtless men have been written, a majority by
Southern writers, which do not place the lives of the Southern people
in the proper light. Soon may such a writer arise to paint in glowing
colors the great Jives of the simple, plain and honest people of the
country and villages."

In the opening paragraphs of the address of the Grand Master are
found some lofty characterizations of the work and worth of masonry.
We quote:

The Grand · Master in his address refers to the circular letters
which this jurisdiction received, in common, we presume, with all
other American jurisdictions within the last year that have recognized
and extended fraternal relations to the new grand Lodge of the
Philippine Islands from one Ramon Mendoza, who appears to bear some
relationship to an alleged Regional Grand Lodge of the Philippines.
The Grand Lodge of Texas was not able to extend to Mr. Mendoza
any more encouragement than he has received from other Grand
Lodges to which he has applied, and the Texas recognition of the new
Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands stands.
,.

"We sometimes hear it said by the enemies of Truth that Masonry
seeks to exercise power, both temporal and spiritual. Masonry seeks
not such powers. It yearns not for the pomp of office, whether exercised by regal hands, or a representative elected by the people. It puts
forth no candidates, nor supports any political party or policy. It
numbers among its devotees royalists and republicans, the subjects of
despots, and the citizens of democracies. It stretches forth no hand to
bestow a crown, nor to pluck the laurel wreath from the brow of constituted authority. Mansonry not only teaches its members loyalty and
obedience to constituted authority but many of the cardinal principles
of eivic life, without which good government could not exist. It
teaches that free speech, free thought and freedom of conscience are
essential to the progress and well-being of all nations, and the liberty
of all people; it should not be unduly restricted, either by government
or any other power. Masonry, by its teachings, endeavors to restrain
men from the commission of injustice and acts of wrong. It is an
advocate of education, enlightenment, and morality. It teaches the
nobility and dignity of labor; that to work with the hands or brain,
to perform our duties earnestly and faithfully, is more honorable than
rank or title, and out of which grow true manhood and genuine
nobility.
''These are some of its simple yet sublime lessons, teaching mankind its duties to country, and to our fellowman. The struggle and
clamor for temporal power, like the restless ocean, may break upon
the distant rocks, but no sound thereof disturbs the serenity of our
peaceful retreats.
"Neither does Masonry endeavor to usurp the place of religion; or
seek to draw men away from the altars of the churches. It stretches
forth no hand to tear away priestly robes, nor to bestow a protestant
gown. It inculcates a belief in the existence of God, the immortality
of the soul, and the brotherhood of man.
"It teaches men to "do unto others that only which they would
think it just and merciful for others to do unto them. It strives to
brush away the fears, superstitions and ignorance that shackle an(!
enslave the souls of men and free them from spiritual tyranny and
despotism, no matter in what creed or religion it may be found.
"It gathers men about its shrine and teaches them great fundamental truths of God, of spirit, of life, and leaves each to seek the altar
of his own church, temple, synagogue or shrine, to worship God according to the dictates of his own conscience. It leaves to other forums all
questions of a sectarian nature, and teaches men to look up to God
and believe that He is not a tyrant, but a .father, infinitely wise, good,
just and merciful, through the power of whose infinite love and mncy
the soul may be lifted into high places of quiet and peace, where the
atmosphere is crystal and the light is resplendent with His beneficence.''

A note of sorrow is sounded by the Grand Master in his feeling
reference to the death within the year of beloved and illustrious Past
Grand Master Augustus Weyman Houston, Sr.

121

The Grand Master renders a number of decisions explanatory of
Texas law. One of the decisions, which we believe will meet general
approval, over-rules a decision formerly rendered by one of the Grand
Masters of Texas, and the decision is in effect as follows:
A certain lodge, after trial, expels a brother. The case was appealed to the Grand Lodge, and the judgment was refused, and case
remanded for a new trial, and change of venue granted by the Grand
Lodge to another subordinate. Upon a re-trial of the case, the defendant was acquitted, and the question presented to the Grand Master
was whether the lodge in which the trial was held in acquitting the
brother, in the absence of a specific reinstatement to membership as a
part of the verdict, restored the brother to membership in his own
lodge. The decision which the Grand Master over-ruled was to the
effect that in the absence of such a specific reinstatement, the brother
acquitted acquired simply the standing of an unaffiliated or dimitted
mason, and was not by virtue of the verdict of acquittal restored to
membership in his lodge. The Grand Master, in this case, held that
the brother was by virtue of the acquittal automatically restored to
membership in his own lodge, and the decision was upheld by the
Jurisprudence Committee and Grand Lodge; all of which will, we
believe, meet with general approval.

Perhaps the one outstanding feature above everything else in
Texas masonry is its Masonic Orphans' Home, located at Fort Worth.
The Home itself represents a monetary investment, according to the
estimate submitted by the Board of Trustees, of $504,846.18. There
are sheltered within the Home 213 children, 112 boys, and 101 girls.
A very complete system of education and manual training is
carried forward within the Home by a faculty of fourteen members
and a course of study, including four years of high-school work, is
carried forward, besides, as previously stated, a manual training department, course of study in music, etc. There is probably no Masonic Orphans' Home anywhere in the world, which has such a comprehensive system of education and training as the Orphans' Masonic

VERMONT.

124

The report on Correspondence is from the scholarly S. H. Goodwin,
Past Grand Master. He reviews in an intelligent and discriminating
manner the reports of most of the Grand .Jurisdictions, although California for some reason fails to receive mention.
His ''Conclusion'' several pages in length is devoted entirely to a
criticism of the Grand Lodge of England in excluding from attendance
upon the masonic lodges of England the members of German or Austrian birth.
It is our theory of the duty of a correspondent, or more properly
speaking masonic ;eporter, to report what takes place, rather than to
criticise, and, in our judgment, it is of doubtful propriety to criticise
any Grand Lodge concerning what it does, or fails to do, touching its
own domestic affairs, and, if the Grand Lodge of England believes
that the safetv of the Empire or the fraternal welfare of the lodges
require the ex~lusion from attendance upon the lodges temporarily of
certain masons of foreign birth, the Grand Lodge of England has a
perfect right to adopt such a course, and it is the concern of no one,
be he a mason or otherwise, residing in some other country, to object
or criticise.

England is fighting for her very existence, and English masons
undoubtedly regard as their paramount obligation unmixed dcyotion
to their own country's cause and welfare, and it is the belief of the
Grand Lodge of ::M:asons of England that that welfare will be promoted
by the ·action taken in reference to foreign born members, and, as
stated, it is the concern of no one else. German Grand Lodges have
taken the same action, so far as England is concerned, and we have
this far heard no criticism of the action of German Grand Lodges,
which illustrates a fundamental difference between the English and
the German method. The English method permits free discussion and
free criticism of any official action, whether it pertains to the Government or any other phase of English life or activity; whereas the
German method, brooks no criticism or discussion; the demand whatever it may be, is simply announced, and that is the end of it.
M.'. W.'. CHARLES C. GRIGGS, Eureka, Grand Master.
R.'. W.'. FREEMAN A. McCARTHY, Salt Lake City, Grand Secretary.

The report on Foreign Correspondence is again from the pen of
Most Worshipful Joseph W. Eggleston. We excerpt the following
from his Introduction as something of general interest:
''Another matter of interest, little known, is the relation of Virginia Masonry to what we fondly call the Mother Grand Lodge of
1717. The fact is that, while our descent can be traced back to that
source, the Grand Lodge of Virginia repudiated and held it clandestine more than one hundred years ago. This Grand Lodge was
formed in 1717 in London by four Lodges, and for years seems to
have had no thought of territorial jurisdiction, even at home. The
idea evidently was to organize and keep records for the first time,
and this was a then modern innovation, so that one or more sece<ling
bodies dubbed them "Modern Masons." These seceding bodies formed
the Grand Lodge of "Ancient York Masons," or "Grand Lodge of
All England,'' and were also called the ''Athol!'' Grand Lodge. They
claimed to be the legitimate successors of what they called the ''Grand
Lodge at York." We know that there was a Lodge there as early as
1630, the constitution of which was in existence and in its possession
fo 1777. The feud between the Ancients or York Grand Lodge (All
England) and the Moderns (England, London, 1717) continued with
bitterness till 1813, when they came together. In 1798 the Grand
Lodge of Virginia passed the following ''Gen. Regulation.'' It may
be found, page 114, in "Masonic Laws," by James Henderson, Master
of Manchester Lodge, No. 14 (afterwards Grand Secretary). This was
our Digest of that day. It reads:
'' '7th. If any member of a Lodge under the jurisdiction of this
Grand Lodge shall visit or work in any Lodge of Masons commonly
called Modern Masons, or any Lodge of Masons not working agreeably
to the ancient usages of York Masons, he shall be reprimanded by the
Lodge to which he belongs; and if he should afterwards be guiltv of
a similar offense. he shall be expelled from the Lodge and excludeG:
from the benefits of Masonry.'
''The above is written as a partial answer to the often asked
question: 'What does 'York Masonry' mean, and why do we call
ourselves 'York Masons~' ' Some writers dispute the existence of a
controlling force at York in ancient times, and essays have been written on both sides of the controversy. Most probably the Masons of
that whole region held there what is often alluded to as 'The General

That it is always unsafe to criticise when one is not in possession
of all the facts, is illustrated in Brother Eggleston 's comments under
the caption of "British Columbia,'' concerning the so-called McGrew
case, and is proven from the fact that California and Massachusetts
have reconciled, in a courteous and amicable manner, the differences
existing between them in this case, and Brother McGrew, a good man
and polished gentleman, was restored before his death by Massachusetts to all the rights and privileges of masonry, and the record
of his death, which occurred soon after his restoration, is inscribed,
with all of his masonic honors, upon the pages of the Grand Lodge
Proceedings of that Jurisdiction.
Brother Eggleston reviews California, 1914, very generously.

and quotes extensively therefrom.
Brother Eggleston especially refers to the "unlimited charity"
of California masonry, the charity feature of our jurisdiction being
especially called into play because of the allurements of our climate
for those seeking restoration to physical health.
Brother Eggleston, in his ''Conclusion'', gives expression to his
ideas as to how a Correspondence Report should be malle up. He
avoids statistics, he ignores local affairs, and necrology, and endeavors to select from addresses and orations enough good stuff to
furnish any mason in search of information, material for masonic
addresses, if this is what he is after, etc.

The thought uppermost in the minds of the civilized world
today is the tragedy of war being enacted upon the continent of
Europe, and that this prevailing thought is in the mind of the
Grand Orator at this time may be judged from the following ;ixcerpts
from his oration:
"I verily believe that the most significant result of the present
conflict in Europe will be to establish one and the same ethical
standards, alike for Nations as for individuals, so that National
pledges, by the common sense and the common conscience of the
people, will be jealously guarded and kept from reproach and shame.
Masonry holds in its hands the threads of the past and the future;
not one of them is broken. There is, therefore, a peculiar obligation
resting upon us to conserve these treasures which make for peace
and the well-being of mankind.
Freemasonry, with her universal language of symbolism, is the
only institution in position to meet this demand for the instruction
of the peoples of all races and nations in ethical and moral development, reduced to the basis of an exact science.''
