Washington has fallen in line with California, waiving the necessity of the formal opening of a Masonic Lodge in order to conduct
a masonic funeral whereby the brethren are permitted, in accordance
with the Constitution as recently amended in California, to assemble
at the place where the funeral is to be conducted, and assume their
masonic clothing and conduct the ritual service without a preliminary meeting and opening of lodge.
The report on Correspondence is again from the scholarly Past
Grand Master RRlPh C. McAllister. He presents his report in the topical or digest form, similar to t.he method employed the last two years
in Alabama. His form of report has much to commend it, and Brother
McAllister's present effort presents a great deal of masonic information in extremely readable form.
Under the caption ''Age of Petitioner'', in considering the ques·
tion as to whether a petition for degrees may be entertained
when the petitioner is actually not of legal age when the petition is presented, but will be before the initiation can take place,

he holds that the weight of authority requires that a man be
of "lawful age" before he may even knock at the door of masonry,
and that no lodge can receive a petition from a candidte until the
candidate shall at the date of his petition actually have attained
lawful age.
Under the caption of "corner stones", the controversy is noted
as to whether the corne11 stone must be actually laid in the northeast
corner, or if placing the stone in some other part of the fo~ndation,
may suffice.
One Grand Master had ruled that a corner stone must be laid in
the northeast corner, but that ruling had been modified by the Jurisprudence Committee, which held that the provision as to the northeast corner was not manditory, and that it might be placed, if neces·
sar_y, at some other point.
1!nder dispensations, he observes a marked tendency that denies
the right of the Grand Master by dispensation to change the ordinary
course of procedure in various matters laid down in the constitution
such for instance, as dispensations which are granted in some juris~
dictions to ballot for and confer degrees short of the constitutional
time.
Under "documentary evidence", he calls attention to the in.demand everywhere for this evidence as a prerequisite to
exammat~on of. a request to visit, and mentions that scarcely a year
goes by m which the proceedings of some Grand Lodge do not disclose the necessity of documentary evidence. This year it comes from

WEST vmGINIA.
1916.

51st Annual, Fairmont, Nov. 10-11.
Lodges, 150; membership, 18,827; gain, 1,073.
Numerous "Special Communication" were held within the year
for the purpose principally of placing corner stones, and if there is
any one feature, more than another, that stands out prominently in
this jurisdictions, it is the frequent exercises of the function of plac·
ing col.'ner stones of public buildings.
The Annual Communication was presided over by Most Worshipful William T. Ice, Jr., Grand Master.
The purpose of holding this Annual Communication at Wheeling,
which city had been selected at the previous Annual Comm•::aication
for the holding of the Annual Communication of 1915, 'l'\'as defeated
because of a fire which destroyed the Scottish Rite Temple, containing
the principal masonic auditorium in Wheeling, and, because of this
disaster, the place for the meeting of the Annual Communication was
transferred to Fairmont.
The Grand Master reports at least sixteen corner stone cere·
monies. He sets forth in his report the usual Grand Master activities, and a few decisions on masonic law, being in the nature of interpretations of the constitution of the jurisdiction.
From his conclusion, we excerpt the following paragraphs which
express his conceptions of the true scope and mission of masonry:
"An observation of world conditions today impresses one with
the great changes taking place in governments and institutions. But
let us remember that the basic structure of Masonry still remains the
same. Loyalty to government, due consideration for the rights of

This Annual Communication, the plans for which contemplated
meeting in the commodious Scottish Rite Auditorium in Wheeling,
was to have been a Semi·centennial Celebration of the founding of
the Grand Lodge, but on aecount of the disaster which compelled the
abandonment of the project to meet in Wheeling, the celebration was
abandoned at the same time.
Judge George W. Atkinson, Past Grand Master, had been as·
signed, in connection with the contemplated celebration, the prepara·
tion of a half century sketch of the Grand Lodge of West Virginia,
and while, as stated, the celebration itself was abandoned, Brother
Atkinson was prevailed upon to present bis sketch to the Grand
Lodge at this time, and this historical document :6.nds place in the
printed proceedings.
The historical resume is interesting, particularly to the brethren
of West Virginia, and it sets forth exhaustively the early trials
and difficulties encountered by the Grand Lodge when it was estab·
lished at the time that West Virginia broke away from Virginia
proper, during the early years of the Civil War.
The Grand Lodge of Virginia was naturally loath to surrender
her jurisdiction over the lodges located in the new State, but the
differences were :6.nally adjusted upon a basis of perfect good will
and understanding, and the kindest fraternal sentiments have always
been maintained between the two Grand Lodges.
There seems to be a prospect of the establishment in this jurisdiction of a Masonic Home through a bequest from one of the wealthy
and prominent masons of the jurisdiction.
There has never been any objection in this jurisdiction to the
masonic home project except that heretofore it has not felt financially
able to support such an institution, and also because the charity obli·
gations of the jurisdiction have always been very capably discharged
by the subordinate lodges.
The report on Foreign Correspondence is as usual from the capa·
ble hand of Most Worshipful Goerge W. Atkinson, Past Grand Master,

Western Australia, like most of the Australian Grand Lodges, had

Brother Atkinson, in his Conclusion, has some kindly observations to make concerning the Order of the Eastern Star, and we take
pleasure in quoting his remarks, and the wider our knowledge becomes concerning the extent and importance of woman's work, the
more inclined we are to agree with anything spoken in her praise:
''I can say in all kindness and good will, that the more I read
about what the members of the Eastern Star are doing as an adjunct
of real :F'reemasonry, the more I feel like praising and encouraging
them. They are lending a woman's hand in bearing alms to the
needy, and doing what thy can to make the world sweeter and happier and better. They are the handmaiden. of their husbands, fathers
and brothers, who are Masons, in carrying on a work which only
women, with true women's hearts, can do. After all, what kind of
a world would we have, if it were not for the work that women only
can do' My, my excuse me! And please remember, I am not a
member of it. I am only an unprejudiced onlooker.
''They talk about a woman's sphere, as though it had a limit;
There's not a place in earth or Heaven,
There's not a task to mankind given,
There's not a blessing or a woe,
There's not a whispered yes or no,
There's not a life-There's not a birth,
That has a feather's weight of worth
Without a woman in it.''
M.". W.". T. WILBUR HENNEN, Grand Master, Fairmont.
M'.". W.". JOHN M. COLLINS, Grand Secretary, Charleston.

WESTERN AUSTRALIA.
1915.

16th Annual, Perth, April 22.
Lodges, 95; membership, 4,042; gain, 17.
The business of this Grand Lodge is conducted at the various
Quarterly Communications, which are held in January, April, July and
October of each year, the communication of April being counted as the
Annual Communication, at which the principal Reports are rendered
and a general review of the business of the year considered.
An inspection of the Balance Sheets of the various Funds discloses the fact that for a Grand Lodge only fifteen years old, splendid
progress has been made in the accumulation of substantial credits to
the various Funds, as well as for satisfactory progress in the matter
of membership.

At this Annual Communication, the Most Worshipful Brother, the
Right Rev. C. C. L. Riley, Lord Bishop of Perth, was re-elected to
serve for the twelfth consecutive term as Grand Master.
The report on Correspondence is rendered by a committee composed of several members, the report being a condensed review of the
proceedings of the various Grand Lodges. California for 1914 is fraternally reviewed by one of the distinguished members of the Committee, with copious quotations from Grand Master Murphy's Address,
and with complimentary references to various phases of masonic activity in California.
M.". W.". BRO. C. 0. L. RILEY, Lord Bishop of Perth, Grand Master,

WISCONSIN.
1916.

72nd Annual, Milwaukee, June 13th.
Lodges, 274; membership, 31,866; gain, 1,315.
The Seventy-second Annual Communication was presided over
by Most Worshipful George 0. Kellogg, Grand Master.
In the opening of his Address, the Grand Master contrasts the
unhappy conditions of strife and blood-shed which prevail upon the
continent of Europe, with the conditions of peace, tranquility and
happiness which obtain in this country, and in order to preserve the
liberties and blessings which we enjoy, he calls attention to the
necessity of the development of the highest type of manhood, such
as is conserved by our great Institution of Freemasonry, and reminds his brethren of the responsibility that rests upon the masons
of this country of counseling the rising generation that they may
become a part of a republic that shall deserve to endure through all
time.
The Grand Master records a year of masonic activity. He· issued
dispensations to form and open three new lodges. Eleven Emergent

The second day of the Annual Communication, that is June 14th,
being what is known as Flag Day, Past Grand Master Charles E.
Whelan entered the Grand Lodge, bearing the flag of our country, the
Stars and Stripes, and from the East of the Grand Lodge, so the
proceedings inform us, ''delivered an oration which was a credit to
him and an incentive to all American citizens to up-hold all the tra·
ditions for which 'Old Glory' stands."
The report on Foreign Correspondence is the nineteenth annual
offering of the Chairman of the Committee, Past Grand Master Aldro
Jenks, in which, in his introduction, he has this to say concerning his
:report and generally touching the spirit of masonry:
''This report is prepared primarily for Masons in Wisconsin and
particularly for those who take an interest in things Masonic; who
are willing to :read and think. Masonry in its teachings and aims is
wonde:rfully practical. It gives to the true Mason a higher conception
of the Infinite One and a more definite mission in life. While this is
the spirit of Masonry too few of us realize it. No man can understand
and appreciate it until he has pondered long and faithfully upon its
teachings. Many a man has taken the obligations from the Entered
Apprentice degree to the Thirty-second, and failed absolutely to under·
stand or get that broader vision of Masonry which they are intended
to give. That man's :Masonry is a failure notwithstanding he may
wear a Knight Templar charm or a Double Headed Eagle; he is neither
an aetive nor a practical :Mason, but merely a hanger-on to the institution. Such is not the fault of the Masonic Institution, but is due to
the fact that such an one was seeking o:rnamental titles and displav
rather than an opportunity of being servicable to his fellow man ancl
improving himself in Masonry.
''The Brother, however, who has progressed in thought and conception to the knowledge that :Masonry is intended to make of him a
better man and give him opportunity for service to his fellow man is
a far higher Mason though he has not progressed beyond the Symb~lic
degrees, than the one of the opposite character who is proud of the
number of steps he has taken.''
His review of the various jurisdictions is characterized by rare
judgment and intelligence and teems with masonic knowledge and
information.

He perhaps under-estimates the ability of the Grand Lodge of
Califo:rnia, without any distress, to take care of the obligations in·
curred in connection with the erection of the magnificent temple in
San Francisco. California does business "with a large auger", and,
while a million dollar investment in a temple with an outstanding
indebtedness of $300,000 might stagger some jurisdictions, the proposition will not in the least disturb the Grand Lodge of California, and
the indebtedness will be absorbed in a short time without much
trouble, and the temple will not only stand as a fitting monument to
the grandeur of masonry in California but will become in a very few
years a magnificent business investment.
M.". W.". CYRUS S. STOCKWELL, Grand Master, Neillsville.
R.". W.". WM. W. PERRY, Grand Secretary, Milwaukee.

WYOMING.

1915.
4lst Annual, Casper, Sept. 8-9.
Lodges, 34; membership, 3,316; gain, 126.
The Forty-first Annual Communication was presided over by the
Most Worshipful J. J. Jewett, Grand Master.
An Address of Welcome to the Grand Lodge was delivered by
Past Grand Master E. P. Rohrbaugh, Mayor of Casper, to which re·
sponse was made, at request of the Grand :Master, by Right Worship·
ful Brother T. Blake Kennedy, Junior Grand Warden.
In the opening paragraphs of his Annual Address, the Grand
Master refers to the well-nigh irreparable loss which the Grand Lodge
suffered within the preceding year in the death of its Grand Secretary,
Brother W. L. Kuykendall. Bro. Kuykendall had served the Grand
Lodge as its Secretary for thirty years, and was known as one of the
most efficient Grand Secretaries in the masonic world. He also filled
the position of Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence
and his reports were regarded as among the most valuable rendered by
Correspondence Committees.
The Grand Master enumerates in a concise manner the various
official aets which he performed within the year, which upon the whol~
was one of the most prosperous in the .existence of the Grand Lodge.

Brethren of the Grand Lodge: •

This Grand Lodge at its Sixty-seventh Annual Communicatio11
invested me with the powers and prerogatives. of Grand Master and
entrusted me with the execution of the duties of that exalted office.
I have striven to comprehend the responsibilities thereby assumed and
have proceeded accordingly. To personal limitations must lack of
achievement be ascribed. \Vherein I have failed, thereat I grieve, as
everything has been done with the hope that it would prove true to
the test of the plumb, the square, and the level.
The year's service will bring recurring joy throughout my life as,
reminiscence, memory will present again and again the events so
,leeply impressed. It has been an inspiration. The pleasure of association with my Brethren and the gratification from observation of the
general understanding and practice. of Masonic precept, dwarf incidents of petty character which have required unpleasant performance
of stern duty. It is not within the range of reasonable possibility to
make personal mention of those earnest, considerate Brethren whose
Jl.fasonic service is the strength of the Institution. To them I am
greatly indebted for co-operation and counsel and must be satisfied
with this general expression of my heartfelt appreciation. May there
come to them that great reward, the satisfaction of duty well performed. I congratulate the Grand Lodge on the efficiency of the Grand
Secretary, Very \Vorshipful Brother John \Vhicher, and the Grand
Lecturer, Very Worshipful Brother Thomas J. Baker. Kot only have
they been faithful in the performance of their respective duties, but
at all times and everywhere have been most courteous and thoughtful.
They have been of great assistance to me.
=!1

In the ultimate analysis accomplishment is the requirement. Effort
sufficient to an understanding of necessary action, but without that
action, is of inconsiderable value as compared with accomplishment.
The ratio is as the unfinished to the finished. The inclination is to
clothe with the mantle of charity misdirected but well-intentioned effort, but it affords little consolation in the inventory of achievement.
In accomplishment, therefore, lies the welfare of our great Institution.
It is required that we be vigilant. Everywhere in the Masonic system

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

is evidence of vigilance in its creation and completion. We are con
cerned in the vigilance of its preservation, understanding its meaning.
and putting it into practice. We have done well at times in California,
but we should not be content witll the attainment of other years. We
feel a pride in the complimentary estimate of R:.
A. O'Sullivan,
Grand Secretary of Missouri and Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence in 1862, that, in point of ability and Masonic talent, California was second to none on this continent. But as level-headed men
we are more concerned with the attainments of the present.

How are we succeeding in California? I think our average is good,
in fact; excellent. We should not judge by comparison. Fully realizing
that I am saturated with the Masonic idea as a result of my tour of
exceptional duty, I shall endeavor to maintain a practical attitude
throughout. Making allowance for human limitations I helieve we can
do better. You are entitled to know upon what I base my opinion
that we might make improvement.

270

w: ·

I conceived it essential to the intelligent performance of my duty
to make thorough survey of the jurisdiction and to that end visited
every district but one in California, regretting I could not go to Hawaii
whither I sent the Grand Lecturer. In all I visited 122 Lodges severally and .in joint session, not including Los Angeles "Get Together,"
and by medium of substantial attendance, came in contact with one
hundred sixty-five Lodges more. The Grand Lecturer will present a
tabulation of visits. Everywhere I was received cordially and, generally, with due deference to the office. The hospitality of the Brethren
was characteristic and I am unable to adequately express my appreciation. My message was received with courtesy and with enthusiasm
which was encouraging. Realizing that by virtue of my office I had
been afforded the opportunity of addressing my Brethren, I conscientiously endeavored to mold my thoughts by Masonic standards.
We assume the practicality of Masonry's "stern morality." The
intelligence of the initiate, using the term in its ordinary sense, is the
all-important factor in the system. With what are we thereafter concerned? Naturally, the mechanism of education, the Lodge, which has
its life from the Grand Lodge. The Constitution and regulations prescribe conduct and all have a direct bearing on the initiate. The moral
system is safeguarded by strict law relative to ritual and landmarks.
The medium for dissemlnation of this knowledge is protected by Constitution and regulations defining organization, powers and government of Lodges.
The self-evident importance of ihe Lodge it would seem should
always inspire action. \Ve know that it frequently does not, and, if we
analyze, we trace the cause eventually to the initiate, who, in association with others, constitutes the Lodge. The effectiveness of the Lodge
is as the average of intelligence and vigilance of the initiates. The
intelligent initiate understands the full importance of qualification for
membership. Vigilance therein maintains the high standard which
creates the voluntary desire in worthy men to become members and
impels them to seek admission. With such material the maximum of
efficiency in the practice of Masonic precepts is attained.

271

If an entirely satisfactory condition existed there would be no com·
plaint of poor attendance, no petty controversy, no peddlers of rumors,
much less countenancing such conduct, not to mention difficulties of
administration. Naturally we are concerned with correction. To correct we must understand the causes.

Poor attendance where it should be better is a symptom. I do
not feel apprehension that non-attendants are necessarily not good
Masons. We have too much evidence that many of our most thorough
Masons are non-attendants. Ordinarily such a condition is due to the
officers. Not necessarily incumbent officers-they may have inherited
the condition. · Remedies which do not attack the root of the evil afford
but temporary relief. There has been a relaxation of vigilance. Inferior officers lack personal magnetism. They are careless in exemplification of the work, disregard the importance of punctuality in meeting and general looseness prevails. They do not maintain the dignity
of, or the decorum so ess.ential in, a Lodge. It has the effect of alienating strong members, failing to attract strong men who should be
members and of admitting substandard material into the Fraternity.
Vigilance in the selection of officers is probably as important a
safeguard as any in maintaining Masonic standards. The strong men
of the Lodge should be selected as officers. The system of promotion
has proved quite satisfactory, but if it so happens that a man who will
best maint~in the standards of Masonry cannot in justice to other demands devote the time ordinarily necessary to advance to the East,
then he should be sufficiently advanced so that the institution may
reap the benefit of his. services. This does not savor of inequality, or
favoritism, it is merely insuring the best service for the Fraternity.
The following injunction from the old charges is pertinent: "To ordain
the wisest of them master of the rest of the work." If the officers in
line are fundamentally sound they will appreciate the advantage of such
a course. In fact they should be alert and from them should come
such suggestion, to avoid efforts of the personally ambitious. Everything that can be done should be done to obtain the service of the
Fraternity's strong men. Ability to understand this depends upon
the intelligence of the initiate.

272

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

That same lack of intelligence manifests itself where there is dis·
regard of the importance, and carelessness in the selection of, the in·
vestigating committee. Vigilance and intelligence of the committee are
of prime importance. They should make careful investigation, witho:ut
delay so that they may be thorough. Masters should exercise great
care selecting men who will earnestly perform the duty and perform
it w~ll, and giving them fu!) instruction where they are inexperienced.
Alphabetical selection will not be productive of best results. Where
a petitioner is rejected by committee a succinct statement of facts
should be reduced to writing by Masters or committeemen and preserved in the files for futllre reference. Where a petitioner has been
previously rejected it should be a requirement that the committee and
the Master of the Lodge by whom rejected should be interviewed. Incidental hereto I have requested the Committee on Jurisprudence to
consider the subject of instructions and formulate something standard.
Another forceful factor in promoting Masonic efficiency is the
influence of the instructor. Good judgment in the selection of Brethren
particularly adapted for the individuals to be instructed will prove
beneficial. By little effort the services of many Brethren may thus be
enlisted who may not have opportunity otherwise to perform service.
Throughout, I have striven in my criticism to observe practical
limitations and particlllarly not to descend to fault-finding. In one
instance it became necessary to suspend a Master. The case has been
directed by me to th~ attention of the Committee on Appeals and
Grievances. Contrary to my first intentions with reference to those
Lodges situated in remote and sparsely settlt><i communities where enthusiasm of Brethren, though few in number, has seemed to warrant, 1
have not arrested charters, concluding that the opportunity should
continue for those well-deserving Brethren and as well afford a haven
for those good men who travel "far from the madding crnwd's ignoble
strife." Rather severe reprimand has been necessary in a few cases.
In some instances marked improvement has been made, other cases are
still :under observation of the Grand Lecturer.
Investigation was initiated through Inspectors by medium of specific questions to disclose comprehensively the condition of Lodges.
The first inquiry covered description of property owned, method of
holding title, bonding of officers, investigation and record of visitors,
records kept, amount of indebtedness, fire protection, insurance, financial condition of building corporations or associations, and other less
important matter. Generally the Inspectors were prompt and thorough, occasionally delayed by Lodges and, in one or two insta_nces,
indifferent. One purpose of this investigation was to develop efficiency
of Inspectors. The result on the whole was most gratifying. The

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

273

duties of an Inspector are onerous, well performed, and to our earnest
Brethren who serve as Inspectors are due the appreciative thanks of the
Grand Lodge. The reports remain in the files as testimony. The
questions, as well as eliciting information, were suggestive of improvement and so intended. Irregularities or shortcomings were checked
that the Lodge might be properly instructed. One answer to the
question, "Arc Trea1>urcrs and Secretaries bonded?" was, "No, they arc
Masons"! Well enough, so long as they do not forget the fact.
Experience has demonstrated that they do forget and it is a precautionary measure against such and should cause no resentment on
the part of any intelligent Mason.
A second list of questions was submitted for the Inspectors' annual reports. The inquiry comprehended attendance, visits of Lodges,
opportunity for social intercourse, dissension, if any, method of appointment of investigating committees, instructions to them, promptness
of investigations and the following concerning financial status:
What is the financial condition of the Lodge?
(a) Has it a substantial bank account?
(b) Is its annual income, that is, dues, interest from investments, rents, etc., greater than its annual expense?
( 1) Does the Lodge depend in part on initiation fees
to meet annual e~penses?
(c) Has it a substantial profit each year?
( 1) Including fees ?
(2) Excluding fees?
(3) If a deficit, what is the amount?
The purpose was twofold, as with the first inquiry. Some Lodges
reported unsatisfactory attendance. I have expressed an opinion that
there is considerable responsibility therefor on the officers. However,
I have observed in some instances what I believe to be a contributing
cause. A few cases I have diagnosed as "high degree fever." Apparently some of our near-sighted Brethren were paying more attention
to the Chapter and Commandery than they were to their local Lodge.
I suggested that the importance of the Lodge should be self-evident
to those Brethren as the source of supply which should afford a practical reason for giving attention to the Lodge even if they did not
understan<I its wonclerful philosophy. The fart that Lodges doing t
great deal of work are compelled particularly to initiate and pa!-3
several candidates in an evening, that under Constitutional requirement
this must be ~everally done, has no doubt influenced attendance adversely. The required repetition consumes so much time that before

275

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

conclusion of the ceremonial many Brethren depart owing to lateness
of the hour. I am satisfied that repetition also influences Brethren to
remain away. Fully appreciating the evident purpose of severally
initiating, passing and raising of -candidates, I am of the opinion that
modification permitting of exemplification of portions of the .ceremonial
on groups would not in the least detract from effectiveness and, by
lessening the time and avoiding repetition, conduce to an increased
·attendance by reason of that fact, and, permitting of the employment
of a portion of the time for educational purposes and social intercourse,
would thereby materially increase efficiency. I therefore recommend
that consideration of the subject matter be referred to such standing
or special committee as . may seem to the Grand Lodge proper for
report and recommendation at the next stated communication of this
Grand Lodge.

The condition of many building associations, as I had anticipated,
was such as to cause apprehension. It warranted the submission of a
blank to Lodges concerned for uniform data to be submitted for reference to the Finance Committee in support of the recommendation I
now make, namely, that a Lodge shall not be permitted to invest funds
in a building association or project without approval in manner to be
determined by Grand Lodge. Consideration should be given the
financial status of some of these building associations by the Finance
Committee to the end that a satisfactory plan of financing be evolved,
if possible. In some instances I have no doubt suggestions concerning records and accounts would prove profitable and very acceptable.

274

I imagine there has been some feeling that the inquiries trespassed
upon Lodge prerogatives. That is not so. It is not generally understood that Lodge funds are impressed with a trust by the Grand Lodge.
These funds must be secure and the investment thereof satisfactory.
Regulation and supervision, therefore, are entirely proper, notwithstanding intelligent and able administration by Lodges generally.
Lodge funds invested in a building association are not immediately
available for purposes of relief and 'if the venture should prove to be
financially unsuccessful the condition is worse. Aside from the discredit of failure to meet financial obligations promptly, in event of
inability of the Lodge to meet charitable obligations, the burden would
fall upon Grand Lodge. Grand Lodge is vitally interested and is
entitled to know. More important, however, is the probable effect
upon membership standards. Troublesome financial obligations will
have a tendency and be a temptation to the lowering of standards of
membership in a. desire for membership fees and dues. Inferior members select inferior officers. Inferior officers produce inferior work
and the result is further contribution to inferiority and the creation of
members who misconstrue and misunderstand the object and purposes
of the institution. It was this that moved inquiry relative to Lodge
finances in addition to the inquiry concerning building enterprises.
Judging from statements of receipts and disbursements of Lodges and
the dependency of many Lodges on fees to meet current expenses, in
part, at least, I am more than ever impressed with the opinion that
minimum dues of $9.00 per annum should be prescribed, except in case
of such Lodges whose income, excluding fees, is greater than disbursements. That amount should not be a burden to anyone and
shnulrl make possible a small accumulation of funds.

This leads to another suggestion, namely, that the functions of
the Finance Committee should be enlarged to include consideration of
many problems which properly come under the classification of Ways
and Means. It would be well to change the designation of the Finance
Committee to "Ways and Means Committee" and, as there are many
questions of importance arising during the year, this Committee should
meet at least quarterly. Such provision will be beneficial to the Grand
Lodge and of great assistance to the Grand Master. It may be said
perchance that there is too much importance placed upon finance.
Healthy financial condition goes hand in hand with healthy Masonic
con.di ti on.
There has been the ever-present desire "to do something" to put
into practice Masonic precept. Frequently the Masonic plan, as I
conceive it, is misunderstood. Many of our well-intentioned Brethren
expect activity in concert. The opportunities for such are infrequent
and unimportant when compared to the great Masonic activity-that
which is manifested by individual achievement. Masonic glory will
be the achievement of individual Masons. The charity which we practice as Brethren, the fraternal relation which we feel, we eventually
understand to be but exemplars for our conduct in our relations with
others whether Masons or not. The Masonic mission is not limited to
the perfection of the Masonic brotherhood. That is but an exemplification of beneficial results to emphasize the importance of the practical
extension of the brotherly relation among all men. Our first great
effort is to educate the initiate who learns by observation the beneficient
results of practice of Masonic precept among the Brethren, whereupon
should follow the fullness of understanding of such precepts put into
practice generally and of the value of educating those who are less
fortunate. The only satisfactory response to inquiry concerning the
reasons for Masonic secrecy is that it is merely a test of honor. That
there is nothing pernicious hidden is evidenced by the independence of
action of every Mason and his activity in all good works. We fully
understand that there can be no interference with a Mason's activities

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

276

277

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

as an independent thinking being or as a citizen. Politics is eschewed
by the Fraternity because it would disturb peace and harmony, but also
because concert of action would interfere with a man's independeqce
and duties as a citizen. Therefore, a Mason as a candidate for public
office realizes that he proceeds on his merits and not on his membership.
Exemplifying our work within the narrow confines, we might do
more charitable work for our own, take greater care of our Masonic
wards by providing for more extensive education, establishing scholarships, obtaining and providing employment for the unfortunate. If we
overlook and fail to perform minor duties we are ill-prepared to
perform the greater service. For instance: In one city "somewhere
in California," Board of Relief funerals are conducted by a "funeral
lodge" composed of a Past Master and twenty Master Masons, "the
vast majority of whom" are members of the different Lodges of the
city and are in needy circumstances. Each of these twenty members
is paid for attendance. It is claimed that the circumstances which led
to the plan were that the individual Lodge was asked to conduct the
funeral of a stranger, and, after making "its best endeavor" would get
out from three to ten Masons. Performance of the last sad rites over
the body of a departed Brother is but a simple duty. It is a sad commentary that it should be claimed that there is lack of sufficient
Masonic spirit for sacrifice, if such it be, of the time necessary on the
part of a sufficient number of Brethren to guarantee a satisfactory
attendance. The representation at Board of Relief funerals conducted
by Lodges in regular manner elsewhere, attended by appointees of, or
those who volunteer to serve on, the Funeral Committee has been
satisfactory. While there may be numerous funerals there is no reason
why it should not work as satisfactorily in this particular city, M. '. W.".
Brother Prescott, Grand Master of Masons of Minnesota, long ago
said: "The Mason * * * who makes prior pleasure engagements,
or the pressure of ·secular pursuits an excuse for not giving his personal presence to a Masonic funeral, should be ashamed to assert any
affiliation with a society which teaches brotherly love." What impresses me is, if our Brethren do not make this simple sacrifice, how
firmly impressed is the requirement of greater sacrifices which are
expected of members of the Fraternity? Whereupon I instructed that
funerals should be conducted by Lodges in rotation, thereby insuring
the attendance of some members of the Lodge conducting the funeral,
who, with three or more delegated by each other Lodge, will give
practical evidence of the sincerity of our intentions in the work in
which we are engaged.

In times like the present when there is plenty to be done those who
are ordinarily on inquiry concerning their Masonic duty have their
work planned for them. The great work has been done individually.
When it became evident that effort would be necessary to insure the
success of the Liberty Loan, I circularized the Fraternity as follows:
"May Seventeenth,
Nineteen Seventeen.

"To the Brethren of the Jurisdiction:
"Enclosed herewith is a circular relative to, and a blank application for, gold bonds of the United States authorized by Congress and
popularly known as the 'Liberty Loan.'
"As patriotic citizens of the Republic it is our purpose 1'o urge you,
if you have n_ot already subscribed, to do so, thereby performing a
small but important patriotic service.
"Lodges should consider an investment of a reasonable amount of
Lodge funds in the bonds. The interest loss, if any, due to the difference in interest on savings deposits, will be negligible. It is unnecessary
that this should impose a burden on anyone, as you will note there are
bonds of the small denomination of $50. No investment can be more
secure and at the same time you will be rendering a service. Such an
investment for yourself and your family should prove a great satisfaction for•more than one reason. Enlist in the cause and arouse your
friends.
"If you need further information consult any local bank.
"With fraternal greetings,"
While the response of Lodges was gratifying, the great response
was by individuals. But even more important was the le1adership of
Masons on general and local committees in every county in the State.
Individual response and activity on committees and as subscribers in
the great "drive" for California's quota for the Red Cross were again
m evidence of the performance of Masonic duty.
The Masonic Ambulance Corps organized through the efforts of
local Masons and generously supported throughout the jurisdiction
was, with enthusiasm and ceremony, duly mustered into the United
States service and the boys are on their way to do their part, not as
Masons but as citizens. Godspeed to them all and to those thousands
who have gone into the service without ceremony.

And so it will be as more calls come for service.
I now direct the attention of this Grand Lodge, Lodges and
Brethren of the jurisdiction to "The Second Liberty Loan of 1917"
with a request to do as well as was done by the first loan and in fact
better. Do not delay.
The issues supporting the great war as defined by foreign statesmen among our allies and the President are not new or strange to
Masons and indicate the course that must be taken now for present
service and service after the war. Masonic doctrines must be transplanted in these benighted countries where they are unknown and
where individualism is unduly subordinated to the state. We are concerned with the solution of the problem of establishing fraternal intercourse with foreign Masonic jurisdictions. It is a means to a great
end and we should not be too conservative. Let us ascertain if after
all the obstacles are insurmountable. Arrangements, or ways and
means, for conferences on the subject should receive immediate attention. The extension of understanding of Masonic doctrine will be the
great contribution of Masonry toward an enduring world peace after
the war. Contemplate the value of a healthy public opinion due to
siuch an educated citizenship supporting just national ideals and
such international compacts as may be necessary.
We have had many inquiries with reference to contributions from
Lodge funds for Red Cross and other mos·t laudable purposes, and I
have been compelled to advise regretfully that under the Constitution
and Regiu:Jations no contribution of Lodge funds can b·e made for
charity other than that which is purely Masonic, or for other purposes,
no matter how meritorious. It may seem peculiar upon hasty consideration that such is the law, but, when it is realized that Masonic
funds must be conserved by reason of the fact that the members can
not be assessed for the important purpose of caring for their own who
may be unfortunate-one of the fundamental reasons why funds are
carefully safeguarded should be readily understood.
For the purpose of co-operation with parents or other relatives at
home desiring reliable information concerning Masons or sons of
Masons temporarily located in military camps in California, particularly concerning their health and condition, on Aug.ust 1st, 1917, I
circularized the several Grand Jurisdictions of the United States, offering the services of Brethren conveniently located near the several
military camps in California, and suggested to Grand Masters that
Lodges in their respective jurisdictions be advised of this service. The
rtsponse from many jurisdictions was gratifying, in some of which a
similar plan was followed.

I am impressed with the importance of Masonic educational instruction and the general desire for it. It is an important work that
should be undertaken by this Grand Lodge without delay. A plan has
been submitted involving amendment to the Constitution which I have
submitted to the Committee on Jurisprudence for consideration and
recommendation.
Pursuant to resolution of the Committee on Appeals and Grievances, adopted by this Most Worshipful Grand Lodge October 12, 1916,
concerning a case tried in Westlake Lodge in 1915, as follows:
"Resolved, * * * That the Grand Master be, and he is hereby
requested to either personally make, or cause to be made by a personal
representative by him appointed for that specific purpose, an investigation of the matters herein referred to; that if as a result of that investigation the Grand Master be of the opinion that in the case referred
to a notice of appeal was actually given, that then and in that event
the Committee on Appeals and Grievances at his direction review the
record in that case and report at the next annual communication in the
same manner as if a notice of appeal was actually on file; and that
finally, if the Grand Master be of the opinion that through the intentional act or omission of any person or persons the notice of appeal
was suppressed and review of the proceedings in due course thereby
prevented, that he direct that charges be preferred against the person
or persons responsible therefor."

I instituted investigation of the entire matter.
I found that notice of appeal was duly filed with the Master of
Westlake Lodge and directed that the record in the case be reviewed
by the Committee on Appeals and Grievances for report thereon at
this annual communication, in the same manner as if a notice of appeal
was actually among the records.
There was insufficient evidence to warrant a finding that the
notice of appeal was suppressed through the intentional act or omission
of any person or persons. The Master has no recollection of receiving
it and probably he paid no attention to it as he said he supposed that
the notice was to be filed direct with Grand Lodge. In this way no
doubt the document was misplaced and lost. Significant of any lack
of intention on the part of the Master to suppress the appeal was his
preparation for appeal and his belief that the case was on. appeal.

situated, such Inspector to investigate and report to the Grand Master
relative to the matter and that upon receipt of such report the Grand
Master take such steps as to him may seem proper."
P.ursuant thereto the matter was fully investigated and it was my
decision that there was no obliiation to reimburse the individuals,
either on the part of Crocker Lodge or of this Grand Lodge, which
has been duly communicated to the said individuals through their
attorney.

DECISIONS
Included herein are interpretations on the application of the law
to facts varying or differing from any hitherto, to my knowledge,
forming the basis of interpretation.
1. Right of visitation-assumed name: A Brother must not be
permitted to visit a Lodge under an assumed name. (Regulation 105 i.)

2. Dispensation fee-death of Master-elect before installation.:
A dispensation for an election consequent upon the death of the
Master-elect before installation may be issued without fee. (Const.,
Sec. 39, Subdivision 3d.)
3a. Past Masters' Association-By-laws subject to approval of
Grand Master: The rules of government of any association of Past
Mastern are sl!lbject to the approval of the Grand Master and the
Grand Lodge. (Const., Sec. 3, Sec. 9, and Sec. 224.)
3b. Past Masters-Sunday meetings: No greater latitude should
be allowed for meetings of Past Masters' Associations than is granted
to Lodges, therefore, Sunday meetings must not be permitted, except
for funeral services. (Const., Sec. 78 and Sec. 224; Regulations
43 K.)
4. Masonic ceremony-memorial tablet: The ceremonial for laying corner stone& is symbolic and cannot 8e performed for placing a
tablet. (Const., Sec. 12, and Regulation 43 J., Corner stone ceremonial.)

5. Degrees-restrictions on con.fer ring-so-called degree teams:
Before permitting a degree to be conferred by individuals other than
those qualified by installation in office, excepting only Past Masters,
their qualifications must be passed upon and approved by the Grand
Lecturer. (Const., Sec. 136, Sec. 137; Regulations 141 A., 142 J.,
143, Subdivisions 2nd, 3rd, and 5th, 138 F.)

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

281

6. Funerals: Where a funeral ceremony is conducted in the
lodge-room the Lodge must be formally opened. (Sec. 164, Const.)
7. Advancement-examination: Where several candidates are to
he examined such examination should be conducted in open Lodge,
questions and answers to be given in a distinct tone of voice and it
will suffice if questions are put to, and answered by, the candidates in
rotation. (Const., Sec. 112.)
8. Funds-how may be used: A trust has been established by
the Grand Lodge defining the use of Lodge funds. The use of funds
of a Lodge cannot be limited to specie.I calls for charity for widows
and orphans to the exclusion of Master Masons. (Const., Sec. 88, Sec.
163.)
9. Ancient landmark--<use of Masonic emblem or reference to
Masonic membership-political advertising: Use of the Masonic em-

blem or intentional reference to Masonic membership for political
advertisement constitutes a violation of Masonic law. (The charges
approved in 1722, VI 2., Const., 167b, 3, 16, Proceedings 1873, page
221.)

10. Funds-expenditures
for social purposes-social fund:
There is HO "banquet fund" or "social fund." Expenditure for social
purposes within limitations is permitted and if the full allowance be
not so expended the balance remains in the funds for prescribed purposes. (Const., Sec. 89.)
11. . Dues-remission: Dues of those who have entered the military or naval service cannot be remitted merely for that reason.
(Const., Sec. 128, Sec. 117.)
12. Grand Lodge dues-exemption from: Unless remission of
dues of a member is made at the stated meeting in July for the preceding twelve months a Lodge is not exempt from Grand Lodge dues
on account of such member. (Const., Sec. 41, Subdivision 3rd.)
13. Grand Master-dispensation for formation of tmve'ling Lodge:
The Grand Master has not the power to issue a dispensation for the
formation of a traveling Lodge. (Const., Sec. 43, Subdivision 1st, and
Sec. 73.)
14. Dispensation-for formation of Lodge: Dispensation should
not be granted for Lodges at military barracks or naval yards situated
within distance of easy access to Lodges regularly chartered. (Const.,
Sec. 73, Sec. 9.)
15. Membership-withdrawal: Notice of intention to withdraw
contemplates reading of such notice, if in writing, at a stated meeting.
(Const., Sec. 158.)

I do not occupy your time or burden the record with my reasons
for many of these decisions. With each decision I have submitted my
reasons to the Jurisprudence Committee with full faith in their review
and that so much argument as may be necessary in support of their
findings will be submitted to Grand Lodge. Neither do I occupy
your time nor burden the record with decisions where the law has
been clearly applicable.
In some instances the subject matter has been of more than ordinary interest or importance and these I desire to draw to your particular attention.

The Case of B.-Sept. 16, 1908, Brother A., Secretary of H. Lodge,
wrote to Brother C., Secretary of a certain Lodge in Illinois, referring
to a letter written May 26, 1908, and con5rming a request for a waiver
of jurisdiction from the Illinois Lodge for the purpose of permitting
H. Lodge to confer the Degrees upon B., who was initiated an Entered Apprentice Mason in the Illinois Lodge, April 1, 1873.
The records of the Illinois Lodge show that a request for a waiver
was received at the stated meeting, June 22, 1908, and that at a stated
meeting, July 27, 1908, the request was granted.
The records of H. Lodge disclose that the petition of B. for
Degrees was presented November 6, 1908, the petition acted upon
December 4, 1908, and rejected.
Nothing further appears until July 4, 1912. In the minutes of a
meeting of H. Lodge, that date, appears the following:
"A communication was received from the Grand Master requesting (H.) Lodge to confer the F. C. and M. M. Degrees on (B.)
and E. A. member of (the Illinois) Lodge."

B. was subsequently exalted and knighted. He attempted to pay
his dues to the Illinois Lodge which refused to accept them, replying
that waiver of jurisdiction had been requested and granted in 1908.
H. Lodge would not accept dues from B., claiming he was not a
member thereof. There followed considerable correspondence between
B. and the Illinois Lodge.
The waiver never became effective because the candidate was
rejected. (Reg.ulation 155d.)
The communication from the Grand Master to H. Lodge had
been misplaced or lost, consequently the notation in the minutes was
the only indication of its tenor. We were advised that the then Grand
Master had no copy of any such communication. There is no copy
thereof in the files of the Grand Lodge. Past Grand Master Delmar
Darrah, Grand Master of the Masons of the State of Illinois in 1912,
had advised the Grand Secretary that he was unable to furnish any
information Le-cause the correspondence of his office had been destroyed. The Secret<!ry of the Illinois Lodge certified under seal that
no request was ever made to have the work done for them.
The provision of our Constitution relative to conferring Degrees
upon request is as follows: "One elected to receive the three degrees
under the jurisdiction of any other Grand Body
may receive the degrees, or any of them, in another Lodge upon the
request of such first nam.ed Lodge, attested, .if it be under the J'urisdiction of any other Grand Body, by the Grand Secretary thereof,
wnder its seal."

* * *

* * *

I held that B. was not a member of H. Lodge and that H. Lodge
had proceeded irregplarly in conferri~g the Degrees by reason of the
lack of proper request.

Subsequently, waiver of jurisdiction having been confirmed by the
Lodge and the Grand Master of Illinois, the petition of B. was received and he was duly elected in H. Lodge and the situation clarified.

The Case of a Masters' and Past Masters' Association-The usual definition of objects of Past Masters' Associations is "to cultivate and
promote social, friendly and fraternal relations among its members, and
to assemble at such periods as may from time to time be by it prescribed for the purpose of conferring the order of Past Master upon
newly-elected Masters of Lodges who may desire to receive such
order, and for such other purposes as may be to the interest of
Masonry."

The purposes enunciated for a certain proposed Association suf
fered by contrast.
The Association was misnamed. Wardens were eligible to membership. This was an attempted innovation. It was misdescribed because theoretically it was proposed to extend its j.urisdiction from the
southern boundary of Inyo County to the northern boundary of California.
For the usual purposes of such an Association the district' was too
extensive. Even some of the so-called districts into which the entire
district was divided were too extensive for the accomplishment of the
ordinary purposes of a Past Masters' Association. Meetings of Past
Masters' Associations comprising the counties set forth in s.everal proposed districts might be conceived, but even one of the proposed districts would have been too extensive by reason of physical obstacles to
communication.
The foregoing was unimportant as viewed in the light of the
object defined in the proposed provisions of Article VIII: "Sec. 1.
All questions of interest arising between the sessions of the Grand
Lodge shall be submitted to the Lodges composing this Association
and decided as follows: Each Master and \Varden to be entitled to
one vote and the Past Masters, collectively, of each Lodge, to one
vote, the minority to abide by the will of and vote with the majority
when such question is submitted to the Grand Lodge. Sec. 2. All
questions of interest arising during the convocation of the Grand Lodge
to be decided by the Executive Committee and each member of the
Association to vote with such Committee."
It was an ambitious scheme of government, but clearly subversive
of the Constitution and regulations of the Grand Lodge. "The Grand
Lodge is the supreme Masonic power and authority in this Srate,
possessing all the attributes of sovereignty and government-legislative, executive and judicial-limited only by a strict adherence to the
ancient landmarks of the Order, and by the provisions of its own:
Constitution and Regulations." (Const., Sec. 7.) The Grand Lodge
of California by creation is an institution whose legislative powers
extend to every case of legislation not expressly delegated by itself
to the Lodges. (Const., Sec. 8.) It has established a scheme of governm'ent including provisions for representation and a method of voting. The fornm for determination of all Masonic problems not within
the jurisdiction of Lodges is in Grand Lodge, and not in ~aucus, as
was proposed. The creation of one or more similar orf§aniz.4\tions in.
unoccupied territory in the State with like purposes w~\c;\ i;~wier the:
Grand Lodge supernumerary.

Judging from the proposal to include the Wardens and by the
provision that the annual meetings of the Association be held, not in
the district (large and comprehensive as it was, with many places
suitable therefor), but in San Francisco during the communication of
the Grand Lodge, there was indicative a politic~! purpose dwarfing all
others.
Though possibly .unintentional, the proposed Association would
have 1usurped powers and prerogatives of the Grand Lodge. It was
further objectionable by reason of its apparent political purpose. It is
expressly provided by our Constitution that no circular or communications shall be sent concerning legislation to be brought before the
Grand Lodge or the election of officers therein.
I directed that the proposed Association, for the purposes specified
and covering territory making it impracticable to hold sessions on
convenient occasions, be dissolved forthwith. (See also Proceedings
1868, p. 399.)

Traveling or Military Lodges: A request for a dispensation empowering Brethren who have entered the service of the United States
in the Ambulance Corps to meet in a Lodge capacity within camp or
post, there to perform all £unctions of a regular Lodge of Masons,
except conferring degrees, was denied for the following reasons:
First : There is no power vested in the Grand Master to issue
dispensations for traveling Lodges;
Second : Rigid observation of the limits of, and diligence in
avoiding intrusion upon, the jurisdiction of other Grand Lodges;
Third: Safeguards provided for the formation of regular Lodges
would to some extent be slighted, namely: the recommendation of a
nearest Lodge as contemplated by the Constitution, near in the sense
of being neighbors; the provision of a safe and suitable lodge-room;
the certificate of an Inspector based upon investigation among, and
the good report of, neighbors, among other things; and thereafter the
requisite supervision;
Fourth: The question of the propriety of so-called army Lodges
of any kind which seems to me to be as important a factor as any
stated. Without question, a man who thoroughly understands the
objects and purposes of Masonry should make an ideal soldier, and,
viewed from the position of one who understands, it would seem that
nothing but benefit should be derived from such an institution. One
of the important elements irt military training is thorough appreciation
of lack of distinction, except such as is due to rank which experience

has demonstrated to be necessary for the system. While the attempt

One of the lessons most thoroughly impressed upon a Mason is that
of loyalty and it should at once be apparent that he should pursue such

such. The establishment of a military Lodge is unnecessary for the
exemplification of fraternity and even more important Masonic precepts, or for instruction and even some ceremonials. It has been said
that California is a conservative jurisdiction. It would be better to say
that tr.ue to tradition the .Masonic system is recognized as a finished
product.

In connection with the subject matter it is interesting to note the
position of our own Grand Lodge in the sixties, at which time the
question was under consideration.
The Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence of the Grand
Lodge for the year 1863 was Brother Gilbert B. Claiborne, Grand
.Master in 1865-66, and an eminent Masonic authority.
The following is from the report of the Committee on Correspondence of 1863:
"New Jersey: The report on Correspondence is from the familiar
pen of Bro. Joseph H. Hough, Grand Secretary, reviewing proceedings
of twenty-seven Grand Bodies in an interesting manner. Ours is very
fully noticed. He takes occasion, in cons·idering the report of Rhode
Island for the year ending June, 1861, to express an opinion concerning traveling Lodges in connection with the army now in the field; and
as there is already developed a difference of opinion, we present his
view of the subject. He says:
"'Have we not all acknowledged that State lines are the territory
exclusively belonging to the Grand Lodge of the States? And do we
n•t expect that they on their part will be true to their vows? But if
we encroach upon them by founding Lodges, traveling or otherwise,

287

"The Grand Lodge concurred in the opinion of the Grand Master
and the Committee. * * * We choose to express an opinion concerning the propriety rather than the legality, at this time. * * *
As we have been in our intercourse honest and true in respect for the
jurisdictional rights of another's, we will not be consistent, at least,
if we do not agree that there is impolicy-saying nothing of the legality
-in permitting Brethren, by the authority of our seal, to hold a Lodge
within the recognized limits of a sister jurisdiction of an American
State. We believe that such an act would damage the interest and
reputation of our Grand Lodge, and accomplish no good which can not
be done by individual Masons who are lovers of our whole Fraternity
wheresoever dispersed."

In the case of application for a dispensation for a Lodge with full

Second: Confusion relative w membership upon surrender of the

Somewhat akin to this was an inquiry whether the Grand Master
would grant a dispensation for the formation of a Lodge at Mare
Island Navy Yard, to which I responded as follows:
"I am of the impression that dispensation for Lodges at barracks
or navy yards situated within a reasonable distance from Lodges regularly established in home communities should not be granted.
"Without reflection upon the character of the men in the army or
navy, the membership of the Fraternity must be safeguarded and it
c_an be no better s.af:guarded than by generally insisting upon application for membership m Lodges in the community where a man has been
reared or wherein he has lived for such a length of time as to have
established. a reputation. Lodges established in towns will proceed
mere cautiously and carefully and will safeguard not only the membership of this j.urisdiction, but do full justice to the jurisdiction from
which the applicant hails and who may only be temporarily removed
therefrom, and in this connection I am of the opinion that the dispensation to ballot upon members of the army and navy should be
carefully safeguarded and extended only in case of those who are
regularly engaged in that service and not temporarily, in due consideration of the jurisdiction to which a man temporarily enlisted in
the army and navy will eventually return."
Many of the reasons assigned in support of my position with reference to traveling Lodges are applicable to Lodges of this character.

Conference of Grand Masters: The Most Worshipful Will Moore,
Grand Master of Oregon, issued a circular announcing a.uthority to
invite a general conference of Grand Masters and requesting advice
as to attenda_nce. I replied as follows:
"At the outset, I must advise that I believe I should not attend
without authority of the Grand Lodge of California. The announcement was received too late to obtain the authority at the annual communication which occurred earlier in October and a special communication at which the matter could be. considered would not be justified
for that purpose alone.
"I cannot refrain, however, ·from expressing my personal impressions with reference to the proposed conference. I feel that a
general Grand Lodge should not be established. While it is true that
there are many benefits which might result from uniformity and centralized government, yet I feel that necessary uniformity can be
attained by means of observation of what is being done in sister
jurisdictions and the adoption of that which proves satisfactory. A
plan of government vested in representatives who would probably be
limited to those who have traveled the long road through the Chairs
of the Lodge and then of the Grand Lodge would not be an improvement on the existing system. The sacrifice of time now required
makes it difficult for the active successful man to serve his Fraternity,
which service would be so beneficial. That which is not official I believe should not be attempted by Grand Masters unofficially.
"With fraternal greetings,"
This it seems is but a reiteration of the position previously taken
by this Grand Lodge. I note from the report of the Jurisprudence
Committee, Proceedings 1858, p. 321-Past Grand Master W. H. Howard, Chairman-"General sentiment of the Craft is adverse to the
formation of such a body."

The management of the Homes is satisfactory. I believe, however, that this jurisdiction might benefit by a suggestion from another
jurisdiction which is as follows: "Residents of the Home are required to engage and assist according to their strength and capacity,
in household, mechanical, or agricultural labor, under the direction of
the Superintendent, so that their time will be occupied and they may
be less dependent." I am satisfied that no self-respecting resident of
the Home, physically able, would desire it otherwise in deference to his
self-respect. Many residents are already voluntarily assisting.
Conditions at Decoto are 'generally ;;atisfactory. In connection
with extensions nothing should be done without a well-settled plan for
the co-ordination of the entire institution. This has received some attention but should have more, as there are difficulties occasioned by
location and architecture of old buildings.
I recommend to your earnest attention and consideration the extension of the scope of the Homes to admit pay residents. It has been
suggested that this might be objectionable by reason of possible discrimination. It seems to me that that may be avoided; that by
planning for a small profit from such residents, income may be obtained to lessen the burden of maintenance; that the Home will be
even more attractive and prove to be more beneficial.
At Covina there has been completed and furnished a Home,
modern in every respect, which should be equal in appointment to any
in the United States. It was dedicated September 8, 1917, with becoming ceremony in the presence of many Brethren, of which the Trustees
make liberal report. During the year I made six visits to that Home
to note general conditions and progress of the buildings.
In addition to furnishing a home, medical attention and education,
there is the far greater problem of equipping the child for its contest
in the cold world. It should not leave the Home, where it has been
recipient of care and attention, handicapped by lack of equipment
eq.uivalent to that of the child who has parental direction. It should
be more fully equipped in lieu of the advice and counsel of father and
mother, which may be massing if, owing to circumstances, it is not
adopted or is deprived of that home environment. You fathers must,

The duties of the Trustees have multiplied rapidly and occasionally

accounts, be kept there and that the Grand Secretary be Secretary of

Some experiences in connection with the Homes warrant me to
suggest that unimportant incidents, as compared with conduct consistent with the greater object to be obtained, frequently result in
fault-finding, not fair criticism, followed by petty differences, magnified
as the point of view is lost. \Ve should never lose sight of the fact
that we are all engaged in the same great .undertaking and should not
permit petty prejudices to befog our vision. It has been well said:
"Feelings strongly aroused by belief fall under control, not of reason,
but of will." Make reasonable allowance and distinguish between
effort which fails by reason of human limitation and that due to intentional malfeasance.

With considerable misgiving I have always approached the task
of uttering anything expansive of the ritual. The undertaking is
a difficult one and no doubt when I shall have concluded, it could be
well said, in light of the ritual and many learned dissertations thereon:
"The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and the thing
that is done is that which shall be done; and there is no new thing
under the sun. Is there anything whereof it may be said, See, this is
new? it hath been already of old time, which was before us." (Ecclesiastes, l, 9-10.)
·whither are we traveling? As one thoughtful Brother put it,
apologizing for the vernacular, "What is the idea?" Endurance of our
institution indicates that it is worth while. It must be worth while to
continue. The Masonic institution must be supported by something
more substantial than the artificiality of an oath. It is sustained by
something entirely substantial, difficult of definition because of its
scope. It is a plan of conduct. Try as we may to formulate rules of
conduct, we shall fail if our rules do not co-ordinate with natural
laws. That accounts no doubt for the abstra'Ction of the Masonic plan.
There is careful avoidance of concrete regulation so as not to encounter
the overwhelming force of the greater law. What, then, is the idea?
The ~1lasoni~l\$ty-stem has to do with individual life and the complex
relation of that life and society. With the individual there is the desire
to live and the same is true of the state, whether right or wrong. The
status of the individual disassociated from society is one thing, and
quite another when he is one of a group. Disassociated from society
the race was to the strong. Physical might made right. Intelligence
increased as an element in the composition of fitness, but has never
become the sole factor and never will. The fittest have ever survived.
Highly organized and civilized states giving way to sheer force of barbarous horde8 may seem not to bear this out beca.use there should have
been a continuation of those ostensibly superior states. They had
failed, however, in some way and were no longer the fittest, else they
would have been equipped to defend themselves. The individual had
been weakened hy the failure of society to conserve and develop individual strength and he was demoralized by frivolity and corruption.
The strength of the individual is the strength of the state. What the
perfect system may be time alone will tell, if it ever will. We believe
that there is in our form of government the correct conception of the

of the same inexorable natural laws. We should do that therefore
which will tend to improve it and perpetuate it. It must be sustained

Our own institution supposedly is safeguarded by its ideals intended to influence and guide its membership. That should insure
satisfactory membership. Apparently it is not always so, because we
find among our regulations concrete restrictions. Every such regulation found is to that extent evidence of failure to live up to Masonic
ideals. Theoretically such restriction is unnecessary. Our performance
has not been satisfactory. \Ve must have a better understanding.
The Masonic system is a chart for the select few. It will be
indeed ·unfortunate if those do not understand. Once equipped it is
immediately apparent that it is not limited in use to Masons alone but
is generally serviceable. That must be demonstrated by education,
always bearing in mind that it is not to think for others, but to teach
them to think and to improve their thinking faculties. It is recognized
by the institution that the individual who must be told every detail as
a rule will fail. He may have no one about him in the emergency.
If equipped with an analytical mind he will be efficient. It is therefore
that we have Masonic symbolism ever challenging thought as· discipline.

In our desire to have this government fulfill its mission of insuring
happiness, too many functions of government should not be assumed
by the people. It is stepping away from representative government and
toward pure democracy. It is not lack of confidence in the people, but
conviction that they will not conscientiously, cannot intelligently assume
the responsibility. One of the human limit•ions is that they think
they have not the time, and it's too much trouble. Can you not see
the possibility of government conducted in this manner? An individual cannot possibly combine the understanding of laborer, mechanic,
merchant, professional man, clergyman and mother. Yet to intelligently legislate in matters affecting each, one should be an expert in
each occupation and in the science of government. Government of
this sort is not for the general welfare but is influenced by class and
it reacts on the individual, thereby affecting the very fibre of the
country.
I think the idea is well defined in the following extract from a
treatise on the French Revolution :
"The French Revolution had supposed itself to be fighting for the
'rights of man'. Really it was trying to replace an autocratic kingship
by an equally autocratic 'general will' of the multitude. And it failed
because no general will could make its voice rise above the conflict of
particular inclination. Thankfolly did men bow to Napoleon."
After the great San Francisco conflagration of 1906, in the midst of
the confusion immediately following, one day a genial friend appeared,
and upon inquiry concerning his occupation, presented a card upon
which was printed his name and the word "Energist.'' He was doing
everything he could to restore order. Masons must be energists.
The service involved, the individual must be ready to perform
regardless of cost. Convenience or pleasure must not interfere.
"The philosopher, as he regarded the hot strife and struggle of
these candidates in the race for Gold, thought with a sigh of the Truth
and the Beautiful, and walked on melancholy and serene." (Thackeray.)
May we perform our duty with the understanding and fullnes·s of
sympathy which possesses fellow sufferers in time of great calamity,
with a constant fire of patriotism like that which burns in time of great
emergency, with the energy to constantly do that which posse&ses one
after refreshing repose at the beginning of an invigorating day, and
with an understanding of the importance of endeavor which confronts
one at the time of a great test.

Pursuant to said resolution five Trustees were appointed (Proceedings 1909, page 210). At the Communication of 1910 (Proceedings 1910, page 38) these Trustees reported that by lot they had determined the tenure of their office.
The Trustees changed the name of the trust to "The Masonic
Home of California" by adoption of new By-Laws. There is nothing
further than a reference to the act by the Grand Master (see Proceedings 1907, page 599).
Another change has evidently been made in the name, of which
the only record seems to be in Sections 33, 34, 35, 36 and 37 incorporated
into the Constitution at the time of the "adoption" of the Annotated
Constitution.
The provisions of the Sections of the Constitution just referred
to, owing to slight variance, demand attention. In considering these
it must be done in light of the "Explanatory Note" appearing after
Section 33 and which formed a part of the Annotated Constitution as
offered to the Grand Lodge in 1911. "The new Article (referring to
Article VIII) is added so that the Trustees of the Homes spending
nearly one-half of our revenue shall have permanent place in our law,
and this Section includes the recommendation of the Committee as to
the number and appointment of the Trustees to be found in Proc. 1909,
p. 165. The provision that the Board is to be the successor of the old
Board may prove of great value in dealing with the title to the real
property now administered by the Trustees."

"AppoinJment and Powers.
"Sec. 33. The Trustees of the .Masonic Homes of California shall be five in number, to be appointed by the M:. w:.

under the resolutions of the Grand Lodge adopted in 1892, and
