It is a logical conclusion that bv action of the Grand Lodge in
1892 a charitable trust was founded and that Trustees appointed pursuant thereto are possessed of specified powers.

INTERPRETATION OF TRUST.
\Vhat power of amendment has the Grand Lodge? The Committee recommending the plan in 1892 used these words, among others:
"Such an organization should he only the executor of the charitable
intentions of the Fraternity." It is my conclusion that thereby a broad
reservation of power in the Grand Lodge to make amendment was
intended an<l effected. Consequently. that such action as has been
regularly taken or approved by the Grand Lodge amending the Trust
by reducing the number of Trustees by providing for appointment of
Trustees from particnlar localities, extending the auth·ority of the Grand
Master to remove
authorizing the change of name of the
Trust, extending the
of the Homes to certain dependent
Masons and others, providiug for the maintenance of a hospital, are
fully within the powers reserved by the Grand Lodge to make amendment.

309

The powers of the Trustees are such only as are conferred by the
declaration of trust or as is otherwise prescribed in Section 2267 of
the Civil Code of California. 1n this connection it should be noted
that it has been held that a trustee with power to mortgage property
had no power to make a covenant to pay money and that in exec•L1ting
a note for money borrowed he is imlividually liable. This reference
is made merely to emphasize the strictness of construction of powers
of trustees for their guidance in the .transaction of their business. The
Trustees have no power of sale; when necessary that power may be
granted by the Grand Lodge. For definiteness and certainty, while
provision is made for election of officers, the Grand Lodge should
specify the officers and define their powers.
RELATIVE TO INCORPORATION.
1 have carefully considered the suggestion which has heen frequently made that the Homes shonld be incorporated. After a careful
of the history of the charity, disregarding the question of
whether or not there be power to incorporate, I am inclined to the
belief that the report of the Brethren who formulated the plan in 1891,
which was approved in 1892 by the Grand Lodge, was based upon careful legal research and consideration of the proper administration of the
charity. Incorporation was considered and, after careful investigation,
I folly concur in the report of the Committee-"that that mode is best
which shall keep the charity most fully under the supervision of the
Grand Master and in the closest relation to the Grand Lodge. Such
an organization should be only the executor of the charitable intentions ..
of the Fraternity and in perfect touch with it at all times. It is to be
a Masonic charity and should receive the hearty support and co-operation of the entire Body. To create for this pmpose an independent
legal corporation, with officers elected by an independent body of
stockholders or members (even if such a body could always be assured) would not be so desirable as to make it and its operation more
immediately dependent upon the Grand Lodge to which reports should
be made and over which it should exercise inspection and control."

It is probable that suggestions of incorporation were made without
careful consideration of the character of the trust, being, no doubt,
uncertain of the powers of an unincorporated association and believing
that by incorporation the trust administration would be more simple,
titles more secure, succession more certain, conveyances more readily
made, financial problems more readily solved and formalities required
of unincorporated associations avoided.
Uncertainty relative to administration of the charity by an unir.,
corporated Boara of Trustees may be dismissed. \Nbere the purpose

310

PROCEEDINGS OF '.l'HE

is to establish a charity and trustees competent to take the legal estate
are named and the class to be benefited are capable of ascertainment,
a court of equity will establish and enforce the charity. That the purpose of the Fraternity in establishing Homes for widows and orphans
and dependent Masons, etc., is a charity, has been established in California. Under such circumstances a bequest made to the Homes for
the purposes specified at the time of the creation of the charity, would
be valid. It has also been established in California that such an unincorporated Board are appropriate persons to accept a bequest and administer it for the purposes specified. For guidance I suggest the
following form of bequest: "I do hereby bequeath (or 'give, devise and
bequeath/ if real estate is involved) unto the Trustees of the Masonic
Homes of California and for the purposes of the charity administered
by them," and direct attention to restrictions on devises or bequests
for charitable uses, particularly, that the will must be duly executed
at least thirty days before decease.
Relative to facility of administration-there might be less difficulty
under the incorporation system \vhere a majority of the Board may
ad, whereas, under the trustee system, all must act. This requirement,
however, is probably advantageous to the proper administration of this
charity which is of such importance to the Fraternity, and, as the requirement will not ordinarily greatly interfere, there is little objection
to it. It might be advisable that the Grand Lodge should empower
such number of the Board, at least a majority (as may be deemed
advisable), when in meeting assembled, to transact business.
Relative to succession and continuity of existence-no provision
for succession can be more continuous than that provided. Corporations cease to exist, but administration of the trust under the plan provided will continue so long as there is a law of the land.
Relative to conveyances, where power is not granted to the trustees, an order of court is incidental to conveyance. It is a proper safeguard of the purposes of the charity. It would not be avoided by incorporation, even under the laws governing business corporations.
Relative to financial problems-power to borrow can only be derived from the terms of the trust. If that power is not granted, there
is none. The Trustees of the Masonic Homes are expressly denied
the power "to create any liability binding ttpon the Grand Lodge or any
subordinate Lodge." Authorization to borrow must proceed from the
Grand Lodge.
.

GHAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

311

It is a proper conclusion that legal provision has been made for the
establishment and administration of a charity, that there is facility of
doing that which it was intended should be done when the charity was
created, and that incorporation is unnecessary and inadvisable.
Respectfully submitted,
F. V. KEl\SLING, Grand Master.

ARTHUR J. RITTER,
HAROLD K. FABER.

At the request of Grand Master F. V. Keesling of the Grand
Lodge of California, the following physical and psychological survey was made of the Masonic Home for Children at Covina, Calitornia, including also an investigation of the housing and feeding,
l'anitary conditions, educational facilities and general management.
The results of this survey are presented in the general report
herewith submitted, and in an Appendix to the report in which

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

314

315

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

detailed recommendations and the results of the individual exammations of the children will be given in full.

I. The buildings of the Home are situated on a thirty-acre
r.-lot of ground in the orange belt of the San Gabriel valley about
twenty-five miles from Los Angeles. There are three large buildings of cement and brick construction, which are of a pleasing
;:irchitectural design. These are connected by covered passage
ways. The equipment and furnishings are modern and in excellent
taste.
The sleeping rooms are arranged on the dormitory plan and
have adequate ventilation. The lavatories are particularly noteworthy, being lined with white tiling and fitted with toilets, handhasins, built-in bath-tubs and showers of the most modern type.
The importance and the value of plumbing installations of this
i.igh character need no comment. A special feature of the lavatories is a device designed by Mr. Spencer for individual toothbrushes, soap and towels.
The dining room is spacious, with tables arranged for eight
and ten children, who are grouped according to age and sex. The
walls are painted a very pleasing French grey, with wood-work
in harmony. This is a very pleasant and cheerful room. The
Htchen and pantry are fairly commodious, and sanitary in every
respect. The gymnasium is one of the best features of the Home.
A large room with abundant air supply for exercises and indoor
drilling is supplemented by a large swimming pool lined with tile.
The gymnasium equipment had not been installed at the time of
inspection.
The septic tank system of sewage disposal is entirely satisfactory.
The examiners took their meals at the Home while making
the survey and found the food to be abundant, wholesome and well
cooked, though certain recommendations have been made in another
part of this report
The daily life of the children appeared, in so far as the time
at our disposal permitted us to judge, to be admirably arranged.
The children carry out most of the housekeeping work, and other
tasks suited to their age and strength are also performed by them.
Ample schooling is provided, given at the public schools of the
vicinity, which in our opinion, is a very wise provision. Besides
this, manual training of some kind is, we understood, to be provided as soon as necessary equipment can be obtained. Recreation
and training in social accomplishments are also provided for, and

in the entertainments given by the children in the evenings the
children show a gratifying absence of restraint and self-consciousness, together with a distinct spirit of co-operation and mutual
encouragement.
Such results as these, are of course, only obtained by painstaking and wise management and we feel that the Home has been
extremely fortunate in its Home Trustee Mr. E. B. Spencer and
its Matron, Mrs. Maude E. Miller. During our stay at the Home
we had an adequate opportunity to observe the management and
care of the children. Both Mr. Spencer and Mrs. Miller manifest
ympathy and devotion in their relations with the children, but,
5
~ore ·important, both a deep understanding of the problems of
childhood and the application of high principles in their solution.
Particularly worthy of mention and commendation is the home-like
atmosphere of the institution. Among the children there is a striking absence of the repression which is too often an unfor~unate
accompaniment of orphanage life, without, however, any evidence
of unruliness or unmannerly conduct. The children are exceptionally well-behaved and courteous and show no self,-consci.ousness
when meeting strangers, in marked contrast to children m most
orphanages or, indeed, in many private homes.
II. Physical Status: A complete physical examination .was
made of each child, and in addition, measurements of :he height,
weight, girth of head, chest and abdomen, and the gnp of b?th
hands. Vision was tested by the Snellen types, and hearmg
(roughly) by the watch test. Special attention was paid to the
condition of the teeth, tonsils and posture.
Taken as a group, the children showed only two defects of any
degree of seriousness: These were dental caries, and postural
defects,-the latter, however, not as a rule of serious grade . . A
majority of the children had had their tonsils removed ~nd with
a very few exceptions this operation had been performed with great
thoroughness, which is to be taken as evidence of c;:msiderable
surgical skill. In regard to the teeth, it may .be. said that the
temporary conditions obtaining before the new bmld~ngs we.re completed made it difficult to have adequate dental mspectton and
treatment carried out. Provison has been made for the necessary
cental equipment at the Home, and we· merely wish to emphasize
the necessity for frequent and regular inspection of the teeth of
all children,-every four months if possible, and in any case every
six months. It will be well worth any extra expense or effort. to
1:arry this suggestion into effect. A few children also reqmre
orthodontic correction. This is expensive but imperatively urgent

316

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

in the few cases noted. As regards postural correction, detailed
recommendations for suitable exercises will gi;en in the Appendix.
Our measurements permitted an accurate appraisal of the
relative forwardness or backwardness in physique of the individuals
and of the group as a whole, and these are of considerable interest.
Jn the table subjoined the term "percentile" has been used. In
explanation, it may be said that the percentile represents the
relation in which a measurement stands to the measurements of
normal individuals. The 100 percentile represents the highest
normal measurement, the zero percentile, the lowest normal measurement, and the SO percentile the average normal measurement.
In other words, the percentiles above 50 represent. figures above the
average, and those under 50, below the average. The use of these
figures is for the purpose of comparing the measurements of
individuals of different ages and sexes.

and favorable environment, and that with the exceptions above
noted there were remarkably few physical defects.
Recent scientific discoveries show the importance of butterfats in influencing the growth and nutrition of children, and we
should like to recommend a somewhat increased ration of milk and
butter for the ehildren, feeling that this should be given even if the
bills for food are somewhat increased. This should not, however,
he regarded as meaning that the allowance now in force at the
Home is unusually low, but rather as a plea for an allowance somewhat more liberal than the average.

The average intelligence and information of the individual
children was rather high, due to the excellent environment and
opportunity for potential development offered by the Home. In
several instances children were found not to be placed correctly
in school as to the age and intelligence, some having been advanced
too far, while others were in grades too low. Re-adjustment was
made in each case. In the course of examining, it was found that
children· of the ages of 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13 years did not know
5, 10, 2S and SO cent pieces.
It is suggested that as an essential part of training for. practical life, children should have an opportunity to make transactions
with monev. This may be done by allowing children, at least the
older ones~ who are assigned work in the Home, some monetary
compensation for their services. This would encourage a sense
of independence, the lack of which is one of the gr~atest dang~rs
1 esulting from institutional life, placing a heavy handicap on a child
making the transition from a dependent to a self-supporting

318

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

existence. The money earned could be placed in individual savings
nccounts. The child should be allowed to make financial transactions of his own, under proper supervision and direction. It is
recommended that the four children of "Borderline" intelligence
and two of the dull normal group be removed from the Home, the
former because of marked mental deviation, and the latter on
account of delinquent tendencies.
We have two other recommendations of a general character:
The first of these is a card index system. Each child on entering
the Home should receive a mental and physical examination, the
record of which should be kept on file in the office. On the same
card or sheet should be recorded the progress of the child, his
record of promotions, his conduct, illnesses, eventual disposition,,
and such other items as may be of interest. The various ways in
which such a record would be of use in scientific investigation and
study are too numerous to mention.
The second recommendation is the establishment of a "followup" system for the ben,efit of children who have left the Home.
An organization of this sort, with a committee in Northern as well
as Southern California, would make it possible for children in times
of stress or doubt to communicate freely for counsel and assistance.
It is a well recognized fact that in the pubescent period the
individual requires more and wise guidance than at any other time,
• and the plan as we conceive it would mean for the children, that
when they have left the protecting influences of the Home behind
them, they still have the opportunity to obtain needed help and
advice.
IV. Conclusion: We feel that the Masonic Fraternitv has
accomplished a remarkable feat in the establishment of an o;phanage of. the standards of the Home at Covina. The physical equipment 1s unusually fine, but the feature which renders the Home
superior to the majority of institutions of its kind is rather a
psychological one. By this we mean the atmosphere of kindliness
good-will, and intelligent sympathy which has been created there'
iargely as a result of the devotion and personality of Mr. Spencer'.
'::'he relationship between the management and the children is
worthy of all praise. As a result, we found a group of children
who in standards of conduct, intelligence, training, physique and
good manners, would not suffer by comparison with children
reared in private homes of means and refinement, and who represent a future contribution to good citizenship of which the Masons
may well be proud.

On the 21st of May a disastrous fire destroyed a large portion
of the city of Atlanta, Georgia, entailing great distress among
the people there, and the Grand Master at once wired to the
Grand Master of Georgia his offer of pecuniary assistance. The
following telegram was received from Frank 0. Miller, Grand
Master of Georgia, in answer to the proffered aid:
"With hearts full of gratitude the Masons of Georgia, and
more especially of Atlanta, thank you sincerely for your expression of sympathy and offer of pecuniary assistance. You will
never know just how much your wire was appreciated, and your
kindly offer will ever be cherished in the hearts of your brethren
in Georgia. I am happy to say .the situation is being met all
right here at home, and assistance will not be needed."

The portrait of Grand Master Burnett, as ordered, was

OUR SOLDIER MEMBERS.
Under date of August 1, 1917, the Grand Master caused the
following circular letter to be sent to the Grand Masters of the
several Masonic jurisdictions of North Americ;a:
"Many young men, Masons or sons of Masons, have left homes
and loved ones and are now in the service of their country,
located temporarily in military camps in California. In many instances parents or other relatives at home desire reliable information concerning 'these young men, particularly relative to their
health and rondition.
"For the purpose of aiding such relatives, we offer the serdces
of Brethren who are conveniently located near the several military
camps in California, and suggest to Grand Masters that Lodges of
their respective jurisdictions be advised of this proffered service.
"Inquiries di~ected to the Brethren below named will receive
prompt attention:
"Concerning men stationed at camps at or near San Francisco
(Fort Baker, Fort Barry, Fort Mason, Fort McDowell, Fort Miley,
Fort Winfield Scott, Presidio, Naval Training Station at Goat
Island), apply to Brother Leo Bruck, 419 Masonic Temple, San
Francisco.
"Concerning men at Mare Island Navy Yard, Vallejo, apply
to Brother Thomas Brown, 1205)1;! Marin street, Vallejo, or to
Brother Samuel Lyttle, box 334, Vallejo.

"Cd~icerning men at Camp Fremont (Menlo Parl~), apply to
Brother Harry N. Vandervoort, 111 Circle, Palo Alto.
"Concerning men at Arcadia or other camps near Los Angeles, apply to Brother J. M. Dunsmoor, 513 Stimson building, Los
Angeles.
"Concerning men at any of the camps at and near San Diego
(Fort Rosecrans, Camp Kearny, Naval Training, Aviation, or Radio
Stations), apply to Brother C. Woodman Potter, Masonic Temple,
Fifth and Ash streets, San Diego, or to Arthur A. Mathewson,
Coronado.
"Assuring you of our desire to be of service in any 'vay. and
feeling as you do a pardonable pride in the fact that so many
Masons are offering their services to their country, I am
"Fraternally yours,
"FRANCIS V. KEESLING, Grand Master."

PROCEEDINGS 01<' THE

.Numerous letters of commendation of the above have been
received from Grand Masters of other jurisdictions, the following
from the Grand Master of West Virginia showing the spirit of all
of them:
":our thoughtful and timely letter of August 1, 1917, calling
attent10n of the Masons of America to the fact that the homes and
hearts of Masons of your grand jurisdiction were open to the
Brethren of the Craft "'.ho _are now in the service of our country,
and who are quartered 111 some of the military camps of America
and particularly those located in California, is just received.
'
"You are to be commended for this forethought, and judging
from the knowledge I have from former acquaintance with a number. of Masons of your State, I am certain that nothing will be
omitted to make camp life of Mason soldiers as pleasant as it is
possible to do.
"Assuring you that I will give your letter and its contents
all the publicity possible among the Craft in this State, and again
thanking you, I remain
"Sincerely and fraternally yours,
"CHARLES E. CARRIGAN, Grand Master."
.

Many of our Lodges are conferring degrees upon men enlisted
the army and navy, as a courtesy for other jurisdictions and
like courtesies are being extended by Lodges in other State's for
us. A recent letter from the Grand Secretary of New York is so
comforting that it is quoted here, as follows:
111

"R. '. W." · John Which er, Grand Secretary,
"San Francisco, Cal.
"M." · W.". Thomas Penney, Grand Master, directs me to inform
you that Morton No. 63 conferred the degree of Master Mason
upon Alfred M. Sheather of South Gate Lodge No. 320, of Los
Angeles, and upon Gordon MacMillan Davidson of Highland Park
Lodge No. 382 of Los Angeles,· on Monday evening, September
24, 1917. The communication may readily be termed a 'rainbow
communication.' It was an event of historical interest. The Masonic Brothers from Camµ Mills who attended this communication
numbered over two hundred and fifty, and in a roll call of States
twenty-five in our Union were represented; also Alaska and Scotland, by Masons who have given their services in the cause of
democracy and liberty. It is the plan of Morton Lodge to have
the minutes of this communication and their subsequent military
communications printed in pamphlet form for distribution among
the members of the Lodge."

UNFINISHED BUSINESS.
Proposal to amend section 17 of the Constitution, so as to fix
the time of election in Grand Lodge for the second day of each
Annual Communication.
Proposal to amend section 30 of the Constitution by adding
the following: "The Committees on Jurisprudence, on Grievances,
and on Finance shall convene at the place of holding the Annual.
Communication of Grand Lodge at least twenty-four hours Qrevious to its opening. All propositions subject to reference to the
above said Committees must be presented in writing and delivered
to the Grand Secretary prior to the time of convening of said
Committees."

Brother Angus MacKillop, for the Committee on Grand
Master's Address and Report of Grand Secretary, reported
as follows:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

$156,769.03

In compliance with our duties as a Committee on the Most W·orshipful Grand Master's Annual Address, we have the honor to report as
follows:

PROCEEDINGS OF '£HE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

A careful digest and close analysis of this most important document has impressed our Committee most deeply. It is indicative of
the high sense of duty and careful and devoted supervision with which
our Most \Vorshipfol Grand Master entered upon his high official
duties.

Relative to increase of minimum dues, to the Finance Committee;
Extension of the powers of Finance Committee and designation as
\Vays and Means Committee, to the Jurisprudence Committee:
Decisions one to eighteen inclusive, to the Jurisprudence Committee.
Relative to the date of report of the Trustees of the Masonic
Homes, to the Board of Trustees;
Relative to report carrying affirmative recommendation, to the Jurisprudence Committee.
Relative to the physical occupation of residents of the Home, to the
Board of Trustees.
Relative to the pay residents at the Home, to the Board ·of
Trustees.
Re-organization of Board of Trustees, to the Jurisprudence Com·
mittee.
As a supplement to the Most Worshipful Master's Address, the
Committee on said message note with pleasure the very thorough and
scientific examination made by the two eminent specialists, Mr. Arthur
J. Ritter and Dr. Harold K. Faber of Stanford University on the
physical and mental qualifications of our orphan wards at Covina. It
is gratifying to note the favorable conditions prevailing, and it speaks
volumes as to the care and administration of Brother E. B. Spencer
and the :Ylatron, Mrs. Maude E. Miller, and will be a valuable aid in the
future management of the Home. We recommend that the unanimous
thanks of the Grand Lodge be officially conveyed to these eminent
professors for their gratuitous and valued services.
Your Committee on the Report of the V. W. Grand Secretary
recommends the document for its lucidity, and in the hands of the
hrcthrcn it will prove a valttablc sottrce of information.
In our jmlgment we beg to rder to the Committee on Charters
the application of Lihertas Lodge of Bakersfield, Culver City Lodge of
Culver City, and Rockridgc Lodge of Oakland, now under dispensation;
To the Committee on Jurisprudence, the special dispensations for
various purposes issued by the Grand Master;

366

In its every line it accentuates his earnestness of purpose to remedy
weaknesses or defects in :\fasonic administration and ritualistic work.
It indicates strongly, by his extensive official itinerary, his earnest
desire to come in close fraternal touch with the brethren of the jurisdiction and by wise counsel, and at times admonition, to impress ,upon
them the responsibility they owe to the fraternity and the line of conduct
to pursue to a void the pitfalls of error and possible contravention of
the ancient landmarks and sovereign rights of the Grand Lodge.

\Ve commend the foresight and judgment of the Most \Vorshipful
Grand Master in forestalling delay and possible litigation in the erection
of the Covina Home and his practical financial solution of the situation
by drawing temporarily on the Endowment Fund, thereby enabling
the work to go on to a successful conclusion.
\Ve are also pleased to recognize the desirability of extending the
fraternal and humanitarian scope of the Homes by means of the annual
Endowment Fund, and in this connection we note with gratification
the donation of an additional $19,000.00 for the betterment and extension
of the Decoto Homes from the same anonymous philanthropic brother
who previously, in the kindness of his heart and love for the orphan
and the needy, had already given $21,0CO.OO to the Home at Covina,
and we therefore fully indorse the action of the Most Worshipful
Grand Master in extending to this most benevolent and practical Mason
the heartfelt thanks of the brethren of the jurisdiction.
Altogether, we recommend to the Brethren a careful perusal of this
ahle document, which ranks high in its conception of what Masonry
stands for and its beneficient influence, not alone on the individual
Mason, but on our State, our Nation and Humanity in general.
'vVith reference to the various suggestions set forth in the Most
\Vorshipful Grand Master's message, we recommend the following to
the various Committees for their consideration and judgment:
Suggestion relative to change of method of initiation, to a speciill
Committee, with instructions that the working of the plan in other
jurisdictions be investigated;

367

To the Committee on By-laws, the various amendments to by-laws
submitted by Lodges, and all resolutions relating to Life Membership
and ap1}lication fees.
Fraternally submitted,
ANGUS MACKILLOP,

CHAs. R. M1u1cR,
C1Bs. H. V1c'l'OR.

The report was adopted.

BOARD OF RELIEF OF SAN FRANCISCO.
To the l\f.". w: .Grand Lodge of California:
We beg to submit the following report for the year commencing
August 28, 1916, and ending August Zl, 1917, both dates inclusive.
We still note with regret the evident desire of Lodges, for whom
we have spent a great deal of money, to try and evade their responsibilities, and we deplore their obvious endeavor to see how little they
can do, instead of realizing how much they ought to do.
The commercial spirit which enters into their dealings seems to
have superseded the Masonic spirit which should be there.

375

It is very refreshing to have the Grand Master of a sister jurisdictio11 defend the actions of this Board in doing its Masonic duty,
and our thanks are due to Brother George R. Malcolm, Grand Master
of the State of Washington, for the able manner in which he presented
the claim of this Board against one of their Lodges; in his address
at the opening of said Lodge.
The .following from the address of the Grand Master of Arkansas
at its Communication in November should be of interest to the Craft, ·
and is hereby submitted to them:
"I have been compelled to make several subordinate Lodges pay
to other Lodges money that had been expended for the purpose of caring for the sick, and in som£ instances burying the deceased. It is a
deplorable fact that some of the Lodges of this jurisdiction have
allowed Sister Jurisdictions to care for their .ick and bury their deal),
and then repudiate the debt, on account of being financially poor.
And in this connection I want to take the time to express lo the representatives of the subordinate Lodges my utter contempt for a Lodge
which refwes to pay for the care of a sick Brother or the burial of
a dead one. If it is wrong to defraud a Lodge of Master Masons,
under ordinary circumstances, it is doubly so to refuse to pay the expense incurred by a sister Lodge in caring for our sick and afflicted,
and a Lodge that 'Will not do that, should have their charter arrested
and have their organization 'Wiped off the map, for of all the contemptible, mean thiings it is possible for a Lodge to do, I think that
it is the worst, and I would' feel more kindly to a Lodge that would
wilfully viola1te every edict of the Grand Lodge than. the one who
obeys every edict implicitly and then refused to pay the {11neral expenses of a deceased Brother, when such e:rpense was incurred by a
sister Lodge."
We also desire to thank our medical Brethren who have so ably
assisted us during the year by generously giving their professional
skill without any remuneration. We refer to Doctors H. L Block,
J. C. Egeberg, D. E. F. Easton, Otto Freyermuth, A. S. Green, William
P. Read, Jacob Schwartz, George A. Wood, Wilhelm Waldeyer and
A. L. W. Zillmer.

REPORT OF THE MASONIC EMPLOYMENT BUREAU OF
SAN FRANCISCO.
Another' year has nm its course. With unabated fnry and horror
the most terrible war of all times continues. The sacrifice of onr
brethren over the seas staggers us; the war's effect now reaches directly to our own land, and there is much distress and suffering to be
alleviated.
The demands upon the :Masonic Employment Bureau of San
Francisco have become greater and greater each succeeding year,
am! fortunately the Bureau h;is kept apace with these demands anrl
has become a more potent factor for good to the unemployed in the
Fraternity. Distress in many instances has meant the want of a job,
and the Bureau finds for the able-bodied brethren, who have still
something to give to the world and mankind, a market for their
honest industry.
The Bureau takes this occasion to thank the Fraternity at large
for the whole-hearted assistance it has received. The members have
put their shoulders to the wheel with the gratifying result shown in
the appended report. Let us hope that the good work will continue,
and that each succeeding year may show greater usefulness on the
part of the Employment Bureltu for the members of our bC'loved
Order.
l<'raternally submitted,
ARTHUR JOEL,
President.

THOMAS IRWIN,
Secretary.

BOARD OF RELIEF OF LOS AI\'GELES.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

The Masonic Board of Relief of the City of Los Angeles, herewith presents the following report of its labors from September 1,
1916, to August 31, 1917.
The Masonic Board of Relief is composed of the Masters (exofficio) of the 27 Blue Lodges of this City and two members appointed
by him, together with the Past Grand Masters residing within the City
of Los Angeles, the Inspectors of the several Masonic Districts of Los
Angeles City, one representative from each of the several Royal Arch
Chapters, the Council. the Commandcries, the Scottish Rite bodies
and the Shrine, the manager of the Masonic Employment Bureau, and
one Past Worthy Matron of the Order of the Eastern Star.
Officers:
President, J olm Hill Bean; Vice-President, Dana
Reid Well er; Treasure:-, Motley Hewes Flint; Secretary, John Marcus
Dunsmoor.
Stated Meetings arc held on the first Sunday of each month.
officers form an Executive Board and are on duty daily.

The

In presenting our report for 1916-1917, we arc pleased to say that
although the '~Great Conflict" has produced the condition of "High
Cost of Living," yet the actual calls for monetary consideration have
not been so heavy as heretofore.

The Employment Bureau has been of great assistance in putting
many in the way of self-supporting, who would of necessity have been
obliged to ask for aid, had it not been for our Employment Bureau.
However, the calls have generally been exceedingly urgent.

1,595.00
Total Cash Available ........................................................................$1,889.17

There have been fewer Masonic tramps, and it is to be hoped that
this class will soon realize that "Once a Mason, always a Mason,"
lloes not hold good unless he shall have deported himself in a manner
to convince the Craft that he is Worthy, and well Qualified.

The Masonic Board of Relief of Oakland herewith presents the
following report of its labors for the year embracing September l,
1916, to August 31, 1917.

Balance on hand September 1, 1917 --··--·······················-··

$2,659.22

The Board is composed of the Masters and Wardens of the Nine
Blue Lodges of this city.
The officers elected to serve until the first W cdnesday in J an11ary.
1918, are: Edwin L. Hiteman, Chairman; Albert B. Cosad, Treasurer;
Robert G. Evans, Secretary.
A continuance of the trade and labor conditions, to which reference
was made in our report for 1916 as affecting the last half of that
fo;cal year. has effected a marked decrease in applications for relief,
causing a falling off, as compared with last year, of about twenty-five
per cent.

following report for the year ending August 31, 1917:

280
61

The Employment Bureau has secured several lucrative positions and
plaees of responsibility and honor. To find employment means more to
the man who is physically able to work, than the loan of money.

The Employment Bureau has stimulated interest in the "Craft" and
a new self respect in those whom we have helped.
\Ve have recorded on our files the names and number, where
located, etc., of different Lodges by whom relief has been given, direct
from Lodge to applicant. These Lodges requested this Board to call
on the one in need, and we have visited thorn frequently and had considerable correspondence. None of this money appeared upon our books,
amOU!Ilting in the aggregate to approximately $3,000 additional business.
This service has been a real pleasure, as it is helping fulfill the object in
maintaining a Board of Relief, and is in line with our idea of Masonic
service.

REPORT OF GRA)JD LECTlJRER.
To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:

I herewith submit my report as Grand Lecturer, giving an ac·
count of my stewardship foc the year just closed.
I have visited every distric;.t in the jurisdiction and have held
schools of instruction, both day and night sessions, in most of the
Lodges therein, also giving private instruction to. many of the officers
and members in my office. I am always glad to have the brethren
call on me for this service when in San Francisco.
The condition of the Lodges is generally good, many of them
having an unusual amount of work, due in ma.ny instances to the
desire of petitioners to receive their degrees before being called to
the colors. Quite a few Lodges have been badly crippled by the loss
of their Masters, ·wardens and other officers who have either enlisted
or have been called in the draft. Most of the Lodges have met this
condition by simply advancing the officers in line and going along with
the work with slight interruption.
It is certainly gratifying to learn from the splendid showing
of the reports that many of our brethren who have enlisted have
received commissions, from Sergeants up. This surely speaks well for
the caliber of our membership and the high standard of the Masons
who have enlisted in this great war.

vVe most sincerely trust, and we offer up our most fervent
t)ra,yers, that a permanent and lasting peace will soon be established.

GRAND LODGE 01<' CALIFORNIA

397

Three new Lodges have received dispensations this year, making
now a total of 379 Lodges, with a membership of over 60,000. There
are several small Lodges throughout the State that are having a
hard time to exist, and I fear they will eventually have to consolidate
with some near-by Lodge, the membership being so scattered that
it is difficult for them to get a quorum. This is indeed an unfortunate condition, for all those Lodges are composed of good men and
enthusiastic Masons, who have worked hard for many years to maintain their Lodges, but who must ere long submit to the inevitable
through lack of numbers. We trust that something unforeseen will
come about to change this condition.
I would suggest that some uniform method be adopted by which
Lodges may check up the standing of visitors. The card system
now in use by many Lodges seems to be the simplest and most inexpensive way to handle this. These cards can be obtained :1t a very
nominal cost. Many Lodges do not in any manner check up the
register of visitors. I trust this Grand Lodge will take the nrcessary
action requiring all Lodges to do this.
I have received reports from all the inspectors, and they report
the Lodges over which they preside to be doing good work, and
most of them increasing numerically and financially. I regret that
space will not permit the printing of some of these reports. Several
Lodges have under course of erection new Temples.

I desire to express to the Inspectors my sincere thanks and deep
gratitude for their able assistance, and for the many courtesies extended to me during the year, and to congratulate them on the
splendid condition of the work in their respective districts. The
work they are doing is worthy of the highest and just commendation
by this grand body.
My thanks are due the V. \V. Grand Secretary and his assistant
for many cou,rtesies extended to me during the year.
It has been my great pleasure to accompany the Most \Vorshipful
Grand Master on many of his visits to the Lodges throughout the
jurisdiction. The Most Worshipful has visited almost every district
in the State, and only the lack of time and pressing business prevented him from reaching all. Most of these vfaits were joint meetings, at which all the Lodges of the Distr.ict were represented by
large delegation~. The inspiring and instructive messages which the
Grand Master left with the brethren at these meetings were certainly
greatly appreciated, and cannot fail to make those who were privileged
to hear the profound lessons illustrated and explained in these masterly
addresses better men and Masons, and which gave the brethren much

ENDOWMENT COM1HTTEE OF MASONIC HOMES.
February 1, 1916:

The Report of the Endowment Committee of the Masonic Homes was read. That portion relating to the purchase of securities from, moneys of the Fund was referred
to the Committee on Finance. In all other respects the
report was accepted as read:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Ca'l'ifornia:

We, members of ycmr Endowment Committee of the Masonic
Homes of California, appointed by the Grand Master at the close of
the last Grand Lodge, beg to report that thiS> very important matter
has received our very best thought and attention during the past year.
When it is taken into consideration that since the close of our last
Grand Lodge session two Endowment Days have been held-namely,
Thanksgiving, :\fovember 30th, 1916, and St. John's Day, June 24th,
1917-it will be apparent that the very large amount of correspondence
handled by your Committee has meant untold labor, but the m,ost
satisfactory results secured have more than compensated for the efforts
put forth.

It has seemed to be almost an impossible task to convince some
of the Lodges that the Endowment Fund is essentially necessary, as
they fail to appreciate that without endowment funds many of the great
universities, colleges, and also many of the i1111portant charities of our
country could not be maintained. In practically every case it has been
noted that where the Masters, and more particularly the Secretaries,
have been deeply interested in Endowment Day, the results have been
more than satisfactory, but where enthusiasm was lacking, the returns
from those Lodges were most discouraging.

The Endowment Fund was increased $11,102.56 during the past/
year through the contribution of the Executive Committee of the 33rq
Triennial Conclave Knights Ternplar. The Grand Commandery o;
Knights Ternplar made a liberal appropriation for the entertainment
of the Grand Encampment, and practically one-half of the total amount
raised was thwugh the Grand Commandery, the balance being raised
locally in Los Angeles. After .all the bills were paid, it was· found
th.at this balance remained, and it was difficult to apportion to the
various funds from which it was derived, the amount on hand; hence
your Chairman of the Endowment Committee, who was also Chairman
of the Executive Committee for the entertainment of the Knights Templar, suggested to his fellow-members the des.irability of recommending
that the entire balance be given to the Endowment Fund. The matter
was presented to the Grand Commandery, Knights Templar; the recommendation approved; the money forwardecl to the Grand Recorder of
Knights Templar, and by him turned over to our Grand Treasurer.
This, as before stated, amountecl to $11,102.56.
No set rules or regulations have ever been made for the pltrchas~
ing of securities for the Endowment Funcl, and so far as we can ascertain the only regulations that we have are that the Grand Treasurer
shall be the custodian of all the funds of the Grand Loclge.
Your Committee believes it desirable that the Grand Treasurer
shall have the co-operation of some of the able men in the Grand Loclge
in the purchase of securities, and also that the securities be uncler
jurisdiction of two or more persons. We therefore offer as a &uggestion or recornmenclation that the Grand Treasurer be the custodian of
the funds and securities of the Endowment Fund, under the joint super
vision of himself, the Grand Master and the President of the Board of
Trus-tees of Masonic Homes, and that these three shall be the Committee to purchase securities for the investment of the Endowment
Fund.
'vVe take pleasure in transmitting in cletail the result of the co:1tribu:tions for both Endowment Days, and earnestly recommend that
each representative at Grand Lodge examine the list most carefully
and note the returns from his Lodge, and if the contribution has• not
been in proportion to their ability, when next Endowment Day is decided upon, will not the respective Lodges urge each member to have
the necessary enthusiasm and appreciate the real necessity of this
splendid undertaking?

Y.our Committee on the Grand Lodge Library herewith i:iresents
the following report :
The Grand Lodge Library, as at present constituted, consists of
a considerable number of books, reports, and ot~er l_iterary matt~r
deposited in rooms adjacent to the ~rand. Lodge ?ff1ces m the Masonic
Temple. There is no catalogue to give either their names or er.ui:ieration. Some are in bookcases, some on shelves, and the rem~mder
piled upon the floor. They have all been secured by exchange, m the
ase of R'eports of the various grand bodies of Freemasonry, and by
~onations from brethren of the craft and others, since the dPstrnction
of the original Grand Lodge Library in the great fire of 1906. Tl~e
books comprise a number of volumes of value to student~ of ~asomc
lore together with many others which have no connect1on with the
ritu;l, history, or symbolism of Freemasonry. Th_e Gra~d Secretary
has. in addition to his other multifarious Masomc duties, collected
anci in some measure co-ordinated the collection.
No appropriation has ever been made by the Grand Lodge for
the cataloguing of the books on han<l, for the acquisition of .new books,
or for the regular care and upkeep of the Grand ~o<lge Library. No

Your committee is of the opinion that the Grand Lodge Lib:ary

BY CHARLES L. PATTON, PAST GRANO MASTER

M.'.W.'.Grmtd l'vfastcr and Brethren:
Samuel Crawford Denson was born near Quincy, Adams Connty.,
Illinois, September 23, 1839. He belonged to an old American family,
am! his forefathers were found
"Where once the embattled farmer stood
And fired the shot heard 'round the world."

MEl\IORIAL SERVICES.
Services in memory of Past Grand Masters Denson,
Nutting an<l Hart were now held, the program being as
follows:
Organ prelude-Samuel D. Mayer, Grand Organist.
Prayer-\Villiam A. Chapman, as Grand Chaplain.
Vocal Solo-Brother Benjamin Liederman.

He was educated in the district school and at Abingdon College,
and commenced-the study of law at Quincy, but before completing his
cou.rse, he came in 1860, across the plains, behind an ox team, to Bntte
county, where for a time he engaged in mining near Oroville; there
continued his legal studies at night, and was admitted to the Bar in
1863. In March, 1864, he located at Carson City, Nevada, and in the
fall of that year was elected a member of the first State Legislature
from Ormsby county, and there practiced his profession, serving as
District Attorney from 1866 to 1868. In December of that year he
removed to Sacramento and there practiced law until 1875 in partnership with Hon. H. ·0. Beatty and with his son, Hon. Wiiliam H.
Beatty, afterwards Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of this State.
In 1875 he was elected Judge of the Sixth Judicial District, composed of the counties of Sacramento and Yolo, and in 1879, when. the
new Constitution went into effect. he was elected Superior J t:dgc of
Sacramento county. In 1882 Judge Denson was the Republican candidate for Justice of the Supreme Court, but the State went strongly
Democratic that year and the nominees of that party were all elected.
J ndge Denson removed to San Francisco in 1839, and from that
time until his death was in the active practice of the law there.
In the early sixties Judge Denson married Mary Beatty, sister of
Chief Justice Beatty, and hy this marriage he had three children, Mary
Beatty Denson, wife of Douglas A. Lindly, now residing in Sacra-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

428

429

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

mento; Henry Beatty Denson, now residing in San Francisco, am.1
Laura Gertrude Denson, wife of George M. Mott, now residing in
Berkeley.
His first wife died many years ago, and about 1906 he married
Laura Ames, who survives him.
Brother Denson's Masonic record is as follows:
He received the degree of Entered Apprentice April 27, 1861; the
degree of Fellow Craft October 5, 1861. and the degree of Master
Mason November 26, 1861, in Oroville Lodge No. 103, served that
lodge as its Steward in 1862, as its Secretary in 1863, and withdrew
from it in 1868. He affiliated with Carson Lodge No. 1, :N'evada, November 19, 1868; withdrew from that lodge March 4, 1869; affiliated
with Union Lodge No. 58, of Sacramento, April fah, 1870, and served
as its Master for two terms in 1872 and 1873.
He was elected the Deputy Grand Master of this Grand Lodge in
October, 1879, and Grand Master in October, 1880.
He became a member of Sacramento Chapter .No. 3, R. A. M.,
March 23, 1875;. a member of Sacramento Council No. 1, R. an•J S. M ..
.November 29, 1880; a member of Sacramento Comtpandery No. 2,
K. T., July 10, 1879, and remained a member of the Ma.sonic bodies
in Sacramento until July 26th of the present year, when, after an illness
of about eight months, at the close of a life exceeding three score
years and ten, our brother passed away, quietly and peacefully, as one
who, at the end of a perfect day, lies down to calm repose.
The record of our brother's professional career and of his Masonic
life cannot give us a distinct or well-defined appreciation of the man
himself or the Mason himself. Would that you could picture him as
he was over a quarter of a century ago when I first entered the Grand
Lodge.
He was of commanding presence, dignified and courteous,
quiet and unassuming. There was that about him that made one feel
he was forceful and successful in his chosen profession, true to his
family, to his friends and to his Brethren, and true to his country
as a thorough American should be.
I distinctly remember him again when Past Grand Master Atkinson
and he appeared before the Grand Lodge and presented for its con·
sideration the reviskm of its ritual. How forcefully he placed before
us the proposition that under our Constitution the ritual of Masonry
could not be changed, and how thoroughly he convinced us that these
proposed changes were simply for the purpose of making our degree
work conform more fully to that which had been handed down from
time immemorial.

In thinking and speaking of a life like this and a death like this
our minds refuse to be content with the philosophy which characterizes
all beyond our finite comprehension as the unknowable. althoucrh
indeed, in regard to matters affecting· life, death, and the Great He~e~
after we are but "infants crying in the night, infants crying for the
light, and with no language but a cry"; yet, we as Masons hold a different be lief as to all these matters, for it is one of the landmarks of
our Institution that there is a life beyond the grave where we will know
each other again. 'Ne can therefore feel assured that in a brighter,
better land, aiter we, too, shall have passed the portals of the grave,
we shall meet our Brother again in that "Celestial Lodge above, where
the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe forever presides." Until
we do so meet, dear Brother, until then, farewell.

IN MEMORIAM

<llqarlrs llilhrr Nutting
BY GEORGE W. HUNTER, PAST GRANO MASTER

Most T-Vorshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
\Ve gather here each year mainly for the purpose of exchanging
friendly greetings, the transaction of business of the Grand Lodge, the
election of its officers and to participate in a work which is in the
interest of humanity and for the general benefit of this great fraternity.
While it is not always so, usually an hour is set apart at each
Annual Communication for memorial services. In the course of nature
many members of this great brotherhood within this jurisdiction die
each year, and rarely does a year roll round without taking as toll
one or· more of our Past Grand Officers, and within the last few
months three of them have passed away and all were held in the highest esteem.
It has been about twenty years since I first attended this Grand
Lodge, and since that time quite a number of the Past Grand Masters
of this Lodge, men who were then strong in mind and body and who
took an active part in Masonic as well as public and business affairs,
have gone from the scenes of this transitory life.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We can in memory and imagination recall their form and features
and listen to their voices in debate or conversation, and we know that
the noble example set by them1the work that they did and the good
thev accomplished while here, has had a wholesome influence upon our
ow~ lives and will continue to redound to the benefit of men and
::VIasonry for long years to come.

childhood and early youth. Four years of his young manhood were
spent as a clerk in a bank, and then he decided to take up one of the
learned professions. Brother Nutting would have succeeded in almost
any profession. He was a man of fine presence, had a clear, logical
mind, strong perceptive and reasoning powers and would have made
a good lawyer, but he chose as his life work the medical profession,
and there is no higher calling, for it is a field in which his. best efforts
were devoted to the preservation of human life and the alleviation of
human suffering.

430

There is nothing so very dreadful about death, and yet most of
us dread it. In this time of stress and destruction, when millions of
men are under arms and almost thousands slain daily, and we read in
the papers of this terrible loss of human. life, we in a m~asure gr?w
accustomed to death by reason of its frequency, and sometimes I thmk
we do not consider it as seriously and thoughtfully as we should.
There is something very .instructive in the reverence and tenderness with which we cherish the inemory of the dead. It is hard for
us to part with family or friends, and when gone from earth, there is
still an affection for them of the sincerest kind. Our thoughts are
frequently of them, and there is a longing for them which causes us
to believe that this tie of sympathy and love is so strong and far-reaching that we have reasonable ground to believe that in some. way they
may be thinking of us, and this is one of the strongest evidences of
immortality.
"No man liveth to himself alone and no man dieth to himself."
In order to have happiness and be useful in this world we mnst
have companionship, and this great fraternity to which we belong
enables us to make friends, enjoy our intercourse with them, and to
do something for our fellow-man.
These memorial services, solemn though they be, give us an opportunitv to express our appreciation of the value of the friendship, character- and worth of departed brothers, three of whom but a short time
since held
rank in this Institudon and who by their zeal, intellect
and power, always wielded an influence for good and left a lasting
impression upon Masonry throughout the great State of California.

It is my privilege to say a few words on the life and character of
Past Grand Master Charles Wilber Nutting, whose death occurred at
his home at Etna Mills on the 20th of September, 1917.
Brother Nutting was born in Georgia, October 3d, 1852, and possessed the chivalrous spirit, the high sense of honor, and the true hospitality characteristic of men of Southern birth and environment. Twice
after coming to this State he made long visits to his old home in the
South, and no doubt enjoyed thoroughly visiting the scenes of his

431

In 1876 he graduated from Atlanta Medical College and for two
years thereafter held the position as demonstrator of anatomv in that
institution, and during the same period was one of the city 1;hysicians
for the city of Atlanta.

Jn 1878 he came to California and located at Etna Mills, in Siskiyou county, where he lived for nearly forty years, built up and maintained an extensive and lucrative practice and enjoyed the confidence,
respect, and esteem of all the people in that part of California.
Dr. Nutting ranked high as a surgeon, and years ago I had heard
of this skill, and knew that his reputation was not confined to hi6 home
county, and had been told of his performing very difficult and critical
operations in the large hospitals of San Francisco. On one occasion
I spoke to him of this, and asked him why he did not locate in San
Francisco, as he was well known here, and I felt confident that with
him it would not be a venture or an experln1ent, but that he would
succeed from the: start and soon become one of the leading physicians
and surgeons of this great city. His reply was characteristk of the
man, and showed that he cared little for wealth or fame. He stated
... to me that a similar suggestion had been made to him many times by
others and he had given it serious consideration, but he had lived in
Northern California the most of his life, liked the people of that part
of the State, had known many of them from the time of thc:ir birth,
was comfortably situated with his family in his own home and he felt
that he could be happier and do more good in Siskiyou county than
he could in San Francisco, and tl.1erefore he would not make the change.
Dr. Nutting took great pride. in. his profession, qualified himself
thoroughly for the performance of his duties, for ten years was a
member of the State Board of Health, was a member of the American
Medical Association, and President of the Medical Society of Siskiyou
county at the time of his death.
On October 3d, 1881, he was married to Janet Parker, rlaughter
of Alexander Parker of Siskiyou county. His wife and seven children
survive him, fonr sons and three daughters, and as an eviden•:e of his

"Masonry is not only the oldest, but the most conservative of

should never be lowered by any act of ours .• and. we should endeavor so

Brother Nutting endeavored to live uir to the principles and teachings of Masonry and to practice them in his daily life as defined in his
own beautiful language. He was honest, generous, charitable and
just; an ideal husband and father, an exemplary citizen and faithful
servant, a true friend and brother, and his loss will be sadly felt not
only by the members of his family, but by the community in which he
lived and his brethren of the Mystic Tie.

BY GEORGE F. RODDEN, JUNIOR GRANO WARDEN

\.Yhen I was invited by the Grand Master to speak to you in
kindly recollection of the Most \Vorshipful Past Grand Master
Edward H. Hart, the commission was accepted with an admixture of
sentiments. It was a great pride that the Grand Master should have
thought me worthy; pleasure that opportunity would be given to
hring heforc you, his beloved brethren, additional evidences of his
great heart and matchless mind; and, conscious of my own weakness,
apprehension lest a subject deserving the master touch should be
all too feebly treated.
And, too, one approaches with greatest trepidation the task of
eulogizing with mere words one whose life work and accomplishments
have spoken so forcefully and so eloquently.
Especially is this true when addressed to an audience composed
of the leaders of Masonry in California, each of whom bv contact
or observation, has been made aware of the virile stren~th: indefatigable energy and splendid efficiency with which Brother Hart prosecuted the many duties assigned to him. and of Masonrv's tremendous
obligation to him, an ohligation which can only be - liquidated by
giving to him his deserved place among our highest and best.
His advent into the world was under conditions none too propitious. Divested at an early age of those tender parental influences
which are the fonts of inspiration of all youth's ambitions, and, in
lives more happily circumstanced, the directing forces of their development, the young lad soon realized the necessity for reliant selfdependence.
Then and there were born those exalted ideals towards which
he continually and tmn;mittingly struggled, and then and there were
laid the foundations of those qualities of mind and character which,
in their elaboration, carried him to such great heights and made
humanity his debtor.

Accepting Abraham Lincoln as his ideal, and the pattern by
which he should shape his .life, he carried bravely over obstacles,
smilingly disregarded adversity, made light of the thousand and
one trials that would have appalled a less gallant spirit, and finally
succeeded in winning his way, with high honors, through the law
department of Ann Arbor University. The first mile post' was
[)assed, but that was all. The goal of his ambition was ·not yet
reached. The practice of the law was not a part O'f his predetermined
scheme of things.

"But the thing a man does practiwlly believe-the thing a man does
lay to heart and know for certain concerning his vital relations to
this mysterious universe, that is in . all cases the primary thing for
him and creatively determines all the rest. That is his religion."

434

All of. those heart-rending, heart-breaking years of toil and selfdenial were but a fragmentary leaf in his program of life; hut
he had fought through them with the fervor of an ascetic for the
general enrichment of his mind, the strengthening of those qualities
which he deemed necessary to success ; and, finally, when all demands
had been met, and all duties to his friends and family had been
fulfilled, that his knowledge of the law, broadened and embellished by
a lifetime of faithful study, might be utilized in the service of his
country and his people.
While still a young man, his talents attracted the attention of
men high in the insurance world, and he was sent to California to
establish and manage a western branch of the Penn J\'Iutual Insurance
Company.
~ow was brought to light his theretofore undiscovered genius
for organization and administration. He attacked the problems which
confronted him with that zeal. attention to detail and steadfastness
of purpose which were so characteristic of him, and which brought.
not only a full measure of success to his undertaking, but likewise made
his name one to conjure by in the insurance world. His knowledge
of the ramifications of the complex business in which he was engaged
was so absolute, his attitnde towards his clients so equitahle arnl just,
it has heen said of him, and truthfully said, that in the more than
thirty years of his business career not a single bit of litigation has
been entered against his company.

Thomas Carlyle has advanc<:d this philosophy:
"It is well said. 111 every sense, that a man's religion is the
chief fact with regard to him.
"By religion, I do not mean the church creed which he professesthe articles of faith which he will sign and in words or otherwise

My brethren, could any of us in any wise familiar with Edward
Hart, with his increasing, undiminishing activities, with the sacrifice of
home and personal comforts made in the name Df Masonry, and the
tremendous influences which he exerted in its behalf, question for a
moment to what he had practically laid his heart-accepted as his
religion ? I think not.
And having accepted Masonry as such, his every thought, act
and deed were moulded and directed by its precepts. Faithfully and
loyally did he adhere to its divine lessons. To those of us who
would falter and complain that our Masonic burdens were become
too heavy; to those of us who would interpret too broadly or even
view with a note of incredulity the demands laid upon us by our
obligations, what an inspiration and support reflection upon his
Masonic life must ever be.
The great honors received at the hands of the brethren of his
mother Lodge, Live Oak No. 61, the exalted place of Most Worshipful Grand Master of Masons in California (in our belief the highest
to which any man can aspire), to which we, his associates of the
Grand Lodge were glad to elevate him, were but the natural and inevitable rewards for faithful and brilliant service.
He was, according to the records, initiated in Wellington Lodge
No. 127, State of Ohio; passed and raised August 21, 1891, by Live Oak
Lodge No. 61 of Oakland, California.
A simple statement that, and cold, but distinctly significant, for
the date of that raising marked an epoch in Masonic annals. On that
date a new and brilliant star rose in the Masonic heavens.
On that day was recruited a mind conceiving the most wondrous
thoughts, a tongue capable .of their adequate expression, and a will and
determination to see them duly executed.
His last months were months of patiently-endured misery of body
and mind, fighting but without hope against the ravages of a dread
disease; accepting and enduring, with mute resignation, the failure of
his last great ambition, that he might be permitted to serve you and
me in the halls of Congress; but to the last a man, to the end a Mason,
tender, courageous and true. May I be permitted to offer this as a
fitting epitaph. But of a great man, especially of him, I will venture
to assert, it is incredible he should have been other than true. It
seems to me the primary foundation of him and all that can lie in him,

There are many standards for our guidance and our government. We establish standards for ourselves in our sessions and
in our intercourse,-we have our traditions and our customs. We
are bound by Masonic law and the Constitution of this body; by the
tenets of our Institution and its ancient landmarks. But by far
the most inflexible standard is imposed neither by ourselves nor
by the law, but by others; by the Masons of California who claim
no membership in this body, by the men of California who never
have knelt before a Masonic altar. The woman who sins is ostracized; the clergyman who is fourid in a compromising position
10rfeits his influence and his career; the judge who swerves from
the path of strict integrity is universally condemned. They are
constituted like ourselves, they have the same instincts and the
s::.me desires; but what is ignored among men means downfall
among women; what is condoned in the business man, the laborer,
the physician, the merchant and the attorney, is condemned in the
clergyman or in the judge. I have no wish to plead the cause
of double standards, but it is an irresistable fact that for each of tis.
according to his position and his profession, society has established
bo'unds which he may not pass. Our mental justification of our
acts is of no effect in this great court of human kind. We are judged
not alone by what we are, and by what we believe, and by that
to which we aspire; but even more by that which we profess, and
Ly the extent to which, in the opinion of our fellow men, practice
goes hand in hand with precept. It is a law more ancient thar; the
law of Moses, as inflexible as the law of the Medes and the
Persians, and as enduring as the word of God itself. The influence
and the effectiveness of this grand body, its leadership among
Masons and its respect among men, depend not so much upon its
organization, its rules and its traditions, as upon its conformity
to the standard which others impose; the standard which in the
mature judgment of men comports with the dignity of such a body,
with the precepts of the Institution of which it is the titular head,
and with the pre-eminence which this Grand Lodge itself asserts.

Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren
of the Grand Lodge:
Masonic custom has decreed that it shall be the duty and the
pleasure incident to this office, to deliver at the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, an address upon matters appertaining to the craft. It would be superfluous, if not presumptuous,
:ipon my part, to attempt on this occasion to eulogize our Institution or to extol its principles; that service already has been too
well performed by those who have preceded me. It is my purpose
to briefly direct your attention to this grand body itself.
While the Grand Lodge of California is the executive head
of the Lodges in this jurisdiction, it is essentially a union of
individuals, and not of Lodges. Upon its rolls are found many of
rhe greatest names in our State, men of honor and of fame, men
who have accomplished much. There are others whose faces are
unknown and whose personality has been impressed only upon their
immediate environment. Every one of them, however, has been,
and every member of this Lodge to-day is, without exception, a
chosen man. Each of them has stood forth among the brethren
of his Lodge and by them has been deemed worthy to be a
Master, with the power, the responsibility and the opportunity,
which that office affords. Because of that fact others have
watched him; his strength has been an encouragement, and where
he has slipped they· have fallen. \Ve glory in the history of
Masonry, in the fact that none but good men and true may enter,
that it represents the best element in every community. If this
Grand Lodge indeed be the select body of such a constituency,
what opportunities stretch before it, what responsibilities rest upon
it, how impressive are the requirements for its standards and its
accomplishments! The time devoted by such men must accomplish

a worthy leader, if it rises above the deadly level of the general
average, should it not possess the consistency and the vision, which

You may have listened to some silver tongued orator; ,his
phrases soothe your , ears, his thoughts hold your attention, his
rounded periods rouse your enthusiasm; but he does not grip your
heartstrings, because you realize that, after all, they were only
words-graphically, scientifically and beautifully arranged, but
words nevertheless. Another speaker follows him; halting in his

perhaps the tears come into your eyes; he has struck the chord
of human sympathy; he holds you because you know he speaks the
truth; he has touched the underlying reverence we all possess, for
simple, elemental truth, in whatever form it may be found. And
if, among the silver tongues, Masonry is to reach the heart of its

When Moses was called from Jethro's flocks and turryed aside
to behold· the flaming bush, which was not consumed, he was
;1dmonished to take his shoes from off his feet because the place
·whereon he stood was holy g.round. Holy, because the bush was

a parting of the ways; because upon the decision of Moses, his

worthy who gather here; the vast number of ·men, clean, intelligent

Masons repudiate the man who prostitutes this body from selfish

A few days ago I stood in this Temple and watched our boys
warch by-to war. And as I watched, I wondered how many of
them would come back to us; I wondered how many of those who
return will be maimed, or blinded or insane; how many of them
will be so diseased or deficient in body or in mind as to be worse
than dead. I thought of the price they pay for an idea, a visionfor democracy and their native land; I thought that no price is too
great to pay for such an idea, and that every one of us, if need be,
stands ready to pay that price. And then as we returned to the
peaceful quiet of this room, with its mighty cross above us, I
thought that no price-in time, in money, in body, or in mindis too great to pay for another idea, a vision, a native land: for the
kingdom, whether it be in the heavens or upon the earth, of the
/dmighty Father who reigns above. One of the leading clergymen
of this coast (a man who appeals to men) said recently, that if
l11asonry fails, the world is lost. He gave as his reason, the fact
that while our churches accept all who chose to come, Masonry
t<.kes only the best; and that if the best shall fail, no one can
succeed. We may or may not agree with his statement, but we
will all agree, that if the church shall fail, and if Masonry shall

fail, it will not be because of any weakness or inefficiency in that
Old Book of ours. It will be because we need less Sunday religion
and more Man religion; because we need less Lodge Masonry, and
more Man Masonry.
Masonry recognizes no creed or dogma, no restricted belief in
Deity, save a belief in the Great Father of All who is worshipped
alike by Jew and Gentile, Mohammedan and Christian. We meet
upon that common ground, and from that meeting point each must
rrspect the individual views and opinions of his brother. By
virtue of that very spirit of toleration, we may freely learn our
lessons from the best of that in which any one of us believes. In
the Book which we all revere, we find a rule of brotherhood which
is greater than the law of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a
tooth, greater than the golden rule that we should do unto ot.h:rs
"s we would that they shall do unto us, greater than the admomt10n
that if a man smite thee on the one cheek thou shalt turn to him the
other: it is the new commandment, that "ye love one another
as I have loved you." It is the greatest teaching ever given to
man· that we render to our brethren the kindly, tolerant, sym11ath~tic and forgiving love, which inspires the Father of all, as He
beholds His children. If that love were embedded in your heart
and in mine, in the heart of Kaiser, President and Emperor, if it
were the motive power behind diplomacy, if it animated the
capitalist and the laborer, and the men of every race and creed,
the strifes and animosities of the world would vanish like the dew
before the sun, and peace and prosperity would reign from pole
to pole.
There dwells in the tropic seas a speck of animal life whose
essential usefulness ls, that it shall die. Its tiny skeleton rests
upon the bed of the ocean, and others gather and die, above, and
l•eside, and around it. Through the centuries, they live and they
die, not knowing whence they come or whither they go; until at
last there arises above the waters an island of coral, upon which
men may live and prosper. So we receive our spark of life, perform
our pygmy task, and, after passing the allotted span, leave behind
what there has been of substance in our lives. Year by year,
through the centuries the countless millions come and go. Though
we strive blindly,' though we never behold. and comprehend but
vaguely if at all, that for which we have lived, there will at last
c>.rise above the seas of time, our coral isle-a goodly land-a land
upon which He who reigns above may establish His eternal
Vingdom.

prosperous condition of our beloved Order and the increased influence
for the good of humanity. Masonry is the shibboleth that opens the
door to charity and good will to our fellow citizens, and is working hand
in hand as an organization and individual Masons with the Red Cross
Association in relieving the distress and afflicted, regardless of nationality or creed. May its good mission continue to benefit humanity
as we meet on the level and part upon the square, and carrying its
influence and blessing like the benediction that follows a prayer. \Vith
kindest regards to the members of the Grand Lodge, I remain
Fraternally and faithfully,
GEO. c. P!lRKINS.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California herewith sl'bmits for your consideration and approval its Annual Report
for the year ending September 30th, 1917.
l\1ost vVorshipfol Grand Master reappointed Elmer E. Stone, vice
self, term expired. The Board held its annual meeting at the offices of
the Grand Secretary on Friday, October 13th, 1916, electing William S.
Wells, President; Motley H. Flint, Vice-President; Elmer E. Stone,
Secretary. During the year the Board has held its regular and special
meetings at both Dccoto and Covina.
This has been a most important year for the Trustees, principally
for the reason that our magnificent new home for Orphans at Covina
has been completed, dedicated and occupied. The wisdom of the
Grand Lodge in authorizing the immediate construction of a home for
uur orphans at Covina has been clearly demonstrated. Anticipating
the great increase in cost of building materials, a number of contract~
were let considerably in advance. The result is that the Grand Jurisdiction of California has probably the most modern and substantial
Masonic Home for Orphans in the entire United States. The buildings are so constructed as to be an enduring monument to Freemasons. Every possible convenience, consistent with safety, has been
installed, and the amendment to our constitution providing for fireproof buildings for our charges has been rigidly adhered to.
The Decoto Home has progressed most satisfactorily, our increased space having amply provided for all the needs of the Fraternity.

In view of the recommendations following for the reorganization
of the Board, and the probabilities that some of the present Trustees
will cease their activities after the meeting of the Grand Lodge, it
might not be out of place to call attention to the excellent service
rendered by our Superintendent at Decoto, Brother. Frank B. Hart.
man. Few realize the responsibilities of the position of Superintendent of the Home of the Aged. There are at present 152 men and
women comfortably installed at Decoto. \Vhen it is understood that

445

there were 23 deaths during the year, you can readily realize that our
Superintenden't, Brother Hartman, in looking after our departed
brothers and their widows, comfortin~ them in their last hours, attending to their many wants when they lay stricken in bed, and last but
by no means least, conducting the Home so that peace and harmony
prevails, has performed a task, the importance of which is appreciated
by hut few except your Trustees, who have observed the faithfulnesB
,1! Brother Hartman, and believe that the entire Fraternity should he
fully advised as evidenc;; that our confidence has not been misplaced.
Your Truf':ees fully realize that no more competent person than
Brother Hartman could be secured for the performance of the exacting duties at the Home.
The question of financing the Children's Home at Covina was
rnost important, and it required the very serious consideration of the
Trustees, who felt that the advice and good judgment of our Gran;\
Master was necessary; consequently each step in very transaction had
the approval of M.'. W.'. Brother Keesling. The Trustees assumed
that, as the Grand Lodge had approved the letting of contracts for the
Covina Home, it was their duty to arrange the necessary finances to
meet the situation, and it was decided that the best method to pursue
was for the Endowment Fund to advance the cash on hand and to
pledge the securities for the balance needed. By this means, the interest paid would accumulate in the Endowment Fund; furthermore,
all funds to be returned to the Endowment Fund as rapidly as possible through the per capita tax raised for building purposes.
In the matter of the Masonic Home property at San Gabriel,
which was disposed of some two years since, it developed that the
owner of the land which we acquired at Covina for our new home,
felt that the Trustees were not altogether fair in their treatment of
him, and in order that no reflection might be cast upon the Fraternity
for any act of the Trustees, it was decided to refer the entire matter
to arbitrators selected by the Trustees and the former owner of the
land. The result of said arbitration was the adjustment of a delicate
situation, and the San Gabriel property was reconveyed to us. We
have recently given an option to purchase the San Gabriel property,
which, if it be consummated, will return to the Masonic Homes fond a
very nice profit.
It is with sincere regret that we announce the resignation of
Mary B. Noble, Matron at Decoto. Said resignation was effective
March 10th, 1917. Mrs. N'oble had served the Home efficiently and
well, bnt impaired health rendered her resignation necessary. She:

1918.
