BoYs' HALL, by Victor Wehe.
"The building forming the east wing of this group is the Boys'
Luilding. It is 82 feet long by 48 feet wide, exclusive of porches, and
44 feet high from basement floor to top of firewalls. The top' floor
i~ made up of several dormitory rooms, a large lavatory room, supply closets and broom closets open from the hallway, and a locker
room or large airy closet opening from each sleeping room. These
locker rooms contain one steel locker 18 x 22 inches for each boy,
with separate shelves for hats and shoes, also a pole for coat hangers on one side of each closet. The window arrangement is so designed that the best ventilation is secured without draughts. An
isolation room is provided so that in case of sickness indicating some
contagion, the boy can be removed from others without inconvenience
or exposure.
"The first floor contains two dormitory rooms for small boys,
with a capacity of twelve beds each, making a maximum bed space for
Beventy-four boys. A large lavatory room, baths and shower room
are also located on this floor. At one end of the hall, commanding
every entrance and exit to building and rooms, is the House Mother'3
room, with private bath and control service to all parts of the buihling. Our study room and· a parlor are on this floor.
"The basement contains a large space given to wood working,
machinery lathe work, and storage for materials for making furniturn, etc. On the opposite end is the indoor play room for smaller
boys, furnished with locker seats for their toys and playthings. The
center space is occupied by storage rooms, private laundry and lavatory
room.
"The building is provided with vacuum cleaning outlets clo'~
enough to operate with fifty feet of hose so that medium-sized boys
can operate it. Drinking fountains are placed in the center hall on
each floor. All lights are operated by switches in reach of the smallest boys.
"The roof of the buildings is designed with firewalls of sufficient height to provide for outdoor sleeping without being in view,
and a full protection from night breezes. We expect to take care of
the building ourselves. We like it very much. We thank you."

TnE GENERJ\L PLAN, by Harry Basenach.
"The plan of this group of buildings is designed for all future
needs and extensions. A line drawn through the center of the main
building gives an equal amount of construction on each side, which
is called the main axis. A cross axis rtms through the center of the
;.tairway and hallway of the girls' hall across the front of the main
building and throl1gh the middle of the hall and stairway of the boys'
hall. These axes cross just eight feet in front of the center of the
main building, which point will always be the center of construction,
regardless of extensions. For this reason, the plan calls for future
buildings for the boys to be erected on the cross axis east of the
present buildings, and future buildings for girls on the cross axis
west of their present building. Any extension to the main building
wiH he built on the main axis to the south.

"All conduits, steam lines, supply pipes, drains, etc., are carried
from the machinery room direct through the pergolas to the other
buildings with connections ready to extend to other buildings in the
future. The front grounds of the buildings will be beautifully parhd
according to designs made by Brother John McLaren, who designed
the gardens for the Exposition grounds at San Francisco. Th~
ground in the rear is divided into two play grounds, one giving tennis and hand ball courts for the girls, with croquet and basket ball
grounds, and the other with a ball diamond and field track for the
boys. About nine acres cast of the buildings will be set out with a
variety of citrus fruits. Three acres west of us arc now in lemon~.
The remainder of the twenty-three acres on the high grounds will be
put in a variety of berries and vegetables that cannot stand frost, as
our high ground appears to be almost frostless. The terraces we now
have in grapes and eucalyptus trees. The lower ground will be occupied by our barns, chicken yards, dairy, a few deciduous fruits, about
four acres of alfalfa, and general garden truck. There are thirtyeight acres in the entire tract.
"Our domestic water comes from the San Dimas \Vatcr Company,
which reaches us with over forty pounds pressure. Our water for
farm use comes from the Covina Irrigating Company. Our drainage
nnd sewage is carried to a septic tank 800 feet from the buildings.
This is connected with a 35,000 gallon reservoir for irrigating the alfalfa, etc., on the lower ground. The soil is all good, and we feel
with the work tis boys can do here, that we can assist materially in
producing much of our own fruits and vegetables. The temporary
Luilding where we have lived the past year will be changed over into
barns, chicken houses, fencing, etc. All the lumber was selected for
this purpose and used in lengths to save waste when the change is
made. \Ve have watched these new buildings go up and we know
every part of them. We are all very, very happy here and think you
bave selected the very best place for us."

0RA'rION, by Robert B. Gaylord, Grand Orator.
'fhe Masons of California are proud of the event for which we
have gathered here today, of the building in whose presence we stand,
f!nd of the spirit of love and generosity which has made it a possibility. It is a spot to which we can bring the children of Masonry
as a hen gathers her chickens under her wings, for consolation and
5helter, for protection and happiness. We realize that in our land
today the orphan does not starve; public charity guarantees that fact.
But when our orphans come to us here, they come to their own, to
that which is theirs by right, to the shelter of the family roof. The
difference which they find should be the difference between the man
who spends his declining years beside the fireside of his children, and
he who enjoys the cold hospitality and the barren comfort of a public
almshouse. If the children of our Order find here a home and not an
institution, if they realize that they are the heneficiaries of love and
not the victims of charity, then this edifice will be worthy of its
name.

I have suggested that we are proud of this day and of this
building, and yet if we look fact soberly in the face there is no
occasion for pride. The man who pays his bills, who tells the truth,
who meets his obligations, may be worthy of commendation, but
there is little occasion for pride. He does his duty and no more.
In caring for those whom it is our duty to shelter, for the children
of our own great family, we merely exemplify that instinct to car~
for our own young which is the law of nature, and which is shared
alike by the beasts of the fields and the vultures of the air. When
~' man raises himself above the level of his daily instincts, when he
proves himself worthier than his fellows, an example whom children
may see and imitate, we are proud to be numbered among his friends;
and when our Order shall prove itself worthy of the principles lt
t·spouses, worthy of the men who founded it, and of the illustrious
names which honor our rolls, when it proves itself worthy of the
leadership to which it aspires,-then, and not till then, may we consistently be proud.
We read in the Holy Writ that in the beginning, the Almighty
urought order out of chaos, that He created the heavens and the
cnrth; that He separated the seas and the dry land, that He placec.I

Masonry has but one lesson to teach. Its great lesson, is not the virtnt's of temperance, fortitude, prudence, and justice, nor the brotherhood of man, nor the fatherhood of God, nor the resurrection from
the dead; these are its ideals, and its beliefs. The great lesson it
teaches, is the practical application of those ideals and beliefs, which
you and I personally and individually make in our daily lives. If
we learn that lesson, we become better citizens, better associates for
th~ man upon the street, worthy examples for little children. If we

wort~y of the name, of the Great Book which God has given us as
a gmde f?r human conduct, is the development of individual initiative.

figned the Declaration of Independence, and who fought at Bunke.Hill and Valley Forge, who fought again in 1812 to preserve their

liberty, entered upon the bitterest of stn1ggles, that of brother against
brother; no one can convince us that the descendants of such for<"·
fathers will be found wanting in the hour of their country's need.
The red blood of patriotism still flows in our veins, and the men and 1
women from North, and South, and East and \Vest will rally around
their flag as long as memory exists and as long as duty calls.
But although patriotism be the noblest of human attributes, we
must remember that for Him to whom a thousand years are as a
day, the greatest war of history, with its sorrow, its sacrifices, its
heart aches, and its desolation, is only an incident in the accomplishment of His will. In one of his addresses, Ingersoll tells of a
visit to the tomb of Napoleon. He says that as he stood gazing down
upon the marble where rest at last the ashes of that restless man, he
thought of the career of the greatest soldier of modern history. He
-;aw Napoleon as a youth in the streets of Paris, he saw him crossing
the Alps into Italy; before the Pyramids in Egypt; at Marengo, am!
t;lm, and Austerlitz, he saw him crossing the barren wastes of Russia, at Waterloo, and finally at St. Helena gazing out across the sea.
He thought of the widows and the orphans whom the Emperor had
made, of the tears that had been shed, for his glory, and of the
only woman who loved him, pushed from his heart by the cold hand
of ambition. And then Ingersol! says that he would rather h<l'le
been a French peasant and worn wooden shoes; that he would rather
have lived in a hut with a vine growing over the door, and grap~s
ripening in the sunshine, with his wife sitting beside him, and his
children gathered about his knees; that he would rather have been
that peasant to go down to the tongueless silence of the dreamte~s
dust, than to have been that imperial personification of blood am!
inurder.
My friends, the men and women of today are laying the foundation upon which our children must raise the superstructure even as
generations gone by have built for us. Regardless of their effect upon
our lives beyond the veil, our virtues and our vices remain to ble5s
or curse our issue. They reap as we have sown, and the influence
which we exert must remain through time, even as it must go with
us into eternity. God grant that from the ashes of this war ther.:
may arise, like the phoenix of old, a rejuvenated America, that her
wings may be outstretched to shelter the oppressed of every land;

SUPJ!RINTENDENT'S REPORT.
Decoto, Alameda County, Cal., October 1, 1917.

~~~~~

To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California.

00

The undersigned presents the nineteenth annual report as Superintendent of the Masonic Homes of California.

<"">

vr

The past year has been one of great interest in the history oi
the Decoto and Covina Homes.
The permanent buildings at the Decoto Home erected during the
past several years have enlarged the work and have enabled the
management to reach a higher standard of service in the care of the
e>lder members of our family.
The completion of the new buildings at the Covina Home has
firmly established the work for the care of the younger members.
Those entering on the evening of their lives, can enjoy the comfort and quiet so much desired by them, while those who are enter-ing the threshold of life will be given the physical, moral, mental anJ
spiritual development to prepare them to meet successfully the experience awaiting them during the coming years.

There has been a greater individual effort on the part of the
Members of our large family to interest themselves in the general
routine work and to contribute their bit, according to their strength,
to the general welfare of the Homes.
Suitable entertainments, school instruction, out-of-door recreatiom,
picnic parties, camping trips, excursions to nearby places of interest,
etc., have enriched the social and family life of the Homes, affording
<liversion for those enfeebled by advancing years, and giving wholesome and beneficial exercise to those who find their strength increasing as the years unfold.
DECOTO HOME.

Since our last report 24 persons have been admitted to the
Home, 15 men and 9 women; 23 have passed away. There are now
present 97 men and 55 women .

bl) -

"'g :§ '()

... ·;; ~

::::: ~ (/)

The health of the Home has been good with the exception vf
those who, by reason of age, have become infirm and helpless.

466

PROCEEDINGS OF TRW

The Coleman Hospital, thoroughly equipped with all the advanced medical and sanitary appliances, enables our physician and
trained nurses to give to those who are ill the best medical attention. Day and night nurses are in constant attendance. There are
now twenty members being cared for in the hospital.
The new water supply is practically inexhaustable. At th:s
season of the year, when the natural supply of water is lowest, there
seems to be no decrease in the service given by the deep-well pump.
At the close of each day there are 700,000 gallons of water in our
rt'servoirs. The springs, our former source of supply, contribute in a
very small way to the storage of water on hand.
The steam plant has supplied all the steam heat during the winter months and hot water for domestic purposes during the entire
year. It also furnishes power for the operation of the laundry and
pumping plant.
The cold storage plant is operated by electric power and enables
the Home to care for a large supply of meat, butter, eggs, etc., and
manufacture at the same time all the ice for our needs.
The steam laundry has attended to all the demands made upon
it in a very satisfactory manner. The hand laundry located in the
basement of the main building has been equipped with two porcelain
tubs, hot and cold watei-, ironing boards and table, clothes rack, electric stove for the making of starch, electric irons. The work done
here relieves the laundry and gives the ladies of the Home, who are
able, an opportunity to do their own work.
The greater portion of the hill ranch has been leased, either •)'.l
ohares or cash rental. The hay crop has been good; about 80 tons
have been stored for our use.
The chicken ranch has given good returns. In addition to the
chickens and eggs sold and for table use, 10,000 eggs have been put up
in water glass. There are now 22()0 chickens on hand.
The hog ranch has supplied us with fresh pork during the year.
There are now 60 hogs on hand.
The dairy has supplied all the milk and cream we need. There
are now 15 Holstein cows on hand. \Ve also have 7 horses in our
stable. Two teams are used to haul freight, etc., and for general
:anch work; three horses for mail and passenger service and oth,::r
work about the grounds.

GRAND J,ODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The vegetable gardens have been eularged and have furnished
a plentiful supply of fresh vegetables for table use and greens for the
form yard.
The orchards have yielded ·a good crop. The new orchard is
now beginning to bear. A large part of the fruit crop was sold. Our
tables were well supplied and the balance dried and stored for future
needs. There is now in storage three-fourths ton of dried apricots,
one ton dried plums, and about four tons· dried prunes.
A large quantity of fruit· has been preserved by the ladies of the
Home; about 700 quarts being now on hand. All of the mending and.
making of household linen has also been done by them. In additio'1
to caring for their individual rooms, they have taken entire care of
the halls, corridors, wash and bath rooms, reception and assembly
rooms in the buildings occupied by them.
All the rooms and halls of the cottages and main buildings have
been tinted, woodwork and furniture varnished and beds enameled.
The woodwork inside of the hospital has been enameled and the
woodwork on the outside has been painted.
A garage building has been built and is located south of the
main building. The labor on this building was furnished entirely by
the brethren of the Home.
A large number of brethren have contributed to the welfare of
the Home during the past year by their labors in carpenter, tailor,
shoe and barber shops, picking fruit, watering lawns, kitchen work
;ind light chores in a general way. One of the brethren looks after
the garage, while another, a graduate optician, looks after the
spectacles worn by the members of the family and keeps them in
good condition.
A flag pole, 84 feet' high, has been erected on the grounds south
of the main building. It was set in a concrete base, 5 feet square
and 7 feet deep. It is surmounted by a halyard block and a gold
ball. The presentation and dedication of the flag pole took place
June 16, 1917.
The following program gives the order of exercises which attended the presentation and dedication of the flag pole and flag. A large
~umber of brethren from the bay cities and towns near the Home
were present and took part in the ceremonies.

Many entertainments have been given for the pleasure and benefit of the family by Lodges, members of Lodges and their friends,
also at times by members of the Home. The following is a list of
the events which have contributed to our enjoyment:
October 21, 1916--Y erba Buena Lodge No. 403; second degree i:1
the Temple, smoker and entertainment.
Oct. 28, 1916--Marietta Chapter No. 256, 0. E. S.; floral degree in
the Temple, followed by a musical program.
Nov. 4, 1916--Lodges of the 37th District; formal presentation of
five hat and coat racks and one pair of massive andirons as furnishings for new Club Room .
Nov. 11, 1916--Live Oak Lodge No. 61 ; first degree in Temple,
entertainment and smoker.
Nov. 30, 1916--Thanksgiving services in Assembly Hall.

10.

Dedication of Pole and Flag-Bro. Thomas Flint, Trustee Masonic Homes of California, and Past Grand Master.

Dec. 19, 1916--Fraternity Lodge No. 399; third degree in the
Temple, entertainment and smoker.

11.

"America," Islam Temple Band and audience.

Dec. 25, 1916--Christmas services in Assembly Hall, attended by
residents and employes; large Christmas tree; rooms, halls and corriclors decorated with green and red festooning, bells and wreath,;
visit of Mr. and Mrs. Santa Claus; distribution of presents.

Since that day, the flag has with appropriate ceremony been
raised each morning at 6 :45 a. m. by the Color Guard. A few
members of the family gather together at that time in the Assembly Hall and sing the National Air as the flag is being raised. The
singing is accompanied by violin and piano. The flag is lowered
each evening at 6 :30 p. m.
New cedar book shelves have been built on the four sides of
the library room by the brethren of the Home. There are now
2700 books, 565 books having been donated during the past year.

Dec. 31, 1916--Reception, musical program, games and dancing; '
watch party at 12 midnight, attended by residents and employes.
Feb. 12, 1917-Lincoln's Birthday; patriotic exercises in Assembly Hall.
Feb. 22, 1917-Washington's Birthday; patriotic exercises in Assembly Hall.

A moving picture and musical entertainment have been given each
Wednesday evening throughout the year at the Temple; the socials on
Thursday evenings, the chorus practice on Friday evenings, and the
services on Sunday afternoons, followed by a musical program by our
orchestra, have been regularly held,

COVJNA HOME.

The Covina Home has been in almost perfect operation. disregarding the inconveniences of the temporary buildings, and the natural disturbances and interruptions by dust, teaming, workmen, anrl
:he noise and confu~ion of the erection of the new buildings. The
health of the children has heen almost perfect, their discipline and
deportment have been exemplary, and their school work very creditable
indeed.
The garden has produced well, but limited in space because of
construction, interruption of water and lack of fencing. No cows o~·
horses have been purchased because the farm plan cannot be installcJ
until the temporary buildings for the children can be taken down.
A portion of the higher ground has been set out to Valencias,
Navels, grapefruit and tangerines. These trees are doing well. A
new reservoir has been built on the highest point of the ground and
connected by pumps in the machinery room to the plunge in th~
gymnasium room, so that our irrigation water for the high ground
can be received through the plunge, thus providing fresh water for
the children at all times. The same pump and pipe used for supplying the temporary buildings is used for this purpose.
The securing of pressure water from the city of San Dimas is a
very desirable and very economical feature. We now have the same
conveniences in the country that those in the most modern city enjoy. It cost $1550 to connect with this system, all of which is returned to us in water, and we thereby saved the cost of a $2000
pressure tank on the roof and the continuous care and cost of
pumping to the tank.
We have also been able to connect with the Covina gas mains
at a cost of less than $100, and our fuel bill for cooking with thts
natural gas is about one-third our former cost with manufactured
gas or distillate.

PROCEEDINGS OF '!'HE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We are on one of the power lines of the Edison Electric Company. Our lighting system is good and the company has made us
a most satisfactory power rate. We can now profitably operate our
new laundry and refrigeration plant at the new buildings, aµd have
the conveniences of vacuum cleaning, plunge, boys' workshop, etc.,, .at
minimum cost.

operated under self government, the children electing their own
officers, caring for all departments of the work by committees, and
publishing a daily paper. The children are all good swimmers, which
can be appreciated by the fact that seven girls swam from Balboa
to the camp, a distance of more than a mile and a half.

472

The basement arrangement is built to install a perfe~t arrangement of receiving, checking and distributing supplies, preventing was"Le
and carrying a continuous inventory of supplies on hand. The system
is taken from that operated in the Masonic Home at. Elizabethtown,
Pennsylvania, which is probably the best regulated institution of its
kind in the country. The records all conform to the accounting system installed by Brother Ruckstell. The new buildings will naturally
:equire some change in operation of general detail, which will take
but a short time, as the scheme was worked out completely before
the buildings were constructed. The limited space in the temporary
buildings precluded much of the training that will now be vigorouslv
renewed, particularly manual training, drills and shop work for the
boys, and domestic science, orchestra, and classic dancing for th~
girls. The play grounds will soon be graded and equipment will be
placed on them from time to time as convenience permits. This wi1l
probably be supplied by sonie of the local Lodges.
Five of our boys, who have comparatively recently graduated
from the Home, are now in the service of our country. Two of
them, although very young, are non-commissioned officers. They
passed their examination largely by their experience in the cadet drills
used at the Home.
Patriotic holidays have been particularly emphasized this yea~·,
although all have been fittingly observed. Indoor diversions were
necessarily limited, but outdoor trips were most enjoyable. Many
"hikes" were made to nearby places. One of particular mention was
a walk of eight miles from car line to Camp Baldy with a rise nf
4000 feet and a further climb of 2000 feet and six mile hike next
day. Again the following day they walked the eight miles down the
mountain. There were twenty-nine children on this trip. All made
it nicely. They held their Easter service in the snow. A rich expe·
rience to nineteen of them who had never been in the snow before.
Another notable trip was the annual outing at the beach, made
possible by the generous contribution of the lodges and individuals
to the Christmas fund. The children are more than g1ad to carry
a portion of their Christmas allowance over to enj~y tl1t'? happy,
healthful camping trip during their summer vacation. The ·camp 15

The intere.ot manifested by the Craft in our Home has been unusual this year. Possibly because of the erection of the new buildings, we had more visitors than any year previous. Many friends
from the north called frequently. Grand Master Keesling and Deputy
Grand Master Hervey visited often, and the children have become
much attached to them. The children also made several visits, particularly just prior to Endowment Day, and their program assisted
materially in stimulating interest in this work. We are pleased with
the visits of Lodges and Chapters where they come in a body and
participate in some entertainment with the children. Some of these
visits of special interest since our bst report are as follows:
September 30th-Hon. Albert G. Burnett, Grand Master, with Mrs.
Burnett, visited the children. Brother Burnett gave the children a
splendid talk and seemed much interested in the Home.
November 25th-Fifteen children with the Matron visited Long
Beach. The children gave a good program and Trustee Spencer
addressed a joint meeting of all the bodies on the Endowment fund.
November 26th-Grand Master and Mrs. Keesling, Deputy Grand
Master Hervey and Mrs. Hervey visited the children. The children
gave a program, and both Brother Keesling and Brother Hervey gave
instructive and entertaining talks to the children.
November 29th-A trip to San Bernardino in the interest of the
Endowment fund was made similar to that at Long Beach, San Bernardino. Masons and their ladies received the children most cordially.
December 17th-Long Beach Day. For several years Long Beach
Chapter No. 173, 0. E. S., has visited the children near Christmas
time, and besides leaving a generous amount of apples and candy,
has always left a dollar bill for each child's bank account. This
year they not only did this same thing, but they brought their strong
ally, The Shriner Club of Long Beach, with them, who also gave the
children a dollar bill each for their bank account. Through this
kindness each child has a bank account, and it is sure to grow with
friends like Long Beach Chapter and Shrine Club. The children responded with a good program.

Special mention must be made of some who are performing exceptional service for the Home. Dr. J. M. Dunsmoor is always generous with his time and always at call for the physical needs of the
children. We are much indebted to him for the good health enjoyed
by the children. His good wife, Dr. Nannie Dunsmoor, and son, Dr.
Robert M. Dunsmoor, have frequently assisted him.

479

Careful attention is given to the general ailments and physical
defects of children. Examinations are frequently made for adenoids,
enlarged tonsils, and similar affiictions, and all cases needing attention
are promptly cared for. In this particular we are indebted to Doctors
F. J. Old, F. D. Bullard, Clarence E. Ide, Agusta Zuber and Lawrence
R. Linhart, all of whom are expert in this character of work. None
of these physicians would accept compensation for their valuable services.
Many others donated in service what would be difficult to estimate
in money value. Brother P. L. Nash of Covina is always at hand in
emergency or otherwise, and Brother Wm. Schneider gives his annual
barbecue and generous allowance of meats, etc .. for the occasion. The
business houses from whom we purchase supplies extend many favors.
The Masons of San Francisco, the members of the San Francisco
Board of Relief, The Southern California Past Masters' Association,
the Grand Officers and Inspectors, several Subordinate Lodges and
Eastern Star Chapters, and many individrials are now contributing generously to the furnishing of the New Orphans' Home. Some are selecting stated rooms to furnish, some pianos, victrolas, hall clocks, drinking
fountains, etc. It is impossible at this time to make the list, but this
splendid Honor Roll will be carefully compiled for our next report,
by which time the several Lodges will have completed their work in
this line, and their donations properly installed.
The Charter Oak Citrus Association, Bro. Wm. Hoogendyk, manager, supplies the children with oranges at all seasons. · Any time the
boys drive up with their wagon they receive a generous supply of the
golden fruit.

Sec. 217. Upon the report of said Committee, if one-third of the
votes shall be in favor of such proposed amendment, it shall be passed
to print, and Hie Grand Secretary shall within thirty (30) days after
the close of such communication of the Grand Lodge, transmit a copy
of such proposed amendment to each Lodge of this Grand Jurisdiction.
Sec. 218. Such proposed amendment shall be read to the Lodge
by the Secretary thereof at the next stated meeting of the Lodge after
receipt, and a vote thereon shall be taken by the Lodge not later than
its stated meeting for the month of July following, a majority vote
determining the approval or disapproval of such proposed amendment
of the Lodge. The Secretary of the Lodge shall make return to the
Grand Secretary at the time of making the annual returns of the Lodge.
If two-thirds of the Lodges shall approve the adoption of such proposed amendment, the Grand Master shall proclaim such amendment
adopted and it shall become a part of this Constitution on the thirtieth
(30th) day after the date of such proclamation.
Sec. 219. No vote upon a proposed amendment shall be taken
after the election of the Grand officers, but a proposed amendment may
be presented, which shall lie over until the next annual communication
of the Grand Lodge.
Sec. 220. All provisions of the Constitution of this Grand Lodge
and all Regulations, or parts thereof, which are repugnant to or inconsistent with this Constitution are hereby repealed, and no Regulation
shall hereafter he adopted which shall be in violation of, or inconsistent
with, any of its provisions.

your Committee to whom was referred the annual report of the
V. \V. Thomas J. Baker, Grand Lecturer, has had the same under co\1sideration, and begs leave to report as follows:

The report and indorsement were adopted.

The report, which details the very satisfactory condition of Lodges

REPORT OF co.:vnnTTEE ON MASOI\'TC
EDUCATION.

\Ve highly indorse the suggestion of the Grand Lecturer that the
Grand Lodge take immediate action to enable the Lodges to carry out
the card system to check the standing of visitors. As it is now, a
brother can produce his recei:pt, be examined, and he can visit the
Lodge for years without ever being asked again to sho.w his receipt.
By adopting the card system, if he is not in go~d stan~mg the Secretary of his Lodge would inform the Lodge of his standmg.
We also note with great pride the interest the Grand Lecturer is
taking in our officers and members wh-0 have been called to the colors,
and without a doubt those that have been promoted can thank the
Grand Lecturer, who no doubt laid the foundation for their success by
his instruction in the ritual, covering the ground of exactness and
punctuality.
\Ve agree with the Grand Lecturer that it is unfortunate there arc
Lodges in communities throughout the State that are having a hard
time to exist, owing to these places being thinly populated and the
members widely scattered; but your Committee is satisfied that under
the guidance of the Grand Lecturer, if there is anything possible to be
<lone, he will attend to it.
It is especialiy gratifying to note that new Temples are being
erected (even with the world at war), as it shows that Masonry is
still progressing operatively as well as speculatively, and it is a pleasure
to know that many of our Lodges are desirous of owning their own
homes.

495

Brother Irving J. ~1itchell, chairman of the Committee
on }f asonic Education, reported as follows:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on sfasonic Education, appointed last year, beg
leave to report as follows :
During the past twelve months we have given the subject referred
to us very earnest and careful attention.
\Ve have endeavored to awaken the active interest of the ablest
thinkers and scholars of the Craft. We have tried to gain their cooperation in the development of this splendid and much needed work.
We have voiced the needs of a deeper understanding of why we arc
here, and have met with enthusiastic response wherever we have gone.
We find a growing conviction that is nation-wide that the rank and file
of our membership lack a proper appreciation of the meaning underlying
the teaching of our Institution.
This is not a cause for despondency or despair, for side by side
with this feeling there is a growing desire to supply this lack in every
possible way.
We believe that in our work we should depend less on formalism
and more on enlightenment. We owe more to the candidates who
knock at our doors than we sometimes give them after they have
entered the portals. Mere ritualism will not suffice; it is appealing so

496

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCF;EmINGS 'OF THE

far as it goes, but it does not go far enough; not every man is prepared to grasp its hidden meaning without adequate instruction. To
that end we bave prepared lectures on the Entered Apprentice, Fellowcraft, and Master Mason degrees to be presented to candidates after
receiving each of the several degrees. These lectures have been submitted to the Most Worshipful Grand Master for his approval. If
found satisfactory by him, the lectures will be printed and will soon he
in circulation among the Lodges of this grand jurisdiction.
1

While these lectures have entailed a considerable degree of labor,
we are quite conscious of the fact that, of ·themselves, without the
earnest co-operation of the brethren, they must fall short of accomplishing the purpose that inspired the appointment of this Committee.

It is personality more than ideas that is the dominant factor of
human progress and development. And so we ask the members of the
fraternity to supplement our effort by commending these lectures and
furthering their uses for the purposes for which they ·are intended.
If the Masters and other officers of our Masonic Lodges will faithfully try the plan that is hereby presented. we are satisfied the results
will amply justify om expectation and we shall know better the virtue
of the plan.
In addition, we would further suggest that the members of our
fraternity should be encouraged and exhorted to do some re.search
work for themselves. To that end we wish most cordially to commend
the following Masonic books as worthy of serious study: Gould's
"Concise History of Freemasonry"; Mackey's "Encyclopedia of Freemasonry"; "The Builders, A Story and Study of :\!Iasonry," by Joseph
Fort Newton; "The Philosophy of :\!Iasonry," by Roscoe Pound, Dean
of the Law School of Harvard L'niversity.
A most helpful plan by which these volumes might be studied is
this: Let the Master of the Lodge, or, if he see fit, let some brother
whom he may appoint, read these books aloud to as many as may be
gathered together. Perhaps this exercise could be incorporated as part
of the business of the stated meeting. Perhaps in some Lodges a half
hour each week could be devoted to this work, preceding the opening
of the Lodge .. If the matter was properly advertised in time, a goodly
company of the craft would come and great advantage would accrue in
developing the understanding of the fraternity in matters which are
fundamental to our Institution. We heartily concur in the sentiment
expressed by our Most \.Vorshipful Grand Master, in his address, when
he said: "I am impressed with the importance of Masonic educational
instruction and the general desire for it. It is an important work that

497

should be undertaken by, this Grand Lodge without delay." We, therefore, sum up this report by submitting the following points for consideration :
First: 1'hat a Committee on Masonic Education, consisting of
three members, be appointed by the Most Worshipful Grand Master to
serve for the ensuing year. That it shall be the duty of this Com·
mittee to exercise a helpful influence toward all Lodges who desire
their counsel and advice. That this Committee shall foster and encourage throughout this jurisdiction the study and research of Masonic
tradition, history, literature, law, philosophy, and dominant purposes of
this Institution.
Second: That a series of lectures to be read in our Lodges at
stated intervals shall be prepared under the direction of such Committee.
Such lectures to be submitted to the Most \Vorshipful Grand Master
for his approval and afterward printed. One lecture to be mailed each
month to every Lodge in this jurisdiction.
Third : That a further series of three lectures be prepared under
the direction of the Committee on Masonic Education, along exoteric
lines, appropriate respectively to the Entered Apprentice, Fellowcraft,
and Master Mason degrees. Such lectures to be first approved by the
Most Worshipful Grand Master and afterwards µrinted. These lectures to be placed in the candidate's hands after he has received each
degree.
Fourth: That the formation of study clubs be encouraged, and
that this feature of the work follow a systematic and carefully-conceived
plan.
Fifth: In view of the expense which the printing and distributing
of the lectmcs noted will entail, vve ask that the sum of one thousand
dollars be appropriated for such purpose.
Respectfully submitted,
IRvrNG J. MrtCHEI:L,
WILLIAM MACCORMACK,

ALFRED W. BusH.

Referred to the Committee on Finance.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred trial record
N.o. 190, respectfully shows: This record first came to your Committee at the communication last year, but had to be sent back to Fairmount Lodge No. 435, in which the case was tried, for correction, and
such correction has since been made. The record is very voluminous
and discloses that all of the issues involved were thoroughly tried and
every opportunity given to both accuser and accused to present any
testimony bearing upon the case. There is a sharp conflict in the
evidence throughout and, while the same might sustain a. different
verdict than that arrived at, there is nevertheless ample testimony to
justify the verdict of not guilty as found by the Commissioners, and,
bearing in mind that the Commissioners had the witnesses before them
and were better able than your Committee to judge of their credibility
and the weight to be given the evidence, your Committee is not disposed to set aside the finding of the trial Commissioners.
The Committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and
recommends its adoption :
Resolved. That the verdict and action of the Lodge in the matter
of trial record No. 190 be, and the same hereby are, affirmed.

. To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Finance begs leave to report as follows :
\Ve have received and considered the reports of the Boards of
Relief of San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Jose, San Diego and Honolulu. These reports, are comprehensive and · reflect credit on those of

solemnly bound in both duty and honor, to be faithful to every trust

REPORT ON DECISIONS OF GRAND :YIASTER.

Your Committee on Jurisprudence has considered the decisions of
the Grand Master as reported in his Address, and report thereon as
follows;
VVe find the decisions generally in accord with our views as to the
law of this jurisdiction.
As to many no comment is necess.iry. These are Decisions 1, 2,
4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15 and 17. All of these are obviously correct.
Vie recommend that they be approved.

Adopted.
Decision No. 8, relative to the use of the funds of a Lodge, evidently refers to the ordinary funds : those described in Section 88 of the
Constitution, as being derived from "fees, dues, rental, profit or otherwise," and to such funds is clearly correct. Section 88 recognizes that
funds may be donated to and accepted by a Lodge in trust for a proper
specific purpose, and that funds so donated and accepted may be limited
to the specific purpose for which they were given. We recommend that
the decision be approved.

Adopted.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

512

Decision No. 11, relative to the remission of dues of those who
have entered the military or naval service, is in strict accord with our
law as it now is. We recommend that it be approved.

Adopted.
Decision No. 14, regarding dispensations for Lodges, relative to a
matter peculiarly within the discretion of the particular Grand Master
to whom the application is made: Subject to the limitations prescribed
by Sections 73 and 74, the Constitution authorizes him to grant such
a dispensation whenever he concludes that it is proper and necessary.
We are of the opinion that in the determination of the question whether
the granting of a dispensation is proper and necessary, he cannot .be
limited by any decision of the Grand Lodge. The Constitution leaves
that question to him. The dispensation terminates on the first day of
the following October (Section 74), when the question whether a charter shall issue or the dispensation be continued is determined by the
Grand Lodge (Section 75). In the· case giving rise to the decision, the
Grand Master concluded that the circumstances were not such as to
make it proper and :necessary to grant a dispensation. We are not to
be understood as intimating that we have any doubt as to the. correctness of his action. We simply hold that such a ruling cannot Operate
to bind any succeeding Grand Master. We, therefore, think that the
decision should not he construed as a dPclaratinn of the law of this
Grand Lodge, limiting the discretion of future Grand Masters.

Adopted.
As to Decision No. 16: We regard it as entirely immaterial that
the corporation in addition to operating a saloon, was also engaged in
a mercantile business. Our law inhibits the saloon business, except
where carried on "in connection with and as a part of. the operation of
a bona fide hotel or restaurant" (Section 129A), and if a saloon is
operated otherwise, either by a person or corporation, it cannot make
any difference that such person or corporation also carries on such
other business. The mere fact that one is a stockholder in a corporation engaged in operating a saloon would not necessarily render him
guilty of a Masonic offense under Section 129A of our Constitution.
But we think that if the circumstances are such that he may fairly be
held responsible for the course of the corporation in this regard, he
falls withi~ the spirit, at least, of the provision. If, for instance, he is
practically the sole stockholder, with full and absolute control of the
operations of the corporation, with only a sufficient number of shares
held by others to qualify them as directors, there could hardly be any
question that the mere adoption of the corporate form in the carrying
on of the saloon business should not render him immune from the law.
We think that ordinarily a majority stockholder in such a corporation

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

513

would be regarded as controlling its operations, and fairly within the
term "owner" used in Section 129A. The decision to our minds may
be construed as implying that the adoption of the corporate form in
the doing of the prohibitive business would be a complete answer to
any claim of violation of the provisions of Section 129A, insofar as any
stockholder is concerned. In this report we believe that the decision
is too broad. We recommend the adoption of this report.

Adopted.
As to Decision No. 18, we find from the papers submitted that the
question presented was whether a member of the National Guard of
California, who had not as yet been mustered into the service of the
United States, came within the exception referred to. Prior to being
so mustered in, he did not belong "to the army or navy of the United
States" (Section 96, Constitution), and the Grand Master very properly held that he did not come within the exception. As our Constitutional provision now reads, we think the exception does include all
persons belonging to the army or navy of the United States. We
recommend that the action of the Grand Master be approved.

Adopted.
As to Decision 3a, 3b, and the matter entitled "The Case of a
Masters' and Past Masters' Association": We regard Past Masters'
Associations as now constituted and existing in this jurisdiction, as
being mere voluntary associations of Masons for the cultivation and
promotion of social, friendly and fraternal relations, in no way amenable to the supervision of this Grand Lodge in their operations, except
insofar as their operations may be subversive of the best interests of
Masonry. They are not recognized by any provision of our law as
parts of our Masonic system, and we have no rules or regulations
concerning them. We find nothing in our law requiring any approval
by either Grand Master or Grand Lodge of the by-laws 0£ such an
association, nor do we think that the Grand Lodge is warranted by
anything in our law in declaring that such an association may not hold
a meeting on a Sunday, except for funeral services. At the same time,
the members of such associations are Masons, and publicly associated
in that character. If they should act in a manner detrimental to the
principles, laws and regulations of the Fraternity, or calculated to reflect
on the good name· of Masonry, they would, of course, be amenable to
our law. To this extent only do such associations come within our
supervisory powers. It is entirely proper, therefore, for the Grand
Master to investigate as to the real purpose and object of any such
associat10n, and to that end, if he deems it advisable, to require its

GRAND LODGE OF CAT~IFORNIA

515

PUOCEEDINGS 01<' '.l'HFJ

514

by-laws and rules of government to be submitted to him for examination. If he finds the avowed purposes of such an association to
be "subversive of the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge,"
as he probably did in the case of the particular association referred to
in his decision, we cannot doubt the propriety of his directing the
members to dissolve the same, or at least to abandon those particular
purposes. We recommend that Decisions 3a and 3b be disapproved,
and that the action of the Grand Master in "The Case of a Masters'
and Past Masters' Association" be approved.

Adopted.
As to Decision No. 5: It is well settled by our decisions that the
Master may permit any qualified brother to confer a degree, he, of
course, remaining present. There is nothing in our law that, to our
minds, requires any approval of the qualification of such a brother by
the Grand Lecturer. The matter appears to be committed entirely to
the Master, whose duty it is to see that the degree is conferred in strict
accordance with the ritual. The same thing is apparently true as to
brethren appointed by the Master to assist in conferring a degree.
The official approval by the Grand Lecturer appears to be confined to
certain officers of a Lodge, who may not be installed without obtaining
a certificate as to their qualifications. We recommend that the Decision
he not approved.

Adopted.
The proposed amendment to Section 17, to fix the annual election
of officers of the Grand Lodge on the second day of the session, has
been given consideration by your Committee, and as at present advised
we can see no good reason for making a change in our law in this
matter. vVe recommend that the proposed amendment be not adopted.

Adopted.
\Vith relation to the proposition to amend Section 30 of the Constitution, to require Committees to meet in advance of the time for
holding the annual communications of Grand Lodge we deem the proposed amendment inadvisable and recommend that it be not adopted.

Adopted.
It is proposed to substantially anrnnd Sections 216, 217, 218, 219
and 220 of the Constitution, relative to the matter of amending the
Constitution.

Briefly stated, the idea is to make it impossible for the Grand
Lodge, declared by our Constitution to be "the supreme Masonic power
and authority in this State, possessing all the attributes of sovereignty
and government, legislative, executive and judicial" (Section 7), to
adopt any amendment. Any proposed amendment may be introduced,
and, after report thereon by the Committee on Jurisprudence, a vote
is to be taken in the Grand Lodge. If less than one-third of the votes
are given in its favor, it is rejected. If one-third or more of the votes
are in favor thereof, it is simply passed to print. This is true even if
the vote be unanimous in favor of the amendment. The subordinate
Lodges are then to be furnished with a copy of the proposed amendment, and each Lodge is to vote on the same at a stated meeting. The
fate of the amendment is to be determined by this vote, cast by Lodges
as such, and participated in by persons not members oi this Grand
Lodge. If two-thirds of the Lodges approve the proposed amendment it is adopted, otherwise it is rejected.
We deem it unnecessary to do more than to thus state the substantia'! feature of the proposed change. \Ve recommend that the proposed amendment be not adopted.

Report adopted.

These amendments are proposed by the present Trustees and have
the approval of the Grand Master. We find nothing objectionable
therein. Those best qualified as to the advisability of the proposed
amendments having concluded that these changes should be made, we
recommend their adoption.

United States or its allies, and no per capita tax shall be payable to the

It is claimed that Lassen Lodge is more accessible to the residents of
said territory than is Sincerity Lodge, and that the convenience of said
residents would be promoted by the contemplated change. Evidence
was taken by your Committee in favor of and in opposition to the
petition. After carefully considering the showing made, we are satisfied the proposed action would work an injustice to Sincerity Lodge
and would be opposed to the best interests of the craft. The Constitution contemplates that such change should be made only in urgent
cases and we do not believe that such case has been made out here.
We, therefore, recommend that the petition be denied.

Report adopted.
Past Grand Master Bledsoe, from the same Committee,
presented the following:
To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:

Brother Jesse M. Whited has presented a number of amendments
to the Constitution providing for the creation of a "Grand Chancellor"
and "Deputy Grand. Chancellors" in furtherance of a scheme of Masonic
investigation, education, etc. With tl;c general spirit and purpose of
the idea entertained by Brother vVhitcd, we are in hearty accord,
believing that anything· tending toward the development of an interest
in the study of Masonic literature and philosophy would he measurably
helpful. But we think the plan actually proposed by Brother Whited
is somewhat too complicated, unsuited to our actual needs at the present time, and possibly wonk! entail too great an expenditure of the
funds of this body. W c, therefore, recommend that the proposed
amcnclments be not adopted.

Report adopted.

PETITIONS FOR RESTORATION.
Brother George L. Jones, fo~ the Committee on Grievances, reported as follows:
To the 11ost Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom were referred certain
petitions for restoration to the rights and privileges of Masonry, report
as follows:
Case No. 154: This is a petition by Ashlar Lodge No. 306 for the
restoration of George B. Caster, who had been expelled from that Lodge
upon the charge of unmasonic conduct in that he had engaged in the
occupation of bartender. The petition shows a compliance on the part
of Ashlar Lodge with the requirements oil the Constitution, relative to
the presentation of such a petition, and, after hearing the statements of
the Master and a Past Master of the Lodge, from which it appears that
the accused has long since abandoned his former occupation and has
followed unobjectionable pursuits, in addition to leading an exemplary
·life, your Committee believe that the petition should be granted.
We, therefore, recommend the adoption of the following resolution:

*For items, see Report of Committee on Returns.

Resolved, That the petition of Ashlar Lodge No. 306 be granted
and that George B. Caster be, and he is hereby restored to all the rights
and privileges of Masonry.

Adopted.

522

PROCEEDINGS OF 'I'HE
GRAND LODGE 01<' CALIFORNIA

Case No. 48: In 1908, the petitioner, Joseph Manoah Smith, then
a member of Fresno Lodge No. 247, was charged with unmasonic conduct, was found guilty and the penalty of expulsion inflicted. The
accused now presents his petition fior restoration, which petition has
been approved by Fresno Lodge No. 247 by the unanimous vote of the
members there present. Accompanying the petition are strong letters
recommending the reinstatement of the petitioner, and his conduct and
standing in the community in which he resides are highly praised.
In view of these commendations, it being evident that his behavior and
actions for at least the last seven years have been above reproach, we
are of the opinion that his petition should be now favorably acted upon.
We, therefore, recommend the adoption of the following resolution:
Resolved, That the petition of Joseph Manoah Smith be granted,
and that he be, and he is hereby, restored to all the rights and privileges
of Masonry.

Adopted.
Case No. 114: The petitioner, who now lives in Honolulu, was
expelled by Golden Gate Lodge No. 30 in 1912, having been in effect
charged with the embezzlement of certain small sums of money received
by him-in one instance, from the Lodge for the benefit of a Mason's
widow; in another instance, from another source for the benefit of the
Lodge. Notice of the intention to petition :£or restoration was given to
Golden Gate Lodge and the petition was approved. As proof of his
character, several letters arc presented urging favorable action upon
the application. There have, however, appeared before the Committee,
certain Masons who vigorously oppose the petition, and, owing to the
fact that they had not obtained knowledge of the petition in time to
present evidence in support of their opposition, we are of the opinion
that definite action should not be taken at this time. The character of
the statements made to the Committee is such that the Committee
believe that further investigation should he made as to the fitness of
the petitioner to be restored.
We, therefore, recommend that action upon this petition be deferred
until the next Annual Communication.
Respectfully submitted,
GllORGll L. ]ONllS,

wALTllR F. HAAS,
E. B. PowllR,

J. P. BllRNHARD.

JUBILEE CELEBRATION.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

525

Past Grand Master Bledsoe in a most gracious and
felicitous speech, every word of which was enthusiastically
greeted by the large assemblage attending, presented to
Brother Mayer, with the love and affection of his brethren,
an ebony cane with black ivory handle, heavily and tastily
mounted with gold. The veteran organist responded with
more grace than was expected under the circumstances,
reciting how he had been first appointed Grand Organist
in 1868, and that he had attended every annual commumcation during the entire time of his appointments. Altogether it was a great event - a real love-feast, and the
fervent prayer of all was that Brother Mayer would maintain his health so long as the Almighty Father would permit him to remain with us.
The thanks of Grand Lodge were extended to all the
brethren who had so freely given of their time and talents
to make this unique celebration a complete success.

SAMUEL D. MAYER
"AS HE IS"

The Grand Secretary in his report has called your attention to the
lack of promptness by a number of Lodges in making their returns.

There has been a net gain in membership for the year of 2634,
making the total membership at the close of the year 60,384.
Your Committee last year called attention to the necessity of encouraging members of outside jurisdictions, who are now residents of
this jurisdiction, to affiliate with us, but the returns do not disclose
that any such effort has been made. We find that in many localities in
the State there are nearly as many non-affiliated as affiliated members,
that such non-affiliated members enjoy all the benefits of the Order
without assuming any of the burdens or responsibilities. This necessarily adds additional burdens to our own members.

536

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Too often, when approached to become members, the excuse offered
is, that the dues they pay are only one-half to one-eighth of what we
pay. It, also, too frequently, happens that when one of these brethren
requires assistance, or we are compelled to advance funeral expenses
and the return of the same is requested from his home Lodge, the reply
is, that the Lodge is not in a position to reimburse us. It is improbable
that any legislation could be enacted to correct this condition which
would not be discourteous to other jurisdictions, but we do think a
concerted effort should be made to have all non-affiliated members who
are permanent residents here to become members of the Lodges in
their vicinity.
Your Committee last year also called attention to the large number
of suspensions for non-payment of dues. This same matter was also
called to your attention in the Grand Secretary's report for that an<l
the preceding year, and yet the returns this year disclose an even greater
number of such suspensions.
This condition can be and should be corrected. The fault seems
to result from the neglect or failure of Masters and Secretanes to take
the delinquencies up promptly, or by other means than a mailed notice.
We recommend that each Lodge have a Committee on Delinquent Members, whose duty will be to personally or otherwise interview each
member delinquent and ascertain the cause for such delinquen~y and
endeavor to have the same paid, or remitted if unable to pay and
deserving, and thus have a concerted effort made throughout the State
to materially reduce the number of suspensions from this cause.
Respect:£ully submitted,
H. D. MEYERS,
JOSEPH ABRAMS,
GEo. W. LEMorn,
ARTHUR
CRITES,
Committee.

their comfort and hospitality. Vallejo, Pico, Alvarado, Castro, Rodriguez and Carillo were types of these Spanish "dons" who figured largely
in those early days. Many of them afterwards became loyal citizens of
the United States and gave their aid in the upbuilding of a new commonwealth.
At this time California was truly a pastoral land. But few of the
excitements and ambitions of our modern civilization had entered
therein. There was no struggling for wealth, no herding into cities,
no effort or desire for the development of natural resources. The
people spent much of their time out of doors, and in the balmy air,
and under the soft skies enjoyed their rough sports. They were contented and happy, indifferent to the accumulation of money, and hospitable to an extreme rarely equalled. Surely this was the land of the
"siesta" and the "mafiana."
Here at their feet were the great valleys which at a future day
were to yield abundant harvests of grain and fruit, but they were yet
untilled. They were carpeted with Nature's luxuriant growth, and
over them roamed countless herds of cattle and horses, of little value
except to provide for the simple wants of the people.
The mountains, God's great storehouses of treasure, ·which were to
enrich the world in after days, but not yet unlocked, towered around
and above the~ in all their grandeur.
Here was the land-locked bay, unsurpassed in beauty, whose waters
washed the bare hills and sand dunes of the future queen city of the
Pacific as far west as what is now Montgomery street. Through the
Golden Gate, now the gateway of the commerce of the world, fhere
ventured a few hardy mariners for their cargoes of hides and tallow.
At this time San Francisco had but a dozen houses, and contained not
more than fifty souls.

Three score and ten years ago, within the lifetime of some of us
here present, California was a Mexican province. For many years
under the dominion of Spain and Mexico, misgoverned and neglected,
there had been no advance in the arts of civilization and progress.
The inhabitants, composed largely of Mexicans and Indians, were
densely ignorant. True, missions had been established in various parts
of the territory by self-sacrificing men who, by wonderful patience and
devotion, had been enabled to make some inroads into the primitive
life of the people and bring some gleams o~ the dawning of a brighter
day.

During the few years prior to 1847, enterprising adventurers who
were to take an active part in the future development of the country,
had found their way to this comparatively unknown land. Sutter,
Stearns, Larkin and Marshall were types of these men.

Here and there in this great domain were to be found the representatives of old Spanish families who had received grants of vast
tracts of land and who had established homes which were noted for

The United States was at this time at war with Mexico. The
struggle was a momentous one in history, for it involved the possession
of a vast domain on this western coast. Here in California the army

Our sunny southland, now so rich in its golden fruitage, with its
marvelous growth and unsurpassed energy, was then sparsely settled
and wholly undeveloped. Los Angeles, world-famed for its growth
and progress, was a small Spanish settlement with but a handful of
people.

560

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and navy were represented by Fremont, Kearney, Stockton, Sloat and
Sherman, who were prominent factors in the acquisition to the nation
of this golden land.
By the treaty of February 2, 1848, which ended the war, California
became a part of our great republic.
Nine days before the signing of this treaty, January 24, 1848, an
event occurred which was to electrify the world and create an empire
by the western sea. On the American river, a few miles from Sacramento, John Marshall, an employe of Captain John Sutter, unlocked
one of the Creator's storehouses by the discovery of gold. The news
oii the discovery spread like wildfire. All lines of business throughout
the territory were deserted, and the people rushed to secure their
portion of the golden treasure.
Soon the wonderful news was heralded to the world. Marvelous
tales were told of the unlimited wealth which was to be easily obtained
by any seeker. Very soon thousands of people were on their way to
the land of gold. By sea, around Cape Horn and by way of Panama;
by land, across the deserts and over the almost inaccessible mountains.
suffering untold hardships, facing sickness, starvation, even death, the
lure of gold drew them on and on to the goal of their amhitio.n and
desire.
By the middle of November, 1849, more than six hundred vessels
came through the Golden Gate, and the largest part of these were left
swinging at their anchors while their crews rushed to the gold fields,
It is estimated that during the year 1849 forty-two thousand emigrants
came overland to California, and at least double that number by sea.
Each succeeding year brought thousands more to this new El
Dorado in search of fortune. The larger part of the early emigrants
were men. In 1850, in the mining counties to which most of the people
rushed, but two per cent were women.
I think we may say that there was no high and lofty motive which
brought thes.e men to this western land. They came to seek a fortune
and then return to their Eastern homes. They remained to build an
empire on the shores of the Pacific.
They were for the most part sturdy, courageous, undaunted spirits.
types of men who, though not remarkable, are the ones who throughout
the world's history have done things worth while. It was the part which
these Argonauts played in laying strong and abiding the foundations of
a matchless commonwealth which makes them prominent figures in our
history.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

561

At least three great problems confronted these pioneers of the early
·
days.
First, law and order: As has always been the case, a great influx
of emigration caused by great excitement has included in the mass a
large number of undesirable citizens-men whose sole purpose in life
is to prey upon society. From all quarters of the globe gamblers,
libertines, outlaws and murderers came swarming to this new field,
which, on account of conditions, gave a free hand for their nefarious
practices.
To meet this situation required men of character, strong, true,
brave men who were ready to sacrifice time, money, even life itself, in
the cause of justice and good government.
Second, the political situation: When Congress ratified the treaty
with Mexico, it left the people of California in a peculiar condition-a
territory with thousands of people, ,thousands more coming, but with
no legally-appointed rulers.
The struggle between slavery and anti-slavery, which was to culminate a little later in the civil war, was fierce and hot. Whether
California was to enter the Union a free State or a slave State, or
whether it was to be divided, half free and half slave, was a vital
question. For two years the giants. of Congress battled, until at last
freedom conquered, and on September 9, 1850, California was admitted
a free State.
An important factor in the decision of Congress was the action
'taken by the Constitutional Convention held at Monterey in September,
1849. This convention was composed of delegates chosen by the people,
a large majority of whom were undoubtedly opposed to slavery. A
constitution was adopted which provided for a free State, with boundaries as they are today. It was taken to Washington by Fremont and
Gwin, who had been elected the first Senators by the territorial legislature. This prompt action on the part of the strong men of that day
had, without question, a mighty influence with Congress, and resulted
in adding one more star to the galaxy which stands for Liberty and
Freedom.
Third: The third problem was one of Humanity-the caring for
stranded, needy, suffering fellow-man.
Among the thousands who flocked to California in those early days
were many who, for various reasons, failed to secure that which they
so eagerly sought. The hardships ofi the journey hither were a heavy
·drain upon physical endurance, and resulted in many wrecks; the

562

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

563

unpreparedness for . the severe toil and exposure at the mines caused
the weaker to succumb; the disappointments caused by the failure to
achieve fortune in a day left many de;pondent and dependent upon
others; epidemics caused by unsanitary conditions were frequent; and
the cost of the necessities of life was enormous.

The delegates thus assembled unanimously adopted the following:
\"Resolved, That the representatives of the several duly warranted
Lodges now in operation in California, and present at this assemblage,
proceed to the organization of a Convention for the formation of a
Grand Lodge for the State of California."

There were no organizations for relief then as there are now.
Many were selfishly seeking for success, unheeding the cry of the
weary and wayworn brother. But there were other men,-men with
liearts of sympathy,-men, who in their Eastern homes had imbibed
the principle of "the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of. Man."
These heard the cry of the helpless and gave relief.

A constitution was adopted and Grand Officers were elected as
follows:

During the past half century, the growth of fraternal organizations has been marvelous. They have met a world-need, brought
men closer together in all the relations of life and done much to
decrease selfishness and promote a spirit of sympathy and love.
In the early fifties these organizations were few. There was one,
however, of ancient lineage, whose precepts, based upon the eternal and
divine, had done much to advance the cause of human .brotherhood
and ameliorate the ills of suffering humanity.
Free and Accepted Masonry, with its sublime and noble teachings
and its beneficent deeds, has accomplished much to uplift man and
advance the cause of righteousness on earth.

The first Grand Master, Jonathan Drake Stevenson, came to California in March, 1847, as Colonel of the First New York Volunteers.
He was one of the first members of C;,ilifornia Lodge, and was chairman of the committee which drafted the constitution for the organization of the first Grand Lodge. Active in all good works, he was a
familiar figure in San Francisco, loved and respected until his death
in 1894, aged 94 years.

"The great benefit of the Order to the human family has been!

As an illustration of the work done for relief, Deputy Grand
Master Radcliff, in his address before the Grand Lodge in May, 1853,
reports that Tuolumne Lodge No. 8, at Sonora, had expended four
thousand five hundred dollars since its organization, November, 1850,
for the relief of non-affiliated Masons. This Lodge had a membership
of fifty-four.
In 1849 the Masons of Sacramento united with the Odd Fellows
in providing a hospita.1 for the sick. During the first year there was
expended in this work over $31,000, the greater part of which was
raised by voluntary contributions.
In the meantime the number of Masonic Lodges was increasing
rapidly. At the first communication of the Grand Lodge, six Lodges
were represented; at the second, 1851, 15 Lodges reported; in 1852, 25;
in 1853, 35 ; in 1854, 56; in 1855, 83.
The numher of members at the organization of the Grand Lodge
was less than two hundred. In 1855, the number had increased to 3,100.
The records of those early years show conclusively that the pioneer
Masons did their part nobly in helping to solve one of the problems
heretofore alluded to: that of caring for the sick and needy and of
bringing comfort to the distressed and bereaved.
What of the other vital questions of the hour, Law and Order and
the Upbuilding of a New Commonwealth?
The scum of the earth had gathered here in large numbers.
Neither property nor life was safe from the depredations of the criminal class. In the beginning there was no organized law, and it became
necessary for the citizens to take the matter m their own hands and
bring order out of chaos.
In all this work of purging society, in earnest effort in the cause
of righteousness, in active participation in the political affairs of the
State, in loyalty to the Nation during the trying days which followed
California's Statehood, we find the names of many Masons who were
true to the principles of our ancient craft and who did their part nobly
in the laying of the foundations of a commonwealth second to none in
the galaxy of States.

It is impossible to enumerate the names of those who did valiant
service for humanity in those early days. In the mining camps as well
as in the towns, Masons were true to the teachings of the Order.

Among the many brothers who figured largely in the pioneer days,

It is with pride and respect that we scan the early records of the
Grand Lodge of California. We find them full of sentiments which
appeal to the highest and best in man's nature. Every address has its
high moral tone and and its exhortations for right living and conduct
worthy of the true Mason.
At a time when temptations assailed man on every side to a degree
which we can hardly realize, the stand of the prominent Masons against
all forms of vice-gambling, intemperance, profanity and licentiousness-exerted a power for good the value of which cannot be estimated.
The Masons o~ those days were not perfect men, no more than we
of today, but they set for us a high standard in acts of charity, loyalty
and righteousness, which we will do well to follow and emulate. We
bring our tribute of lo~e and respect in memory of what they accomplished, of their high ideals, and their exemplification of the true principles and teachings of the Order which has done so much to alleviate
suffering and uplift manhood.
Those pioneer days were days which "tried men's souls." Men
were found true and we enjoy the inheritance. Today we are in the
midst of a struggle more terrible in its exhibition of hate and barbarity,
more fearful in its possible consequences to the race, than any in ,vhich
mankind has ever been engaged.
Humanity, love of liberty, righteousness, yea, even the Great
Master, calls upon each and every one of us to be faithful and true in
this hour of peril.
Be not despondent, for out of this awful travail shall be reborn a
redeemed and better world. God lives and the teachings of the ~;fan
of Galilee shall yet prevail.
"God of our fathers, known of old,Lord of our far-flung battle line,
Beneath whose guiding hand we hold
Dominion over palm and pine ;
Lord God of Hosts, be with us yet,
Lest we forget-lest we forget."

Whereas, It is pre-eminently desirable that the "Universality of
Masonry" no less than the "Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood
of Man" shall be something more than an empty phrase; and
Whereas, The readjustment of the world's affairs that will result

were believed to be fundamental differences between Anglo-Saxon and

on either side of any essential principle or matter of conscience; and
be it further
Resolved, That any inhib.ition upon the right of visitation heretofore imposed by this Grand Lodge be, and the same hereby is, modified

"MOON" DATES FOR STATED MEETINGS.
Past Grand Master Bledsoe, for the Committee on Jurisprudence, reported as follows:
To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:
A suggestion has come from Lafayette I~odge No. 126 that the
"Moon schedule," as issued by the Grand Secretary, gives in some
instances more than one meeting in a "lunar month," and requesting
that Regulation 78d · of the Constitution be eliminated, and that the
times of meeting be determined by Section 78 of the Constitution. The

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF C'.ALlFORNlA

so-called Regulation is really a ruling, a construction of the law, made
by the Grand Master and approved by the Committee on Jurisprudente
and the Grand Lodge in 1912. \Ve ·understand that the Grand Lodge
may by appropriate action amend the law, but we do not understand
that it can change it by the elimination of an approved construction
thereof. As was said by this Committee in 1912, the subjecf matter is
"somewhat complicated," and we suggest that if a change is desired an
amendment to the Constitution which will properly respect the practices
of Lodges relating to times of· meeting be presented.

was elected Junior Grand \Varden.

ALABAMA.
1916.
96th Annual, Montgomery, Dec. 6-7.
Lodges, 557; Membership, 28,596; Gain, 680.

Largest Lodge, Birmingham Temple Lodge No. 636, 532 Members.
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Ancient, Free & Accepted
Masons of Alabama held its 96th Annual Communication in the Masonic Temple in the City of Montgomery, Dec. 5th and 6th, 1916,
Most Worshipful Walter Smith, Grand Master, presiding.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
In the opening paragraphs of his address, Grand Master Smith
congratulates the Craft upon its progress within the jurisdiction, stating
that not only is the Craft growing stronger numerically, but is growing every year in the knowledge of what true Masonry is, and striving
each year to live in closer accordance with the knowledge attained.
ACTIVITIES OF THE GRAND MASTER
Dispensations were isstted for the formation of five new Lodges.
Corner-stone ceremonies, seven in number, took place under the auspices
of the Grand Lodge. Lodges which received charters at the preceding
Annual Communication were duly constituted.
The Grand Master attended the annual meeting on Feb. 21st and
22nd at Alexandria, Va., of the George Washington ·Masonic National
Association. The work of that organization is commended by the
Grand Master and he recommends that the support of the Grand
Lodge of Alabama be continued to that organization.
MASONIC HOME.
The Masonic Home of this jurisdiction, which has now been in
existence, perhaps a half a dozen years, is calling for the best efforts
of the jurisdiction to maintain it upon a proper and efficient basis.
Great and useful undertakings of all kinds call for effort and sacrifice, and the responsibility assumed by this jurisdiction in connection
with the Home is proving the truly Masonic character of the Brethren,
and is developing those high Masonic qualities which distinguish genuine Mason.ry, and while it is true that the Home is a burden and
responsibility, it is through responsibility of this kind that real character is developed. Alabama will meet this, and all other responsibilities, in the lofty Masonic spirit which characterizes the jurisdiction,
and the Home will in future years prove, as it has proven elsewhere,
a monumel)t to· Masonry.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

CONSTITUTION AL AMENDMENTS.
We· have, we believe, in commenting upon this jurisdiction in previous reports, referred to the method pursued therein of amending the
Constitution, which, in brief, requires, in the first place, that the proposed amendment be submitted in Grand Lodge and supported by a
vote of one-third present, asking for the consiueration of the proposed
amendment. After this affirmative vote of the Grand Lodge that the
amendment be considered, the proposed amendment is then submitted
to each and every Lodge of the jurisdiction, and each and every Lodge
is required, some time within the next ensuing Masonic year, to con.sider the proposed amendment and vote either "yes" or "no" for its
adoption, and no amendment of the Constitution can be adopted except
after being thus submitted, and approved by at least two-thirds of the
Lodges of the jurisdiction, and any Lodge failing to give consideration
to and take action upon any proposed amendment is subject to the
severest kind of Masonic discipline, such, for instance, as the arrest
of its charter. The result of this method of procedure in the adoption
of a constitutional amendment is that every Lodge must have an intimate knowledge of any changes in the Constitution; not only this, but
hasty action is prevented in connection w"ith changes of the organic
law.
