4

At this Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge an amendment
to the Constitution concerning physical qualifications was adopted, as
follows:
"If the petitioner be physically defective by reason of deformity
or being maimed, his eligibility shall be determined by the Lodge to
which he has applied, and if determined favorably to the petitioner he
shall be eligible to receive the degrees of Masonry when the action of
the Lodge has been approved by the Grand Master in writing."

COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN CORRESPONDENCE.
In accordance with the recommendations of the Committee on
Foreign Correspondence, recognition of an alleged Grand Lodge of the
Argentine Republic was denied.
Recognition also was refused to the alleged newly created so-called
Grand Lodge of France.
The new Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence is Worshipful Brother Oliver D. Street, who presents an extremely interesting
and comprehensive report on Foreign Correspondence.
For the past two years, under the chairmanship of Brother Mewhinney, the report had been arranged in the "topical" form. Brother
M ewhinney's reports were interesting and instructive, and bore evi-

Brother Street, the ~ew Chairman, has combined the ordinary
method of individual review of each jurisdiction with a comprehensive
index of the Report, which gives the Report the advantages of the
ordinary form of review and also the topical form, for the reason that,
by reference to the extremely carefully prepared index, any subject
treated in the various reports under review may be readily located .
In the report before us, California, 1915, is reviewed in a courteous
and painstaking manner with favorable comment upon many of our
Masonic activities.

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Eleventh Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Alberta, Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons, was
opened in the Masonic Temple in the City of Banff, Province of
Alberta, on May 31st, 1916, the Most Worshipful Brother S. Y. Taylor,
Grand Master, presiding.
EXPRESSION OF LOYALTY TO THE CAUSE OF THE ALLIES
IN THE PRESENT WORLD WAR'.
Preliminary to the Address of the Grand Master, the following
resolution, expressive of the loyalty of Canada and Canadian Masons
to the cause of the British Empire, was introduced and unanimously
adopted:
"Resolved, That the terms of the following resolution be cabled
through the proper channel to His Majesty the King:
"The Grand Lodge of Freemasons of Alberta, now in session,
humbly desires at this time to assure His Majesty the King of its
loyal fealty to His August Person and to the Empire.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPO~DENCE.

"As the duration of the present war lengthens from months into
years, \'lie realize more fully the justice of the cause for which Our
Empire and Our Allies are contending, and the necessity for a successful issue of the conflict, if the principles of liberty and justice
are to be preserved for civilization and the world.
"Numbers of our Brethren under this Grand Jurisdiction are now
serving His Majesty at the front, and many more are preparing so
to serve. Several of our brave Brethren have given their lives while
fighting in the trenches for the honor of Canada and the cause of the
Empire.
"\Ve hereby renew our assurance to His Majesty that the Freemasons of Alberta remain ready and willing to perform their <lnty to
their King and Empire."

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
Expressive of the exalted character of the Grand Master's ideals
concerning Freemasonry and its functions, we quote the following
paragraphs from the opening portion of his Annual Address:
"The centuries of the existence of Freemasonry sweeping onward
like a stately river toward the ocean of eternity make the course of
one year seem like a little tributary on whose waters we have briefly
glided to the outlet, where they mingle with the majestic flood. Yet
on a journey so short and eventful, the determination of our course
from time to time may have created influences which will extend beyond our lives and help to mould for weal or woe the hearts and
lives of our fellow-men.
"'No man liveth to himself.' May we all endeavor to perform our
allotted task with the utmost fidelity, remembering that
"'Life counts not by hours, or joys, or pangs,
But just by duties done.'
"The year has been an eventful one, particularly on account of the
mighty conflict which is now waging on the continent of Europe.
Many unusual conditions existed which called for judicious solution
without violating the Constitution and the Landmarks of our Order.
"During the year peace and harmony have prevailed within our
Subordinate Lodges. Not a single appeal has been made to me in this
regard. Our annual records show a net increase in membership of 494,
which is highly satisfactory, when we consider the faet that so many
of our brethren have enlisted for service at the front. that in some
instances it has been difficult to properly officer the Lodge; 10 per
cent of the total membership in this province have joined the ranks
of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces."

hundred in number; another Grand Master two hundred fifteen; and

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
The Grand Master states that he dedicated during the year the
Masonic Hall of Patricia Lodge, constituted the Lodge and installed
the officers. He constituted in all five new Lodges. He made a number of official visits to subordinate Lodges; he rendered only one
decision.
FRATERNAL DEAD.
This jurisdiction suffered the loss of many of its Brethren, many
of whom perished on the battlefields of the world. The Grand Lodge
mourns the loss of Grand Tyler R.". w:. Bro. R. C. Bruce, who efficiently filled his office.
We quote the Grand Master in his Conclusion, referring to the
awful calamity of the war in Europe, as follows:
"The outstanding events of the war during the last twelve months
have been the Russian revolution and the entry of the United States
as a combatant. From the one will eventually come greater strength
and a purer purpose; from the other has come a conviction beyond all
doubt of the ultimate triumph of those ideals for which we are fighting. Now, as truly as in the dark days of the Civil War, is the great
American republic fighting for that government 'of the people, by the
people, and for the people' for which their immortal President prayed.
Never before in the world's history has there been such an inspiring
spectacle of mighty nations united in the great contest for the freedom
of free peoples; never has there been anything so nearly approaching
that actual brotherhood of man for which we feared to hope. But
now through the clash of armed nations the dream of the poet may
yet become the business of the statesman.
"It is not for us, however, at this time, to discuss the war in its
greater phases. Our purposes must be to consider those matters that
have become our especial business as the result of this conflict. The
ever-increasing burdens that are being imposed on the peoples of the
world by this struggle are being felt in a constantly increasing degree
by the people of this province and members of our Order. Many
funds unconnected with Free Masonry have been established to help
to relieve the situation, and I am glad to say that in my visits throughout the province I found that these funds are receiving substantial
assistance from our Lodges. That, Brethren, is good Free Masonry.
"As I went from place to place I saw in our Lodges the names of
our men who have gone, the records of the men who have fallen.
Very many of our Brethren are now at the front; many of them will
never return. All this is throwing upon us a responsibility which we
cannot ignore, and which it will be our greatest honor and our highest
privilege to meet. The welfare of the widows and children of our
departed Brethren must be for years to come the principal concern of
this Fraternity. Our obligation in this regard will not be answered

9

"If it were a question of the price to be exacted from us that we
be allowed to remain in our own country that we might be with and
care for our loved ones, what would we not give, what would we not
do? This I take it is the nature of our obligation. This great privilege is being purchased for us by the sacrifices of our brothers overseas, by the anguish of their wives, by the sorrows of their children.
To pay this debt we may easily do too little; we cannot do too much."

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of Arizona commenced its Thirty-fourth Annual Communication at
Tucson on Tuesday, the fourth day of March, 1916, the Most Worshipful George M. Bridge, Grand Master, presiding.
INTRODUCTION OF VERY WORSHIPFUL JOHN WHICHER,
GRAND SECRET ARY OF CALIFORNIA.
After the formal opening of the Grand Lodge, and preliminary
to the Address of the Grand Master, a pleasing incident occurred in
the introduction to the Grand Lodge of Very Worshipful John
Whicher, our genial Grand Secretary of California.

10

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The event took place with full ceremony, Past Grand ~faster

East, where Brother Whicher thanked the Most Worshipful Grand

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
Masonry in our sister jurisdiction of Arizona is progressing in a
satisfactory manner, there being a substantial increase in membership,
and the Grand Master reports the constitution of three new Lodges
within the year.
The Grand Master was able to make only a limited number of
visitations to subordinates, but his official activities were manifested
in other directions, such, for instance, as the placing of not less than
three corner-stones of public buildings tmder Masonic auspices; and
the conducting of correspondence concerning mooted Masonic questions with Lodges of the jurisdiction, and with other Grand Jurisdictions.
DECISIONS.
Under the above caption, he makes some pertinent remarks which
may be of general interest upon the subject of "physical qualifications," and we quote him upon the subject of "decisions" as follows:
"Many questions have been submitted to me for my decision,
interpretation or advice. Several of these matters have been disposed
of by reference to the Constitution or Anderson's Manual. Others
have either appeared ambiguous in their meaning, or are entirely new
so far as the Constitution and decisions of this Grand Lodge reveal.
"First. I have received several communications concerning the
question of the physical qualifications of the candidate. To all of these
I have replied by reference to Regulation 10 of our General Regulations. Each Grand Master is the recipient of many similar inquiries
and this Grand Lodge has most emphatically called the attention of
the Subordinate Lodges to the plain nature of this regulation and the
ease with which each Worshipful Master can decide these cases without
applications to the Grand ~faster. In spite of Regulation No. 10 and
its undoubted import, many members of the. Craft in this State do not
sancticn the application of physical tests for candidates, who are to
practice progressive moral science.. which we claim our Organization
teaches. I
that an expression of opinion on this matter be
obtained from
Grand Lodge session."

REPORT ON CORRESPON.DENCE.

11

Concerning one of the decisions of the Grand Master, declining
to lay a certain corner-stone, the Jurisprudence Committee remarks
as follows:
"Your committee does not agree with the answer given by the
Grand Master. The Grand Lodge shouJd lay the corner-stone of a
public building only by invitation from the proper authorities. As they
and not the Grand Lodge furnish the stone, the decision as to what
if .anything should be put upon it (or in the box) rests with them.
A sense of propriety usually leads them to confer with the Grand Lodge
or the local Lodge, and if any disagreement should ensue the Grand
Lodge should deeline to perform its ceremonies. There is nothing
wrong or inappropriate in placing a Masonic inscription or emblem upon
a corner-stone when the same is laid by the Grand Lodge."
There is no report on Foreign Correspondence.
FREDERICK WELLINGTON PERKINS, Grand Master, Flagstaff.
GEORGE J. RosKRliGE, Grand Secretary, Tucson.

"Question-\Vill it be a violation of the law of our Grand Lodge
for a Mason in this State to sign a petition asking for the repeal of

, "Answer-The Edict passed by the Grand Lodge of Arkansas at
its. sessio"! of 1914 sa.ys it is a Masonic offense to sign a petition for

a Masonic offense to sign a petition to repeal the State-wide Prohibition
l~w,_ so that saloons may be brought into the State again, therefore
stgnmg such a petition will subject any Mason living in this jurisdiction to expulsion or indefinite suspension, and lodges are hereby
directed to proceed accordingly on every case of such violation."
The last decisions quoted above, and which was approved by the
Jurisprudence Committee and the Grand Lodge, seems to go to the
point of making the holding of an opinion a Masonic offense. It certainly does so, if the opinion takes the form of a written expression
of one's views against the policy of a State-wide Prohibition law. In
other words, in Arkansas, if one disbelieves in the policy of Statewide prohibition, it is advisable for him to keep his mouth shut on the
subject.
MASONIC ORPHANS' HOME.
There is in this jurisdiction one of the best Orphans' Home in
America. One hundred and seventeen children are enrolled at the
Home, which institution is under the efficient management of very
competent superintendent and matron; and the report of the. Board
of Trustees of this beneficient institution states in its concluding paragraph that all that is necessary to make a'!ly Mason an enthusiastic
supporter of the Home and School is a visit of a day or so to the
institution. Everyone, so they state in their report, after making such
a visit, has gone away singing the praises of the Home, an~ if not
loyal friends of the Home before such a visit, are certain to become
such after going through the institution.
In addition to the Home and School for Orphans, preliminary
steps have been taken looking to the establishment of a Home for
Widows and Aged Masons of Arkansas, as is evidenced in the following resolution adopted at this Communication:
"Resolved, 'That the recommendation, of the Grand Master be
approved; and that a committee of five be appointed by the incoming
Grand Master to consider the feasibility of establishing a Horne for
Widows and Aged l'vlasons of Arkansas, and to report at the next

sells whisky and brandy, but riot to be consumed upon the premises.
I can see no distinction between this grocer and any other person who
sells intoxicating drink. The blind tiger is often run in connection
with a .cigar stand, a drug store, a livery stable, a barber shop, and
some years ago I knew of one out in Kansas in connection with a
blacksmith shop. The boot-legger sells whiskey to be consumed elsewhere. In my humble judgment our worthy brother makes a distinction without a difference and overlooks the spirit of the law because
of a mere technicality."

The Sixty-first Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, A. F.

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
A large portion of the Grand Master's address is devoted to the
great war, in which Canada is fighting side by side with another ·country, and the Grand Master calls attention to the significant fact that
every dependency of the British Crown is fighting as loyally for the
· preservation of the Empire as is England herself, and that Canada
and other dependencies of Great Britain realize that the preservation
of their liberties is inseparably linked with the success and integrity
of the Empire.
The Grand Master calls attention to another lesson which this
war has emphasized, perhaps the greatest lesson of all, which, however,
both individuals and nations in their ambitions are apt to forget, and
in the case of Germany to scoff at. This lesson is summed up in the
motto of one of the degrees of Knight Templarism, "Magna est ·veritas
ct prevalebit"-"Great is Truth, and it will prevail."

FOREIGN CORRESPONDENCE.
The report on Foreign Correspondence is, as usual, by the Most
Worshipful A. T. Freed, Past Grand Master.
He reviews California, 1913, and quotes extensively from the
excellent address of Grand Master Bledsoe.

In Brother Freed's Conclusion, he discusses several subjects of
general interest, and we quote from his "Conclusion" his remarks upon
the subject of "Landmarks," as follows:
"In 1914 a suggestion was made by this correspondent-hesitatingly and tentatively put forth-that the landmarks of Masonry had
been misunderstood, especially on this continent; and that, in fact,
there never had been any Masonic landmarks except those safeguarding the reserved rights of the four old lodges which formed the first
Grand Lodge of England. The suggestion was made with a view of
getting opinions and comments from brother correspondents and
possibly from others. But the attempt was a failure; except for a few
brief passing notices the overture met with no response.
"It has been pointed out that when Anderson used the word landmarks in Article XXXIX of the first Book of Constitutions, he meant
figuratively the posts or signs which marked the bounds of lodges,
and that the proviso made in Article XXXIX was a stipulation that
in any future amendments to the Constitution the reserved rights of
the old lodges must not be impaired. It is also possible that the
peculiar customs of the operative lodges were to be secured to them.
It is in evidence that for some time the old lodges exercised their
reserved rights, notably in the particular of attending the communications of Grand Lodge and scrutinizing the elections of Grand
Masters. In a few years the old lodges fell into decay with the exception of St. Paul's. the reserved rights ceased to have much value, and
the meaning of the word landmarks was forgotten. The term continued to be employed, but in a vague and indefinite way, as a name
for the general principles of the fraternity.

19

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

"And so the matter stood for a century and a quarter. In 1858
Dr. A. G. Mackey came to the conclusion that 'a comprehensible form'
should be given to the landmarks, and he elaborated a list of twentyfive, which list has been generally, but not wholly, accepted by Grand
Lodges in the United States. Dr. Mackey said the first requisite of
a custom or rule of action to constitute it a landmark was that it must
have existed from 'time whereof the memory of man runneth not to
the contrary.' The second was that it must be absolutely unchangeable. To use his own language, 'The landmarks of the Order, like the
laws of the Medes and Persians, can suffer no change. What they
were centuries ago they still remain, and must continue in force until
Masonry itself shall cease to exist.'
"Now a very superficial glance at Dr. Mackey's landmarks ·will
satisfy the observer that they do not meet his own requirements. For
example, his second landmark is 'the division of symbolic Masonry into
three degrees,' while it is well known that three degrees in craft
Masonry did not exist till after the formation of the Grand Lotlge of
England. Another of his landmarks is 'the government of a fraternity
by a presiding officer called a Grand Master, who is elected from the
body of the craft.' Again it is quite certain that, previous to the
formation of the Grand Lodge of England, there was no Grand Master
elected from the body of the craft. Indeed, there was no Grand
Master at all in the modern sense of the term.
"In the year 1911 Brother Axel ]. A. Poignant read a paper before
the lodge Quatuor Coronati, in which he asserted that not one of
Mackey's twenty-five landmarks was a landmark at all; that no two
writers could be found to agree as to the character of the landmarks
and that in fact the landmarks were neither more nor less than th~
moral teachings of the fraternity. In the discussion wbich followed
the reading of the paper, and in the written criticisms afterwards sent
in by leading students of Masonry in England, not one ventured to
say what the landmarks really were. And the more a man knows
about Masonry the less disposed is he to be dogmatic on this subject.
If we have ventured to express an opinion that possibly the term had
no meaning except the safeguarding of the reserved rights of the old
lodges, and possibly the customs of operative Masonry, it has not
been put forth as a settled conviction, but at the best as a plausible
conjecture. In support of that conjecture much may be said. At
present we shall content ourselves with saying that such was ·the
assertion of members of the old lodge of St. Paul. In 1778 there was
an unfortunate disagreement in that lodge, resulting in a division.
The C?ne P'.lrty applied to the so-called Grand Lodge of All England,
then m existence at York, for a warrant. In the statement made in
support of their application the brethren of St. Paul's Lodge said:
"'And whereas in the year 1717 the Fraternity in London agreed
to cement under a new Grand Master, and with that view the old
lodge of St. Paul, jointly with three other lodges, assembled in form.
constituted themselves a nominal Grand Lodge pro tempore, and
elected a Grand Master to preside over their future general meetings,
whom they afterwards invested with a power to constitute subordinate
lodges and to convene the fraternity at stated periods in Grand Lodge,
in order to make laws, with their consent and approbation, for the
good government of the society at large. But subject to certain conditions and restrictions then expressly stipulated, and which are more
fully set forth in the thirty-ninth article of the General Regulations in

the first Book of Constitutions. This article, with thirty-eight others,
was afterwards, at a meeting of the brethren in and about the cities
of London and Westminster, in the year 1721, solemnly approved of,
ratified and confirmed by them, and signed in their presence by the
Masters and Wardens of the four old lodges on the one part, and
Philip Duke of Wharton then Grand Master; Dr. Desaguliers, Deputy
Grand Master; Joshua Timson and William Hawkins, Grand Wardens, and the Masters and Wardens of sixteen lodges which had been
constituted by the fraternity betwixt 1717 and 1721, on the other part.
And these articles the Grand Master engaged for himself and his
successors, when duly installed, in all time coming, . to observe '.Ind
keep sacred and inviolable. By these prudent precaut10ns the Ancient
Landmarks (as they are properly styled) of the four old lodges were
intended to be secure against any encroachments on their Masonic
rights and privileges.' "

ANOTHER UNUSUAL EVENT.
Another unusual event occurred at one of the sess10ns of this
Annual Communication in the introduction to the brethren by the
Grand Master of Most Worshipful Brother Lawrence N. Greenleaf,
who sat in the South fifty years ago when Brother Chase Withrow
was Grand Master.
Brother Greenlcaf's response to his introduction was as follows:
"Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand
Lodge: I am always glad to be among you. While I was sitting
here with Brother Chase Withrow, it occurred to me that fifty years
ago he was sitting in the East and I sat in the South as Junior Grand
Warden. The flight of the years seems hardly possible; how swiftly
they have passed away, leaving behind half a century in the service of
Masonry. I believe I have served in the Masonic bodies for fifty-three
or fifty-four years, having been made a Master Mason in 1863. I have
served in nearly all the capacities in Blue Lodge Masonry, and have
been your Correspondent since 1870---thirty-two years, I believe, consecutively-which makes me, I believe, the oldest Foreign Correspondent
in the United States. I have hardly realized the passing of these years.
It has always been a pleasant duty to serve in any capacity in the
various Bodies with which I have been conn~cted, and I assure you
I fully appreciate the kind words which I have received from the
Brethren. I only feel, Brethren, that I have been unworthy of the great
confidence that has been reposed in me. I thank you.''

20

Under the caption, "Condition of Craft," he makes the following
observations concerning Masonry in Colorado, and his remarks on
electioneering for office may be read with profit by Masons generally:
"The Craft in Colorado, Brethren, is in good, healthy condition.
Our Lodges are active along all proper Masonic lines, they are blessed
with a reasonable amount of prosperity and in most instances have
increased in strength and influence.
"I wish to call your attention to the fourth paragraph of Section
163 of our Constitutions: 'Electioneering for Office is Strictly Prohibited.'
,
"Reports have reached me of the ill effects of this most pernicious practice in one of our Lodges. Brethren, I caution you in the
most solemn manner to vote only as your conscience shall dictate to
you to be right; seeking neither to influence others nor permitting
yourself to be influenced by them. The good of Masonry must be
our sole guide."

This lodge received its charter from the Grand Lodge at its Sixth

Teller was appointed Grand Orator; and at the Fiftieth Anniversary
of Black Hawk Lodge No. 11, Brother Withrow, still in vigorous
health, and the Dean of Colorado Masons, was re-elected Master of
the Lodge, and he graciously consented to preside over the Lodge for
another year as Worshipful Master.

FOREIGN CORRESPONDENCE.
The report upon Foreign Correspondence is by Past Grand
Master George A. Kies, who is also the Grand Secretary, this
being his third report.
Bro. Kies reviews California, 1916. He refers particularly
to our Masonic Homes at Decato and Covina, and is evidently of
the opinion that California, in her charitable w~rk, is entitled to a
high place among the Grand Lodges of America.
He comments upon the law of California, whereby the word
"orphan" has always been construed to include a daughter, whatever her age, and regardless of whether she has been married; our
law being, that, if in distress, such a person is entitled to Masonic
aid, and he rises to ask if this also includes adult sons of Masons?
and expresses his opinion t"o the effect that donations to any
adult children of Masons is purely a matter of favor, rather than
of duty. We, however, can see a distinction between adult daughters in distress and adult sons. Adult sons may, of their own
volition, become Masons, and thereby gain all of the privileges,
and assume all of the duties incumbent upon Masons; adult
daughters cannot attain this position, which is at least one excellent reason why they should be considered upon a basis different from adult sons.

COMMUNICATIONS.
The 106th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, A. F. &
A. M. of the District of Columbia was held in the Masonic Temple
in the City of Washington, D. C., on December 20, 1916.
Various Special and Stated Communications were held within
the year, at which various business matters were considered and
disposed of.
At the Annual Communication, after the formal opening, and
preceding the Address of the Grand Master, the following distinguished visitors were received with appropriate honors and
invited to the East.
Brother George Fleming Moore, Sovereign Grand Commander
of the Supreme Council of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish
Rite for the Southern jurisdiction.
Past Grand Master Martin A. Morrison, of the Grand Lodge
of Indiana.
Past Grand Master Milton J. Hull, of the Grand Lodge of
Nebraska.
Past Grand Master John C. Muerman, of the Grand Lodge of
Idaho.

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
The Grand Master in the opening paragraphs of his Address
congratulates the Fraternity upon the progress of Masonry within
the jurisdiction, his report indicating that the gain is the largest
recorded since the foundation of the Grand Lodge.
MASONIC AND EASTERN STAR HOME.
There apparently has been a little friction between the Grand
Lodge and the Grand Chapter of the Eastern Star over the administration of the Masonic Home, although not of a character to.
in any sense, impair the usefulness of the Home, and we gath~~
from reading the reports that the differences have been recon·
ciled, and complete harmony restored to the management of this
great Masonic charity.
A MOVE IN THE INTEREST OF CLOSER COOPERATION.
The Grand Master refers to the fact that the Scottish Rite of
Freemasonry for the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States
has its headquarters in the City of vVashington, and that the
Sovereign Grand Commander of the Scottish Rite is not only
interested in the Scottish Rite of Freemasonry but is, also, in
hearty sympathy with the aims and purposes of Ancient Craft
Masonry, and that his counsel, and advice, and sympathy are
of great benefit to the Craft in general, and the Grand Master is
pleased to note that co-operation along all of the lines of Masonry
within the District is producing splendid results, and is of vast
benefit to all branches of the Order.
·
The Grand Master recommends that the Sovereign Grand
Commander be invited to deliver an Address before the Grand
Lodge at the May Communication, and that the occasion be made
the most notable in the new Masonic year.

ST. JOHN'S DAY COMMUNICATION.
The usual St. John's Day Communication was held at the
Temple in the City of \Vashington on St. John, the Evangelist's
Day, Dec. 27, 1916, for the purpose of installing the newly elected
Grand Officers for the ensuing Masonic year.
Most vVorshipful Brother Jam es W. Witten was installed
as Grand Master, and in his Address accepting the important
trust, indicated in eloquent words his conception of the high
mission of Masonry, and to indicate the trend of his thought in
this direction, the following paragraph from his thoughtful production is quoted:
"If Freemasonry has a mission in the world, and it has a large
one; if Freemasonry, or any other institution, justifies its existence,
and the efforts necessary to its support and maintenance, it must do so
through the good it does, through the lives it touches and betters,
through the fruit it bears; and when it fails, and as soon as it fails,
to fulfill its true mission. to meet the needs that gave it birth, and becomes fruitkss, it must follow the fate of the barren fig tree, because
the time is shortly coming, if it has not already come, when there is
and will be no room in society for institutions that make no contributions to its welfare."

Brother Baird's report, as usual, is replete with interesting

Brother Baird continues to question the efficacy of prohibition as a means of reducing the evils of intemperance and upon

28

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

this subject we quote from his Conclusion as follows:
"That bete noir, prohibition, is still active in the Fraternity, and
notwithstanding prohibitive laws have become effective in eighteen
States of the Union, there was an increase of 11,602,661 gallons of spirits
distilled during the fiscal year ending June 30, 1916, over that reported
the previous year. These figures were obtained from the Revenue
Officers of the Treasury Department.
"But, during the fiscal year ending June 30, 1916, there was brewed
1,182,192 less barrels of malt liquor than during the previous fiscal
year.
"The population of the eighteen dry States aggregates about 4.4%
of the total population of the United States (figured from the 1910
Census returns), and from this one would suppose the consumption of
distilled spirits would diminish in about that ratio; but for a fact the
output of spirits was 136,570,695 gallons during the fiscal year ending
June 30, 1915; and 149,849,180 gallons during the fiscal year ending
June 30, 1916, which is an increase of 9.16%. These figures are
significant.
"It is evident that the prohibitive laws have not diminished the
production nor the consumption of distilled spirits (which makes
drunkards), while on the other hand the output of malt liquor has
diminished nearly 2%; and beer, be it remembered, is less harmful
than distilled spirits.
"That distilled liquor does go into the dry States there is abundance of evidence. A reputable dealer in the Capital City informs the
writer that in his shipment of liquor into the State of Maine, claims
were made for breakage, by his customers there; and upon investigation it was proven that even express employees purposely broke
the packages that they might obtain portions of the 'juice.'"

MASONIC HOME AND ORPHANAGE.
At one of the sessions of the Annua1 Communication, Brother
Charles A. Wilson of Louisville, Ky., was introduced to the Grand
Lodge, and delivered a stirring address upon the functions of
Masonic Hornes, this being a subject in which Florida is at this
time particularly interested, the Grand Lodge having under consideration the question of the location of its contemplated Home.
The report of a Special Committee upon this subject was rendered
at this time. At the conclusion of the report a resolution was
adopted whereby a committee was appointed to determine the
selection of a sife for the Home, with power to proceed, after the
selection of a site, "to erect such a Home as in their judgment
will meet the needs of this Grand Jurisdiction.''

"It has been claimed by many that 'Masonr.y knows no flag' and
that Masons owe no allegiance to any special banner. With this statement, in a broad way, we agree, and the claim that the flag should
always be displayed in a Masonic Lodge and should float from every
Masonic edifice, does not appeal to the writer. \Ve claim that we
firmly believe that patriotism and love of country should he a prevailing element in the breast of every Mason, and the flag of the American Masons is the Stars and Stripes and it should always he shown
proper respect on every occasion. The flag of our English Brethren is
the Union Jack, that of the Germans and the French is the flag of
their respective countries, and so on, and Masons owe allegiance to
the civil representation of the country in which they hve. In our
opinion, Masons who are so ethereally constituted that they get restless when sitting in a Lodge under the flag of their country, are not
practicing one of the fundamental precepts of the Order, nor do we
feel that the omission to display the flag in every Lodge meeting is
any lapse or lack of patriotism or love of country. Every Mason must
be proud of the part the Order has borne through every srtuggle in the
nation, from the Boston Tea Party to the Initiation of Maj or General
Leonard E. Wood, Chief of Staff of the United States army of recent
date.

"THE !'LAG."

"The wide discussion which has taken place anent the introduction
of the flag in Lodge and Grand Lodge meetings, shows a great diversity of opinion and some considerable opposition. The Grand Lodge
of Indiana has adopted a law requiring every Lodge in that State to
display the flag in the East at all times when the Lodge is open, and
they have formulated and adopted a certain form or ceremony for the
introduction of the flag after the opening of the Lodge or Grand Lodge.
"A ceremony has also 0een adopted in the Grand Jurisdiction of
Illinois and has been used at all of the schools of instruction in the
State during the year. It was exemplified in Kenwood Lodge, Milwaukee, not long ago and was very much appreciated and complimented
by the Wisconsin Masons.
"In Missouri the Grand Master advised that every Lodge should
be instructed to display the flag at all meetings, but the Grand Lodge
refused to adopt the recommendation.

"BLUE" LODGE.

"A number of requests for information have appeared in the
Masonic periodicals of recent date, and in one or two instances Grand
Masters have ventured a criticism upon the appellation 'Blue Lodge' as
applied to the Masonic Lc-dge for the Craft Degrees in the English
and American Jurisdictions. There are a large number of historical
incidents and much Masonic data on this subject. Probably the best
is by Dr. W. J. Chetwood-Crawley, late Grand Treasurer of the Grand
Lodge of Ireland and a noted Masonic writer. Much of his work has
appeared in the 'Ars,' that most excellent periodical published in
London.
"He says that the use of the word 'Blue' as applied to Lodges
first came to us from many centuries ago and the first authentic Masonic record in regard to the color 'hlue' is in the English and Irish
Grand Lodge minutes of 1731 and 1734, where they ordered the tJiree
Grand Lodge officers to have 'blue silk lining to their aprons and blue
ribbons for their jewels.' Jn the Scottish Grand Lodge, green was
used and their color records date hack to 1637, but the first three
degrees are known with them as the 'Blue Lodge' and in their third
degree work they make a very marked preference to 'blue.!.. In· the
English Grand Lodge records, the shades of blue were at one time
termed as of 'a watery tinge,' which is very near what is now called
'garter blue.'
"Going hack beyond the Grand Lodge of England to ancient and
biblical history we find an abundant field, and there 'blue' was almost
universally associated throu?hout Christendom with the 'Virgin Mother'
and it was one of the principal colors of the Orders of Imperial Rome,
Byzantium, and Egypt.
"Going hack to the tabernacle erected under the direction of
Moses, we find blue especially mentioned. In Exodus, 25th chapter,
8th verse, we find that Moses said, 'Of this is the offering which ye
shall take of them, gold and silver and brass, and blue and purple
and scarlet, and let them make me a sanctuary that I may dwell
among them.'

33

REPORT ON CORRESPONlJ"P'.NCE

32

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

"Again in Exodus, 26th chapter, we find the instructions, 'And
shalt make loops of blue upon the edge of one curtain,' etc.
"In summing up the matter from these and from other references
not given above, it seems a natural sequence that the Lodges of Craft
Masons should be known as the 'Blue Lodge.' "
"ROMAN CATHOLIC MEMBERSHIP."

"The Grand Master of Texas decided that there was no law or
rule of Masonry prohibiting a member of the Fraternity from becoming a member of the Roman Catholic Church, so long as he is faithful to his Masonic obligations, but he doubts if it is possible to be
faithful to Masonic vows and be a good Catholic.
"It was held that Masonry does not attempt to dictate to any
member with reference to faith or creed. Masonry opposes ignorance,
tyranny, fanaticism and intolerance, regardless of what faith or creed
may foster it. \Ve require of our initiates a belief in the existence of
God, but do not deal with questions of sectarian nature. While it is
generally understood that the Roman Catholic Church forbids members uniting with any secret society not under Roman Catholic control, it is a matter which should address itself to the conscience of
every member, whether he can consistently maintain a membership in
both institutions."
M.". w:. APJ\LLE:s S. YoRK, Grand Master, Live Oak.
R.". W.'. \VlLBER P. WEBSTER, Grand Secretary, Jacksonville.

DECISIONS.
The Grand Master rendered a number of decisions within
the year, from which we quote the following:

"Query-A member of this Lodge has drifte~ into a life that is
very unbecoming and has almost gotten on the !me of a dead-beat;
will not pay his debts when he can; has been accused of embezzlement
in another territory, and is also accused of arson. His presence in o~r
Lodge is very repulsive to a majority of the membership, .and wh!le
we as yet are unable to make a specific charge of un-Masomc conduct,
a general 'charge can be made and all necessary evidence for conviction can be had.
"Answer-I am not sure whether the Masonic Code authorizes
charges in the case stated, but I am going to give the Grand Lodge the
opportunity of either making such a rule or else declaring that it cannot be done. Therefore, you are authorized to prefer charges on the
grounds that the man's reputatio!l in the c.ommunity is. su.ch that it reflects discredit upon the Fratermty and his membe~shtp 1s h'.lrmful to
the general interest of the Lodge on account of this reputation. The
Lodge would be authorized to fin.d ~im guilty <_in such c~arges as
stated in your letter and to expel him 1£ they see ht. 'vVe will at least
make a test case of it."
The Committee on Jurisprudence held, in the above instance,
if any Brother, by any overt act, or by continuous improper
practices, should bring reproach upon the Order of Freemasonry,
or if he should do anything contrary to the good of the Order,
he is subject to charges, trial and discipline; but where charges
were based solely upon rumor of disrepute, to permit charges
would tend to encourage slander and backbiting, themselves
offenses under the Code.
, )¥e quote again:
"The question that the result of a ballot when once declared cannot
be reconsidere'd is a well established fact in our jurisprudence. The
Edicts of the Grand Lodge have gone so far as to state that, although
a man throurrh blindness made a mistake in casting his ballot, it could
not be reco1;;,idered. So many appeals along this line have come to
me that I am convinced that certain modifications of this rule should be
made. 'Where a Lodge certifies to the Grand Master that they believe
an honest mistake has been made. I believe that the Grand Master
should be permitted to authorize a new ballot, which shall .be. final.
This wiJI in no wise affect the secrecy of the ballot. It will m no
wise inquire into the reason for ~h.e ?bjection.. I~ would often save
an honest applicant from the hum1hation of reiect1on, and !he L?dge
from the same humiliation in that they had, through an unmtent1onal
error, prevented the applicant from becoming a Mason."

Some exalted ideas are expressed by the Grand Master in the
opening paragraphs of his Address, as follows:
"Let us contemplate this glorious scenic landscape and d~aw from
it if we can a lesson that will upbuild the Craft whereby an important
step forward may be taken for the advancement of civilization. For
the untold centuries of time the snow that fell. upon the Tetons, together with snows that fell on other mountam ranges here about,
melted and the waters ran down to the great and beautiful Snake
River. The floods of each year carved deeper and 1eeper the bed of
the river until it formed a deep canyon, also along its course formed
numerous great and wonderful waterfalls as if nature bad run riot in

The 77th Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of A. F. & A. M. of Illinois was held in the City
of Chicago at the Oriental Consistory Building on the 10th, 11th
and 12th of October, 1916.
The Grand Lodge was opened in due course by Brother
Austin H. Scroggin, Right ·worshipful Deputy Grand Master.
ANNUAL ADDRESS OF GRAND MASTER.
Previous to reading his report, the Grand Master announced
that fifty out of fifty-one District Deputy Grand Masters were
present and that the entire membership of all of the committees of
the Grand Lodge, with the single exception of a brother who was
detained at home on account of serious illness in his family, were
present.
The Grand Master reported a year of unusual Masonic activity
and mentioned among the official acts of the Grand Lodge the
constitution of twelve Lodges which received charters at the preceding Annual Communication, the issuance of dispensations to
form eleven new Lodges; the dedication of six Masonic Temples,
and the placing of comer-stones of nine public buildings.
The Grand Master displayed a marked degree of zeal in the
matter of visitations, he having favored with his presence within
the year 103 :Masonic Lodges of the jurisdiction, not to mention
the many visits paid by him to clubs and many organizations
consisting entirely of Masons, and among these visitations were
not less than three Fiftieth Anniversary celebrations of subordinate Lodges.
DECISIONS.
Apparently the only decision touching Masonic law rendered
by the Grand Master within the year concerned a question which
was raised as to whether Lodges should carry life members on
their roll and pay Grand Lodge dues upon them when they had
not been heard of for more than seven years.
In the absence of anything in the Code upon · the question,
the Grand Master decided "that the Worshipful Master should
direct the Secretary of the Lodge to report the names of such
missing Brethren in the Grand Lodge returns as being 'legally
dead' and drop their names from the roll of active membership."
MASONIC HOMES.
From the report of the Board of Managers of the Masonic
Homes, it appears that the conditions in both of these institu-

39

The family at the Old People's Home is large and gradually
increasing. The Royal Arch Memorial Hospital, established about
two years ago, is filling a long-felt want, and provides the means
of caring for certain of the infirm among the elderly people,
whose needs before the establishment of the Memorial .Hospital
could not be properly taken care of.
MONITOR.
It seems that in this jurisdiction, the Monitor had been for a
great many years held under a copyright by a prominent Mason
of the jurisdiction, and latterly by his estate, and to remedy this
unusual and unsatisfactory condition, the Grand Lodge authorized
a new edition of the Monitor to contain a few slight changes
from the one previously held by copyright, and then provided
that the Grand Lodge itself should be the sole owner of the
Monitor, with the recommendation that each Lodge provide each
candidate upon his attaining the third degree a Monitor free
of charge. The complete new Monitor, as adopted, is set forth in
the Proceedings and differs in no essential particular from the
Monitor in use in California, and we presume in other jurisdictions.
NECROLOGY.
From the report of the Committee on Obituaries, we find
special mention made of the death within the year of Most
Worshipful \Villiam H. Scott, the Senior Past Grand Master of
the Jurisdiction.
Brother Scott was well known in California; he was a frequent
visitor to various Blue Lodges, and had been seen many times
in the Annual Communications of the Grand Lodge, he having
made California his home for many years preceding his death,
which occurred in San Francisco, and his remains were interred
in the military cemetery in the Presidio of San Francisco.
A PLEASANT INNOVATION.
In the second day of the Annual Communication, while the
Grand Lodge was at ease, the children of the Illinois Masonic
Orphans' Home were introduced to the Grand Lodge by the
Superintendent and Matron of the Home. The children rendered
a short programme and retired from the platform "amid the
tears and applause of the Brethren."

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

DECISION OF SUPREME COURT.
The Supreme Court of Illinois, Mr. Justice Dunn delivering
the opinion, in the case of Herbert Ashley representing the
Masonic Orphans' Home against the Board of Education, held
that the seventy-nine children between the ages of six: and fifteen
years, inmates of the Illinois Masonic Home, situated at La
Grange, Illinois, and within a certain school district within the
County, were entitled to all the privileges of the school; whereby
the effort to exclude these children from the schools of the
district, unless the Illinois Masonic Orphans' Home would pay
tuition for them in accordance with a resolution which had been
adopted by the Board of Education, was defeated; and the
children of the Home are thereby accorded the same privileges
of free tuition; etc., as are accorded to other children of the
district. Certainly a very righteous and proper decision; and
the only surprise caused in connection with this case is the
action of the Board of Education in attempting to exclude the
Home children except upon payment of tuition fees not exacted
from other children.

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
Preliminary to the formal opening of the Annual Communication, and in accordance with the custom in this jurisdiction, the
Grand Lodge assembled in the Auditorium of the Masonic Temple,
and listened to a program of welcome, consisting in this instance
of patriotic music, and an address by Brother Frank L. Loveland,
D.D., Pastor of the Meridian Street M. E. Church of Indianapolis.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Brother Loveland's Address was appropriate to the occasion,
being a blending of Masonry and Patriotism, whereiri he pointed
out the high duties incumbent upon Masons in this crisis in the
world's history, and wherein he indicated that Masonry forever
stands for certain things and stands forever against certain other
things.
Brother Loveland's Address was greatly appreciated by the
assembled Brethren, and was greeted at its close with prolonged
applause.
After the preliminary ceremonies, the Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of the Ancient and the Honorable Fraternity of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of Indiana, convened in 96th annual
meeting, the date of the opening being May 22nd, and the Communication was presided over by Most Worshipful Harry B.
Tuthill, Grand Master.
RECEPTION OF THE AMERICAN FLAG.
Immediately upon the declaration of the Grand Master that
the Grand Lodge was opened, there was an alarm at the door,
and it was announced that the American Flag "seeks admission."
The Grand Lodge was called up, and two flag bearers entered
the Grand Lodge, led by the Masonic Quartet singing the "Star
· Spangled Banner," the Colors were received by the Grand Master,
and placed upon the rostrum amid great enthusiasm.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
The place of honor in the Grand Master's Address is given
to the American Flag, to which he refers as follows:
"The American flag has been for years a mandatory article of
furniture in all regular and well governed Lodges within this Grand
Jurisdiction. Next to the three Great Lights, the American flag has
been· placed, not by order of the Grand Lodge alone, but by reason of
ou: universal love for our country, in the most honored place therein.
Without 01;der or direction from the Grand Lodge it is, scarcely without except10n, saluted by the Brethren as a part of the opening ceremony. This speaks volumes for our patriotism and for our common
love of country.
"May I not ask at this session the proper committee be authorized
and directed to prepare a salutatory service; that the national anthem
be included as a part thereof; with power vested in the incoming
Most Worshipful Grand Master to oromulgate the service as an executive order throughout the length a~d breadth of Indiana?"

OFFICIAL ACTIVITIES.
The year 1916 was Masonically one of the most active years
in the history of the Grand Lodge of Indiana. Four Lodges
which received their charters at the preceding Annual Communication were duly constituted, and dispensations were issued to
form four new Lodges.
Twenty-five public ceremonies of the placing of corner-stones
of public buildings took place within the year under Masonic
auspices, and besides these functions, the usual routine of official
duties were performed by the Grand Master.

PLEDGE OF SUPPORT TO THE PRESIDENT.
The Grand Lodge, at one of the sessions of the Annual Communication, passed unanimously, preceded by preambles of patriot·
ism, and amid enthusiasm, a Resolution, authorizing and directing
that a message be forwarded to the President of the United States
pledging the faith, loyalty and devotion of the 78,000 Masons of
Indiana to him and all constituted authorities of the United States.
This resolution, as stated, was unanimously adopted, and by a
rising vote, and a telegram to the President embodying tr.e resolution was forwarded, and in due course a telegraphic reply came
back from the President of the United States. thanking the Grand
Lodge for its patriotic resolution, and expressing the sense of
gratitude which he experienced in the assurances of support
from such a magnificent body of men.
GEORGE WASHINGTON NATIONAL MEMORIAL
ASSOCIATION.
This jurisdiction, in common with most of the American
jurisdictions, has fallen in line in cordial support of the George
Washington National Memorial Association, which contemplates
the building of a Memorial, befitting to the Father of his Country,
and one of America's most eminent Masons, at Alexandria, Va.,
and, incidentally, it may be stated that at the last meeting held in
February, 1917, the funds in hand aggregated, in round figures,
$75,000, with promise of a rapid increase within the next two
or three years. It may also be stated that the site for the proposed Memorial has already been selected, being a commanding
elevation in the City of Alexandria, which had originally been
fixed upon as the site for the Na ti on al Capitol, before it was
located across the Potomac in the City of Washington. Furthermore it is expected that within a year, plans will be accepted
for the proposed building.

The Stated Communication of the Grand Lodge of Ireland was
held in Dublin on St: John's Day, Dec. 22nd, 1916.
The Communication was opened and presided over by the Deputy
Grand Master, owing to the fact that the Grand
the Earl of
Donoughmore, was unable to be present, on account of his work in
connection with the Red Cross in France.
He, however, sent letters of cheer and encouragement to the
Deputy Grand Secretary, and also the Deputy Grand Master, in which
he referred particularly to the hope which he had expressed the year
before that the great war might terminate within the year, and while
this hope had not been
he had an abiding faith in the absolute
certainty of ultimate victory.
He calls attention to the fact that there is probably not a Lodge
of Freemasons in Ireland that had not sent representatives into the
great army that on the continent of Europe were fighting for human
freedom.
He expresses gratification at the progTess of Masonry in Ireland;
he calls attention to the fact that when he was initiated in the year
1858, there were only fifteen Lodges in the Citv of Dublin. while the
number of Lodges in that city at the present- time has ~eached the
splendid total of fifty-three.
REPORT OF DEPUTY GRAND SECRET ARY.
From the Deputy Grand Secretary's report, we learn that the
Jurisdiction had enjoyed a year of unusual growth and prosperity.
He refers at some length to the reeoent action of the Government
in introducing a bill in the House of Commons, withdrawing the permission previously enjoyed by the Royal Irish Constabulary and the
Dublin Metropolitan Police of joining the Masonic Order. The introduction of this bill caused a decided stir in the Masonic circles of
Ireland, and protests from various sources were addressed to influential members of Parliament expressing the earnest hope that the bill
would not pass, and the Grand Lodge itself unanimously adopted, on
Dec. 7th, 1916, the following Resolution upon the subject:
"That we, the members of the Grand Lodge of Freemasons of
Ireland, present at a meeting held in Dublin on the 7th day of December, 1916. having heard read a copy of the letter to the Right Hon.
H. E: Duke, K. C., M. P., Chief Secretary for Ireland, dated the 17th
day of November, 1916, and written by our Grand. Master, the Right

46

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Hon. the Earl of Donoughmore, emphatically endorse the protest
therein contained against the proposal to alter the existing law, and
thereby to prohibit the admission to our Order of members of the
D. M. Police and R'. I. Constabulary, and we solemnly declare that
the Masonic Order in Ireland is a benevolent, charitable, and social
society only; that it has no connection with any religious or political
body ; that it contains members of all shades of religious belief and
political opinion; and that both by its principles and in its practice
controversial subjects of a religious or political character are strictly
excluded from discussion at all meetings of the Order.
"That a copy of this Resolution be sent to the Righ Hon. the
Chief Secretary to the Lord Lieutenant."

MASONIC HOME.
The saddest chapter in the history of Masonry in Kansas is recorded in the cur.rent year in connection with the Masonic Home of
this Jurisdiction.

which Masonry fosters involves performance of the duties which
we owe to the public; it means a fraternity or community interest,
and a desire to know how the other half lives; a good citizenship
that stirs an instinctive spirit of fellowship; a desire to be our
brother's keeper and an impulse to take him by the hand and
help him over the hard places of life.

48

In the early morning of Dec. 22nd, 1916, the building was destroyed
by fire, which involved a loss of life of several of the residents and
at least one employee of the Home.
The Jurisdiction, with its accustomed vigor, immediately took
up the problems of the temporary care and comfort of the residents of the Home, and the matter of the permanent restoration
of the destroyed property, and the task of rehabilitation is going
forward rapidly in spite of the severe financial loss which the
Grand Lodge suffered.
The one great regret in connection with the destruction of the
Institution was the loss of life of four of the elderly residents of
the Home, and the faithful employee.
In connection with the sad affair, reference is made in the
report of the Secretary of the Home of the Grand Lodge to an
incident that is worthy of mention, which illustrates that in
moments of great disaster there is the "one touch of nature that
makes the whole world kin." The incident referred to is thus
spoken of by the Secretary in his report:
"I wish to pay high tribute to the citizenship of Wichita for the
magnanimous offers to assist, and in this no denomination nor creed
was known. One of the first offers of assistance came from the Sisters
of one of the Catholic institutions, located south and west of the
Home, in which they offered to care for at least twenty of our children. Later, this was supplemented by an offer from the Right Reverend John J. Hennessey, Bishop of the Diocese of Wichita, in which
he tendered assistance to the limitations of the various establishments
under his control. This proposal was later made to the Board in session, as you will doubtless remember, and thanks of the Board were
directed to be conveyed to him and to the good people of 'Wichita."
ORATION.
The Grand Lodge was greatly edified in one of the sessions
of the Annual Communication by the scholarly address ddivered
by Worshipful Brother William A. Johnson, Chief Justice of the
Supreme Court of Kansas, and a member of Lodge No. 143.
The oration was of a high, patriotic order, wherein the orator
pointed out that our Institution fosters civil and religious liberty,
and the patriotism which makes for good citizenship; and that it
is not all of patriotism to live decently, to break no law, and to
pay taxes, etc., that it means more than simply to keep out of the
penitentiary and the poorhouse, but that the good citizenship

The orator pointed out some of the great names in our
country's history associated with our Fraternity and indicated that
Masonry has been from the very foundation of our government,
one of the great factors in the up-lift which our country's influence has wrought in world affairs.
At the conclusion of the address, the thanks of the Grand
Lodge were extended to the Grand Orator, the oration was ordered
printed in the Proceedings and extra copies in pamphlet f ..)rm were
ordered for distribution among the Lodges.

"May I not say that a meeting of the Grand Masters of our own
land, and of the world if possible. might become a mighty influence
in the direction of universal peace? No thought or endeavor could
be more appropriate for such an assembly. Our Organization is itself
a plea for peace and an argument for peace. Freemasonry makes for
the dissemination of the spirit of brotherhood throughout the world,
and teaches us that peace and harmony are the strength and beauty of
all institutions. Freemasons need not dwell on the fact that seventenths of the income of our nation is expended for war and its equipment, and that in other lands the tax is even greater. As Freemasons
we cannot fail to deplore the barbarity of war, the awful sacrifice of
human life and human hope, not merely on the field of carnage or in
the hospitals of the world filled with groaning victims, but in the
widows and orphans left helpless, starving, dying, because their protectors are taken away. Surely it were well for us to consider this,
and to support every thought and movement calculated to secure the
peace of the world.
"All the Masoni"c Grand Bodies and individual Freemasons could
not engage in a wiser. more righteous, more human or more useful
endeavor than to try in every proper way, with all their power, to·
influence their particular governments to make treaties with all other
nations looking to the perpetuation of the peace of the world."

The Grand Master asserted that all fair-minded jurlges pronounce Freemasonry as our social mordant. "The student of
legislation, the observer of our domestic and social prosperity,
appear in the excellences of our educational systems. One and all
find everywhere the influence of national reverence for Freemasonry."
Further he calls attention to the fact that in its unobserved ·
workings, Freemasonry is the element that has broui;;ht out the
choice beauty of the best things of which we boast. "Largely to
it, are we indebted for juster laws, better schools, happier homes,
greater security of social order, than can be found in any other
land."
The Grand Master observes certain weaknesses inherent in
the rapidity of growth of the Fraternity, and, referring especially
to his own Grand Jurisdiction, he thinks it lacks the solidarity and
cohesiveness which gave th~ Fraternity strength in by-gone days.
In these later days, he thinks that we hear too much of the
"play ground of Freemasonry" and the "Flower garden of Freemasonry," catch phrases put forth frequently by well-meaning
Masons; but, in his opinion, Masonry has no "play ground" nor
"flower garden," but is a progressive moral science, with pro-

the offense would have to be proved in the Lodge and to its satisfaction, just as if the trial had not been had in the courts."

There are a great many Masons who fully agree with Grand
Master Purser's opinions upon these subjects.
Grand Master Purser is also opposed to the idea of large
Lodges, and believes that more effective Masonic work can be
accomplished through Lodges having a smaller number of members, but yet enough to carry forward the charitable and other
Lodge functions efficiently.
He advised the recognition of the Grand Orient of France
as a Sovereign Grand Body, but this recommendation was reported on adversely by the Committee on Forceign Correspondence,
simply because of a lack of ev'idence at this time concerning the
character of this Grand Orient, the recommendation of the Correspondence Committee not to be construed as prejudicial to the
future consideration of the matter when additional evidence is
presented.
RULINGS.
The Grand Master ruled upon a large number of questions of
a local nature, and all of the rulings were apparently in accord
with the law of the Jurisdiction, and all were approved by the
Committee on Jurisprudence and sustained by the Grand Lodge.
We refer to one ruling touching the weight to be given in a
Masonic trial to the verdict of a Court of Justice after trial for
the same offense; from which it would appear that Grand Master
Purser entertains serious doubts as to the accuracy of verdicts
in courts of justice, and believes that such verdicts, after all, are
not entitled to a great deal of weight in a Masonic trial.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

57

Mason.' Masonry means more than the assembling in our Lodges,
reciting our ritual and making the applicants into members. It means
the teaching of the truths of Holy Writ which treat of the Fatherhood
of God and the brotherhood of man. :.Jo man can be made a Mason
unless he profess belief in Deity, and no man can be a Mason unless
he recognizes his duty to his fellows and neighbors and discharges
that duty with honor to himself. We cannot escape the Fraternity
being judged by the lives of members, and should so live that in our
communities each 'may be known as one to whom the burdened heart
may pour out its sorrows, to whom distress may prefer its suit, whose
hand is guided by justice and whose heart is expanded by benevolence.'"
MISUSE OF THE "WHITE" BALL.
We read a great deal; and hear a great deal, about the misuse
of the black ball, but the Grand Master Bodge calls attention to what
is possibly even a greater menace to our Institution than the misuse
of the black ball, in that sufficient care is not exercised in the use of
the high prerogative whereby unworthy material is often admitted to
our ranks because of lack of moral courage in refusing to use the
black ball when it should be used.
We quote upon this subject as follows:
"The matter of the black ball still holds its usual prominent place
in the correspondence. While it is doubtless true that it is occasionally
used by members in an unworthy manner, I am frank to state, Brethren,
I am more afraid of the misuse of the white than of the black ball.
"We are all human and most of us reasonably charitable, and I
think we more often err in admitting those who are not suitably qualified than in rejecting those who should be accepted; and when the
reverse occurs it is generally evidence someone was permitted to enter
who should have been refused admittance. But for that we cannot
reasonably argue that the black ball is wrongfully used. I wish moral
defects might be as clearly defined as physical imperfections and legislated against as strictly; but there is a wide latitude granted the Craft,
and each member is to determine from his own knowledge, observation or information what shall be his conclusion and consequent action.
\Vhile we teach it is the internal and not the external qualifications
that govern, there is no denying social prominence and financial success, inherited or acquired, have their influence.
"If the black ball is used with discrimination it is not likely any
will be admitted who will later use it viciously. In nearly every case
where a member is strongly suspected of interfering with the w'ork,
will be expressed the sentiment 'he should never have been admitted.'
Think this over, Brethren, and when you ballot bear in mind the reputation and harmony of your Lodge and Masonry arc at stake as well
as the good and pleasure of the petitioner.''

CHARITY FUND OF THE GRAND LODGE OF MASONS.
The State of Maine, Masonically speaking, is one of the comparatively few large Jurisdictions in the United States that has not a
Masonic Home. Its obligations of relief and charity, however, are
capably discharged through its Charity Fund, administered hy a capable
Board of Trustees.
This. Fund is applicable to the following cases, and the classification, it will be noticed, presents a rather comprehensive system of
relief. Following is the classification:
First, to poor and worthy members of Lodges under this Jurisdiction, in cases where the funds of their own Lodges are not adequate
to the exigeucy of the case.
S ecoiidly, to poor and worthy Masons resident in this State, not
members of any Subordinate Lodge, and being in circumstances to
ren~er such membership not a Masonic duty.
Thirdly, to poor and worthy Masons being sojourners in this State.
Fo11rthly, to other cases of distress.

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Most Worshipful York Grand Lodge of Mexico, Free and
Accepted Masons of the Republic of Mexico, held its Fifty-seventh
Annual Communication in Masonic Hall, April 5th, 1917, the Most
Worshipful Wayne A. White, Grand Master, presiding.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
The Grand Master in his Address refers to the unsettled conditions prevailing in the Republic, which conditions have affected Masonry, as well as everything else.
He states, however, that all of the Lodges have been able to keep
open, and the four larger ones have been doing the usual amount of
work.
He refers to personal ill-health, which prevented his getting out
of the City of Mexico, in consequence of which ·he was unable to visit
the outside Lodges.
FRATERNAL RELATIONS.
The Grand Master refers to the relations of the Grand Lodge with
foreign Grand Jurisdictions as being most cordial; and he furnishes
a list of Grand Jurisdictions throughout the world that have recognized the Grand Lodge of Mexico, recognition having been extended
by twenty-nine Grand Lodges of the United States, and not less than
fifteen other Grand Lodges throughout the world, whereby it would
appear that the York Grand Lodge of Mexico had attained a very
substantial stamp of approval as a legitimate Grand Lodge.
REPORT OF GRAND SECR:ET ARY.
From the report of the Grand Secretary, concerning the condition
of .:V!asonry in the jurisdiction, it appears that the membership of one
Lodge remained stationary during the preceding year, four Lodges
showed a total increase of thirty members, ten Lodges showed a total
decrease of fifty-three members, leaving a net decrease of twenty-three
members, which ought not to be considered discouraging in view of
the difficult conditions under which the jurisdiction has labored.
The retiring Grand Master, Wayne A. White, was elected Grand
Secretary, and Brother \Vhite presents a condensed report on Foreign
Correspondence, being a review of a limited number of jurisdictions.
California is not in the list.
M:. W.'. STEPHEN MOTTA, Grand Master, Mexico City.
M.'. w:. WAYNE A. WHITE, Grand Secretary, Mexico City.

Grand Master Hawks sets forth very briefly the affairs of his
office during the year; he comments on the awful calamity of the war
m Europe and its relation to Masonry, and says :

"Jr:; this national eris.is, Masonry must not and will not play the
cowa_rd .s part. The meanmg of the word 'fraternity' will be intensified,
and it. is patent today as. never before that the world needs the conserva~1s~ and. steady1pg mfluence ~f Freemasonry. It appears to me
that 1t is the 1mperat1ve duty of this Grand Body to think soberly to
;eason acc~rat~ly, :;md to be ready at

greatest. No one can tell
what the commg year will bring forth, but God grant that we, as
brotI:ers, .shall stand .sho~ld~r to shoulder in the defense of our country, its liberty and its Justice. May prudence and fortitude be our
watchword as we move forward in our attempt to further the interests

62

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

of civilization God grant that the teachings of our Order may become
the working tools of our everyday life and not a mere veneer to be
cast off in the heat of passion or in the throes of a great national
crisis. Let us rededicate our illustrious Order to the human virtues
of Friendship, Morality and Brotherly Love. Without hate we will
stand true to the colors made glorious by the sacrifice of our fathers."
The Grand Master speaks feelingly of the Brethren who have
answered the summons of the Supreme Grand Master since the last
Annual Communication, and makes mention of the fact that since the
incumbency of Michigan's first Grand Master, Lewis Cass, down to

ORATION.
A stirring and eloquent Address was delivered at one of the

of the Grand Lodge and his oration is published in full in the Proceedings.
MASONIC HOME.
Perhaps the most interesting feature of this Annual Communication was the discussions and actions centered about the Masonic
Home proposition.
Some years ago, this jurisdiction committed itself to the establishment of a Masonic Home, but provided that the actual construction of the Home should be deferred until a fund of $100,000 had been
accumulated as a foundation. A year ago, the fund thus accumulated
amounted· to about $75,000, and the present Grand Master, Brother
Alfred G. Pinkham, determined, if possible, to bring this fund, during
his incumbency of the Grand East, to the minimum of $100,000 required, before the actual work of construction should commence, and
throughout the year of his administration he devoted strenuous efforts
to the completion of the task, adding within the year to the $75,000
already in hand at the beginning, something like $10,000, and at this
Annual Communication, through the enthusiasm awakened for the
cause, additional subscriptions, which were asked for at the conclusion
of the report of the committee upon the subject, were made in a few
moments to the extent of $17,200, which more than covered the amount
needed, and as a result the project has now been definitely entered upon,
and, by resolution, duly adopted. the Trustees of the Minnesota Masonic Home were authorized, empowered and directed to proceed
forthwith to acquire a suitable site for a Home, to adopt plans for the
required buildings, and to go ahead speedily with the construction of
the same.
The Grand Lodge also, by unanimous vote, extended its· sincere
thanks to the Grand Master, for his constant and persistent work for
the benefit of all of the Masons of the Grand Jurisdiction in his untiring efforts in behalf of the Home.

THE NINETY-NINTH ANNCAL COMMCNICATION.
The Ninety-ninth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge,
Free and Accepted Masons, was held in the City of Jackson, Feb.
13th and 14th, 1917.
Previous to the opening of the Grand Lodge, a public reception
was tendered to the Grand Body by a large number of Brethren and
citizens of Jackson in the Century Theater, an elaborate program of
addresses and music being carried out to the delight and edification
of the· Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master in the remarks made by him in connection
with the ceremonies referred to the war in Europe, and stated that
not a silligle crowned head in all of the belligerent countries belonged
to the Masonic Order, and he stated that he had no doubt the war
would never had taken place if the kings and rulers of war-stricken
Europe had taken the vows and obligations of Masonry.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
At the conclusion of the public reception, the Grand Lodge wrts
opened in Ample Form, Most \Vorshipfol George B. Power, Grand
Master, presiding.
In the opening paragraphs of his Annual Address, he enumerated
a number of the illustrious men in the long line of Grand Masters who
had seryed before him as rulers of the Grand Lodge of Mississippi in
the ninety-nine years of its existence, some of the names being household words throughout the length and breadth of our broad land.

UNNECESSARY LODGES.
The Grand Master refers to the tendency, which has existed in
years gone by, to create Lodges unnecessarily, and under conditions

that contained no promise of their becoming vigorous, self-sustaining
