THE NINETY-SIXTH ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Ninety-sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons of Missouri, was convened at
Scottish Rite Cathedral, St. Louis, Sept. 19th, 1916, the Most Worshipful Frank R. Jesse, presiding.
Preliminary to the formal opening of the Grand Lodge, the justly
celebrated Moolah· Orchestra, composed of musicians, members of the
Shrine, in conjunction with the children of the Masonic Home, rendered a program of instrumental and vocal music for the entertainment
of the Grand Body, which program was highly appreciated, as expr.essed by the Grand Master in appropriate words of thanks rendered
at the conclusion of the program.
ADDRESS OF THE GRAND MASTER.
In the opening paragraphs of his Annual Address, the Grand
Master refers to the great war in progress in Europe, and gives expression to a sense of gratitude that our country was not involved
in the world struggle.
This condition is, regrettably, not true at the present time, but
America has never in her history evaded any responsibility which has
been thrust upon her, and has not refused now to take her place by the
side of those who are battling, as we believe, for the rights of humanity and liberty, and for the vindication of the principle of selfgovernment.
Grand Master Jesse expresses his belief that Freemasonry has
always been at the front of every movement which has for its purpose
the amelioration of the condition of mankind, affirming that it has
always stood strong and unfaltering for the right, amid the throes
and turmoil of contending factions, affirming that it has defied bigotry
and superstition in the middle ages, and that it has taken part, with
its influence, in all of the conflicts for right in the world's history;
that it has ever been the defender of justice and the protector of the
defenseless ; that it has been the guardian of the weak ; the friend of
education and the foe of ignorance; that it has been a bulwark of

68

REPORT ON CORRESPONDmNcm.

freedom, a comfort to the oppressed, and a relief to the distressed,
the widow and the fatherless, and he closes his eloquent tribute to
Masonry with the declaration "that it has withstood the acid test of
time, the horrors of war and the wreck of empire, and stands today
unchanged and changeless; faithful among the faithless; firm among
the faltering; steadfast in its purpose; supreme in its integrity; grand,
glorious, and eternal in its devotion to mankind."
MASONIC HOME.
The Grand Master refers with justifiable pride to the Masonic
Home of Missouri.
We quote his words concerning this great Masonic charity:
"Out on Delmar avenue in this city the Freemasons of Missouri
have erected a monument to that Masonic virtue which, 'next to a
belief in Deity, lies at the foundation of Freemasonry'; it is the
Masonic Home. In this splendid building and equipment we have a
concrete manifestation of that truly Masonic virtue, charity, without
which our beloved Institution could have never survived the shock
of the ages. The very genius of Freemasonry is Love, the spirit of
which not only unites its member5 in an unbroken phalanx as a band
of brothers, but overflows those bounds and expands into a stream
of Charity for all mankind."
DECISIONS.
The following are quoted from the decisions of the Grand Master,
as containing perhaps information that may be generally interesting:

"Question-An expelled Mason petitions for reinstatement, receives a two-thirds vote and is granted a certificate of good standing.
Does this entitle him to any other Masonic privilege than to petition
for membership? If so, what? Also, may he petition any Lodge in
the State for membership, or can he petition only the Lodge which
expelled him and which also .issued the certificate of good standing?
"Answer-Upon the case stated the party is not entitled to any
privilege other than to petition for membership. He may petition any
Lodge in this State if he has been a resident of this State for one year.
He is not required to petition only the Lodge which expelled him."
"Question-A brother is made a Master Mason in a Lodge in
Illinois which does not require an examination as to his proficiency
in the third degree. On demit from his Lodge in Illinois he is elected
to membership in a Lodge in Missouri and is elected an officer therein.
Will he have to stand an examination as to his proficiency in the third
degree before he can be installed?
"Answer-No. The Masonic status of a brother is fixed by the
law of the jurisdiction wherein he was made a Mason. Our law requiring an examination as to proficiency in the third degree, and imposing penalties for failure to do so, only applies to Master Masons
raised in this jurisdiction."

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

69

"Question-Is one who is engaged in the manufacture of Weiss
beer containing two per cent alcohol eligible to petition for the degrees? Weiss beer is not considered an intoxicating liquor.
"Answer-No. Ten drinks of beer containing two per cent of alcohol is just as intoxicating as one drink of whisky containing twenty
per cent of alcohol, and makes you feel a great deal worse."
This decision might be defended, perhaps, upon the general principle of homeopathy,. that the higher the trituration, the higher the
power.
Of course, the ordinary mortal may fail to comprehend this process
and, in accordance with the same principles, a tankful of liquor, if the
human system were capable of absorbing it, might be intoxicating as
a glassful, with the same absolute quality of alcohol. condensed into
1.he smaller portion; and we would imagine that if a beverage containing not more than two per cent of alcohol is intoxicating, that
ordinary tea and coffee are equally as stimulating, and the habitual
user thereof ought to be as ineligible for the degrees of Masonry as
the one who partakes of the concoction declared illegal in the above
decision of the Grand Master.
MISCELLANEOUS.
The traveling silver trowel that we had almost lost track of, turns
up, so it appears from the report of Grand· Master Jessee, in Illinois,
for he speaks of a visit to Stephen Decatur Lodge No. 979 at Decatur,
Ill., held in honor of the Traveling Silver Trowel. This emblem and
symbol of Masonry, started on its journey several years ago by one
of the New York Lodges, will need to "speed up" or it will take an
eternity in getting around the world, and back home.
The Grand Master reports an interesting visit made by him to
Alexandria, Va., on Feb. 22nd, to the Washington Masonic Memorial
Association. This enterprise is receiving an increasing volume of support, but a number of years, we imagine, will need to elapse before
the enterprise is placed upon the substantial financial basis that will
enable it to go ahead with the construction of the proposed memorial
building.
ORATION.
The Annual Oration was delivered by the Grand Orator, Right
Worshipful George F. Rixey, in which he traces the origin and teachings of Freemasonry, asserting that the Institution exists today because
it is s·ought after, and has endeavored to teach the truth only; that
it has been free of sectarian bias; free of fraud and ostentation,
and that its practice and tenets have been addressed toward the uplift
of humanity; that it teaches self-control and charity in the best and
broadest sense; that it proclaims the universal Fatherhood of God and
the houndless Brotherhood of Man.

Born amidst the turmoil and strife incident to the influx into the Territory of men in the search of wealth, to be obtained lawfully by some,
and unlawfully by others; and when we revert to the beginning of this

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Grand Lodge of the Most Ancient and Honorable Society
of Free and Accepted Masons of Nebraska met in Annual Communication in Freemasons' Hall, Omaha, on June 6, 1916, Most
Worshipful Samuel S. Whiting, Grand Master, presiding.

73

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
_The subject which receives the position of honor in the Grand
Master's Address is the Nebraska Masonic Home, several pages
of the Address being devoted to consideration of this beneficent
institution. He is glad to observe that the Masonic Home is on
a firm foundation, the Brethren manifesting a marked willingness
to contribute to the maintenance of the institution. The trustees, he observes, have no complaint to make touching the liberality of the Grand Lodge in supplying funds, and the only reward
the trustees desire is the appreciation and the good will of the
Brethren.
In addition to the regular Masonic Home, there has been, in
accordance with instructions .issued by the Grand Lodge a year
ago, erected at Fremont, a substantial cottage for girls, and he
announces that there are now thirteen children at the Home at·
Fremont, in addition to a number of boys still at the Home .at
Plattsmouth. Nebraska has seen the wisdom, as did California,
of separating the beneficiaries of our Masonic Homes, placing
the elderly people in one Home, and children in a separate institution.

Dispensations were granted to form two new Lodges within

Public ceremonies of placing comer-stones of public buildings

of visitations to Subordinate Lodges were made by the Grand

favored.

ORATION.
At the evening session of the first day of the Annual Communication, the Oration was delivered by Worshipful Brother Charles
L. Richards, Grand Orator. The Grand Orator's address consisted
of an exposition of Masonic principles. He pointed out the fact
that there is no conflict between Christianity and Freemasonry,
but rather a co-operation between the two.
He shows clearly that Masonry stands for true and genuine
charity, for enlarging the facilities for the care of the unfortunate,
and that Masonry, by her acts, shows that we are living in an
age of deeds as well as words, whereby the Brotherhood of Man
means more today than it has ever meant before, which permits
us to cherish the belief that the day of hatred and distrust is
passing away, to be succeeded by an era of generosity, unselfishness and kindness.
At the conclusion of the Oration, the Past Grand Master,
John A. Ehrhardt, moved, and it was voted and carried unanimously, that the thanks of the Grand Lodge be tendered to the Orator,
and that the Address be published with the Proceedings.
PROMOTION· OF WORLD'S PEACE.
In accordance with the fashion of 1916 among Masonic Grand
Lodges, there was the appointment, at this Communication, and in
due . course, the report of the Committee on Promotion of the
World's Peace. There was an idea prevalent about a year ago
that the promotion of the world's peace might be brought about
possibly by the adoption of Resolutions of Fraternal Organizations and the issuance of polished rhetoric from authoritative
sources, urging upon the warring nations of Europe that the only
sure pathway to tranquillity was "peace without victory," and
Nebraska was no exception to the rule, in that a committee of this
character was duly appointed, but developments in the world's
history within the last twelve months has demonstrated that the
only way to secure peace, and peace with the triumph of the
principles of liberty and freedom, is to fight for it; and not only tb
fight, but to fight until peace with victory is attained and military
despotism is eternally destroyed.

The Fifty-second Annual Grand Communication of the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge of Nevada was held at the Masonic Temple, in the City of Reno, commencing Tuesday, June 13th, 1916,
Grand Master Benjamin \V. Coleman presiding.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
The Grand Master made a business-like statement of his official activities within the year, stating there were no matters of
great importance demanding his consideration.
He states that while many from the -constituent Lodges have
been called to their reward, the members of the Grand Lodge
have been spared.
OFFICIAL ACTIVITIES WITHIN THE YEAR.
The Grand Master made a large number of visitations during
the year to Subordinate Lodges.
At the last Annual Communication, a resolution was passed
to appoint a Master of Instruction, and the Grand Master made
such appointment. The work of the Master of Instruction is to
hold schools of instructions in several places in the jurisdiction,
saving the expense of having the Master of Instruction, Brother
Past Grand Master.David, visit every Lodge in the jurisdiction.
Grand Master Coleman did not find it necessary to render
any decision on Masonic law; he issued dispensation to form one
new Lodge; he received an invitation to attend the Washington
Masonic National Memorial Association, held at Alexandria, Va.,
but was unable to attend, and appointed Brother William H. Sands
to represent him; he recommended a Masonic Magazine to be
published by a Supreme Grand
of Free and Accepted
Masons.

"May the spirit of this great Fraternity so permeate our o~~ation

NEW BRUNSWICK.

49th Annual, St. John, April 25-26.
Lodges, 39; Membership, 3768; Increase, 101..

THE FORTY-NINTH ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Forty-ninth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of the Ancient and Honorable Fraternity of Free and Accepted
Masons of New Brunswick, was held at Freemasons' Hall in the
City of St. John on Tuesday, the 25th day of April, 1916, the Most
Worshipful Hedley V. B. Bridges, LL. D., presiding.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
The thought uppermost in the minds of all of the Canadian
Jurisdictions is the great war in which the British Empire is
involved, and this thought is emphasized in the opening paragraphs
of Grand Master Bridges' Address.
He states that it has been estimated that Canadian Masons
to the number of ten thousand have already enlisted for foreign
service, and that many Brethren of the Craft have laid down their
lives in defense of liberty and freedom.
He refers with pleasure to the increase in membership within
the year, but takes greater pleasure in the knowledge that Masonry
is capably fulfilling her mission and discharging her duties within
the Province.
He refers feelingly to the Brethren who have been called to
their reward within the year, giving especial honor to those after
whose names are written the words "killed in action."
His official visitations within the year included practically
every Lodge in the jurisdiction. He accords special praise to the
District Deputies, whose activities have been highly commendable,
thereby showing themselves to be strong and efficient officers in
discharge of their duties.
In closing his excellent Address, he refers with pride to the
progress made by Freemasonry in the Province in the last fifty
years, noting particularly the increase within the last few years
of the element of enthusiasm, whereby a higher standard has been
created, to the end that the outlook for the future of the Craft
is exceedingly bright. He affirms his belief that Masonry is an
organization of strong and sturdy men, who are striving, according

80

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

to their best light, "to act upon the square, to uphold the leaven
of truth, and to walk uprightly before God and man."
As he comprehends Masonry, it impresses itself with especial
force in these times of war and stress and tragedy that it is a liie
of duty and service, and he feels that each individual Mason is
learning the lesson, as the Great Empire, to which the Province
belongs, is learning the lesson, that through pain and peril,
through distress and danger, through want and suffering, that
war is the curse of the ages; that peace is a divine boon; that
selfishness is almost the supreme evil, and that it is "more blessed
to give than to receive."

NEW MEXICO.
1916.

39th Annual, East Las Vegas, Oct. 9-10-11.
Lodges, 45; Membership, 3737; Gain, 173.
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Thirty-ninth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons of New Mexico was held
in the hall of Chapman Lodge No. 2, i~ the City of East Las
Vegas, beginning Oct. 9, 1916, the Most ·worshipful Amos W.
Pollard, Grand ::\faster, presiding.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
The Grand Master's high conception of Masonry is set forth
in the opening paragraphs of his Address, from which we quote
as follow~:
"Masonry is vastly important to us as it is our inspiration, our
philosophy and our religious guidance; to some of us it is our religion,
if it may be so termed.
"Masonry has always been a potent influence for good in every
community, a builder of character and of good citizenship, ever subservient and obedient to the laws of the state and never waivering in its
allegiance. It is a leveler· of persons in every rank and state of life,
recognizing every Mason as a brother and an equal. Our lives are but
passing events in the world, pawns in the game of life, living entities
today and gone tomorrow, but Masonry will continue in its present
high plane so long as this world shall survive. The whole world may
be at war and nations and empires crumble and fall, but the ravages
of warfare will not affect the principles upon which Masonry is founded
and it will rise up from the ashes of such devastation and ruin unsullied
and unchanged.
"Is it not an honor to be enrolled a member of an institution that
stands for right living, correct thinking, a high standard of morality,
with tolerance for the belief of every man, with charity for all mankind?
"It is the inspiring and elevating things in Masonry that have drawn·
us together today as one band of fellows, and not the legislative or
social functions of this meeting. So in our deliberations let us not
forget the beautiful tenets of our institution, ever remembering to encompass them with legislation that will reflect credit and honor upon
us as Masons."
DECISIONS.
As evidence that the ever-present question of the status of a
Mason in arrears for dues is troublesome in New Mexico, as well
as in other jurisdictions, the following is quoted from the "decisions" of Grand Master Pollard:

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

85

Question-Is a member of any Lodge in: good standing if he has
allowed his dues to become delinquent one or more years, taking into
consideration the fact that the said member has not been suspended,
that his dues have not been remitted and that the Lodge is paying his
per capita tax to the Grand Lodge? When does a member cease to be
in good standing?
"Held-The good standing of a member of a Lodge is affected
solely by suspension or expulsion. Non-payment of dues is not of itself
a Masonic offense. A member ceases to be in good standing only upon
conviction after due trial."
This apparently passed the Jurisprudence Committee, but can
hardly be the law, even in New Mexico.
ACTIVITIES OF THE GRAND MASTER.
That every Lodge in the jurisdiction might receive the benefit
of an official visitation from either the Grand Master or one of
the other elective Grand Officers, he divided the Lodges of the
jurisdiction into four groups, allowing one group to each of the
principal Grand Officers, and in this manner every Lodge in the
jurisdiction received an official visitation from one of the high
officials, and a number of the Lodges were favored by visitations
from more than one of the Grand Officers.
The recommendation of the Grand ~faster that this method
of division be adopted as a permanent regulation of the jurisdiction, however, was not adopted, the presumption being that this
feature of the Masonic work ought properly be left to the judgment and discretion of future Grand Masters from year to year.
Numerous dispensations for various purposes were issued by
the Grand Master, and extensive correspondence between the Grand
Master of New Mexico and the Grand Masters of other jurisdictions over controverted points is set forth in the Grand Master's
Address, a spirit of fraternity and good will characterizing the
exchanges of letters between the ruling officials of the different
jurisdictions.
ANTI-LIQUOR LEGISLATION.
Legislation was adopted whereby not only are those who are
engaged in the retail liquor business rendered ineligible to membership, but those already members of the Fraternity who, after
becoming members, engage in this business are rendered liable
to expulsion from the Fraternity, which legislation is along the
lines of the provisions of our California law, and in harmony with
the general trend of Masonic legislation throughout the United
States.

He reviews in a painstaking manner the various Grand Jurisdic-

tions, giving courteous consideration to California, 1915. In his
report on California, he states that the Grand Orient of Italy was

for recognition from the Grand Lodge of California.
Our personal opinion upon the subject as to whether or not
the Grand Orient of Italy, entirely aside from the question of her
invasion of the territory of other Grand Lodges, is entitled to
recognition as a Sovereign Grand Lodge of Ancient Craft Masonry
may be of slight impurtance, but, in our opinion, even if the question of the invasion had not been charged against her, the Grand
Orient of Italy is not entitled to recognition as a Sovereign Grand
Lodge of Ancient Craft Masons, for other good and sufficient
reasons.

GRAND LODGE COMMUNICATIONS.
The Volume of Proceedings under consideration embraces the
reports of the various Quarterly Communications from Sept.· 8,
1915, up to and including the Quarterly of June 14, 1916. which is
also the Annual Communication.
In the Volume are also recorded the Proceedings of the
Special Communications of June 13, 1916, and July 7, 1916, at
which time the Investiture of Grand Lodge Officers for the ensuing Masonic year took place.
The various Communications were presided over by the Most
"Worshipful Grand ~faster, Brother \Villiam Thompson, who was

87

at the Quarterly Communication of June, 1916, re-elected to succeed himself as Grand Master for the third term.
The outstanding feature of all of the Communications throughout the year concerns the great war in which the British Empire
is engaged, and the highest memorials contained in the book are
the various "Rolls of Honor" printed in connection with each
Quarterly Communication, being lists of Brethren, active members of the various Subordinate Lodges, who have enlisted with
the Australian Expeditionary Forces, and the lists of those reported "killed at the Dardanelles," and elsewhere. The individual
names listed in these "Rolls of Honor" aggregate several thousand, and indicate that probably from ten per cent to fifteen per
cent of the Masons of this Jurisdiction have enlisted in the cause
of liberty against military domination and oppression.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
At each of the Quarterly Communications, the Grand Master
delivered an Address, setting forth official actions, from which it
appears that the year was an active period for the Grand Lodge,
in which several new Lodges were constituted, and dispensations
issued to form other new Lodges, and that, notwithstanding the
great war, this Jurisdiction shows a degree of growth and prosperity greater than any year, perhapS, in the history of the Grand
Body.
In one of his Addresses, the Grand Master refers feelingly to
the death of one of the eminent English Masons in the person of
Lord Kitchener, who was Grand Warden of England in 1897,
District Grand Master of Egypt and the Soudan in 1889, and District Grand Master of the Punjaub in 1902.
The Grand Master refers to Lord Kitchener's famous message
to his soldiers, which breathed the true spirit of Freemasonry, and
to his untiring efforts in promoting amongst the soldiers the great
principles of temperance. sobriety and morality. It afforded evidence that he ever had before him the high ideals of our glorious
Institution.
The Grand Master refers to Lord Kitchener's visit to Sydney,
some six years ago, and states that the Craft will ever treasure
the memory of that great occasion.

OFFICIAL ACTIVITIES.
As is usual in this great Jurisdiction, the one who presides
as Grand Master is called upon to devote practically his entire
time to the duties of his exalted station.
In his Report, the Grand Master enumerates a long list of
his activities, and of the many "ceremonies" conducted by him
within the year; possibly greatest prominence being given to the
official visitation on June 25th to the Masonic Home at Utica. On
this occasion, the Grand Master was accompanied by his staff of
Grand Officers, and probably more than one hundred distinguished
Masons from' various parts of the Jurisdiction.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Another notable visitation made by the Grand Master was to
the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania at
Philadelphia on Dec. 29th, 1916, upon which occasion he was
accompanied by a large number of his associate Grand Officers.
Dispensations were granted for the establishment of six new
Lodges.
MASONIC HOME.
Concerning the great Masonic charity of the Jurisdiction, that
is, the Home at Utica, the Grand Master refers to it as a splendid
monument of the Fraternity, expressing in concrete form the great
heart and generous instincts of the Craft.
This institution gathers within its sheltering arms probably
the largest number of beneficiaries of any institution of its kind
in the world. The membership of the institution at this date consists of 171 men, 117 women, 83 boys, and 67 girls, a total of 438,
who are receiving the benefits of this wonderful Masonic charity.
The investment in the Home, and the properties sustaining
the Home, amount of several million dollars, and the annual disbursement for the care of its beneficiaries runs into hundreds of
thousands of dollars.
PATRIOTIC DEMONSTRATION.
At one of the sessions of the Annual Communication, patriotic demonstrations took place in which the Masons of New York
pledged themselves to the support of the government in this
crisis in the world's affairs; and the following resolution, expressive of these sentiments, was unanimously adopted:

"Resolved, That we, the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of New York, in annual communication assembled,
pledge to the government of the United States our unswerving support,
and to our country our best efforts, our fortunes, and our lives, to the
end that victory may crown our arms, and government of the people, by
the people, for the people, may not perish from the earth."
After the adoption of the above resolution, Brother Theodore
Roosevelt, a member of the Fraternity, former President of the
United States, was introduced to the Grand Lodge, and favored
the Grand Body with a stirring and thoroughly American address,
from which we quote two brief paragraphs as follows:

"It was a fine thing for the Grand Lodge as its first work to pass
this resolution that I have in my hand. I congratuate you, Brothers
and Master. It is a fine thing to have laid down so clearly the principles ~or which we are fighting no:w. the principles of freedom and justice,
the liberty of all peoples, the nght of small nations to govern themselves free from aggression, the duty of this great democracy to try
to support the common policy of the free peoples as they have against
the governments which deny freedom to their peoples.

"Now I for one-and one of the odd amenities of our political life
has heen th~t some of the same gentlemen who have been most active
in preventing us from organizing in our own defense, and who have been
able to remain in safety behind the shield of the British flag, have
passed their time in making faces at Great Britain. But l am not content
to owe my safety or owe the safety of this nation to the British flag
or any other flag or any other army than our own. I want to see
Uncle Sam able to help his neighbors, when they do right, and to defend himself from them if they go wrong. And T want to see us take
steps that will make ns a factor for the peace of righteousness throughout the globe."
The address of the former President of the United States was
listened to with rapt attention, and was followed, at its conclusion, with a whirlwind of prolonged applause.
The Grand Lodge was also visited at this time by Hon. vVilliam Renwick Ridell, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Ontario; and Brother Ridell was, at the conclusion of the address· of
Brother Roosevelt, introduced, and he, too, made a stirring and
patriotic appeal.
Brother Ridell was followed by Brother Louis A. Watres,

FOREIGN CORRESPONDENCE.
The report on Foreign Correspondence is from the usual committee, of which Most Worshipful Brother William Sherer is
Chairman.
As being of general interest, the following is quoted from the
"Introduction" of his report:
"At this time your Committee feels that it would not be out of
place to call attention to the high stand taken by the Brethren two
hundred years ago. It is just two hundred years since, on St. John
Baptist's Day, June 24th, 1717, an assembly was held at the Goose and
Gridiron Alehouse in London and 'with the oldest Master Mason
(now the Master of a Lodge) in the chair,' elected and installed Anthony Sayer Grand Master and formed the Grand Lodge of England.

*

*

*

"Ancient Charges and ceremonies, called from many sources, were
compared, digested and adapted to modern conditions and a Constitution and Charges were formulated which enunciated the highest ethical
platform of that time. For the age was decadent. The Grand Lodge
was formed at a time when individual and social morality was known
only to be scoffed at. Religion seemed dead and worship a farce. The
bigotry and intolerance of a cold and formal Church-in which a few

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

devout worshippers only served to mark the drunken ignorance of
many of its ministers and the lewd degeneracy of the mass of its
adherents-were matched on the other hand by a fierce dogmatism
and a narrow and cold religion which spent itself in cruel hatred of
all men rather than in pious love of any. Men and women alike were
utterly worldly, society utterly base and degenerate.
"It was in such a time that Freemasonry received an organized form
which, in its first general statement of belief, purpose and command, expressed itself as follows: 'A Mason is obliged by his Tenure to obey
the moral law; and if he rightly understands the Art he will never be a
stupid Atheist nor an irreligious Libertine. But though in ancient times
Masons were charged in every country to be of the religion of that
country or nation, whatever it was, yet it is now thought more expedient only to oblige them to that religion in which all men agree, leaving their particular opinions to themselves : that is, to be Good Men and
True, or Men of Honor and Honesty, by whatever Denomination or
Persuasion they may be distinguished; whereby Masonry becomes the
Centre of Union and the Means of conciliating true Friendship among
persons that must have remained at a perpetual distance.'
"This statement may verily be called the Magna Charta of our Fraternity. It is not surprising that at a time of bitter intolerance in politic3 and religion, this great Masonic platform of Morality, Toleration
and Good Will challenged the sympathetic attention of good men everywhere. In this spirit of tolerant morality Freemasonry 'has spread its
beneficent influence wider and wider over the earth.' In all lands and
among all peoples Freemasonry has been found on the side of individual, social and political righteousness, it has stood against wickedness
among the high and the lowly, it has spread the light of social and political truth, it has proclaimed a high code of ethics for men and governments; it has withstood evil and promoted works of private and
public beneficence. It has passed through periods of misunderstanding,
misrepresentation, obloquy and persecution and has gradually won the
respect of the world. In the few places where its ministry has been
refused and repelled, religious bigotry has kept men in ignorance or political despotism has held men in thrall.
"For two hundred years the progress of Freemasonry has so closely
kept pace with the progress of civilization and human liberty that it
would be only fair and moderate to claim that the Ancient Craft has
been, at least, a willing agent in the advance.
"The two hundred years now ends in a welter of blood. Into this
world conflict our American Republic has been gradually drawn through
no desire of ours either for contest or conquest. In this conflict every
Freemason of our jurisdiction-so cosmopolitan in its origin, so polyglot
in its speech-stands devotedly loyal to the United States of America.
'In the State we shall be quiet and peaceable citizens, true to our government and loyal to our country. We shall not countenance disloyalty or rebellion, but submit to legal authority and obey the laws of the
country in which we live.'
"And in whatever of conflict we may be engaged as Free Masons
we shall never forget that we war not against men, but against powers,
not for conquest nor territory, but to establish human rights, to proclaim human liberty and promote human happiness. We shall be tolerant, patient and sympathetic with those at home and abroad whose

hearts are saddened and whose lives are hroken by this cruel warfare.
We ,shall remern,ber that 'Man's love of man is, next to Love of God,
mans first duty. And we shall look forward to the time when Freemasonry, practicing charity and benevolence, shall assuage the bitterness
of contest, quench the fires of hatred, bind up the wounds of strife
renew and reanimate the spirit of World Brotherhood, draw all me~
tog~ther. in th<; bonds of the mystic tie and establish a confraternity of
nations m which Love of God and of men, God's children, shall alone
be regnant."

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Grand Lodge of Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons of
North• Carolina, convened in its One Hundred and Thirtieth Annual Communication in the Masonic Temple, in the City of
Raleigh, Tuesday, January 16, 1917, Grand Master A. B. Andrews
Jr., presiding.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
The Grand Master reports that the year has been one of
unusual Masonic activity, and that the gain in membership and
quality of the work are ample reward· and genuine satisfaction.
Under the heading of Necrology, he calls attention to the
vacant chair of the Grand Secretary, John C. Drewry, who performed his duties in the capacity of Grand Secretary for twentytwo years unstintingly, and whose influence and inspiration did
much to bring North Carolina Masonry up to its present standard.
In his will, Grand Secretary John C. Drewry bequeathed the sum
of $10,000 in trust, to be .known as "The Drewry Memorial Grand
Secretary's Fund." This sum is to be handled by a Board of
Trustees and invested until it by accumulation or additions shall
amount to $20,000, when its earnings are to be used to pay the
salary of the Grand Secretary.
DECISIONS.
The Grand Master rendered a large number of decisions
within the year, among which were the following:
"A Mason made in a Lodge under the Grand Lodge of Porto Rico
and petitioning a North Carolina Lodge for affiliation can be healed
as provided in Regulations 149 and ISO of the ::Vlasonic Code."
"Regulation IS!, forbiclcling healing' any degree conferred in a
clandestine Lodge, does not apply to the foregoing as the Grand Lodge
of Porto Rico is not a clandestine Lodge, though it has not been recognized by our Grand Lodge."
"A <limit takes effect from the time it is ordered granted. When
a <limit is ordered and delivered by the Secretary to the Brother, he is
then a non-affiliate Mason, and can only re-connect himself with the
Lodge issuing the climit or any other Lodge by petitioning the Lodge as
a non-affiliate."
"A person of illegitimate birth, if otherwise qualified, is eligible to
the degrees of Freemasonry. The Masonic order looks to a man's moral
character and not his antecedents, and only requires he must he a man
of good character and standing in the community.
"'Honor and shame from no condition rise,
Act well your part, there all the honor lies.'
"A Master can invite a Brother from another jurisdiction (in this
instance a former Grand Lecturer of a sister Grand Lodge) to confer
work, and it would be entirely proper for the Brother to give the lee-

MASONIC RELIEF.
During the year a nttmber of individual applications for relief
were made to the Grand Lodge, and assistance given. This Jurisdiction accomplishes a great deal of good through its Orphan
Asylum at Oxford, which institution cares for 375 children. There
is also a Masonic and Eastern Star Home now caring for thirty
guests, and it is proposed to build additions at the Home to provide for the care and maintenance of an increased number of aged
Masons and their dependents.
GRAND ORATOR'S ADDRESS.
The Annual Oration by Grand Orator Hon. F. C. Harding
was a magnificent and splendid effort, and a rising vote of thanks
was extended by the Grand Lodge to Brother Harding.
At the second day's session of the Grand Lodge, a delegation
from the Grand Chapter, Order of the Eastern Star of North
Carolina, appeared before the Grand Lodge, and extended an invitation to the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge, A. F. & A. M.,
of Nor th Carolina, to attend their next Annual Session. This invitation was prompted with the spirit of co-operation of the Order

of the Eastern Star in its great works of charity to humanity, and
of making the world better,

TRUSTEES OF RELIEF FUND.
North Dakota is one of the comparatively few Grand J urisdictios that does not administer relief through the tnedium of a
Masonic Home, but if one may judge of the aspirations of this
Jurisdiction from the report of the Trustees of the Relief Fund,
one might reasonably conclude that a Masonic Home is still atnong
the hoped-for things in North Dakota. The report of the Trustees
touching this theme is as follows:
"Could we but look into the future some years to come, we would
be enabled to see a magnificently equipped and endowed Masonic Home
in North Dakota, endowed with the wealth of willing, generous brothers who of their substance had provided means for the honor and glory
of their faith in the Order, by endowment and other sources of their
material belongings, for the housing and the caring of those of
their Brotherhood who were less fortunate in their struggles for competence; building a monument to themselves which would last for all
time, enduring and abiding for ages.
"The needs of the· brethren of this State is not a poor house, or
alms house, but a comfortably equipped Home for the convenience and
comfort of our aged and infirm friends who could be pleasantly situated
in the place provided for them as guests without the feeling that they
were objects of charity in its commonly accepted definition, but as
guests in a warm wholesome atmosphere of love and light."
This Jurisdiction is fortunate (or unfortunate, as one may look
at the subject) in that the Trustees of the "Relief Fund" were
called upon to disburse from this fund just $100, and that as relief
to just one case, during the year, and upon the subject, the Trustees report as follows:
"During the past year there has been but one call for financial
assistance which was promptly met, the circumstances being made plain
to your Trustees that it was an exceptionally deserving case. The relief
bestowed, $100.00, brought letters of thankfulness from the worthy distressed brother as well as from his home Lodge, which had granted him
·
substantial aid."
This Jurisdiction must indeed be fortunately situated to have
only one call made within the year upon the Relief Fund of the
Grand Lodge.

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Fifty-first Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons of Nova Scotia
was held in the rooms of the Baptist Church, Bear River, N. S., beginning Wednesday, June 14th, 1916, with M:. w:. Bro. Donald Fisher
Fraser, Grand Master, in the Chair.
DISTINGUISHED VISITORS.
The Grand Lodge was favored with distinguished visitors in the
persons of M:. w:. Bro. J. T. Whitlock, Past Grand Master of the

100

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Grand Lodge of New Brunswick, and M:. W:. Brother Walter P.
Doull, Past Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Prince Edward
Island, who were accorded Grand Honors, and invited to take seats in
the Grand East.
The Grand Lodge then repaired in a body to St. John's Anglican
Church, where Divine Service was held, and an eloquent and instructive sermon preached by the Grand Chaplain, R. '. W:. Bro. Rev. Edward
A. Harris, after which the Grand Lodge returned to its place of meeting, where a vote of thanks was tendered to the Grand Chaplain for his
masterly effort.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
There is an excellent address by Grand Master Don F.
who makes note of the fact that the Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia is
now starting upon the second half of their first century as an independent Grand Body, and he reviews the splendid growth and strength
of the jurisdiction in the half century just passed.
He comments on the war now raging in Europe, and we .excerpt the
following in reference to Masonry and its relation to this subject:
"Tradition says that Masons were first known as 'Noachida,' or
sons of Noah, and that the actual sons of Xoah believed that when the
waters which covered the earth subsided, an era of peace would be established for all generations. It also says that Moses was a Grand
.Master of the .Masons, and dreamed that when the Children of Israel
reached the Promised Land they would rest there in peace and undisturbed. If there is no history to warrant this tradition, the idea behind
it may well give inspiration and hope to Masons of today, who in common with millions of people in Europe, are marching through strife and
sorrow, and the Shadow of Death, though not without hope. It was
not given to Moses to enter the Promised Land, and it cannot be given
to the Masons of today to walk the field of universal peace ; but in spite
of all that is happening, true Masons, strong-hearted and faithful, will
still believe they are marching forward not falling backward, and that
the Masons of tomorrow will, through the scribes of the Masonic Lodges
of the world, write in their archives that the brotherhood of man which
they have cultivated has prevailed."
Nova Scotia Masonry has many members in every branch and
rank of military service in the present world-war, and already has
sacrificed many of her Brethren in defense of world liberty and freedom.
Within the year, the Grand Lodge was called upon to mourn the
passing of one of its most valued members, M.". \V:. Bro. T. A. Cossman, P. G. M., a Mason of sterling worth and honesty of purpose.
The Grand Master issued a Charter to one new Lodge; two Lodges
under dispensation were chartered, one being the Nova Scotia Lodge of
Research, unique in that it is dependent upon the support of the entire
jurisdiction, and is to be devoted to .Masonic education and research.

James C. Jones, Acting Grand Secretary, presents his first report
on correspondence, and we quote his opening remarks as follows:
"Herewith I submit my first review of the doings of sister Grand
Lodges during the past year. In reviewing the various Proceedings I
have refrained from making any comment or criticism, feeling that this
had better be left until I was more comfortably placed in my seat at the

has been reviewed. I am indebted to my good friends the Representatives of New- York and Louisiana for reporting on their respective
Jurisdictions."
His review is very comprehensive and painstaking. California,
1915, is considered, with liberal quotations from Grand Master Bledsoe's able address. His comment upon attending religious service is
quoted:
"The Committee on Report on Correspondence review Nova Scotia's proceedings for 1914 and rather slur at our Grand Lodge attend"
ing Divine Service at the opening of our sessions. We can assure our
good friends of Califo!nia that we have never yet heard of any of
our members compla1mng of any part of the services we have held,
no matter what sect or church we attend, and like all Grand Lodges,
ours .is composed of various religious ideas and thoughts."
Far be it from us to "slur" any such action as attending divine
service; we only questioned the propriety of a .Masonic Grand Lodge
attending all(V sectarian religious church.

VISITATIONS.
Concerning official visitations to Subordinate Lodges, the

A PLEASANT INCIDENT.
A pleasant incident occurred at one of the sessions of the
Grand Lodge at this Annual Communication, in which the oldest
living Mason of the Jurisdiction was introduced to the Grand

REPORT ON FOREIGN CORRESPONDENCE.
The report on Foreign Correspondence by its Chairman, Most
Worshipful Nelson Williams, contains the usual Review of the
Proceedings of other English-speaking Grand Lodges, this report
being the sixth in number from the present Chairman.
He states in his Introduction that little has been gleaned from
the Volumes of Proceedings of the current year which is of interest to the Fraternity in general, as the business of the Grand
Lodges for the preceding year had been largely of a routine
character.
·
He refers, however, to the action of the Grand Lodge of
England, in barring from the Lodge Rooms of its Subordinates
members of German birth, and expresses the opinion that the
action of the Grand Lodge of England is foreign to a just and
proper conception of Masonic teaching, etc.
Opinions differ upon this subject, and, as we stated a year
ago, even before our own country was involved in the Great War,
that what the Grand Lodge of England did upon this subject was

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

the concern of the Grand Lodge of England alone, and that the
safety of the British Empire was the matter of paramount importance; and that, if, in the opinion of the Grand Lodge of England,
exclusion, for the time being, of German members from Subordinate· Lo<lges was necessary to safeguard the Empire, the action
of the Grand Lodge of England was justifiable; and what has
occurred since we expressed those views a year ago has confirmed
us in the opinion voiced at that time.
Brother Williams reviews California, 1915, Grand Master Bledsoe presiding. He expresses various forms of criticism of some
of our Masonic activities, referring to the Masonic Temple at San
Francisco. as presenting an unfortunate form of Grand Lodge
financiering, although he is not probably as familiar as we are in
California with the manner in which Masonry in this State undertakes and carries through successfully large affairs, as it will the
financing of the Temple in San Francisco. California, Masonically
and otherwise, bores with a large auger.
He finds fault with the action of the Grand Master in failing
to regard as of material importance the "War Relief Association"
started in Ohio for the purpose of extending Masonic relief to
the war-stricken nations of Europe. The purposes of this organization were undoubtedly of a high order, yet its puny efforts were
so insignificant as to be totally discouraged even by the proposed
beneficiaries, which is historically true; and we can find nothing
to criticise in Grand Master Bledsoe's opinion that the project
was one to which he could not give his official approval.
Brother Williams also criticises the opinion expressed by the
Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence of California, that
we entertained serious doubts that the Throne of Grace would
be greatly moved by the repetition of a certain made-to-order
printed prayer for peace, mailed out from one of our American
Jurisdictions with the request that everyone repeat it. We ventured to express the opinion that these so-called "prayers" printed
on a handbill, and repeated parrot-like by individuals, would be
about as effectual as running a phonograph record on a talking:
machine in moving the Almighty. We are still of that
opinion, but Brother Williams apparently holds otherwise, and
refers to the Lord's Prayer as a parallel case. When we recall,
however, who was the Author of the Lord's Prayer, Brother Williams' parallel becomes funny. We do not quite remember, but
believe that the name of the author of the N cw York supplication
was Pretzman.

THE NINTH ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Ninth Annual Communication was held in the .City of
Oklahoma.
Preliminary to the official opening of the Grand Lodge, the
Grand Body was entertained by children from the Masonic Home,
who rendered a program, musical and otherwise, to the edification
of the assembled Masons and their friends.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
At the opening of the Grand Master's Address, he made a
recommendation which was apparently forthwith unanimously carried by rising vote to the effect that the UNITED ST ATES FLAG
become a part of the paraphernalia of the Grand Lodge and of
each of its constituent Lodges, which flag shall be spread upon
the altar and upon which shall rest the Three Great Lights of
Masonry,
DECISIONS.
That peace and harmony prevail among the Craft may be inferred from the statement of the Grand Master that no question
of importance has been brought to his attention for an official
ruling, and that such questions and answers as have taken place
have been of a routine nature, mostly answered by the Constitution, and which cannot, therefore, be properly called decisions, and
are, therefore, as the Grand Master states, omitted from his report.
MASONIC HOME.
The Grand Master reports progress and efficiency in the
affairs of the Masonic Home at Darlington. There are now sheltered at the Home 146 children and 31 adults, all of whom appear
to be comfortable, happy, and contented.
MASONIC ACTIVITIES.
The year preceding was evidently a prosperous one, Masonically speaking; four new Lodges were constituted; a large number
of dispensations for various purposes were issued, including three
to form new Lodges; numerous corner-stone ceremonies were performed, and the Grand Master paid not less than seventy-nine
visits to Subordinate Lodges.

"Finally Brethren, since life was given to the germ which grew
and developed into the Masonic Order this old world has witnessed
many changes. Nations have risen to might and glory on land and
sea, have fallen, their heroes enslaved and their banners trailed in the
dust; cities of marvelous beauty and wealth have vanished, covered
with the ashes of volcanic fires and the sands of the desert, forgotten
until some venturous explorer sheds light upon their hidden treasures
and reads their story to a wondering world. Men have come and gone
and the handwriting on the wall which tells of their having lived is a
sculptured bust, a painting rare, or verse of deeds of bravery and daring bold. But the principles of this order change not, nor age, nor
decay; shining with the light of Purity within, glowing with the energy
and vigor of achievement, heedless alike of the sound of strife, and the
battle's cry. They are embodied in a spirit, deathless, sublime."
ORATION.
The Grand Orator, Worshipful Brother ·woodson Easley Norveil, delivered the Annual Oration, his subject being "Federations
of the Future."
The entire trend of thought of the Grand Orator was in the
direction of the wisdom of America keeping out of the European
war. "He kept us out of war" was the slogan and battle-cry on
which a President was re-,elected in November last.
This oration was delivered on the 21st of February, after the
slogan "He kept the country out of war" had served its purpose,
and a few brief weeks before war was actually declared.
A few quotations from the Orator's Address will indicate that
the address would have been more appropriate had it been delivered in October, 1916, instead of just prior to the second inauguration of President \Vilson, and a few days before he appeared
before Congress and demanded a declaration of war against Germany:
"\Vhy is this great repuhlic, so long consecrated to the cause of
peace, now trembling on the verge of war? Because, we too, would
achieve mastery in the fields of trade. It is saiq that we have a right
to the freedom of the seas. The individual has many rights that he does
not use. He has a right to he upon a thoroughfare of the city while a
riot is in progress, but his judgment tells him to make his right subordinate to his safety. He has a right to travel a given part of the
highway, but he willingly turns aside to avoid a collision. It will be a
sad hour in the history of human freedom when we abandon the· principle promulgated by \Vashington and followed by all the great patriots
whose service has g·iven power to the republic and glory to our flag, by
engaging in a war ahroad, where the spirit of commerce instead of the
devotion of the patriot has called millions to march beneath the banners of nations, whose governments promise nothing to benefit mankind.

At the opening of the Grand Lodge, the Flag was escorted
into the Lodge Room according to the form outlined by this committee. After it had been placed on its pedestal, the Rev. W. W.
Youngson, behind a screen, with the Flag floating in the breeze
of an electric fan, impersonated the Flag, and gave the following
address, as quoted below:
"The Flag of your Country greets you! I am grateful to the Grand
Lodge for having made me a necessary part of its equipment and for
having ordered all lodges in the jurisdiction to accord me a special position of high distinction and to welcome me with befitting ceremony
at the opening of each session of the Lodge.
"I am the symbol of the brotherhood of man. I stand for courage,
for chivalry, for generosity and honor. No man must touch me roughly;
no hand shall touch me irreverently; I am the birthright of privilege
and integrity. I have floated since June 14, 1777, over a country of
benevolence, refuge and progress. To bear me is an honor, to own
me a sacred trust. I am the emblem of Freedom, of Equality, of Justice, for every person and creature as I float unvanquished, untarnished,
over the open door of free education.
"Let me tell you who I am. The work that I do is the making of
the real flag. I am not the flag, not at all. I am but its shadow. I am
whatever you make me, nothing more. I am your belief in yourself,
your dream of what a people may become. I live a changing life, a life
of moods and passions, of heartbreaks and tired muscles. Sometimes I
am strong with pride, when men do an honest work, fitting the rails
together truly. Sometimes I droop, for then purpose has gone from
me, and cynically I play the coward. Sometimes I am loud, garish and
full of that ego that blasts judgment. But always I am all that you
hope to be and have the courage to try for. I am song and fear, struggle and panic, and ennobling hope. I am the day's work of the weakest man and the largest dream of the most daring. I am the constitution and the courts, statutes and statute makers, soldier and dreadnaught, drayman and streetsweep, cook, counselor and clerk. I am the .
battle of yesterday and the mistake of tomorrow. I am the mystery of
the men who do without knowing why. I am the clutch of an idea and
the reasoned )}Urpose of resolution. I am no more than what you believe me to be, and I am all that you believe I can be. I am what you
make me, nothing more. I swing before your eyes as a bright gleam of
color, a cymbol of yourself, the picture suggestion of that big thing
which makes this nation. My stars and my stripes are your dreams and
your labors. They are bright with cheer, brilliant with courage, firm
with faith, because you have made them so out of your hearts, for you
are the makers of the flag, and it is well that you glory in the making.
There are many flags in the earth-the union jack, the tricolors of
France, the Nether lands and Belgium, the yellow field of Spain, the full
moon of Japan, the star and crescent of Turkey, the lone star of Chili.

DISTINGUISHED VISITOR.
The Grand Lodge was honored by the presence of a distinguished
visitor in the person of Harry A. Raser, the personal representative
of the Grand Master of the Grand Encampment of Knights Templar
of the United States for the Jurisdiction of Oregon.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
The Grand Master's Address was a very complete statement of his
activities during his term of office, showing that he had devoted unselfish care and attention to the discharg~ of his duties.
He constituted one Lodge that had received its charter at the last
Annual Communication; and instituted three new Lodges. He laid
corner-stones to two Masonic buildings, by proxy. He granted a number of dispensations of a local nature.
GR'AND LODGE CONFERENCE ..
The Grand Master issued a call for a Conferei1ce of the Grand
Masters of the various Grand Jurisdictions of the United States, to be
held in Portland, but, it being impossible to get a good representation, or at least one-half of the jurisdictions present, the call was
withdrawn.
MASONIC WAR RELIEF ASSOCIATION.
There is a Charity Fund set aside for relief . of members of the
Fraternity at war, which is growing, and it is expected will finally be
placed where it will achieve the greatest relief and be ready for distribution immediately at the close of the present world war.
MASONIC HOME.
There is no Masonic Home in this jurisdiction, although there is
a growing sentiment in this direction, the Grand Chapter of' the Eastern
Star having already started a small fund for that purpose, and it will
not be long before Oregon will be able to extend charity and relief
through the means of a Home, which, as stated, there is a strong
desire to establish.

COMMUNICATIONS.
The business of this jurisdiction is transacted in four Quarterly
Communications, and one so-called Annual Grand Communication, held
at Philadelphia on St. John the Evangelist's Day, Dec. 27th, of each
year, for the installation of officers who are elected at the regular
December Quarterly, and, also, for the reception of reports.
At the Annual Communication on St. John the Evangelist's Day,
this year, distinguished visitors from other jurisdictions were present,
particular mention being made of the Worshipful William R'. Meakle,
Grand Master of Masons of New Jersey, accompanied by his Staff
of Grand Officers; Most Worshipful Brother Thos. J. Shryock, Grand
Master of Maryland, accompanied by his Director of Ceremonies; and
the Most Worshipful Thos. Penny, Grand Master of Masons of New
York, with a large number of his Grand Officers.
All of the Quarterly and the Annual Grand Communications were
presided over by the Most Worshipful Brother Louis A. Watres,
Grand Master.
ADDRESS OF GRAND MASTER.
Grand Master \Vatres sets forth in business-like form a resume
of his official activities within the year, particular mention being made
of the constitution of the five new Lodges which received their charters at the preceding Annual Communication, whereby the total number of Lodges within the jurisdiction was carried forward to a total
of 502.

Important corner-stone ceremonies, eight in number, are enumerated by the Grand Master, these Ceremonies being performed only for
important public buildings, such as mentioned by him-a Federal
Postoffice building, a Municipal building, High School bnilding, Masonic Temples, etc.
The Grand Master issued a large number of so-called "edicts,"
otherwise interpretations of the law of the jurisdiction; and in this
jurisdiction there is no appeal from the decision of the Grand Master,
that is, no review of his "decisions" by any Jurisprudence Committee
or by the Grand Lodge itself. In other words, his "edict" is the law,
unless and until changed by some other subsequent Grand Master.

MASONIC HOME.
Probably the most complete Masonic Home establishment in the
world has been developed by the Grand Lodge at Elizabethtown, Pa.
The number of guests of the Homes at Elizabethtown is at this
time 285. The community life is reported as ideal with the reign of
absolute harmony. The Committee reports that the spirit of fraternity,
helpfulness, gratitude, forbearance, and consideration one for another,
is plainly apparent to all upon entering the sacred portals of the
Homes, and mingling with those whose happy surroundings have been
made possible by the beneficence of the Grand Lodge.
The Homes are complete, in that provision is made for the attendance at the public schools of the children of the Home. The religious and social life of the residents of the Home have been provided
for; an extensive library has been installed, and hospital service for
those in need thereof has been provided for upon a most scientific
scale.
FINANCIAL.
The Jurisdiction of Pennsylvania is distinguished among the Grand
Jurisdictions of the world by its high-class methods of finance. The
Chairman of its Committee on Finance, Worshipful Clement B. Newbold, is one of the ablest and most distinguished figures in the American World of Finance; and it is largely because of the high character
of men that Pennsylvania has always chosen to fill its important· and
exalted stations, that it has attained its commanding figure in the
:Vfasonk Jurisdictions of the world.
· The· Statements of the various Funds rendered at the. Annuai'
Grand Communication, and at the different Qµarterly Communications,
particularly the Quarterly Communication of December, are ·more
comprehensive and complete, we believe, than similar Statements rendered by other jurisdictions; and the open, financial methods of Masonic Jurisdictions, exemplified, for instance, by Pennsylvania, is in
pleasing contrast with the financial· methods of certain •great religious
organizations, and some others, that are not religious, where the evident
purpose is not to afford information, but to conceal the same.

REPORT ON COR:RESPONDENCE.
The Report on Correspondence is presented by \Vorshipful Thomas
F. Penman, Chairman, this being his first report, he having succeeded
as Chairman of this important Committee the late Brother James M.
Lamberton, who, for sixteen years, presented this report on behalf of
his Jurisdiction, and who was universally regarded as one of the most
capable reviewers belonging to the reportorial gttild.
In his introductory remarks, Brother Penman states, after giving
the matter consideration, that he conceives his occupation as that of
a "chronicler" rather than a "critic," his reason for this conclusion
being stated by him as follow:s :
"The fact is, there is little common ground in the affairs of Grand
Lodges from which to proceed. to profitable controversial discussion.
In their independence of one another they differ in laws, regulations,
policy and methods-even, to some extent, on the subject of Landmarks; they may be said to agree entirely only on the fund?-mental
moral truths, which admit of no controversy. All we want is news
of the Masonic world which keeps us in homogeneous touch with our
world-wide Fraternity and from which we can note its progress and
neutralize a tendency towards isolation."

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

His initial report ·is scholarly and excellent, and bears evidence
of thoughtful care in its preparation.

RECOGNITION OF THE GR'AND LODGE.
Almost universal recognition of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine
Islands by the other Masonic Grand Lodges of the world has now been
extended, there being only three Grand Lodges in the United States
which have thus far failed to take action, and the total number of
Grand Lodges which have granted recognition is now seventy-seven,
twenty-four additional recognitions having been received within the
preceding year.

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Fifth Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the Philippine Islands was
held in the Masonic Temple in the City of Manila, Feb. 13th and 14th,
1917, Most Worshipful William H. Taylor, Grand Master, presiding.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
In the opening paragraphs of his Address. Grand Master Taylor
felicitate~ the Craft upon the fact that the Fraternity is domiciled, as
its headquarters, in the splendid new Temple in the City of Manila,
one of the most magnificent buildings in the entire Far East.
He calls attention to the splendid growth of the Fraternity, both
numerically and financially, the net gain in the six chartered Lodges
being 112, in addition to the 1039 members in the thirty-two Lodges
under dispensation.

119

UNIFICATION OF MASONRY IN THE PHILIPPINES.
The great work accomplished in the preceding year in the Masonry
of the Philippine Islands was the practical unification of all of the
Masonic Lodges, with the exception of possibly one or two under the
Scottish Constitution, whereby the old Lodges chartered by the Grand
Orient of Spain surrendered the charters received from that authority,
and all of them have come under the Grand Jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of the Philippine Islands by dispensations from that Sovereign
Grand Body. There were thirty-one of these old Lodges, all of which
received charters 'at this Communication, making, with the Lodges
previously in existence under the Grand Lodge of the Philippine
Islands, a total of thirty-eight Lodges in that Grand Jurisdiction.
There now remains in the Philippine Islands one Lodge, or possibly
two Lodges, still in existence under the Scottish Constitution, but it
seems altogether likely that both of these Lodges will surrender their
Scottish charters, and accept charters under the new Grand Lodge.
which will complete the absolute unification of Masonry in the
Philippines.
ANNUAL ORATION.
The Annual Oration was delivered in the afternoon session of the
first day of the Annual Communication by the Grand Orator, Worshipful Brother Charles S. Banks, who developed the theme "The
Practical Na tu re of Our Craft." His Address was interesting and
instructive, and upon motion of Brother George R. Harvey, Past
Grand Master, the thanks of the Grand Lodge were tendered to the
distinguished Orator, and his ·Address was ordered printed in the
Proceedings.
FOREIGN CORRESPONDENCE.

Walter William Webber. In his Introduction, he calls attention to
some of the features of universal Masonry that have impressed themselves upon his observation in his review of the various Grand Lodges,
and states among other things that "Masonry is Action," and believes
that this fact is especially emphasized in Masonic Homes and other
Benevolences, and finds that the reading of reports of these various
Masonic Activities is truly inspiring.

Brother Webber has the correct idea, also, of the true character
of the "Grand Master," in that the "Grand Master" is a creation of
the Grand Lodge, and that, regardless of the theory of his original
position in Ancient Craft Masonry, he now has only such powers as
are delegated to him by the Grand Lodge, and that any attempt to
misuse those powers, .or to exceed his authority, may be checked by
the Grand Lodge, and his "decisions" may be modified or reversed.
This, in our opinion, is the correct exposition of the character and
province of the Grand Master, although in certain Grand Jurisdictions,
Pennsylvania for instance, the Grand Master still retains much of the
original conception of his autocratic power, and his "decisions" are
not subject to review by the Grand Lodge, but stand absolutely as the
interpretation of the law of the Jurisdiction, unless and until modified
or reversed by some succeeding Grand Master.

QUEENSLAND.
1916.
12th Annual, Brisbane, June 12 .
N llmber of Lodges, 66; Membership, 2610; Gain, 220.
IXSTALLATION OF GRA::\D MASTER.
At the Stated Communication of August 10th, 1915, Most Worshipful Brother A. M. Hertzberg was installed as Grand Master for
the seventh consecutive term. This practice of re~electing the Grand
Master for a large ntlmber of years obtains in most of the Australian
Jurisdictions, and Brother Hertzberg has served as Grand Master for
more than half of the entire existence of the Grand Lodge of Queensland.

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
After his installation, the Grand Master made a patriotic and
inspiring Address to the Grand Lodge. He also set forth in a businesslike form the Grand Lodge activities, indicating the capable manner in which Masonry is performing its functions in the Grand Jurisdictions of Queensland.
There have been, as is well known, many obstacles placed in the
way of this Grand Lodge by the Grand Lodges of England and Scotland, which Grand Lodges were loathe to surrender the jurisdiction
in Queensland which had been exercised by their District Grand
Lodges for a great many years; but from the report of the Grand
Master, it appears that nearly every Masonic Jurisdiction in the world,
outside of England and Scotland, has recognized the regularity of the
Grand Lodge of Queensland, and this Grand Lodge is, therefore, firmly
estahlished as a Sovereign Grand Lodge of Ancient Craft Masonry.

124

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE. ·

Since the last Communication, Queensland has received formal
recognition from five Grand Lodges, viz., Iowa, New Hampshire,
Prince Edward Island, California and Manitoba, with a membership
of 123,734, making a grand total of nearly two million Masons who
have recognized the sovereign character of this Grand Lodge.
MASONIC HOMES.
This Grand Jurisdiction, while one of the youngest in the world,
is looking forward to the establishment of a Widows and Orphans
and Masonic Home, and the Brethren are urged by the Grand Master
to spare no effort in speeding the day that will see this exalted ambition realized.
A fund amounting to something like $25,000 has already been
created as a nucleus toward the establishment of an institution of this
character.

M:. w:. A. M. HERTZBERG, Grand Master.

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Grand Lodge of the Most Ancient and Honorable Society of
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations was opened in Ample Form in Freemasons' Hall,
Providence, May 15, 1916, Most Worshipful Reuben S. Bemis, Grand
Master, presiding.
ADDRESS OF THE GRAND MASTER.
The Grand Master presents a concise, businesslike statement 9f
his official acts within the year, his duties consisting in the usual
routine of affairs, incident to his exalted station.
This is one of the comparatively few American Jurisdictions that
encourages the attendance of Lodges upon divine service, and nnmerous dispensations were issued within the year to permit Lodges to
attend church in regalia.
The Gran'd Master manifested an unusual degree of activity in the
matter of official visitations to Subordinate Lodges, and his efforts

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

125

in the direction of stimulating interest by these official visitations were
greatly appreciated by .the Lodges of the Jurisdiction.
He states that he received a number of requests for advice from
Masters of Lodges, but that no official decisions were necessary, all
questions that arose being decided by reference to the Constitution
and Laws.
The Grand Master makes a recommendation along the lines of
simplifying, if possible, the rule respecting the physical qualifications
of the candidate, his idea being, we assume, that greater latitude
be allowed to Lodges in accepting those having visible physical <lefects, but possessing the necessary moral and mental qualifications.
A PLEASING INCIDENT.
An incident of a pleasing nature occurred within the year in the
unveiling of the bronze tablet placed on the Chamber of Commerce
Building of Providence, a ceremony which took place under the auspices of the Grand Lodge on May 9, 1916, the building having been
occupied as far back as 1797 as a place of meeting of several of the
Masonic Bodies of Rhode Island, and in which Grand Commandery
of Knights Templar and appendant Orders of Massachusetts and
Rhode Island were organized in 1805.

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
This Annual Communication, being the tenth since the foundation
of the Grand Lodge, the Grand Master, in his Address, takes occasion
to institute a few comparisons between the Province of Saskatchewan
as it was ten years ago, and as it is today, and also a few comparisons touching Masonry as it was then, and is now.
He calls attention to the fact that Saskatchewan is essentially an
agricultural province, and referring simply to one of the staple crops
of the Province, he mentions that in 1905 there was produced in the
Province 42,600,000 bushels of wheat, whereas in 1915, this crop had
increased to 263,000,000 bushels, which, as a matter of fact, is almost
half the normal production of this cereal in the United States.
. Referring to Masonry, he finds that when the Grand Lodge was
launched upon its career of usefulness, there were twenty-nine Lodges
with a membership of about 900, whereas now to these twenty-nine
Lodges have been added ninety-six, making a total of 125 Lodges, with
a membership of over 7000.
From these statements, it is manifest that, not only has the Province of Saskatchewan, within the past ten years, made wonderful
progress, but Masonry itself in the Jurisdiction has made wonderful
strides.
OFFICIAL ACTIVITIES.
The Grand Master was active in the discharge of his official duties
within the year. All the Lodges which received charters at the preceding Annual .Communication were duly constituted, most of them
by himself in person. He granted dispensations to form nine new
Lodges; he was active in official visitations to Subordinate Lodges;
numerous dispensations for various purposes were issued by him, and
he, otherwise, manifested a marked degree of official activity.
DECISIONS.
Among the "approv.ed rulings," here is one that is not the rule
in American Jurisdictions:
"The position of the S. W., when ruling the Lodge in the absence
of the W. M., shall be in a chair placed on the dais in front of the
E. He shall be addressed as Brother S. W."

"(1) That Grand Lodge of Scotland should approve of and act

"'That in order to prevent the peace and harmony of the Ci;aft

done to such vital questions until after peace shall have been restored."

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The 140th Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Ancient, Free Masons of South Carolina was held in the
Masonic Temple in the .City of Charleston, S. C., Dec. 12th and 13th,
the ).fost Worshipful Brother R. A. Cooper, Grand Master, presiding.

130

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

AGE OF THE GRA:\'D LODGE.
This Jurisdiction for several years last past has been agitated over
the question of the age of the Grand Lodge. The Volume of Proceedings before us is designated as the Proceedings of the "140th
Annual Communication," but about two years ago some of the members
of this Grand Jurisdiction, who had been delving into the subject as to
the ages of the various Grand Lodges in America, became convinced
that the Grand Lodge of South Carolina was entitled to the
position of greatest honor, so far as age is concerned, among the Grand
Lodges of America; and a Committee was duly appointed to inquire
into this important subject and ascertain if South Carolina had not,
as a matter of fact, been cheating itself to the extent of forty years,
in the matter of age, the desire being not to make itself appear as
young as possible, but on the other hand, as ~d as possible; and the
findings of this Committee were to the effect that South Carolina, in
some manner, had lost in the discard forty years. In other words, that
instead of dating its existence from 1776, the date should have been
1736, which would make this Annual Communication the 180th instead
of the 140th.

Following introductory remarks incident to his Address, the Grand
Master places, apparently in his judgment, the subject of most importance to the Jurisdiction, what he designates as the
MASONIC HOME FUND.
In this connection he states that a great deal has been said on the
floor of the Grand Lodge within the several years .last past concerning
the work of the Masonic Home Trustees, and the method followed
in this Jurisdiction of dispensing charity.
The Grand Master states that he is each year more fully convinced
that the plan adopted by South Carolina tentatively several years since
should be made the permanent policy of the Jurisdiction, which policy
contemplates the administration of the charity functions of the Grand
Lodge, so far as widows and orphans are concerned, which is the
"individual" or "annuity" method, as distinguished from the "Home"
method; and the Grand Master recommends, which recommendation
was subsequently adopted, that the word "Home" be stricken from the
title of the Fund, and the title subsequently adopted at this Communication is "Masonic Relief Fund" instead of "Masonic Home Fund."

South Carolina, therefore, is one of the comparatively few Jurisdictions in the United States that has definitely decided against the
Masonic Home system, and from the standpoint of economy, there is
undoubted wisdom in South Carolina's action.
GRAND MASTER'S ACTIVITIES.
The Grand Master reports nine official visitations to Subordinate
Lodges.
The activities of Grand Masters in respect to official visits have
a wide range, the nine visitations reported by Grand Master Cooper
of this Jurisdiction being, perhaps, the smallest number of visitations
indicated by any Grand Master, and the largest number, so far as our
reading of current Proceedings has gone, being 215 visits to Subordinate Lodges, reported by Grand Master Jermane of the District of
Columbia.
Five Lodges that received charters at the preceding Annual Communication were duly constituted within the year; dispensations were
issued to form three new Lodges; four corner-stone ceremonies took
place under the auspices of the Grand Lodge, and the Masonic Temple
at Columbia, S. C., was dedicated.

131

The Grand Secretary. however, apparently overcome by a sense
of modesty, has continued to number the Proceedings on the old basis,
and some action of the Grand Lodge will probably be needed to advance the serial, whereby the Grand Lodge of South Carolina will
become the oldest on the American Continent.

COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE.
The Committee on Jurisprudence, commenting upon the work of
the Grand Master, pays special tribute to his great industry and zeal
in favoring with his personal presence such a large number of the
Lodges of the Jurisdiction. His activities deserve the high praise
paid him in the report of this Committee, as follows :
"The work of your Grand Master throughout the year has led
him into .great diversity of activities and his record is unprecedented
for comprehensiveness and efficiency. He comes to you from a harvest field of Masonry, made richer far by his earnest, intelligent and
loving labors, and that will, we trust and believe, become yet stronger
and far more golden by reason of the great work he has wrought,
the words of encouragement, and the instructive lessons he has so
widely and generously carried to the Tennessee Craft. His record
of 'Official Visits' is without parallel, whether considered in point
of number, diversity, or territory covered. He has not waited for,
but has made opportunitY. for visitation. He has been with the
numerically strong and. well-equipped Subordinate, and has traveled
far and wide to reach and to help, instruct and encourage the weak
and struggling rural Lodge. Instant in season and out of season, his
travels have been brightened by the sweet songs of the birds of
springtime, bathed in the sunshine and melting heat of summer and
chilled by the shivering winds of bleakest winter time, marked always
by a zeal unbounded, a devotion that knew no rest. Impartial always,
and seeking ever to improve conditions and accomplish all possible
good for the Brethren, he deserves and will, in rich measure, receive
your commendation. We must heartily congratulate our worthy Grand
Master upon the abundance of his labors during the year and felicitate
the Craft upon their good judgment and wisdom in selecting such an
able, aggressive and faithful servant."
