The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Texas, Ancient, Free and
Accepted Masons, held its Eighty-first Grand Annual Communication
at the Masonic Temple, in the City of Waco, commencing Tuesday,
the 5th day of December, 1916, the Most Worshipful Dan S. McMillin,
Grand Master, presiding.

R.". w:. Bro. George W. Treadwell, Grand Senior Warden of
the Grand Lodge of the State of Louisiana.

"The history of Masonry in Texas is the history of Texas, because those who were foremost in making Texas a free country,
making it what it was, what it is, and what it is destined to be, also
planted Masonry in Texas. Many of her most noted soldiers, statesmen and jurists have occupied the prominent positions in the Subordinate Lodges and the Grand Lodge of Texas and directed its destinies
with the same intelligence and patriotism displayed in the formation
and guidance of the new Republic and State, and leading to the great
success it has now attained and the even greater success which no
Mason doubts it will attain in the future. For we see before us the
flower of the young manhood of Texas, strong in their knowledge and
zeal for the principles of Masonry, which they have learned to love
and practice in the years of their young manhood, and it is a joy to
know that those who are following after us are so much better qualified than we have been to carry on the great work that means so much
to humanity."
He refers to the present condition of ::'vfasonry in his Jurisdiction
as follows:
"I am glad to report to you that Masonry in Texas was never in a
more flourishing condition than now. Peace and harmony, with very

PHYSICAL DISQUALIFICATION.
'Texas is still one of the comparatively few American Jurisdictions
that holds to a strict construction concerning physical disqualifications,
and the Grand Master, in his Address, gives a list of thirty-eight
defects ruled upon by him within the year as disqualifying applicants
for admission, and among some of these defects, we find the following:
Monahans Lodge No. 952-Defect: Loss of first joint of little
finger of right hand.
Lee Scott Lodge No. 793-Defect: Sees but little out of one eye;
the other eye perfect.
Nolan Lodge No. 1003-Defect :Loss of first joint of second
finger of right hand.
\Ve may say, however, that notwithstanding the apparent strictness of this Jurisdiction touching the subject of physical disqualifications, it is nevertheless very much more liberal than formerly, and
there has been within the last three or fol1r years a very decided relaxation of its rules upon the subject of physical defects.
MASONIC FUNCTIONS.
A marked measure of activity was manifested in the performances
of Grand Lodge ceremonies; there were not less than twenty-five
corner-stone ceremonies; numerous dispensations were granted to publicly install officers; dedications of not less than five Lodge rooms
took place, and otherwise, the year was an active period for the
Grand Master.
DECISIONS.
A number of rulings were made by the Grand Master upon questions of interpretation of the Constitution and laws of the J urisdiction, all of which interpretations were apparently upheld by the Jurisprudence Committee and the Grand Lodge.
We quote as follows from the decisions, as possibly presenting
questions of general interest:
"Question-Is it permissible for the Order of Eastern Star to form
a procession and precede the Masonic procession to the place of installation?
"Held-It would be improper for any, except Masonic Bodies,
acting as an escort. to precede the Lodge in procession on public
occasions. The Order of Eastern Star not being recognized by our
Grand Lodge as a Masonic Body, it would he improper for them to
form a procession and precede the Lodge to place of installation."

MASONIC ORPHANS' HOME AND SCHOOL.
Texas has a _just pride in its Masonic Home and School, this
being one of the finest institutions of its kind in this or any other
country, and concerning this institution, we quote from the Grand
Master's Address as follows :
"No Grand Master's report would be complete without reference
to the Orphans' Home, though I have no intention of going into details of that institution, as that will be given you by our Board of
Directors and Superintendent.
"During the year I have visited the Home repeatedly, and met
with the Board of Directors in their deliberations, and observed the
care with which they considered every question affecting that noblest
work of Masonry in our State today, which is the visible and valuable
manifestation of the tenets of our profession of Brotherly Love, Relief
and Truth. Under their careful management 'Our Home' stands preeminent among like. institutions in the whole world as to successful
financial management, comfort of our children, and their moral, physical and spiritual training, under the excellent direction and management of our peerless Superintendent, Brother Walter Acker, and his
noble and devoted wife. Brethren, go see the actual workings of our
Home, as I have done, and you will come away with a renewed inspiration of their great work.
"Our Brethren cannot fully appreciate. because they do not know,
the labor, the time and the tremendous responsibility involved in the
successful management of this most important trust. It is seldom that
the most extensive business enterprise demands such sound judgment,
so mnch laborious attention to details, and such careful circumspection, yet all this is freely rendered by our excellent Board of Directors
without compensation or reward, save the happy consciousness of duty
well done. Their devotion and fidelity deserve all praise. We shall
never know how much we are indebted to the Directors of our Home
until they have gone to their reward, and we come to fill their places.

"If our Home is not the most symmetrical and magnificent of
structures ever erected by human hands, it is to every true and devoted Mason the most beautiful Masonic emblem ever contrived. In
its structure there are no cedars from Lebanon, nor marbles from the
quarries of the East, but its foundation is Trust in God, and its pillars
are Faith. Hope and Charity. The gold of Ophir does not adorn its
portals, nor precious stones from afar gem its corridors, but the smiles
of cheered widowhood and orphan children illuminate its hall, and its

gems are the teardrops of gratitude sparkling in the eyes of orphan
children.
"My Brethren, that Home is our Mount Moriah, that is our Temple, sacred to Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth."

The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of Utah held its Forty-sixth Annual Communication in the Masonic
Temple, Salt Lake City, Utah, on January 16th and 17th, 1917, Most
Worshipful Charles Clifton Griggs, Grand Master, presiding.
GRAND ORATOR'S ADDRESS.
After the opening of the Grand Lodge, a departure from the
usual order of procedure took place in that the Grand Orator, Brother
John E. Carver, was introduced, whereupon the Annual Oration was
delivered, which consisted principally of a review of the traditions
and history of Freemasonry.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
Upon the re-assembling of the Grand Lodge in the afternoon of
the first day of the Annual Communication, the Grand Master delivered his Annual Address, which consisted of a resume of the business of the preceding year.
The Grand Master reported personal and official v1s1tations to all
of the Lodges in the Jurisdiction, with the exception of one Lodge,
which was visited by the Deputy Grand Master.
OUR NATIONAL EMBLEM.
Th·e Grand Master states in his report that in all of his visitations to Subordinates, he drew especial attention to the spirit of patriotism which prevailed throughout our country, and, in this connection, called the attention of the various Lodges of his Jurisdiction
to the history of the American Flag, which is inseparably linked with
the history of American Masonry, and in his visitations he mentioned
to all of the Lodges that it is right and proper to display our National
Emblem in the East in all Lodge rooms, and in the official visit which
he made to his own Lodge-Tintic No. 9-he presented the Lodge with
a large silk American Flag, and received their assurances that at all
future meetings the Flag would be displayed. He states further that
many of the Lodges have always displayed the Flag in the East, and
he states that the few that have not observed the custom have since
been notified by him to do so, and he is pleased to inform the Grand

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.
The Grand Master's Address is a very complete resume of his
activities during his term of office. In his introductory remarks,
touching upon the awful calamity of the war in Europe, and its relation to Masonry, he has this to say:
"It may be that among the blessings to the world that are bound
to emerge from the world-wide welter of war there shall come a
clearer vision than we have ever known of what is meant by universal
brotherhood. Groups 'of Masons that hitherto have stood apart and
looked askance at one another are standing face to face. We are
learning what are the essentials of our Craft. Emphasis is being laid
less upon the question 'from whence come you' and more upon 'whither
are you traveling.' The devout Christian beholds with sorrow the
various sects of Christendom divided and too often opposing each
other. They earnestly pray as Chris.t himself prayed that 'these all
may be one.' So let the Mason who prays at all pray that the divided
ranks of Freemasonry may be closed up and, united in heart and
action, work together for the good of all mankind. Sure it is that
there can be no permanent peace so long as warfare of any kind
exists, commercial, industrial, social, political, or even fraternal. All
these must be done away and all nations stand side by side as do
the States of our country, independent yet united in the bonds of the
Union, before the vision of England's seer can be realized-'The Parliament of Man, the Federation of the World.'"
He makes extensive and fitting comment on the harvest of the
Grim Reaper, which included two beloved Past Grand Masters,
M.". w:. Charles Arba Calderwood and M.". w:. Kittredge Haskins,
Masons who had given active Masonic service of usefulness in promoting the best interests of the Craft.
OFFICIAL ACTIVITIES WI'.I'HIN THE YEAR

the largest of any year in its history. He called one Special Communication to lay the corner-stone of the Henry W. Putnam Memorial

GRAND LODGE CHARITY FUND.
The Grand Lodge of Vermont has a Permanent Charity Fund
which is gradually increasing, but does not warrant the building of
a Home as yet, but as evidence of the broad vision of Vermont charity,
we quote the Grand Master upon this subject, as follows:

Jurisdictions maintain, as it were, a law department, a sort of an attorney-general, who passes on the questions of law before they are
promulgated. In North Carolina questions of law are passed on by
the Grand Master in case only of appeal from the Subordinate Lodge.
Some of these methods have an advantage over our method in which
the Grand Master announces the law, makes a ruling, renders judgment and the same is acted on ; after which the correctness of the
Grand Master's ruling is submitted to the Committee on Jurisprudence of the Grand Lodge, whose report is affirmed or disapproved
by the Grand Lodge. Under this method the judgment has been enforced before the validity of the law has been established; and,. if the
Committee on Jurisprudence overrules the decision of the Grand Master and the Grand Lodge approves the Committee's report, it is then
established that the law is different from the law given the Subordinate Lodge by the Grand Master, which has been acted upon by the
Lodge. Probably a majority of the Jurisdictions are in accord with
our practice. It requires some care in reporting a decision from another Jurisdiction, in order to ascertain just what the decision was
as rendered by the Grand Master and then follow the same up to determine how far the decision was sustained, modified or overruled
either by the Committee on Jurisprudence or subsequently by the
Lodge in acting upon the Committee's report. Many errors creep into
the reports of the Committee on Correspondence through oversights
in this regard. A careful judicial foreign correspondent and compiler
who would specialize in gathering these decisions for a number of
years, would perform a service for his own and all the Jurisdictions."

"I feel sometimes that we are a bit selfish in our charity. \Ve
do little outside our Fraternity, and I am aware that Lodges sometimes give grudgingly when it should be a delight to give. It is true
that we have given for the general relief of sufferers from fire, flood,
earthquake, and pestilence. But for the most part our benefactions
have been to our own. I would have the Grand Lodge of Vermont
and its constituents in such condition that no worthy Brother in need,
no Masonic wife or widow should be without the necessities and comforts of life, no Masonic children lacking in all that we regard so
essential for our own little ones, should grow up without the opportunity of developing into useful manhood and womanhood. Are anv
sick, I would have nursing care at their service; are any in need o"f
such surgical skill as those in better circumstances can command to
prolong life and comfort, I would have it, too, within their reach. I
hope to see the time when in every public hospital within this Jurisdiction there shall be an endowed Masonic bed or sum of money set
apart to care for any who may need its advantages. I trust the time
may speedily come when we can say to any suffering Mason, 'My
Brother, you are ill and in need of the best medical skill. It is provided for you by your Brethren. By your consistent life as a Mason
you have acquired the right to these things. The best in medicine
and surgery is yours.' "

THE GREAT WAR.
The Jurisdiction of Victoria, in common with all other Masonic
Jurisdictions of the British Colonies, treats as the subject of uppermost
importance the great World \Var in progress, in which the British
Empire is struggling for existence, and, with her allies, to carry forward to victory the great principles of Liberty and Freedom.
From an inspection of the current report of Victoria, it is observed that probably ten per cent of the entire Masonic membership
of the Jurisdiction is enlisted under the colors and battling bravely
at the front.
The last words of the Grand Master, in closing the December
Quarterly Communication, were upon this very vital topic, as follows:
"Before I .close Grand Lodge, I wish to say a word or two with
regard to the future. We have been buoyed up with hope that each
Quarterly Communication and each New Year would see the coming
of peace. Surely our hopes will not be disappointed during the coming year. Surely in His own good time will the Great Architect of
the Universe bring about that peace, which is so much desired. So
far as we are concerned, we hope to have peace with honor, and, above
all, peace with certain security for the future. We have many of our
Brethren at the front. I do not know of any organization which has
done as much as Freemasonry has done. Only last evening I attended
the Australia Felix Lodge of Hiram, which has no fewer than 25 per
cent of its members serving at the front; but this is only typical of the
Fraternity throughout Australia. Increasingly heavy demands will be
made upon us, and there is at the present time urgent need for greater
economy, and it is only by individual sacrifice and personal economy
that we can hope to meet these demands. As Freemasons we are.
looked upon as men of some substance, and it is generally agreed that
we ju·stify this by contributing what is expected of us, and it is up to us
to show our proper appreciation of our further responsibilities. It is useless to look to the State or Federal authorities alone to take steps to provide means to meet these added demands, so I would ask you to
exercise in your homes and in your daily lives that economy which
has proved during this present war one of the most potent factors in
the success of our nation. I would ask you to look forward with
confidence to a happy and prosperous New Year. Our land of the
Southern Cross has been blessed with seasons which we have rarely
had before. We hope that during the coming year, and as early as

"Question-The candidate for initiation was prepared and alarm
had been given, when information of his serious moral turpitude was
communicated to the Master. Was it right for him to arrest the
initiation at that stage?
"Answer-Yes ..

"Question-Can an Entered Apprentice be prevented from advancement by an objection secretly communicated to the Master of his
Lodge?
"Answer-Under section 129, the Master may decline to confer
the degree, in which case the candidate stands rejected, and his fee
must be returned; or he may delay the advancement for investigation. If the objection be a serious one, he must give it consideration,
no matter how communicated."

FOREIGN CORRESPONDENCE.
The report on Foreign Correspondence is, as usual, by Most Worshipful Joseph W. Eggleston, Past Grand Master, Chairman.
We quote the following paragraph from his "Conclusion" as worthy of thoughtful perusal:
"Striving for members is un-Masonic. All degree work, and little
or no social life or instructive features, is a sad mistake. But, perhaps, worse and most destructive of all, is permitting our peace-loving
institution, which is in its very essence the antithesis of controversy,
to be drawn into religious contention. We have our work to do in
the world, and have no mission to fight or contend with anybody.
That we are sometimes attacked today by the Roman Church, as we
have been for centuries, is no excuse whatever. Wordy defense is
confession of weak vulnerability, and just that is what Rome wants.
Their fulminations have never hurt us in all the ages, and, if we only
have the sense to leave them to beat the air, they never will. If on
earth there ever was a set of people who could afford to smile in
silence at any and all attacks, we are just those people. What we
choose to do as individuals is another story.
"Our fathers had none of these mistakes in their Masonry. These,
and some others, are modern innovations, and should be rigorously
weeded out. Let us keep our Masonry pure and simple; do what we
can for our fellow-man, especially those of our household, and let
other organizations do as they will."
Brother Eggleston's review throughout is characterized by intelligent selection for quotation and beneficent and killdly criticism.
California, 1915, is reviewed with generous selections from the
Address of Grand Master Bledsoe, and favorable references to the
Masonic activities of our Grand Jurisdiction.

those who have the strongest possible claims upon us."

FOREIGN' CORRESPONDENCE.
There is a review of a large number of Jurisdictions arranged in
topical form, by Ralph C. McAllaster, Committee. He quotes the
Grand Master of California upon acquiring new members into the
Fraternity, but m'ore especially in maintaining harmony between those

Sacred Law" :
VOLUME OF THE SACRED LAW.
"Iti deciding upon the petition for a new Lodge at Peking, China,
the Grand Master of Massachusetts was confronted with the problem
that the Bible is not the 'Volume of the Sacred Law' to all peoples,
and there was a certainty of such Lodge receiving applications from
those whose obligations would be considered more sacred if taken on
their own particular volume. His conclusions were:
"'To the Christian, the Volume of the Sacred Law is the Holy
Bible, and upon it he should be obligated. The Christian religion is
the prevailing religion of our Lodges and, therefore, the Holy Bible,
as the Volume of the Sacred Law, is and must always be part of the
furniture of each Lodge. Its sanctity, however, does not appeal to the
Islamite, and the ceremony of initiation would lose much to him in
binding effect if his obligation should be taken thereon. While the
Holy Bible should not be removed from the Lodge, the conscientious
Islamite who so desires may be permitted to take his obligation upon
the Koran : the Hindu, otherwise qualified and accepted, may be permitted to have the Vedas spread open before him; and the rite of
initiation may be so far adapted to the conscience and religious belief
of a candidate as to permit his taking the ohligation in a manner and
form regarded by him as sacred and binding, and upon that work
which to him is the Volume of the Sacred Law, providing always that
such Volume of the Sacred Law teach Monotheism.'"
The Committee, to whom the matter was referred, agreeing with
the Grand Master.

COMMUNICATIONS.
Communications of this Grand Lodge are held quarterly, and the
Quarterly Communication held in April of each year is considered,
also, the Annual Communication, upon which occasion in 1916, the
Most Worshipful Brother C. 0. L. Riley, Archbishop of Perth,
Grand Master, presided.
ADDRESS OF GRAND MASTER.
At the Annual Communication, the Grand Master Riley instituted
a few comparisons between the condition of the Jurisdiction at this
time, and at its inception sixteen years ago.
The grand total of the various Funds belonging to the Grand
Lodge aggregate £34,411, the equivalent of which would be about
$170,000, which is an impressive amount to belong to a Grand Lodge
m existence no longer than sixteen years.
The Grand Master also contrasts the membership sixteen years
ago with the present membership, there being only thirty-three Lodges
on the Grand Lodge roster then, whereas there are now ninety-seven
Lodges with a membership exceeding 4100.
WORLD WAR.
The theme uppermost in all of the Addresses of the Grand Master delivered within the year, is the great World War rocking the
civilization of the earth since August, 1914.
Western Australia has done its duty manfully, and Grand Master
Riley calls attention to the fact that even as long ago as April, 1916,.
more than three hundred Master ~fasons, members of the Western
Australian Jurisdiction, were serving at the front ; and he also refers
to the active part which Masonry is taking in the· actual life of the
troops on the firing lines. He mentions the fact that there are several
Military Lodges, with traveling warrants, holding meetings and conferring degrees behind the firing line, and within sound of the guns,
special reference being made by him to the Seventh Royal Irish Fusiliers and the 16th Royal Irish Rifles, and others.

WAIVER OF JURISDICTION REFUSED.
We quote the Grand Master on this subject, showing the period
of time this Jurisdiction retains jurisdiction over rejected material:
"September 7, 1916, I received a letter from :Vfost Worshipful
Thomas J. Shyrock, Grand Master of Masons in Maryland, containing
the request of King Davids Lodge No. 68. Baltimore, :Viaryland, that
Mannington Lodge No. 31 grant said Lodge a waiver of jurisdiction
over Mr. Hyman Kaplan, who was rejected by Mannington Lodge in
February, 1911. I replied advising Most Worshipful Brother Shyrock
that in this jurisdiction we only attempted to retain jurisdiction over
rejected material for a period of three years, and since more than that
length of time had passed since Mr. Kaplan's rejection, we did not
claim jurisdiction over him, and so far as we were concerned thev
were at liberty to act upon his petition without consulting us."

"A Lodge U. D. can not conduct a Masonic trial. Charges of
Un-Masonic conduct against a member of a Lodge U. D. who stands
quasi dimitted must be filed with and disposed of by the Lodge from
which the brother became quasi dimitted when he signed the petition
for a dispensation for the new Lodge; except when the charges ·originate with some other chartered I~odge, in which case the Lodge above
referred to as having jurisdiction, could, at its discretion, delegate the
disposal of the charges to the complaining Lodge."
CHARITY.
There is a Grand Lodge Educational Committee in this Jurisdiction· that has been active during the past year, extending. monetary
assistance to a number of worthy children of deceased brethren.
Many cases of merit were investigated and assistance extended,
although there is no Masonic Home in this Jurisdiction where de
pendents may be placed.

GRAND :\!ASTER'S ADDRESS.
The Grand Master sets forth with businesslike precision his
activities within the preceding year, referring particularly to tl1e
Special Communications held by the Grand Lodge at Cheyenne, Cody,
and Laramie, for the purpose of placing corner stones of public
buildings. His official visitations extended, apparently, to all parts of
the Jurisdiction and his administration was capable and efficient.

In Brother Lowndes' present review, California, 1915, is given
courteous consideration with quotations from the masterly address of
Grand Master Benj. F. Bledsoe.

156

DECISIONS.
We quote the following ruling of the Grand Master upon the
subject of "physical qualifications" to indicate that the law of vVyoming is apparently in harmony with our own upon this subject, and in
harmony with the prevailing trend of opinion throughout the
Masonic world :

"Question-We have a party who is desirous of becoming a
Mason, but owing to a stroke of infantile paralysis, one of the lower
limbs is under-developed and causes him to use his hip excessively.
His limbs are complete, but are out of proportion to each other. Can
we accept his petition ?
"Held-That where a candidate can take all the positions required
in giving and receiving the work that he is qualified, physically, to
make application for the degree."
MASONIC HOME FUND.
There is in this Jurisdiction in process of accumulation a fond
which, when it reaches adequate proportions, will be used, according
to the present purpose of this Jurisdiction, for the foundation of a
Masonic Home.
FRATERNAL CORRESPONDENCE.
In accordance with the custom which has prevailed in this Jurisdiction for a great many years, the report on Fraternal Corre~
spondence is made by the Grand Secretary, and the late Grand Secretary Brother William L. Kuykendall for nearly thirty years performed the service of Chairman of the Correspondence Committee in
a most capable manner, his annual reports having been read with
a great deal of interest throughout the Masonic world.
Since
Brother Kuykendall's decease in 1915, the duties of foreign correspondence have devolved upon the present Grand Secretary, Very
